The *Vālmīki-Śrīvāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, together with its commentary titled *Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa, edited by Vāsudeva Śarman, son of Paṇaśīkara Upāhv Lakṣmaṇa Śarman.
Edited by Vāsudeva Laxmaṇa Śarma Paṇśīkara.
The First Section: On Dispassion (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa).
First Chapter.
1. Salutations to the two lotus-feet of the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Om. Salutations to Brahman, to those who know Brahman, and to those who are the transmitters of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman.
To Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Śuka, and others, and to the illustrious Rāmabhadra;

to that which is unborn, undecaying, beginningless, endless, inwardly consisting of its own bliss and consciousness, eternally non-dual, full, auspicious, manifesting within the hearts of all as the play of the universe unfolded by its own *māyā*—to that we have offered our salutations. (1)

I take refuge within my heart upon that beautiful gem known as Lambodara— the very fortune of the lap of Śiva and Bhavānī, which fulfills every desired object through the blossoming of mindfulness and is like the rising sun.
The orb of his moon-like face was charming, graced with a gentle smile;
his beautiful, compassionate side-glances were like smooth nectar;
and he was followed by the foremost sages among the company of seers.
Let us take refuge with our teacher at his dwelling at the foot of the banyan tree.

May Narakesarin— the lion among men— be our eternal refuge; he whose rising is for the sake of protecting the three worlds, who is non-dual bliss arising from true fearlessness, stainless awakening, and happiness, and who is a lion in the mountain caves of the hearts of the virtuous.

Holding a rosary and the gesture of fearlessness in her right hands, and a book and a lotus in her left, she— whose eyes are like lotuses and whose splendor is like the autumnal moon— is to be meditated upon according to the ritual as Śāradā.
May your speech remove the darkness from my heart. || 5 ||
Those who are the eyes of Hara; by whom this world is illuminated and set in motion;
upon whom alone Dharma—praised by the Śruti and Smṛti and the source of the rise of bliss—is established;
and who, like the Supreme Self, possess their own supreme light and measure out time.
May the Sun, Moon, and Fire become suns for the lotus of my awakening within my heart. || 6 ||

I take refuge in that primordial teacher of the knowledge of Brahman, who dispels the darkness in all directions with the moons of his faces, who pours forth the nectar of the essence of the Vedas' meaning, and who is cherished by the goddesses of speech for the attainment of one's desired goals.
For those who drink the nectar of his words, every step is true ambrosia; through the investigation of the meaning of his speech, even the desired heaven becomes a prison-house;
and for those whose minds are filled with the clarity of his voice, the world is as worthless as cotton wool.
To that venerable Guru, the sage Vasiṣṭha, we offer perpetual salutations. || 8 ||
To him whose Vedic mother— renowned as the Ṛṣi, renowned as the Yajus, and beneficial to the three worlds— is supreme; and who,
desiring to create other worlds, brought the hosts of gods under his control through austerity.
I repeatedly bow down to that sage Viśvāmitra— the ocean of awakening, the wish-fulfilling gem adorning the crown of ascetics, the sinless refuge— and I pay him homage once more.
To him by whom Rāma— whose majesty was revealed by the Śruti as none other than Brahman itself— to him Vasiṣṭha returned Sītā in the assembly, purified by truth like the very form of Brahman;
he whose speech, yielding a flood of world-bliss, quells the root of delusion.
To that Vālmīki, the most venerable of gurus, we bow with profound devotion. || 10 ||

He whose nature is perfect bliss, having assumed a body through *māyā* for the sake of the welfare of his own kin, desiring out of compassion to uplift people who are incessantly submerged in the mire of delusion,
entered Vasiṣṭha within and, manifesting externally as well in the form of a disciple, brought him forth.
I take refuge in that Rāmacandra, who, through his own testimony, is the ocean of the nectar of the scriptures. || 11 ||
Blessed are those whose mouths are frequented by Sarasvatī along with the sciences; whose hearts are firmly established in Brahman through the excellence of their being and meditative concentration;
and upon whose lotus-feet the sacred waters, together with all prosperity, constantly take refuge.
I worship those illustrious gurus, known as Śrī Sarvajñasarasvatī. || 12 ||
Fortune has taken refuge at their feet, Rāmacandra is in their hearts, and Sarasvatī, with her abundance of virtues, resides in their mouths; therefore,
they bear names marked by those very titles.
I perpetually bow down to the glorious gurus, who are most venerable. || 13 ||
To the venerable Rāmānanda Muni, whose compassionate glances are ever active in destroying the suffering [of others],
whose every limb is satisfied by the speech of his exegesis, who is the refuge for all,
and whose conduct is wondrous—
I bow perpetually to the noble and excellent teachers. || 14 ||
Even Hari, the Lord of the Universe, whose feet are the refuge for all, spoke thus out of friendship: "I shall always follow those who are peaceful so that I may be purified by their dust," he said;
and the Śruti always prescribes his worship for the sake of accomplishing every desire of the wise.
I worship those established in Brahman, whose minds are full with the bliss of the Self and liberated while living. || 15 ||

Where, alas, are these compositions difficult for even the skilled to master, and where is this creature of mine with its childish intellect? Nevertheless, my sole support in composing this is the compassionate glance of the true gurus. (16)

For me, in this [undertaking], the remembrance of the lotus feet of those virtuous ones—those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of all branches of knowledge, who have cast off the mental impurities such as passion, and who are mines of compassion—is my helper. (17)
I perpetually worship those venerable gurus known as Śrī Gaṅgādharendra, by whose mere trace of compassion I have crossed the ocean of worldly existence. 18.
By the ascetic Ānandabodha, this *Vāsiṣṭhārthaprakāśa* is being expounded according to his understanding, through the nectar-like words of the venerable Guru. (19)
Let the wise praise me at their will or revile me with their intellects;
for my conduct does not proceed from a desire to please the world.
Under this pretext, [I shall remain] filled with the words of Vasiṣṭha, which are like the essence of nectar.
I desire to dwell every day in the ocean of bliss that arises from honor. || 20 ||
Just as one would offer assistance to those seeking knowledge during times of distress, according to my own understanding, I shall exert my efforts to clarify the meanings of these difficult verses.
Established in a single flavor, the manifestation of manifold flavors occurs through reasoning;
let this Vāsiṣṭha delight you, just as salt enhances a fine meal. 22.
Even a word that is difficult to understand due to limited intelligence shall be clearly explained;
moreover, that which was previously explained two or three times shall be released [from further difficulty], even if it is hard to grasp. (23)
As I desire to explain this work, which has never before been commented upon by others, may the virtuous who understand my labor kindly forgive any errors I may commit here and there. (24)
Śrī! Salutation to that True Self, from whom all beings manifest and abide, and into whom they alone reach their final rest. 1.

Now, this world—sleeping through the night of beginningless great delusion, awakened by the thunderous roar of the drum of the Teacher; wandering through a succession of incessant bad dreams; beset by the terrifying tigers of the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa*); crowded with the garlands of flames from the forest fire of the three types of suffering;
and tormented by the hunters of the six internal enemies—[is thus situated].
Beholding the multitude of living beings being bound in the great forest of saṃsāra— bewildered, blinded by a lack of discernment,

and despondent due to the rarity of the means for awakening— the [author] proceeds, both by the command of the lotus-born Lord and by his own accord, through the rising of the sun of the scriptures, in order to awaken them.
The most compassionate Blessed One, Vālmīki, for the sake of achieving the unimpeded completion and widespread propagation of the great treatise he intends to compose,
[performs] that which is prescribed by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous, and which is capable of uprooting all obstacles.

Performing the auspicious invocation characterized by prostration before the Supreme Brahman— the inner Self which is non-dual, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss— he incidentally sets forth the subject matter and purpose of the treatise,
as well as its incidental and essential definitions: "That from which [all beings] are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at death— that you should seek to understand."

He pays homage to the referent of the word *tat* (That), whose nature is non-dual Being established by the "incidental" (*taṭastha*) definition stated in the scripture as "That is Brahman," with the words: "From which... From which—that ultimate reality, the non-dual Self-substance which serves as the primordial source—at the time of creation and so forth, all the great elements such as space, as well as elemental objects, [proceed].
The meaning is: that by whose very existence [all things] obtain existence, shine forth, and manifest;

likewise, during the time of persistence, they remain by whose very existence alone; and at the time of dissolution, they reach their cessation or disappearance into that very [source] where only its own existence remains—to that True Self (Satyātman).

Salutations to the Supreme Brahman, who is the ultimate essential nature of all phenomena superposed by one's own mind, and who is the true self of all living beings. And in saluting Him, there is that state where all the gods become one, as declared in the Śruti: "Where all the gods become one."

Because no other deity remains [to be worshipped], through the accomplishment of all prostrations, this auspiciousness—being the most excellent of all—brings about the attainment of results such as the destruction of all obstacles. Here, by the two phrases "from which beings" (*yataḥ...bhūtāni*), one refers to the [Brahma-sūtra]:
"From which indeed these beings are born; from which [comes] the birth etc. of this [world]."

Because this [definition] is recognized through the characteristics stated in the *Śruti-sūtras* composed by him, it is rooted therein; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the causes such as *mahat* imagined by the Sāṃkhyas and others, nor to the intermediate causes shown by Yāska. Here, since the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) is obtained precisely from the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) applied to *prakṛti*, the triad [of categories] has *prakṛti* as its material cause.

Some say it is for the purpose of demonstrating the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇatraya*). Furthermore, since the ablative case is seen even in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), the statement that [the Lord] is the substratum of dissolution (*layādhāra*) serves to establish his status as the material cause (*upādānatva*). As for the statement that he is the cause of persistence (*sthitihetutva*), this is intended to exclude any other agent, because protectors are observed to be sentient beings, and thus [the Lord’s] sentience is established.

Others maintain that the single defining characteristic is the state of being the non-different material and efficient cause (*abhinnanimittopādānatva*), which is obtained from all three [definitions]. In reality, however, for the purpose of providing acquaintance with the non-dual reality consisting of pure existence—which was introduced as the object of knowledge in such scriptural passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"—[the text proceeds] from "from this very Self... (*tasmād vā etasmād ātmanaḥ*).

Since the definition by way of external indication (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) is introduced through such passages as "From [Being] ether was produced" and "That [Being] created fire," and since, according to the direction shown by the scripture— "All this is indeed Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him"— the effect does not deviate from *Sat* (Being) throughout the three periods of time, namely origination and so forth.
Furthermore, since no existence apart from the causal reality is perceived, Brahman— the very essence of the cause—

is the only ontologically real entity; thus, the definition composed of these three elements is adopted in order to establish the subject matter and purpose of the "devoid-of-multiplicity" (niṣprapañca) state through the methods of superimposition (adhyāropa) and negation (apavāda).

For the illusory nature (*vivartatva*) of an effect is not established by the adoption of each individual [cause] alone. Therefore, in the Śruti, the words "they are born" (*jāyante*) and "they enter back into" (*abhisaṃviśanti*)—which refer to manifestation and disappearance characterized by appearance and non-appearance—are intended to indicate that they are not concerned with modification (*vikāra*); thus it is said that "they appear and then go to their cessation."

Since increase and transformation are included within manifestation, and disappearance within concealment, and since persistence is merely the permeation of the existence of the substrate, there is no modification other than superimposition.
The knower is knowledge; likewise, the object of knowledge is the ground of the seer, the seeing, and the seen.
Salutation to Him whose nature is pure consciousness, for from whom the agent, the cause, and the action arise. || 2 ||

Having indicated in general that [the Self] "shines forth," he now bows once more to that very reality which constitutes the true meaning of the term *tvam*, establishing its nature as the singular essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*) through the fact that it is proven by universal experience— saying, "known" (*jñāta*). Having entered by means of this living self (*anena jīvenātmanā*), [He differentiates] name and form...

Because of the Vedic revelation, "I shall manifest," from that Being— which is the archetype (*bimba*), the immutable (*kūṭastha*), whose sole essence is consciousness— the knower himself, by way of becoming a reflection (*pratibimba*), emerges as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of the two sheaths of the collective and individual cognitions and mind;
having overcome the inertia born of that [organ] and illuminating it, he is the knower, like sparks [issuing from a fire].

Illuminating its own modifications (vṛtti), it is knowledge. When the modification has assumed the form of the object, the Self also, by means of that [modification], assumes its form and becomes as if it were that very state;
this is what is to be known. This was stated in a manner applicable to both direct and indirect perception:
"having taken up the sense organs, it is seen"; [this refers to] having taken up the modifications produced by contact with those [objects].

Vision (*darśana*): having pervaded objects by means of its nature as their fruit, it becomes itself an object of vision through its coloring by the form of those objects; thus it is the "ground of the visible" (*dṛśyabhūḥ*). Likewise, that very same [vision], assuming the instruments of action, the vital breaths, and the body, is the agent.
It is the cause because it is the motive for the production of action through its state as the enjoyer of the fruit.
Action arises from the conceit of agency, thinking "I alone am complete" or "I am incomplete," regarding the totality or deficiency of actions. For this very reason, the scripture states:

"This seer, hearer, thinker, doer, knower, and conscious self—the Person—becomes known as 'breath' when breathing, as 'speech' when speaking, as 'the eye' when seeing," and so forth. Thus it is in all worldly transactions.
Because it sustains the manifestation of both self and other, consciousness (*cit*) is established by universal experience as being of the nature of pure awareness;

nevertheless, due to the delusion caused by its coloring by diverse limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is not perceived distinctly—just as the radiance and whiteness [of a surface] are not distinguished on a variegated painting. Therefore, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed in the word "yasmāt" (from which) for the purpose of isolating it.

The sense is this: the manifestation of the agent and so forth is caused solely by its proximity [to it], and not because it constitutes their essential nature; for, being subject to deviation, it cannot logically be the essential nature of the visible object. Therefore, to that Witness of the knower and the rest—who is in the ultimate sense of the nature of consciousness (jñapti), and who remains as pure consciousness alone—[salutation].
The meaning is: "Salutation to the inner self. || 2 ||
Salutations to that essence of Brahman-bliss, from whom sprays of joy radiate throughout the sky and upon the earth, providing life to all. || 3 ||

Having thus purified the two categories of reality, he realized that the ultimate locus for the definition by external characteristics (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) is the Supreme Goal, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss as shown in the scripture: "He understood that Brahman is Bliss.
[This bliss exists] up to the end of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), meaning among the gods in heaven; likewise on earth, from humans down to the blades of grass.

Due to the gradation in the overcoming of obscurations according to the degree of freedom from defects, the drops of bliss appear like droplets, being perceived through various degrees of conditioned differentiation— just as the reflection of a mountain appears in different ways in a thorn, a mirror, or a gem.

Sprays of water droplets are shimmering; that is to say, they are experienced by everyone through delusion as being non-self, as subservient to the self, and characterized by distinctions of limitation, manifoldness, the intermingling of suffering, perishability, and so forth.
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is not so; rather, that very [reality], with its distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) extracted, is the same for all.
That by which all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass live is "jīvana," the very essence that is the reality of the Self (ātmatattva).

"No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna); rather, they live by something else, upon which these two depend. Of this very bliss, other beings subsist on only a fraction. Who [could perceive it]?

For the Śruti says: "If this bliss did not exist in the ether (ākāśa), who indeed could breathe or live? Therefore, because there is no differentiator and because their essential characteristics are one and the same, it is that very [Brahman] regarding which the Śruti says: "From whom words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it; he who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere."

And the Self is the well-known, undivided bliss of Brahman. There is no other so-called Self, according to such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer than this; there is no other knower than this. The meaning is: "Salutation to that Self which is the bliss of Brahman, whose nature is the supreme human goal. Herein lies the performance of an auspicious invocation (maṅgalācaraṇa).

However, there is no tautology, because [the first half] is for the purpose of beginning the composition of the treatise, whereas [the second half] is for the purpose of beginning the instruction of that [treatise] to the disciples in the subsequent chapter. || 3 ||
A certain very sharp-witted Brahmin, his mind drawn by doubt,
went to the hermitage of Agastya and respectfully questioned the sage.
In this regard, the dialogue between the Sage and the Deity is described for the sake of purifying the tradition,
as well as for the purpose of removing ignorance concerning Rāma and as an introductory preface.

Having thus briefly presented the subject matter of the treatise by way of demonstrating the auspicious objects and so forth for the sake of easy understanding, and now commencing the treatise to explain that very same subject in detail through arguments, proofs, and the like, [the author] acts in order to strengthen the conviction of the listeners therein.

[This is established] by such statements as: "obtained through the tradition beginning with Brahmā, which is cherished by the great sages who are the foremost among those possessing supreme knowledge of Brahman. [The name] Sutīkṣṇa [is used] because his meaning is beautiful and difficult to grasp, owing to being purified by the practice of austerity, ritual action, and meditation.
The mention of "Brāhmaṇa" indicates that Brāhmaṇas alone possess the primary qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

For the sake of illumination: the meaning is "one who desires to know" (jijñāsu), whose mind has been drawn toward inquiry by means of doubt. Sutīkṣṇa spoke with reverence, [demonstrating] through the performance of prostration, surrender, and so forth, as prescribed by the injunctions regarding the carrying of sacrificial fuel (samit) in hand.
O Blessed One, knower of the reality of dharmas, you who have reached certainty in all scriptures, there is one great doubt; please speak upon it out of compassion. (5)

One who knows the reality of Dharma is a *dharmatattvajña*. One whose certainty (*niścaya*) is distinguished and fixed among all the scriptures is likewise [described]. Regarding the many Vedic and Smṛti texts that propound mutually contradictory meanings—such as whether action is the cause of liberation or knowledge is the means to liberation—one who has reached a definitive conclusion is so called.
Or, having determined both, state the single reason.

A cause (*kāraṇa*) is that which produces; a means (*sādhana*) is that which manifests. In this context, liberation (*mokṣa*) is indeed the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). According to the Vedic scripture: "That happiness which is unmixed with pain, not immediately swallowed by it, and brought about by desire—that is the state of heaven (*svarga*)," because it is common to all. Thus, it would be heaven.

And because its being such is established by the words of Jaimini; nor can its destruction be inferred from its being produced, for inference does not arise regarding a matter contradicted by Śruti. Furthermore, if it were unproduced, the instruction on the means [to liberation] would be purposeless—[as stated in texts such as:
"Not by action, not by progeny... for these forms of sacrifice are unstable rafts."

Based on such scriptural passages as "The path to liberation," which negate any means other than knowledge for attaining liberation, and because knowledge produced by the valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) is not known to have any fruit other than the manifestation of reality—this is the view of the followers of the Upaniṣads. [Objection: But there is the injunction, "One who desires to live [should perform rites] for a hundred years," which establishes that ritual action (karman) must be performed throughout one's life; [and] "Surya are the names of those worlds... [Thus, action is necessary.]

Having introduced the knowledge of Brahman preceded by a censure of the ignorant through the passage beginning with "Enveloped in blind darkness," [the text states] that neither of those two alone is a means to liberation: "Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance"—
where Mahīdhara explains that "ignorance" refers to ritual action characterized by the Agnihotra and so forth.

Then, having censured them with the words, "But for those who delight only in knowledge, it is as if they enter deeper darkness," [the text] declares that the cause of liberation— characterized by the absolute cessation of all misfortune and the attainment of unsurpassed bliss— is the combination of both, stating: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together, having crossed over death through ignorance, enjoys immortality through knowledge."
The meaning is: "Tell me the cause of the definitive conclusion."
Agastya said:
Just as the movement of birds in the sky is achieved by means of both wings, even so the supreme state is attained through both knowledge and action. (7)

Because the statement "that which is not [associated] with suffering" contradicts numerous other scriptural passages and so forth, it must be understood as referring to a relative eternity; thus, the impossibility of the first alternative regarding those [states] was established. Then, [the author] gave the answer concerning the second and third alternatives—that the fruits of actions lead to the purification of the mind—beginning with the words "by both," and so on. Just as for birds in the sky...
The "supreme abode of Viṣṹṇu," as celebrated in the Śruti, is liberation (kaivalya), which is the further shore of the path of saṃsāra.
However, prior to that state, since engagement and withdrawal cannot occur simultaneously due to their contradictory objectives for specific types of practitioners,
both cleansing and illumination are necessary upon the arising of a reflection [in the mind], just as purification of the mind through action is likewise required.

The meaning is that since the modification (vṛtti) produced by valid means of knowledge is necessary for the cessation of ignorance, the fruit of knowledge is not seen even when [the teaching] has been heard hundreds of times by those with impure minds. || 7 ||
Liberation does not arise from action alone, nor indeed from knowledge alone;
rather, liberation comes from both. The wise know that both are the means.

Strengthening that very point, he says again: "From the solitary" (*kevalāt*). "They know the means to be the manifestor" (*vyañjakam*); the words "the knowers of Brahman" (*brahmavidaḥ*) are to be supplied. Thus, the sense is that since this is established by the experience of the wise, there should be no disagreement regarding it. Furthermore, the scriptural passage "Knowledge and ignorance" (*vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca*) is intended to teach the combination of meditative worship (*upāsana*) and ritual action (*karman*), and not [the combination of knowledge and ignorance].

The knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is intended for combination with ritual action; however, there is no contradiction, as the Commentators have already explained at length that this is refuted by the injunction for renunciation found in the opening passage, "By that which has been abandoned, you shall enjoy. One should not, however, grasp the meaning here merely according to the literal surface reading.
One should not be deluded into thinking that this text intends the position of the synthesis of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*).

For, as in the story of Maṇikāca, it is said: "For those who have not attained the vision of knowledge, mere ritual action is their ultimate resort; if one has no silk garment, what need does he have for a woolen blanket? and so forth.
Furthermore, because it would result in a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, since liberation is established later as occurring through kevalajñāna alone. || 8 ||
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history from the past:
long ago, there was a certain Brāhmaṇa named Kāruṇya who had studied the Vedas.
The son of Agniveśya, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
returned home after having completed his studies under his teacher.
At that time, Agniveśya, seeing his son standing silently in the house, abstaining from performing his duties and filled with doubt, observed him to be devoid of action.
Agniveśya said:
"O son, why do you perform this? You are not tending to your own duty."

"He said this" is without euphonic combination (*asaṃdhi*) because the *saṃhitā* is not mandatory here. "Blameworthy" refers to a son who deserves censure due to abandoning his duties contrary to the prescribed rule.
"Tell me, how will you attain perfection if you are not devoted to action? Let the reason for this cessation from action be explained. (13)
He speaks of success, the warding off of obstacles, heaven, or liberation.
Kāruṇya said:
"One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives and should constantly observe the Sandhyā;
this is the dharma of worldly engagement (pravṛtti-dharma) enjoined by both Śruti and Smṛti. (14)
"He performs the Agnihotra"—this is the completion of the sentence. "Enjoined" means prescribed. || 14 ||
Liberation does not come through wealth, nor through ritual action, nor through progeny;
rather, some ascetics consume the nectar of immortality through renunciation alone.
"Eke" means "the principal ones. The particle "ca" (and) serves to include the cessation of what is not beneficial. || 15 ||
"O Guru, between these two scriptural statements, what should be done by me?
Having fallen into such doubt, I remained silent regarding my duty. (16)

"Of two [things] having contradictory meanings," that is to say. "The state of being doubted" means the state of being in doubt. Because it is intransitive, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *gaty-arthā-karmaka-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72). || 16 ||
Agastya said:
Having spoken thus, O dear one, that compassionate brahmin became silent;
seeing his son in such a state, the preceptor spoke again to his son. (17)
Agniveśya said:
Listen, my son, to a certain story; having grasped its entire meaning from me within your heart, O son, do as you wish. (18)
First, I shall state the primary discourse, which cuts through ignorance—the root of all doubt—that is yet to be explained:
Knowledge is neither an attribute nor a quality of the Self in any way;
the Self is of the very nature of knowledge, eternal, omnipresent, and auspicious.
I am the Self of all beings, the Supreme Lord;
I alone am the sole reality, and all objects are imagined within me, O Six-faced One.
Those of unawakened intellect perceive this entire consciousness as having the form of the universe;
however, the wise see this world as the single form of the Self.
In the past, this which is difficult to comprehend was told by Vasiṣṭha to Rāma.

Thus, having extensively taught the nature of ignorance and the reality of Brahman to the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), Śiva addressed him by the name "O Knower of Brahman" (brahmavit) in order to instill firm confidence in his words; this appellation serves to indicate that he is the most trustworthy person known for such knowledge, and to manifest his fitness to receive the paternal inheritance characterized by the meaning of the narrative. || 18 ||
A certain woman named Suruci, the most excellent among the host of Apsarases,
was seated upon a peak of the Himavat mountain covered with peacocks.
It is "supreme" because it is the most excellent, being endowed with the specific qualifications required for the knowledge of Brahman. || 19 ||
There, the Kinnara women, tormented by desire, take their pleasure with the Kinnaras at the confluence of the celestial river,
which destroys the flood of great sins.
She beheld Indra’s messenger traveling through the atmosphere;
Suruci, the most excellent of apsarases and highly fortunate, spoke to him.
She is "highly fortunate" (*mahābhāgā*) because she partakes in the fruit of the instruction in knowledge. The particle *ca* (and) implies that her name alone does not constitute her excellence;

rather, it serves to include the fact that a beautiful inclination toward the science of Brahman has arisen in her—this being the sense of the term *suruci*. Furthermore, she possesses divine vision, which is capable of discerning the true nature of the messenger and his knowledge of Brahman.
Suruci said: "O illustrious messenger of the gods, from where have you come?
Where are you going now? Please tell me all of that."

Suruci said this: The address "O highly fortunate one" (*mahābhāga*) is intended to illuminate the fact that, by virtue of his worthiness, he had already performed the rites of rising to greet him, saluting him, bringing offerings, honoring him, and so forth. Furthermore, it serves to indicate the appropriate inquiries arising from the context: "Where was he before? "From where has he come? "Being released from here, where will he go?"—these being the questions prescribed by the scriptures.

It is understood that the intended meaning of the question, "In what essential nature will you go? concerns precisely the reality of Brahman as the substrate of all; this same meaning of the question is also understood from the natural force of the words, "Tell me all that, which is full. || 22 ||
The divine messenger said:
"O fair-browed one, you have asked well; I shall relate it to you exactly as it is.
The royal sage Ariṣṭanemi, having indeed bestowed the kingdom upon his son—"

Having understood that the great purpose of the question, which was intended in secret, had been indicated by the play of her eyebrows, he, signaling his own intention that it was known by himself, addresses her in that very manner with the words "O fair-browed one.
He speaks of the reality of the Self exactly as it is, according to its occurrence, and according to its true meaning. || 23 ||
Free from passion, that righteous-souled one departed for the forest to practice austerities;
that king was performing penance on Mount Gandhamādana.
"Having performed my duty there, I am now returning from that place;
I shall go to the side of Śakra to report that account. (25)

Having made his own purpose fulfilled by means of the knowledge of the Self—having accomplished that which was necessarily to be accomplished—he became one whose end, the limit of saṃsāra, had been reached; such was the king, and this is the meaning. || 25 ||
The Apsarā said:
"O Lord, tell me what happened there;
I am humble and desirous of asking, so you should not feel any agitation. (26)
The divine messenger said:

"For this very reason, desiring to know that which is of such a nature, she spoke. 'What king was he who reached the end of worldly existence, and in what form did he abide?'—this is a hidden question. Much remains to be told here."

Since the defects such as the lack of faith in that [truth] are not pacified by a mere [brief statement], there is a prayer for freedom from agitation. Furthermore, because the gods prefer what is indirect, even though the question and answer are under his own control, they are expressed here in an obscure manner rather than through explicit speech.
Listen, O blessed lady; I shall tell you in detail exactly what occurred while that king was performing difficult austerities in that forest.
Thus was I commanded at that time by the king of the gods, O fair-browed one:
"Go quickly there as a messenger, taking this celestial chariot."

"In this manner," refers to the method that will be explained. There, on Gandhamādana, the suffix *kan* is employed in the word *vimānakam* to indicate that if one is dispassionate, each of those [objects] is slight, contemptible, and thus worthy of indifference. 28.
It was joined by hosts of Apsarases, adorned with various musical instruments, and graced by Gandharvas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and others. (29)
The specific characteristics of the celestial palaces have their extremities adorned. || 29 ||
Having gone to that auspicious mountain Gandhamādana, which is filled with various trees and resounds with the sounds of palm-claps, flutes, drums, and other instruments, [they remained there]. (30)
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "even outside the celestial chariot, the soldiers took up palm-clappers, flutes, drums, and so forth. (30)
"Having placed King Ariṣṭanemi upon a celestial chariot, O messengers, bring him to the city of Amarāvatī for the enjoyment of heavenly pleasures. (31)
The messenger said:
Having received this command from Śakra and taking that celestial chariot,
which was equipped with all necessary implements, I went to that mountain.
The *upaskarāṇi* are the means of enjoyment provided with excellence; [the suffix] *suṭ* is applied according to the rule "upāt pratiyatne.

Now, because he himself possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñatva*), regarding his own departure—which is mediated by the body and so forth and is thus regarded as such by the ignorant—he employs the periphrastic attribution of being out of sight (*pārokṣyāropa*). Consequently, just as one might say "I spoke while intoxicated," he uses the perfect tense (*liṭ*) in the form *yayau*. || 32 ||
Having arrived at that mountain and gone to the king's hermitage,
I reported all of Mahendra’s commands to Ariṣṭanemi.
Having heard these words of mine, he spoke while still in doubt, O auspicious lady.
The King said:
"O messenger, I wish to question you; therefore, you ought to tell me that. (34)
Tell me, what are the virtues and what are the defects there in heaven? Having understood the conditions prevailing there, I shall act according to my inclination. (35)
The state—that is, the established condition of the deficiency or excess of virtues and faults—pertaining to that [place] or situated in heaven. || 35 ||
The messenger said:
"In heaven, supreme happiness is enjoyed through the fullness of merit;
indeed, by means of the highest merit, one attains the most excellent heaven. (36)
"By the completeness of the totality" means by the abundance even of minor merits. He says "by the highest" to indicate that supreme happiness is thereby obtained. || 36 ||
Likewise, by a middling [merit], a middling heaven comes to be, and not otherwise;
but by the least merit, such a heaven comes to be. (37)
In this way, even regarding the culmination of the Middle Way, it should be understood through both its abundance and its excellence. || 37 ||
Intolerance of the excellence of others, rivalry even with equals, and complacency toward those who are inferior—these persist until the exhaustion of one's merit. (38)

Regarding the faults within the fruits of unsurpassed merit, he says "pareti" (and others). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "competing with those superior ones. Thus, the sense is that the suffering caused by that is unbearable. The word "yāvat" (as long as) applies universally to all. || 38 ||
"When their merit is exhausted, these men enter this world of mortals;
O King, such are the virtues and defects that reside in heaven. (39)
And humans exist when there is a remainder of pleasant karma; the word "ca" (and) is used to indicate that this is difficult to obtain.
Having heard these words, O blessed lady, that king replied.
The king said:
"O messenger of the gods, I do not desire such a fruit as heaven. (40)
"Heaven is the fruit"—this is the construction based on non-difference. || 40 ||
After that, having performed most severe asceticism, I shall indeed cast off this impure body, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin. (41)
Because of the complete exhaustion of sins through austerity, and because there is no longer attachment to meritorious deeds, rebirth does not occur.
O messenger of the gods, take this celestial chariot and go back to the presence of Mahendra just as you came; salutations to you!

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "this very celestial chariot (*vimāna*). Alternatively, it is an epithet of the divine messenger (*devadūta*), meaning "one whose pride (*māna*) has departed (*viga-*) due to the refusal of his arrival. In this case, *vimāna* is a separate word. For this very reason, there is the expression "salutations to you" (*namo 'stu te*) for the sake of seeking forgiveness for that [insolence]. || 42 ||
The divine messenger said:
"Having been addressed thus, O blessed lady, he went to report it before Śakra;
having reported exactly what had occurred, he was then filled with great wonder. (43)
The marvelousness and the cause of wonder of those great beings who share the assembly of Śakra. || 43 ||
Again Mahendra spoke to me with gentle and sweet words.
Indra said:
"O messenger, go back there once more and lead that king to the hermitage."
The connection with the following verse is as follows: "To console the messenger who was distressed by an impossible command, [he spoke] to the hermitage of Vālmīki in sweet words. (44)
"Announce my message to the great seer Vālmīki, who has realized the truth and is free from passion, for the sake of his own awakening. (45)

"For the sake of your own awakening" means for the knowledge of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*). By the pun on the word "your own" (*sva*), it is suggested that you too will attain the awakening to your own self.
"Message" (*saṃdeśa*) refers to a verbal communication. || 45 ||
O Great Sage, please enlighten this humble king, who is free from passion; he does not desire heaven for himself. (46)
[For one who is passionate, there is passion; for one free from passion: "The activities directed toward objects of desire have their root in passion;
for one in whom these have been removed—that is, gone away—solely through the departure of passion, he does not desire heaven. (46)
"Afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra, he shall gradually attain liberation.
Having spoken thus, I was sent into his presence by the King of the Gods.

By that awakening to reality, [through the sequence of instruction], because the meaning taught has been transmitted into the mind step by step, or through the sequence beginning with the dissolution of the mind and the cessation of mental activity; || 47 ||
Having returned there once more, I informed King Mahendra that the means for liberation had been revealed by the king to the one born from an anthill.

I informed the king along with the message of Mahendra; the connection [of the sentence] is through ellipsis (*vipariṇāma*), meaning that the king informed [him] of his own desired means for liberation. || 48 ||
Then that one born from an anthill, with great affection, inquired after the king’s well-being through a message of greeting concerning his welfare. (49)
The meaning is that, by means of inquiries regarding the welfare of his kingdom, treasury, sons, ascetic practices, and so forth, he effectively inquired after [the king's] health. || 49 ||
The king said:
"O Blessed One, knower of the essence of dharma, you who have known all that is to be known, best among the wise!
I have achieved my purpose by the sight of you; that alone is my well-being. (50)
By the first qualification, knowledge of the secret of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is shown; by the second, knowledge of the reality of Brahman;

and by the third, knowledge of the reality of the world. By "your vision"—that is, by your sight and by the glance of your grace—that fulfillment of purpose brought about by your vision [is attained].
The state of having accomplished what was to be done is indeed the fulfillment of one's purpose. || 50 ||
O Blessed One, I wish to ask; tell me that without obstacle:
how may I be released from the suffering of the bonds of saṃsāra? Tell me that.

The phrase "I wish to ask" is used even though the subject of the question is already known from the messenger's message; this is to prevent the possibility of neglecting one's duty based on the rule that "one should not speak to anyone unless asked. Regarding that [subject], which is of the nature of the highest good (*śreyas*):
he wards off the apprehension of obstacles, which might arise from the common saying that "all blessings are beset by many hindrances."
"Without obstacle" means: because of the Vedic scripture, "Therefore, that is not dear to them which men might know.

For if there were hostility from the gods, there would be the possibility of obstacles; however, that is not the case, since I am asking [this] by the very command of the King of the Gods—this is the underlying sense. "Affliction" refers to the suffering caused by the bonds of saṃsāra as previously described.
Because of that repeated destruction, I am released; I become liberated. The first question concerns the nature of liberation, while the second concerns the means to liberation. || 51 ||
Vālmīki said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the Rāmāyaṇa in its entirety;
by hearing it and grasping it with effort, you will become liberated while living. (52)

Just as Rāma, having been displaced from his own station due to Kaikeyī’s pretext of boons, conquered the *rākṣasas* and attained the prosperity of returning to his own place; so too, he who was displaced from his true nature due to the pretext of a curse,
by following the instruction of Vasiṣṭha, destroyed the *rākṣasas* such as ignorance and attained the prosperity of regaining his own essential nature.

Having ascertained the impossibility of the means of valid cognition through reflection, and having dispelled the impossibility of the object of cognition and contrary mental impressions by means of effortful meditative contemplation— [the remainder being] "by means of direct realization"— (verse 52).
O wise King of kings, having realized the true nature of reality, I shall relate the auspicious dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma concerning the means to liberation; let it be heard. (53)

How could this [teaching] on the means to liberation—which proceeds in the form of a dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma—not be known as it truly is? For the scripture states: "This is not easily understood by an inferior man, even when reflected upon in many ways. Thus, its nature is not unknown to those who have realized the truth. || 53 ||
The King said:
Who is Rāma? Of what nature is he? To whom does he belong, or is he perhaps liberated?
O best among the knowers of reality, tell me this with certainty.

In the compound *vasiṣṭha-rāma-saṃvādam*, because the word with fewer syllables (*alpācaḥ*) is placed last according to grammatical rule, it indicates that Rāma is the disciple; however, such a status is possible only for one who is ignorant (*ajña*), not for the Lord (*īśvara*). But since Rāma is an incarnation of the Blessed One (*bhagavad-avatāra*), [the name] refers to Viṣṇu—who is eternally liberated—rather than to some person merely named Rāma. The meaning is that he is the well-known, eternally liberated Viṣṇu. [The term "Rāma"] is so called because by him everything is known (*jñāyate'nena*).
Knowledge is the cause of certainty; this is the meaning of the other term. || 54 ||
Vālmīki said:
By the very pretext of a curse, Hari, assuming the guise of a king, was deprived of his omniscience;
thus your lord became one possessing only limited knowledge. (55)

He says that very thing: "By a curse," etc. *Vyāja* means a pretext. Having become as if ignorant—having become one who was mostly ignorant by means of the ignorance accepted (*āhṛtena*) through his own will for the sake of fulfilling the truth of the words of his devotee—the verb *abhavat* (he became) takes the form *bhavat*, the absence of the augment *aṭ* being Vedic. || 55 ||
The king said:
"Tell me the cause of the curse upon Rāma, who is indeed the very nature of consciousness and bliss, the embodiment of pure awareness; tell me who cursed him and who was the one cursed."

For great sages pronounce curses only upon those who have committed an offense; indeed, an offense can only belong to one who is ignorant and whose desires are unfulfilled. Since Rāma is not such a person—because his essential nature consists of the bliss of consciousness—an offense is impossible for him. Furthermore, if it were claimed that he was cursed, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Bearing this in mind, [the author] says: "consciousness-bliss" (*cidānanda*).
In reality, he whose nature is consciousness and bliss, inseparable from consciousness;
and even in the realm of conventional discourse, he in whom consciousness alone has transformed into a physical form out of compassion for his devotees—
Vālmīki said:
Sanatkumāra, free from desire, dwelt in the abode of Brahmā;
Viṣṇu, the Lord and sovereign of the three worlds, arrived from Vaikuṇṭha.

The form "niṣkāma" is a Vedic (Chāndasa) shortening of the vowel. It means "that from which desires such as passion and the like have departed," or it refers to the "abode of Brahman" (brahmasadmani) which is free from desire. || 57 ||
Honored there by Brahmā and the inhabitants of Satyaloka,
the Lord Īśvara, seeing that Kumāra was absent, spoke.
The connection [of the previous verse] is that he was worshipped by the inhabitants of Satyaloka, with the exception of the youth Sanatkumāra. || 58 ||
"Sanatkumāra, you have become paralyzed by pride through your desireless conduct;
therefore, become afflicted by desire, known by the name Śarajanman."
*Kāma* is pervaded by *ṛtu*; and because it is a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), there is *vṛddhi* [of the first vowel]. || 59 ||
By him also Viṣṇu was cursed: "Since you possess omniscience, for a certain period of time you shall indeed become ignorant. (60)
*Kiṃcitkālam* is a *karmadhāraya* compound. The accusative case ending is used according to the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*. || 60 ||
Seeing his wife slain, Bhṛgu, overwhelmed by anger, said:
"O Viṣṇu, you too shall surely suffer the loss of your wife. (61)
He was fainting with rage, deluded, and highly exultant. || 61 ||
"Viṣṇu was cursed by Vṛndā because of the deception you committed;
therefore, by my word, you shall suffer separation from your wife. (62)

By Vṛndā, the wife of Jalandhara; "deception" means a fraud consisting of the violation of wifely devotion by deluding him with the guise of her husband's appearance. "Cursed" means he was accursed. [The verse continues: "For Devadatta’s wife was indeed situated on the bank of the Payoṣṇī river."
Seeing Viṣṇu wearing the guise of Nṛsiṃha, she met her death.
"Veṣadhṛgviṣṇu" is a *karmadhāraya* compound [meaning "Viṣṇu who wears the disguise"]. || 63 ||
For Hari, already afflicted by grief due to separation from his wife, was cursed by him:
"Indeed, you too shall suffer separation from your own wife. (64)
Although Nṛhari was directly perceived by him through well-performed deeds that were accomplished with great hardships, he was nonetheless cursed by him.
Thus cursed by the prince Bhṛgu and by Devaśarman, Viṣṇu was cursed by Vṛndā; because of that, he attained human birth.

Through the first curse, ignorance was attained by direct means; through the others, it was attained by implication. For this very reason, Rāma experienced the separation from Sītā three times: first by her abduction by Rāvaṇa, second by false accusation, and third by her entry into the earth. Furthermore, Tārā’s statement, "She will not dwell with you for long," was merely an insult and not a curse, since she [remained] even while Vālin was still alive.
Because it is well known from Aṅgada’s words that he— who, being loathsome, would rightfully accept as his mother one who has been abandoned by Sugrīva—
lacked the power to bestow a curse upon the exalted Rāma due to his violation of the duty of devotion to his wife and his base conduct, [he remained] merely a human being in human form.
The human [attains] that state. || 65 ||
All this has been told to you regarding the cause of the pretext of the curse;
now I shall tell you everything else—listen with an attentive mind. (66)
That which was previously asked— the means to liberation, together with all its associated details— has been explained, O Great King.

Thus ends the section titled "The Laying of the Foundation" within the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa* (Chapter on Detachment) of the *Śrīmadvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of Vālmīki, spoken by the Divine Messenger, in the compendium of thirty-two thousand verses concerning the means to liberation.
The First Chapter. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first section, titled "The Chapter on Dispassion," in the *Vāsiṣṭhamāhārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*. || 1 ||
Second Chapter. 2.
Salutation to that Self of all, the pervasive Lord, whose nature is luminosity, who shines as the light within and without, in heaven, on earth, and likewise in the sky.

Now, so that this great treatise which he intends to begin may reach completion without obstacles and proceed with success, [the author] demonstrates—following the method shown in the Mahābhāṣya—that there exist mantras which bring about the protection of heroes and the protection of long-lived persons; thus he says:

"In heaven," etc. That is, in heaven (*divi*), meaning in the celestial world (*dyuloka*); on earth (*bhūmau*), meaning in the terrestrial world (*bhūloka*); and likewise in the sky (*ākāśe*), meaning in the intermediate space (*antarikṣaloka*).

To Him who shines forth externally as the objective world (*adhibhūta*), internally as the subjective self (*adhyātma*), and— by the force of the word "and"— as the divine principle (*adhidaiva*), my pervasive Lord, who manifests and expands in manifold forms through His own ignorance (*svāvidyā*);
yet who, in the ultimate sense, is of the nature of luminosity, whose essence is unchanging pure consciousness (*nirvikāra-cinmātra*).

The meaning is "salutation to the Self of all. Alternatively, having heard from scripture that "the earth is the prior form and the sky is the posterior form," here too—in the sky, which is the upper lid of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) made of gold;
on the earth, which is the lower lid made of silver; and in the space between them, which is the subtle ether—[one should offer salutation].

He who shines with particular distinction both outside and inside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), even more intensely than the sun, moon, fire, speech, and so forth, because his nature is self-luminous and unlimited—whence is this? Because he is the self whose essence is illumination, the illuminator even of the sun and other luminaries; for by him the sun shines, kindled by his splendor, and he alone is its very self.

This is because of such scriptural and traditional texts as, "He becomes light; He is the light even of lights. The meaning is: "Salutation to Him, the Self of all, who constitutes the ultimate reality of all things. Alternatively, [it refers] to that which is in the heavens (*divi*)—in the nature of the Fourth State (*turya*), whose sole essence is luminosity (*dyotana*) and which consists of the bliss of plenitude (*bhūmānanda*).
In the two states of arising— the waking state, which is the external space of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is experienced by outward-directed consciousness,

and the dreaming state, which is experienced by inward-directed consciousness— and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), in their transition as well as in states such as death and fainting, that which shines forth in various ways as gross and subtle [objects]— [This is the *ātman*.]

"Of the nature of light" means having consciousness alone as one's essential nature (*cinmātra-svabhāva*). "To him" means to that which is non-different from the Seer (*dṛk*) of the visible (*dṛśya*). Alternatively, [it refers to Him] who shines in heaven—that is, in the causal adjunct (*kāraṇopādhi*) endowed with omniscience and other qualities—and likewise on earth—that is, in the effected adjunct (*kāryopādhi*), the ground where the seeds of karma sprout—and likewise in the intermediate space.

The meaning is: "Salutation to the Self" (Ātmane namaḥ), which—by the etymology "that which shines all around"—either refers to that which is abundant in the manifestation of its own nature during the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), or to the inner aspect of the Self when all adjuncts have been removed, having cast out the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) and the *māyā* contained within the adjuncts of cause and effect, and existing externally as the unconditioned essential nature; or alternatively, to that which shines in the sky (*divi*), whose nature is luminosity.

The meaning is: "Salutation to Me, whose nature is full bliss, who exists within fire, earth, water, space, the intermediate regions, and the external elements of water and air, as well as in the manifest (vyākṛta) world— and by the word 'ca' (and), in the unmanifest (avyākṛta)— or else, in heaven, the world of the gods."

Externally, by way of being a bystander, as the self of the worshipful deity, the Lord, and so forth; internally, within the body on the earth-plane (*bhūrloka*), as the self of the worshipper; and in the intermediate space (*ākāśa*) between them, as the means for accomplishing the fruit of the ritual action—he whose nature clearly manifests through the arising of the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*).

The All-pervasive One (*vibhu*), who is devoid of the threefold limitations, clearly shines forth; salutations to that Self of all. The word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the Full (*pūrṇa*); therefore, the meaning is: "Salutations to Him whose nature is full bliss," just as it is said, "He became all this.

Alternatively, [the meaning is]: "In heaven (*divi*)—above; on earth (*bhūmau*)—below; in the sky (*ākāśe*)—in the intermediate space; outside (*bahiḥ*)—and within (*antaḥ*)—in the directions such as the east, etc."

To that Self of all, who— by the force of the word "and" (ca)— shines as the essence of pure consciousness, consisting of the experience of bliss within the body, as well as before and after it, for me who perceives reality; [to Him] of whom the Śruti says, "The Self alone is below, the Self is above," etc.,
and who remains as the residue when the entire phenomenal world has been sublated by the realization that "the Self alone is all this."
The meaning is "salutation to the Supreme Self" (paramātmane namaḥ). In this way, other meanings may also be inferred according to the power of one's own intellect.
Furthermore, it is indicated that the purpose is the state of abiding in that [Self] through knowledge, which is the nature of supreme liberation.
This very point will be clearly demonstrated later as well.
The qualification, the subject matter, the means, and the connection [of this work] are established by the command of the Creator;
the composition of this treatise and the conduct of the liberated one are now proclaimed. (1)
Vālmīki said:

He who possesses the firm conviction, "I am bound; may I be liberated"—neither entirely ignorant, nor a knower of that [ignorance], nor yet a knower [of the Truth]—is the one qualified for this scripture.
Now, who is the qualified candidate for this treatise: the ignorant or the wise? It cannot be the former; for he identifies with the body and so forth as the self.

Nor can it be argued that his qualification arises once he has attained the desire for liberation (mumukṣā) through the emergence of dispassion (vairāgya), resulting from perceiving the defects in sense objects and witnessing the suffering of birth, death, and so on.

It does not proceed from one who is passionate, because such a person—driven by the desire to protect against intense sensory objects, by seeking means to eliminate their defects even while those objects are present, by searching for superior objects, and by desiring the means to achieve them both in this world and the next—acts accordingly. Nor does it proceed from one who possesses knowledge; for him...

Anticipating the objection that engagement with this treatise would be untenable because one who has already achieved their goal, or one who merely desires the results to be accomplished by the text, would not apply themselves to it, [the author] shows the qualified candidate by saying "I am" (*aham*).
The word *uta* is used in the sense of "also. It is true that neither the absolutely ignorant nor the fully wise person is a candidate for this scripture; rather—

I grieve because I am bound in this saṃsāra from beginningless time, like one imprisoned by shackles and fetters, experiencing the sufferings of birth, old age, death, and the rest, which involve limitation and helplessness; and for the ultimate crossing over of sorrow, self-knowledge alone is the means, according to the Vedic scripture: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow."

The firm conviction, accompanied by an intense desire to know, that "by means of that knowledge of the Self I shall be liberated," leads one to approach a guru through humility, offerings, and so forth; such a person is qualified for this scripture.
The meaning is that he becomes a partaker of the fruits of hearing the scripture and other practices. Thus, it is only for the ignorant one who possesses abundant merit [that this occurs].
The meaning is that the qualification belongs to one who desires to know [the truth], whose defects such as passion have been exhausted through the arising of discernment. || 2 ||
Having first reflected upon the means of worldly discourse, the wise man who then reflects upon these means of liberation is not born again.

Now, if a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) whose defects such as passion have been exhausted is eligible only for hearing the Vedānta preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), then [one might object]: even though a member of the three higher castes is eligible for rituals accomplished through the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), this eligibility is not common to those who have not maintained the fires (*anāhitāgni*). However, the performance of the duties of the former section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) serves as a means to the purification of the mind, which in turn leads to eligibility for the latter section (*uttarakāṇḍa*). Thus, there is no contradiction.

The qualification for performing *smārta* (tradition-based) rites exists even in our own work; furthermore, it extends until the attainment of knowledge. This is because this [work] also serves to supplement the Vedas, just like the *Smṛtis*. Thus it has been said: "When the son of Daśaratha was born, he who is to be known through the Vedas and is the Supreme Spirit, the Veda itself emerged directly from Vālmīki in the form of the *Rāmāyaṇa*. In that regard:
The first six sections (*ṣaṭkāṇḍa*) constitute the *Pūrvarāmāyaṇa*, which serves as an elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) on the story of Rāma’s life under the guise of the *Pūrvakāṇḍa*.

This present work, consisting of six chapters (*ṣaṭprakaraṇa*), is the *Uttarakāṇḍa* along with its supplement (*sottara*). Just as women and Śūdras possess a common right to perform certain Smārta rites, so too do they have the right to hear this [work], owing to its nature as a Purāṇa.

One should cause the four castes to hear [the scripture] after placing a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront; for there is scriptural evidence such as, "Even a Śūdra person may attain greatness. However, statements such as, "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One," and "I ask you about that Puruṣa who is known through the Upaniṣads," refer to those ignorant of the Veda.

Some maintain that this [text] is intended to exclude those who lack qualification for knowledge derived from the Śruti; others hold that it is intended to exclude those who do not culminate in immediate, intuitive knowledge (aparokṣa-jñāna);

still others maintain that it is intended to praise the fact that [knowledge] is preceded by the Vedas. In any case, there certainly exists a qualification for others as well in the knowledge common to the Purāṇas, for that Self is to be sought after by all.

Based on such statements as "by castes (*varṇas*) and likewise by stages of life (*āśramas*"), [the author] demonstrates the logical connection of cause and effect between the *Pūrva-rāmāyaṇa* and the *Uttara-rāmāyaṇa*, wherein knowledge of the Śruti is the cause for the [subsequent]. Thus, he presents the means that lead to the qualification for knowledge— namely, the knowledge of the true nature of Dharma, its practice, and surrender to the Lord— which are the destroyers of all misfortune.

In this treatise, that work known as the *Pūrvārāmāyaṇa* serves as the means for the narrative. The plural number is used with the intention of referring to the various divisions of the *kāṇḍas*. Having first investigated those [works], the qualified seeker—who has attained the right to practice their meaning—investigates the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*) consisting of the six chapters (*ṣat-prakaraṇa*) that are about to be described.
The wise one, whose seeds of ignorance—the latent impressions of desire, action, and karma—have been scorched by wisdom, is not born again;
he does not become a partaker of the sufferings of birth and so forth. The meaning is that he is liberated. || 3 ||
O crusher of enemies, having first performed these great and powerful means for subduing Rāma's anger in this Rāmāyaṇa in ancient times, I [composed it].
In this present Rāmāyaṇa, consisting of fifty-six thousand verses, I have bestowed it with single-minded focus upon that humble and wise Bharadvāja, who had been my disciple since time immemorial—
just as the ocean gave the jewel to the one who asked for it.

The qualifications of the disciple indicate the perfection of his eligibility (*adhikāra*). He is one whose preeminent chief disciple alone is foremost (*agra*)—that is, preeminent (*agram*)—and is skillful in receiving, retaining, and practicing [the teachings]. Out of affection for his grace...
therefore, these means of discourse were [spoken] by the wise Bharadvāja.
In a certain thicket of Mount Meru, they were proclaimed in the presence of Brahmā.
These, which constitute the form of the *Pūrvarāmāyaṇa*, have been obtained from me; they have been cited and proclaimed. || 6 ||
Then the blessed Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds and the magnanimous one, being pleased with him, said to him, "O son, choose a boon."

He is one whose great resolve (mahān āśayaḥ) is the intention that "the scripture of liberation (mokṣa-śāstra), which is the means for the upliftment of the world, must be composed under the pretext of [describing] excellent boons"; thus he is so described. || 7 ||
Bharadvāja said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, this boon now pleases me:
declare that by which these people may be liberated from suffering."
"Bhūtam" means that which has arisen in the past; "bhavam" means that which is about to arise. Today, having reflected upon the purpose of his former delight, the illustrious Brahmā said:
"Quickly and with great effort, request the preceptor Vālmīki here."
Therefore, this faultless Rāmāyaṇa has been commenced.
In this regard, concerning this matter asked: because it has been only commenced and not completed in its entirety. (9)
Upon hearing this in its entirety, a person shall cross over delusion by means of it,
just as one crosses to the far shore of the ocean by means of a bridge endowed with boundless virtues.

From the context of what has been heard, it is understood that this occurs immediately after the complete attainment [of the goal]; for he is endowed with infinite qualities well-known in the Smṛtis, such as: "By seeing the bridge over the ocean, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin. (10)
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus to Bharadvāja, the Supreme Lord,
the Creator of all beings, arrived at my hermitage together with that Bharadvāja.
Quickly honored by me with water for the hands, feet, and other offerings,
that Great Being, who delights in the welfare of all creatures, spoke to me.

Although Rajas predominates during the process of creation, nevertheless, O blameless great sage, because you have manifested compassion for the sake of uplifting the world and have described the true nature of Rāma,
he must not be abandoned by you out of agitation until his final conclusion.

The fifth case ending is used in the sense of "lyablope" (omission of a word ending in a lyap suffix). The meaning is: having introduced the description of Rāma’s true nature, [the narrative] should be composed in its entirety, including all details, due to the intensity of the agitation; that is to say, it must be told in full. || 13 ||
By means of this treatise, this world will quickly cross over the peril of saṃsāra, just as one swiftly crosses the ocean by means of a boat. (14)
The ablative case (*pañcamī*) in *saṃsārasaṃkaṭāt* (from the peril of saṃsāra) denotes the point of departure for one who has completely crossed over saṃsāra;

it is [the meaning of] the first [word]. Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy with the word *āśu* (quickly). If the reading were *kṣiprapotena* (by a swift boat), there would be no concern at all. *Āśu* means at the very same time as the arising of knowledge. Now, one might object: "Is not the crossing of the ocean by means of a boat [a well-known fact]?"
In this context, "crossing over" (samuttaraṇa) is intended to mean precisely "the lifting up of the foot," due to the natural force of the word *āśu-pada*.
For this very reason, the ablative case (*apādāna*) is employed in the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*). || 14 ||
"The Unborn One (Aja) said: 'I have come for this very purpose—to speak. For the sake of the welfare of the world, compose a scripture. (15)

Therefore, for that reason, although the command and message could have been conveyed through Bharadvāja, he—who is honored by the whole world—came himself to speak this matter; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 15 ||
From that meritorious hermitage of mine, he vanished in an instant,
rising up again in a moment like a great wave from the water.
By the touch of the foot of Brahmā, this hermitage has become most meritorious.
When that Blessed One had departed, I was filled with wonder;
then, with a composed mind, I questioned Bharadvāja once more. (17)
Because of the statement "with a steady mind," [it was asked: since his mind was previously distracted by the arrival of Brahmā, joy, and wonder, why did he not speak?
When thus addressed, that Bharadvāja spoke again to me: "Tell me quickly, what was this spoken by Brahmā? (18)
Bhāradvāja said: "O Blessed One, as you have instructed, compose the Rāmāyaṇa for the welfare of all the worlds, which serves as a means of crossing the ocean of worldly existence. (19)
Just as the *Kathopāya-rāmāyaṇa* was previously composed, so too [is] the *Mokṣopāya-rāmāyaṇa*;
this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 19 ||
And tell me, O Blessed One, how Rāma and the high-minded Bharata conducted themselves within this narrow strait of saṃsāra.
How did Rāma conduct himself? Did he act like one ignorant, grieving like others, or like one liberated while living? (20)
Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as the illustrious Sītā, and those highly intelligent sons of the ministers who were followers of Rāma—[all these went forth]. (21)
By the use of "ca," the inclusion of Daśaratha is indicated; the two instances of "ca" also imply the inclusion of his retinue.
[Regarding the phrase] "nirduḥkhatāṃ yathaite tu": "Tell me clearly how these have attained such a state of freedom from suffering."
In that very same way, I shall become [one with them], together with the people.

It is clear that this culminates in my awakening. O King of kings, when I was respectfully addressed by Bharadvāja—"Speak for the sake of the people who have fulfilled their purpose by hearing your instruction"—I then proceeded to speak in order to carry out the command of the Lord. (23)
"With reverence" means accompanied by respect, such as bringing offerings, approaching, prostrating, and making supplications. || 23 ||
Listen, dear Bharadvāja, I shall speak to you according to what was asked;
by hearing this, you will cast the impurity of delusion far away. (24)
Delusion (*saṃmoha*) is the lack of thorough knowledge regarding the reality of the self; it is the impurity or the mud of that nature. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *alam*.
O wise one, conduct yourself in such a way that you may live happily, just as the lotus-eyed Rāma conducted himself with an intellect entirely unattached. 25.
Unattached, because of the certainty that [it] is false, and thus unclinging. || 25 ||
Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and the high-minded Śatrughna;
as well as Kausalyā, Sumitrā, Sītā, and Daśaratha. || 26 ||
"Mahāmanā" refers to one whose mind is of such a nature due to being fixed upon an object that is undifferentiated; the "ca" particles are as before. || 26 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and the other eight ministers were masters of weaponry, free from enmity, and had attained the perfection of awakening.
Rāma’s two companions, skilled in weapons and free from hostility, have reached the ultimate awakening— the final realization beyond which no further object of knowledge remains.
Dhṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Bhāsa, Satya, and Vijaya;
Vibhīṣaṇa, Suṣeṇa, Hanumān, and likewise Indrajit. || 28 ||
Satya is one who speaks according to reality; Indrajit is quite another, a minister of Sugrīva.
These eight ministers have been described as having minds free from passion;
they were great-souled ones, liberated while living, who followed whatever came to them. || 29 ||
Internally their minds are free from passion, while externally they continue to follow worldly affairs as they have begun. || 29 ||

"O son, if you conduct yourself exactly as that which was offered, given, taken, stolen, remembered, and [otherwise dealt with] by these [ancestors], then you shall indeed be liberated from this peril. (30)
"Huta" and "datta" are indicative of the Śrauta and Smārta rites respectively. "Smṛta" refers to the former practices pertaining to both domains.
Having obtained supreme yoga in the midst of the ocean of boundless saṃsāra, the noble-souled one—[as if fallen into the middle of the ocean]—[attains liberation].
He does not fall into grief, nor does he succumb to dejection; free from fever, he remains eternally satisfied. || 31 ||

Through reasoning, he has attained internal equanimity (*samarasatva*) by means of the certainty regarding reality. Possessing noble courage, his superior power of knowledge is firmly established. Sorrow (*śoka*) is the suffering born from separation from the beloved; wretchedness (*dainya*) is the state of being miserable and pitiable.
He is one from whom the fever of egoism—the root of those two—has departed, and who abides as the self of unsurpassed bliss.
It is because of the lack of satisfaction with impermanence. || 31 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Casting of the Sutra," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vālmīki’s *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Rishis. || 2 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Sutra-Laying," in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Third Chapter.
Bharadvāja said: O Brahman, having first described the state of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) regarding Rāghava, [please speak further].
Tell me in due order so that I may eternally be happy.
In this [work], the means for cleansing the visible world, the characteristics of the various types of latent impressions (vāsanā),
and Rāma’s pilgrimage to sacred sites are described in detail.

Having been told, "Act as Rāma and others, who were liberated while living (jīvanmukta), have acted," Bharadvāja—desiring to know the means for attaining that state of liberation while living by means of hearing the description of the sequence of Rāma’s attainment thereof—asks, beginning with the descendant of Raghu: "O Jīvanmukta... and so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "Having made the state of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) the primary subject of description, please tell it. Alternatively, the connection is: "Having gradually brought Rāghava to the state of one liberated while living—that is, having fashioned him into the condition of a jīvanmukta—tell me from the beginning; [tell me] in what manner (yathā) I shall become eternally happy."

Alternatively, the meaning is that one should treat Rāghava as the questioner from the beginning of the dialogue and Vasiṣṭha as the speaker. Thus, having fashioned Janaka and Yājñavalkya, you too should enlighten [the disciple] through a dialogical discourse, just as the Śruti itself reveals the Truth through such a dialogue.

Likewise, in this context, there is no contradiction with the *pūrva-rāmāyaṇa*— which describes the absence of liberation through the display of deluded conduct by those such as Daśaratha who were imagined to be knowers of reality (*tattvajña*), nor with the description of Rāma, who is eternally liberated, as being ignorant due to the cause of a curse that contradicts such scriptural passages as "Neither gods nor powers prevail over him" (*tasya ha na devāśca nābhūtyā īśate*).

There is no harm [to the doctrine] because, for the purpose of making known the non-difference of the beginningless jīva from Brahman, it is logically consistent that the very Brahman—by entering into limiting adjuncts (upādhi) which are its effects—assumes the adventitious state of being a jīva, as described in the Śruti. || 1 ||

Śrī Vālmīki said: O holy one, for this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky, I consider its non-recollection to be better than its remembrance; indeed, forgetting it is preferable.

Thus questioned regarding the characteristics, nature, means, and results [of liberation], Vālmīki, desiring to explain the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in detail, first presents the characteristics and nature of liberation in brief for the sake of easy comprehension,
beginning with the words "Of the delusion" (bhramasya). O virtuous one, [this is like] imagining an extreme impossibility, such as blueness in the sky.

I consider that very state of forgetfulness— whereby there is no further recollection due to the severance of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the root-ignorance (*avidyā*) concerning the world-born, worldly, and superimposed (*adhyāsa-lakṣaṇa*) ego-sense— to be the best, the most excellent, the very nature characterized by liberation.

The meaning is: "I have ascertained through both valid means of knowledge and direct experience. Although even for one who possesses indirect knowledge there is a forgetting of the visible world during deep sleep and in non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), nevertheless, that is not a "re-remembering" (*punah-smaraṇa*). Alternatively, "re-remembering" refers to that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by which [the world] is remembered again.
"That in which there is no [cognition] is thus" refers to forgetting, which is the absence of recollection;
this is an indication of the absence of even the mere appearance of duality. Alternatively, "forgetting-like" means like forgetting;
just as for one who has forgotten an object, there is a non-perception [of it] even while the experiencer exists, so too [is there non-perception] even while consciousness exists.

The meaning is the non-perception of the visible object. If it is asked, "In that case, is there merely a non-perception of the visible object—which is ultimately real—just as in the liberation accepted by the Sāṃkhyas?", he says "no," with the words "of the delusion" (bhramasya).
