The meaning is "below this" [in the following verse]. How can that be a delusion, given that it is not produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)? [To this he replies: "Because of the appearance of another form. This means: because of the appearance of a different form. Therefore, since it is produced by an impression born of error, it is indeed a delusion. The meaning is: "of that which is established by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the worldly transactions of each preceding [moment]. Now, one might object: "In that case, since it does not arise from a defect (*doṣa*) and lacks a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhāna*), it cannot be an error (*bhrama*). Anticipating this, he says: "Like the color of space for that which has arisen. Just as, due to distance and lack of discernment—
The meaning is "the delusion of the world. And likewise, its characteristic is the absolute eradication of the visible;
its essential nature (svarūpa) is the state of pure consciousness (cinmātra) as indicated by that [eradication]. || 2 ||
Without the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible world, that [Self] is never experienced by anyone at any time; therefore, let one's own consciousness be sought. (3)

By the word "I think" (*manye*), the fact that those two are established through one's own experience is shown. To the question, "If so, why is that not experienced by us?", he says: "dṛśya" (the visible). Sublation (*bādha*) is the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible; that is the aforementioned definition and essential nature. [This applies] to the non-experience [of sublation] in terms of time and space.
The phrase "sometimes by someone" is used to demonstrate its pervasiveness. If one asks, "By what reason, then, is there sublation of the perceptible?", he says: "by one's own realization.

That [sublation] occurs precisely from the direct realization of the reality of the Self, which is non-different from the inner witness and the substratum of the entire world; therefore, for that purpose...
And that [liberation] is indeed possible here; for this purpose, this scripture has been composed. If you listen to it, you will attain the truth, and not otherwise.

If so, what is the means for that? To this he says: "And he... The ellipsis is: "when this [work], this treatise, has been mastered. "If there is attraction" means: until the determination of reality. || 4 ||
O sinless one, through this inquiry, it is experienced without weariness that this delusion of the world, though visible, does not exist at all— just as color does not exist in the sky.
He states the very same point more clearly with two verses beginning with "jagat":
by means of this [teaching] presented in this work. || 5 ||
If, through the realization that "the visible does not exist," the cleansing of the mind's objects of perception is accomplished,
then the supreme bliss of Nirvana has arisen.

Regarding the statement "it is experienced," one might ask: is experience (anubhava) identical to the consciousness of the Self (ātmacaitanya), or is it something else? It cannot be something else, because that which is distinct from consciousness is insentient (jaḍa) and, as an object (viṣaya), cannot be experience itself. If it is the Self alone, then since that already exists [prior to the scripture], what is the purpose of the treatise? Anticipating this objection, he says: "the visible" (dṛśyam).

It is true that experience is indeed the Self; nevertheless, when that [experience] is accompanied by the visible object, it is not the experience of the Self, but rather a modification (*vṛtti*) of the mind through which the Self appears as if it were the visible object.

If, however, [the mind] becomes established in the form "the visible object does not exist even in the three periods of time," then [the Self], though its nature is eternally established, [shines forth].

The supreme liberation (*parā nirvāṇa-nirvṛtiḥ*) arises as if produced from that knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); thus, the meaning is that experience, though being one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-bhūta*), is the fruit of the scripture solely by means of that [knowledge]. || 6 ||
Otherwise, for you who roll about here in the pits of the scriptures and possess unrefined ignorance,
there will be no peace even in aeons.

One might ask: "Could liberation not possibly occur through the very means shown in other scriptures? To this, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). If the aforementioned means are not adopted, then for those base men who repeatedly take birth here in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), whose ignorance (*ajñāna*) is uncreated (*akṛtima*), unborn (*ajanya*), beginningless (*anādi*), and characterized by non-self (*anātman*), there is no end to their suffering.
The meaning is that [ignorance] is not removed even by thousands of means other than knowledge. || 7 ||
O Brahman, that supreme abandonment of all latent impressions without exception is called liberation; that alone is the stainless path.
Now, it may be objected that other forms of liberation, such as *sālokya* and others, which are accomplished through means like meditation (*upāsanā*), are also well-known. [To this we reply:

That which is the complete abandonment of the seeds of birth—the absolute eradication by cutting them off at the root—is the primary liberation. This is because the verbal root *muc* is conventionally established in the sense of the cessation of bondage, and it is only the various births that constitute bondage.

Because it is the primary bond, while that [bond] is absent in states such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world), the term "liberation" (*mokṣa*) is used figuratively there; thus, liberation is attained by those who are pure—meaning free from the impurities of ignorance and the like—and not by others. Through rituals, meditations, and practices such as hearing the scriptures, day by day, one attains the very purity of the mind, culminating in the destruction of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Or, the meaning is that he is one whose manner of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is of such a kind. || 8 ||
But when latent impressions are exhausted, the mind dissolves quickly,
just as a speck of frost vanishes when the continuity of cold is spent, O Brahmin.

One might object: "Even when latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have disappeared, since their cause—the mind—still exists, latent impressions will arise again, and consequently, bondage will also persist. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "When [the mind] has perished" (*kṣīṇāyām*). The meaning is that the mind consists essentially of a mass of latent impressions. || 9 ||
This body, a cage of elements, is sustained by latent impressions (vāsanā),
just as a multitude of pearls is strung together by a fine thread inserted within.
Fearing that even when the mind has perished, bondage might still persist in the gross body itself, he says: "This...

It is a cage of elements (*bhūtapañjara*), meaning either composed of a collection of elements, or serving as a cage for living beings, such as animals and birds. Thus, upon the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*)—that is, the destruction of all latent impressions—that too [perishes].
The meaning is "turn back. || 10 ||
Impression (vāsanā) is said to be of two kinds: pure and likewise impure.
The impure is the cause of birth; the pure is the destroyer of birth. 11.

Having thus described supreme liberation by way of an introduction, and desiring to discuss the topic at hand—liberation while living (jīvanmukti)—the author states the twofold nature of latent impressions (vāsanā) for that purpose: "Vāsanā... (verse 11).
The wise declare that impure latent impression (vāsanā) is characterized by a dense form of ignorance, is possessed of thick egoism, and brings about rebirth. (12)

Therein, he characterizes the "impure" (malinā) as follows: "Through ignorance," etc. In the sprouting of the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), ignorance is the excellent field; within that, the seed is the latent impression, which takes a very dense form through the cultivation of the habitual pursuit of sense-objects. Because it is nourished by the soil of passion, hatred, and so forth, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is the thick, dense irrigator, acting as the farmer.
For she, being cultivated and continuously maintained, flourishes and shines. || 12 ||
Having abandoned the sprout of rebirth, she remains like a parched seed; she who knows what is to be known, who sustains or dies for the sake of the body, is called "Pure. (13)
He perceives that [pure state] as pure— [he perceives it as pure]— again. Just as subtle sprouts already existing within a seed manifest through contact with time, water, and so forth,
so too do the successions of births existing within latent impressions (vāsanā) truly exist.

They manifest by the power of causes such as desire and karma. Since it is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to be born, when the sprout of birth within [the self] is destroyed through the burning of the field of ignorance (*avidyā*) by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), even though the impressions (*vāsanā*) of one's own and others' experiences remain, that [consciousness] is called "pure" (*śuddha*). This is the meaning. || 13 ||
In embodied beings who are liberated while living, a pure latent impression (vāsanā) that prevents rebirth remains, like the whirling motion in a potter’s wheel even after the clay has been removed.

He clarifies the very point already stated with the words "anupana" and "dehiṣu. The sense is that the existence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in those [beings] is inferred by the fact that they perform the function of maintaining a body. || 14 ||

Those of great intelligence whose latent impressions are purified so that they are no longer vessels for the misfortunes of rebirth, and who have known that which is to be known, are called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 15 ||
He defines *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) by means of its basis, presented along with its fruit—beginning with the words "yaḥ" (he who).

Thus, it is established that the defining characteristic of one liberated while living is the state of possessing a body sustained solely by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), whose power to produce the sprout of birth has been scorched by the knowledge of reality; for [the term] *vāsanā* here implies that which possesses such power. || 15 ||
Listen as I shall tell you how the high-minded Rāma attained the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), for the sake of pacifying old age and death. 16.

He promises to describe the means for that attainment with the words "jīvanmukti" (liberation while living). I shall explain the auspicious sequence of Rāma’s practice, by which and through what method of spiritual discipline such a state of liberation while living was attained by Rāma— O Bṛhaspati-like Bharadvāja of great intellect, this sequence characterized by the transcendence of old age and death.
Listen, I shall speak; by that very means you will always understand everything.

Clarifying the very meaning already stated, he speaks of another result, beginning with "Bharadvāja": the meaning is that the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is also its result. || 17 ||
Having departed from the house of learning, the lotus-eyed Rāma spent his days at home, free from all fear, with playful diversions.
Having emerged from the house of learning— that is, from residence in the teacher’s family appropriate for the stage of student life—
he [the king] then, while protecting the earth as monarch,
found his subjects free from sorrow and established in a state devoid of affliction. (19)

"Free from fever" means that due to good governance, even afflictions such as fever do not exist for the subjects; this is intended to indicate, all the more so, that no other afflictions exist. || 19 ||
Once, the mind of the virtuous Rāma became intensely eager to behold the series of holy fords and hermitages.
The connection is that Rāma’s mind became eager to behold the series of holy hermitages at the sacred fords;
the locative endings from the previous verse of grief are also to be construed here. 20.
Having reflected thus, Rāghava approached his father’s feet and grasped them by their nails and hair, which were like fresh lotuses and their filaments.

If it is argued that, in this treatise on spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*), it would follow that the description of pilgrimages (*tīrtha-yātrā*)— as well as the upcoming descriptions of the hunt, the abduction of Sītā, and Rāma’s birth— must also be narrated here, thereby rendering the *Pūrva-rāmāyaṇa* (the earlier portion of the Rāmāyaṇa) purposeless, we reply as follows:

regarding the phrase "having investigated the means of the narrative" (*kathopāyān vicārya*), [it refers to] those actions such as sacrifices (*yajña*) appropriate to one's respective caste (*varṇa*).

It has been stated that purity of mind is required for eligibility to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). However, for one who is unable to perform sacrifices and other rites due to the lack of youth, learning, or other qualifications, the description of pilgrimage is provided to indicate that the fruit of sacrifice can be attained through pilgrimage and similar acts as well—according to the scriptural statement: "Sacrifices have been fashioned in the form of sacred fords (*tīrtha*). Thus, the description of pilgrimage is given.

For this very reason, one should not imagine Rāma to be advanced in age, because that would result in the failure of the indicated meaning—namely, the description of his desire for self-knowledge (*ātmajijñāsā*). As for the description of the hunt, however, even the longing to see a spectacle previously witnessed acts as an obstacle to the desire for self-knowledge; therefore, if...

If one’s longing does not subside without experiencing that curiosity, then only by experiencing it and ascertaining its worthlessness can one dispel that longing and become established in listening and other practices without hindrance; thus, all is consistent for the purpose of providing this specific instruction. Rāghava, [having heard] this matter thus stated...

Having reflected thus, he prostrated at his father's feet; the sense is that for one whose father is living, the right to perform religious duties exists only in the presence of the father and preceded by the father's command. || 21 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Father, O Lord, my mind is yearning to behold the sacred fords, the abodes of the gods, the forests, and the temples. (22)
The word "nātha" (Lord) is used for the purpose of indicating one's own state of dependence. || 22 ||
Therefore, you ought to make this former request of mine fruitful;
for there is no petitioner in the world, O Lord, who has not been honored by you.
"Former" means the first. "Not honored" means not satisfied by the fulfillment of his desired object. || 23 ||
Thus entreated by Vasiṣṭha,
the king then deliberated and released Rāma first, as he was the primary petitioner.
He did not release her at all, nor did he consent [to her departure], out of grief for the separation from his son.

On an auspicious day under a favorable constellation, Rāghava, his body adorned with auspicious ornaments and having had benedictions performed for him by the twice-born, set out together with his two brothers.
Accompanied by Brahmins sent by Vasiṣṭha who were well-versed in the scriptures,
and together with a few affectionate and excellent princes.
Having been adorned by his mothers, who repeatedly embraced him and bestowed their blessings,
he departed from that house, intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
He departed from his own city, accompanied by the citizens who sounded the music of musical instruments,
while being gazed upon by the eyes of the city women, which were as tremulous as swarms of bees.

Like the Himalaya mountain scattered with showers of snow, he was covered by showers [of flowers] from the lotus-hands of village women— showers that were as flickering as swarms of bees, meaning they fell upon the flowers. (29)
By those who have driven away [the darkness] and impelled [the light]. || 29 ||
Winning over the hosts of brahmins, hearing the blessings of the people,
and surveying the regions of the world, he wandered through the forest lands.
Winning them over by means of gifts, honors, and so forth, he brings them under his influence; "jāṅgalāni" refers specifically to "jāṅgalān," that is, dilapidated forests.
Then, beginning from his own treasury and mandala,
he beheld [the world] preceded by bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation.
The word "dadarśa" (he saw) is to be connected with "pāvanān āśramāñ śubhān" (the purifying and auspicious hermitages) at the end [of each clause] throughout the entire passage. || 31 ||
Sacred riverbanks, forests, and sacred abodes;
wildernesses within the reach of men, and the shores of oceans and mountains. (32)

The "abodes" (āyatana) are the abodes of divine sages; "at the borders of people" (janānteṣu) means, by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇayā), at the borders of inhabited districts (janapadānteṣu). || 32 ||
The Mandākinī, which resembles the moon; the Kālindī, with its stainless blue lotuses; the Sarasvatī, the Śatadrū, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī. || 33 ||
The Veṇī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the Nirvindhyā, and likewise the Sarayū; the Carmaṇvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā, and also the Bāhudā. || 34 ||
The Veṇī alone; that Kṛṣṇaveṇī which is conjoined with the Kṛṣṇā. || 34 ||
Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, and likewise Gayā;
Vārāṇasī, Śrīgiri, Kedāra, and likewise Puṣkara. || 35 ||
Śrīgiri is Śrīśaila. || 35 ||
And he respectfully visited Mānasa, Kramasara, likewise Uttaramānasa, Vaḍavāmukha, and the multitude of other sacred fords.
Next in order is Sāra, the Vaḍavāmukha Hayagrīva Tīrtha. || 36 ||
The great pilgrimage site of Agnitīrtha, as well as Indradyumna-saras,
the lakes, the rivers, and likewise the series of streams and ponds.
"Mahātīrtha" is an epithet for the Indradyumna lake. || 37 ||
[He saw] his master Kārttikeya, as well as Śālagrāma Hari,
and the sixty-four sacred sites of Hari and of Hara.
And the shores of the four oceans, variegated with many wonders;
and the Vindhya, Mandara, and Kuñja mountains, as well as the regions of the principal mountain ranges.
From the groves and bower-houses; the principal mountain ranges such as the Himavat and others. || 39 ||
And likewise, he saw the auspicious hermitages that purify the great royal sages, the brahmin sages, the gods, and the brahmins.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include those various locations that have not been explicitly mentioned. || 40 ||
That bestower of honor wandered again and again with his two brothers through all the regions of the earth, reaching even the four extremities of the quarters. (41)

"Again and again" means that even regarding those previously seen who have now returned, there is a going back once more out of curiosity or to manifest their extraordinary greatness when they are present. (41)

Honored by gods, kinnaras, and humans, the joy of the Raghus, having surveyed this entire earth, returned to his own home, having traversed all directions like the Lord [Śiva] returning from the realm of Śiva.

The connection [of the narrative] is as follows: Honored and worshipped by the gods and others who were present in various places, the son of Raghu (Rāma), having thoroughly surveyed the entire earth consisting of Jambūdvīpa, returned to his own home, Ayodhyā. Īśvara refers to Śiva. || 42 ||
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Undertaking of the Pilgrimage," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Undertaking of the Pilgrimage," in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrī Vasiṣṭha-Mārkaṇḍeya-Mārkaṇḍeya-Rāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-Prakāśa*.
The Fourth Canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Rama was showered with heaps of handfuls of flowers by the city-dwellers.
The illustrious Jayanta entered his home, as if entering heaven itself.
In this [chapter], the delighting of Rāma’s friends at his home upon his arrival from a pilgrimage to sacred sites,
as well as his conduct such as hunting expeditions, is described.
"Rāma" refers to [the mountain] strewn with multitudes—that is, groups—for the purpose of auspicious rites. "Viṣṭapa" means heaven (triviṣṭapa);
the name is used here by taking a part of the full name. || 1 ||
Then Raghava, having arrived first, bowed down to his father Vasiṣṭha, his brothers, his kinsmen, the brahmins, and the elders of the family.
Having reached the first stage, he has returned from his first journey abroad. || 5 ||
Rāghava, his conduct repeatedly embraced by friends, brothers, mothers, his father, and the assembly of brahmins, could not contain himself for joy.

He was one who, being embraced by them again and again, performed the appropriate actions such as salutations and affectionate speech; [the ellipsis implies] his own body did not find enough space [to move]. The sense is that he was blossoming with joy. || 3 ||
In that house of the son of Daśaratha, the quarters of the sky vibrated through their mutual conversations concerning his beloved,
as if by the sweet sounds of soft flutes.

In that house of Daśaratha— [the house] of Daśaratha, the father of Rāma— the people, [as is understood from the context], were delighted by pleasant reports and agreeable words; they whirled about, wandering from one direction to another, or rather, they experienced a confusion of the quarters due to the delusion caused by their joy.

The same applies to the simile as well. Alternatively, by the word "direction" (dik), the people residing there are indicated. The meaning is that those who had gathered together, their hearts refined by the beloved stories of Rāma’s son, wandered about as if playing with the soft sounds of flutes during a special festival. || 4 ||
Then, for eight days, there was a festival celebrating Rāma’s arrival,
filled with the tumultuous, joyful clamor released by people intoxicated with happiness.
It was filled and pervaded by a deep and melodious clamor, uttered with great intensity by intoxicated and joyful people. || 5 ||
From that time forward, Rāghava lived happily in his home,
describing the various customs and manners of the different regions he had visited here and there.
The grammatical connection is with the words "sumukhavāse" (in the beautiful-faced one). || 6 ||
Having risen early in the morning and performed his twilight devotions according to the prescribed rules, Rāma beheld his father seated in the assembly hall, resembling Indra himself.
The phrase beginning with "prātar" (in the morning) intends to express repetition; "tathā" (likewise) serves to include what was stated in the preceding verse. || 7 ||
Having spent a fourth part of the day with Vasiṣṭha and the others, he remained respectfully engaged in most diverse conversations filled with the essence of knowledge.

That Rāma, having stayed with Vasiṣṭha and the others and being attended by them with appropriate conversation for a fourth part of the day—the accusative case here denotes duration (atyantasaṃyoga), meaning during the fourth division of the day—went to the forest out of a desire for hunting; this is to be connected with the following verse. || 8 ||
Permitted by his father and accompanied by a vast army,
he went to the forest crowded with excellent elephants and buffaloes, according to his desire for hunting.
Ākheṭaka means hunting. || 9 ||
Then, having returned home and performed the sequence of rites beginning with bathing,
he ate together with his friends and kinsmen and passed the night with his companions.
Rāghava, whose daily conduct was of this nature, returned with his two brothers from his pilgrimage and dwelt in his father’s house.
The word "prāya" is used to indicate the impermanence of hunting and other such pursuits. [He was accompanied] by his two brothers, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna. || 11 ||

O sinless one, he passed his days with these activities— which were pleasing in the king’s worldly dealings, like moonlight in the heart of a virtuous man, and as delicate as the essence of praised nectar.
The word *anagha* is either an address to King Bharadvāja or a description of Rāma himself. That Rāma, by means of a conduct appropriate for kings—

conduct which is pleasing, captivating, and as refreshing to the hearts of virtuous people as moonlight, and therefore praised, extolled, and as sweet and clever as the essence of nectar— [conducted himself].
In this manner—with this aforementioned activity, which was tender with a sweetness like that of nectar (sudhā) flowing forth—she passed the days, spending them in this way. (12)
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Description of Daily Activity," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Description of Daily Activity," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa.
The Fifth Canto.
Vālmīki said:
Now, while the sixteenth year was underway for that scion of Raghu’s lineage...
Likewise, [he was established] in Śatrughna, who follows Rāma, and also in Lakṣmaṇa.
The emaciation and other conditions of Rāma’s body, as well as his despondency and so forth, are described here;
then follows the king’s inquiry regarding their cause, which initiates the discourse of Vasiṣṭha.

Having thus described the conduct of Śrī Rāma in performing the practices for the purification of the mind, the author now begins with the words "atha" (now), desiring to explain the attainment of the means such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) which are the fruits of that practice. The connection is as follows: when the sixteenth year was current, being deficient by a fourth part, Rāma attained emaciation (*kārśya*).

The phrase "in the descendant of Raghu" (raghūdvahe) is an adjective qualifying either the king Śatrughna or Lakṣmaṇa, who are mentioned in proximity, but it does not refer back to Rāma. This is because there would otherwise be a lack of syntactic connection with the statement "Rāma attained emaciation. Furthermore, if it were intended to indicate an interval of time (bhāvāntarāla), the locative case used as a *bhāvalakṣaṇa* (indicating a temporal condition) would be untenable.
While Bharata remained constantly in his maternal grandfather’s house in happiness,
the king protected this entire earth in accordance with the law.

Regarding the word "bharati": from this very [verse], even though it was not mentioned in the earlier *Rāmāyaṇa*, it is inferred that Bharata went to his maternal grandfather’s house without Śatrughna and returned before his marriage. Furthermore, by the word "constantly" (*nityam*), it is understood that Bharata had previously gone there and stayed many times. || 2 ||
And while King Daśaratha— the highly wise, discerning, and sagacious monarch— was deliberating daily with his ministers regarding the matter of obtaining sons, [the following occurred].
Those who carry the bride are called *janyas*; that which provides for them with garments, ornaments, and so forth is the *janyatras*, meaning the wedding intended for that purpose. || 3 ||
When his pilgrimage was completed, Rāma remained in his own home;
day by day he grew emaciated, like a stainless lake in autumn.
Emaciation and other such symptoms are described as the signs of despondency, anxiety, and suffering. || 4 ||
The prince’s large-eyed face took on a pallid hue,
like a white lotus with its petals slightly opened by the frost.
The phrase "sālimālam" is used as a comparison for that which is distinguished by having large eyes. || 5 ||
With his palms resting upon the surface of his cheeks, seated in the lotus posture,
he became silent and inactive, entirely overcome by anxiety.
Non-activity is the absence of effort. 6.
With a wasted body, filled with anxiety, exhausted, and deeply dejected,
he said nothing to anyone, appearing as if fixed in a painting.
He whose likeness is bestowed upon the work of a painter, depicted in a painting. || 7 ||
Being entreated again and again by his attendants out of weariness,
he performed his daily ritual with his lotus-like face withered.
Āhnika: that which must necessarily be performed daily. || 8 ||
Beholding Rāma, who was distinguished by such qualities and was a mine of all virtues, his two brothers fell into that very same state. (9)
King Rāmadeva, a mine of a multitude of virtues distinguished by the aforementioned qualities such as reflection and so forth—
[thus he was]— while those sons were distressed and emaciated,
the protector of the earth, together with his wife, fell into a state of being overwhelmed by anxiety. (10)
"O son, what is this heavy anxiety of yours? Thus he questioned Rāma again and again with affectionate words, yet Rāma did not say anything to him at all.
He did not speak at all; the sense is that he was certain that the purpose for speaking would not be accomplished. || 11 ||
Having said, "Father, I have no sorrow at all," Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, sat upon his father's lap and remained silent.

The intention was that "suffering cannot be avoided by you"—since this is not found anywhere as being untrue, there is no falsehood. *Tiṣṭhati sma* means "he stood"; the present tense (*laṭ*) is used here in place of the past tense (*liṭ*) due to its connection with *sma*. 12.
Then King Daśaratha asked Vasiṣṭha, the best of speakers and knower of all affairs, "Is Rāma distressed? (13)
The phrase "for what reason" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 13 ||
Having been addressed thus by the sage Vasiṣṭha, that king reflected:
"O illustrious one, there is a reason for this; O King, let there be no sorrow for you. (14)

Thus questioned, the sage Vasiṣṭha spoke to that king in this manner. He states that very point with the half-verse beginning "There exists here... together with the following verse: [He spoke of] the auspicious outcome of the thought of Rāma—[namely,] anger, the state of despondency, and widespread joy.
The virtuous do not act on account of a trivial cause;
O King, in this world, great beings do not undergo transformation except through the impulse of creation or the force of destruction.

The peaceful do not harbor anger or the influence of dejection on account of even a slight cause; just as the great elements, such as earth and the rest, do not undergo transformation—nor do they experience the changes of increase and decrease—without the impulse of creation (sarga), that is, the fruit of manifestation, or the force of dissolution (saṃhāra). || 15 ||
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Declaration of Emaciation," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Declaration of Emaciation," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa.
The Sixth Canto.
Vālmīki said:
When the lord of sages had spoken thus, the king was filled with doubt.
Remaining in a state of weariness, one should maintain silence while waiting for some time.
The arrival of Viśvāmitra, the king’s formal worship of the sage,
and the king’s joyful promise regarding the task are described here.

"By the Lord of Sages, Vasiṣṭha"—that is, in the manner thus described; the meaning is "in a general form. For this very reason, while there was doubt regarding the particular earthly king, and while there was a waiting for some time—that is, one characterized by a certain duration for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion—[the word "sati" is not found in some versions]. || 1 ||
While all the queens in the royal palaces were utterly exhausted and remained on guard,
keeping watch everywhere for every movement of Rāma.

The connection is: "while the queens were staying in the royal palaces. The plural number is used because it is well known that there are different palaces corresponding to the different queens. They were attentive in order to ascertain the causes of their despondency by means of the signs of their particular gestures. (2)
At that very time, however, the great seer known as Viśvāmitra arrived to see that king of Ayodhyā.

Regarding the phrase "in this": although a specific time is already obtained through locative cases used to indicate a condition (*bhāvalakṣaṇa-saptamī*), nevertheless, the term "at that time" (*kāle*) is specifically employed to suggest, from the perspective of worldly convention, that Viśvāmitra’s arrival occurred at an inappropriate moment. He was heard of and renowned. (3)
Then, it is said, the sacrifice of that wise man who was devoted to dharma was indeed torn apart by Rākṣasas, who were intoxicated by their power of illusion, heroism, and strength.

For one for whom dharma alone is the task that must necessarily be performed, his sacrifice was so utterly destroyed that it reached that lord of men; this is the connection with what precedes, or rather, with the subsequent phrase "he desired to see the king. || 4 ||
For the sake of protecting that sacrifice, he desired to see the king;
for that sage was unable to bring the ritual to completion without obstacles.
To complete, to bring to an end, or to attain correctly until completion. || 5 ||
Then, intent on their destruction, Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of asceticism and possessed of great splendor, went to the city of Ayodhyā.
Udyata means exerted or striving. || 6 ||
Desiring an audience with the king, he spoke to the gatekeepers:
"Quickly announce that I, Kauśika, the son of Gādhi, have arrived. (7)
It was told; "to the king" is the ellipsis. || 7 ||
Having heard those words of his, all the gatekeepers, their minds agitated and urged by that speech, went to Rājagṛha.
Their minds were agitated by the fear of a curse due to the delay. || 8 ||
Then those doorkeepers, having gone to the royal palace, announced to the lord that the sage Viśvāmitra had arrived.

A *sadana* is a place where one sits or rests; it refers to an assembly hall (*sabhāsthāna*). *Pratīhāras* are gatekeepers. [The term applies] to a staff-bearer (*yāṣṭīka*) who stands outside the door of his own master, or to one standing at the door of the assembly hall. [This concludes the section on] "motion and cognition" (*gatibuddhi*). Now, [the verse describes] the king who has gone to the assembly hall, adorned by a circle of subordinate kings.
Approaching with haste, that staff-bearer made his request.
Having been informed of the matter by the doorkeepers, he was a staff-bearer, one whose weapon was a staff; [the suffix] *īkak* is applied after *śakti* and *yaṣṭi*. (Pāṇini 4.4.59)
O King, at the gate stood a glorious man of great splendor, radiant as the rising sun, with a mass of matted hair ruddy with flames. || 11 ||

Possessing great majesty and great power, he was radiant with beauty like the rising sun; to illustrate this, the term "jvālāruṇa" (red as a flame) is used. He was illustrious and possessed the splendor of asceticism.
He made that region, including its banners, horses, elephants, men, and weapons, appear as if strewn with gold by his splendors.

That region of the royal gate, from its upper reaches down to the tops of the assembly halls' banners, was filled on all sides with horses, elephants, men, and weapons; strewn with gold, it appeared tawny as if entirely covered in gold.
While the King was looking at the staff-bearer, the latter announced with a humble voice: "The sage Viśvāmitra has arrived. (13)

The connection with the following verse is as follows: while the staff-bearer was announcing the report to the king, saying in a humble voice, "The sage Viśvāmitra has arrived," and as soon as he was seen, that best of kings rose up. || 13 ||
Having heard these words of Yashthika, that best of kings,
together with his ministers and vassal lords, rose up from his golden seat.
To show that this is not without careful consideration, he says: "Having heard these words of the staff-bearer.
The *sāmanta*s are the lords of small territories. From the *viṣṭara*, that is, from the lion-throne. || 14 ||
On foot alone, he was suddenly garlanded by a multitude of kings;
praised by the vassal lords, he was accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva. || 15 ||
"Mālitaḥ" means adorned or garlanded. The connection with the subsequent verse is that "that best of kings went together with Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva. (15)
He went here and there until he reached the place where the great sage Viśvāmitra was;
there he beheld that tiger among sages standing at the gateway.
The syntactical connection is: "He went to where the great sage Viśvāmitra was. || 16 ||
For some reason, the sun had descended to the surface of the earth,
overwhelmed by both the spiritual luster of a Brahmin and the great martial power of a Kshatriya.
The distinction between *ojas* and *tejas* consists in their respective manifestations of ascetic power (*tapas*) and prowess (*parākrama*). || 17 ||
His shoulders were covered by a mass of matted locks that was perpetually withered by age and made rough by the expansion of his ascetic penance,
resembling a mountain enveloped in the clouds of twilight.
By old age, worn out by the extreme of advanced years and grey-haired. || 18 ||
He bore a radiant body that was both tranquil and lovely, luminous yet non-obstructive, modest yet possessed of majestic form. (19)

It was radiant, difficult to behold due to its excellence of splendor; tranquil and gentle; unimpeded and invincible; lovely and pleasing to the sight; "ūrjita" means its form and physical configuration were bold and confident; "nibhṛta" means it was endowed with modesty; and it was resplendent.
"Radiant" (*kāntimat*); if the reading is "the sun" (*bhāskaram*), it means resembling the sun. The suffix *kan* is elided according to the rule beginning with "devapatha.
The adjectives are to be applied to both [the moon and the sun]. || 19 ||
Its radiance was colored by a splendor that was both charming and most formidable, serene yet agitated, profound and exceedingly full.

With a gentle gaze that delights the mind and is clever; with one that is exceedingly formidable and terrifying; with one that is agitated and intensely moving; with one that is profound and unfathomable; with one that is perfectly full and immeasurable—the splendor (*tejas*) conjoined with his physical form is the radiance (*prabhā*) extending outward; it is distinguished by the excellence of that splendor.
Thus it is said. || 20 ||
He held in his hand a single, smooth, stainless water-pot, which was like a companion to the state of infinite life, while his own mind remained unfading.
The state of infinite life is the state of long life; the meaning is that he was a friend who had been associated with her for a long time.
"Ślakṣṇām" means smooth or glossy. "Kuṇḍīm" means a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). "Amlānamānasaḥ" refers to one whose mind (mānasa) or heart (manaḥ) is untainted and serene. || 21 ||
Because his mind was overcome with compassion, he seemed to sprinkle these women with nectar through his glances and his clear, sweet words.
The meaning is: those [speeches] which consist of sweet syllables; that is to say, by means of these sweet conversations. || 22 ||
His limbs were adorned with the sacred thread, his white eyebrows were raised high, and he seemed to bestow infinite wonder within the beholder. || 23 ||
He whose body was adorned with sacred threads suited to his advanced age. || 23 ||
Beholding the sage from afar, the king, with his body bowed low, prostrated himself until the ground was honored by the jewels falling from his crest.
The connection is that the king, having first seen [the sage] from afar, bowed to the sage with his body already bent;
the final word is an adverbial modifier of the action. 24.
There the sage also greeted the lord of the earth with sweet and noble speech, just as the sun greets Indra.
He saluted him with an embrace; the meaning is that he returned the greeting with blessings. || 25 ||
Then all the twice-born ones, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
respectfully honored him according to the sequence beginning with a welcome.
They worshipped and praised him; "ādṛtāḥ" means filled with respect. || 26 ||
Daśaratha said:
O virtuous one, by this radiant sight of yours, which has appeared unexpectedly,
we have been graced as beds of lotuses are by the sun.
"By that which was brought without suspicion and approached without deliberation. The genitive case in "te" (of them) is used either in the sense of the object or the agent. || 27 ||
O Sage, through the sight of you, I have attained that blissful joy which is unbroken from speech onwards and free from the realms of misery.
Manifesting grace alone in accordance with the future destiny [of beings], he describes it with the word "yat" (that which):

[it is] devoid of a beginning cause; by this, there is a rejection of its birth, growth, and transformation. It is unimpaired and free from decay; it is devoid of loss and destruction. [It is] through adventitious [conditions]...

The meaning is that he has attained that very bliss which is well-known as the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha)—that which gladdens all beings with even small fragments of its own inherent happiness. || 28 ||
Today we truly stand at the forefront of the blessed by virtue of our dharma, since we have become the object of your arrival. (29)

It is to be observed that [he stands] at the forefront, in the position of preeminence, among the fortunate ones who have accomplished their purpose. This is an expression emphasizing the abstract state;
let it be observed. || 29 ||
Thus conversing there, the kings and the great sages,
having reached their seats in the assembly hall, sat down together.
Thus, speaking in the very manner described by Daśaratha, the kings and great sages, having reached the assembly hall, sat down upon their seats; such is the grammatical connection. || 30 ||
Seeing that best of sages adorned with splendor, the king was struck with awe;
yet, with a joyful countenance, he personally offered him the guest-offering (arghya).

The meaning is that, fearing the splendor of her asceticism (tapolakṣmī), he himself brought the water intended for the guest-offering (arghya) and presented it, out of apprehension that there might be an offense in having it fetched by another person. || 31 ||
Having accepted the guest-offering from the king according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
he honored the king by performing a circumambulation.
He worshipped and praised him. || 32 ||
Honored by the king, he then, with a joyful countenance,
inquired after the welfare and the well-being of the lord of men.
It is "auspicious" (kuśalam) in reference to the body, ministers, prosperity, and so forth; it is "imperishable" (avyayam) in reference to treasuries. || 33 ||
Having met with Vasiṣṭha, that bull among sages smiled,
honored him as was fitting, and then inquired after his well-being.
Having thus honored Vasiṣṭha as was fitting, he enquired after the welfare of his disciples, the Ṛgvedic students, and others; such is the meaning. || 34 ||
Having honored one another for a moment as was appropriate and having come together,
they all, with joyful minds, entered the residence of the great king.

The connection with the following [verse] is as follows: having met one another and honored each other, they sat upon appropriate seats and, being virtuous, inquired after each other's well-being. || 35 ||
Seated upon their respective appropriate seats, their mutual splendor increasing, they all respectfully inquired after one another's well-being.
To that wise Viśvāmitra who was seated,
he repeatedly offered water for his feet, the guest-offering (arghya), and a cow.

By the first "ca" (and), there is a conjunction of unmentioned items such as perfumes, flowers, garments, and ornaments; by the second, of items such as sacrificial fees, fruits, and betel-leaf. And because these are of many kinds, the phrase "again and again" (bhūyobhūyaḥ) is used. || 37 ||
Having honored Viśvāmitra according to the prescribed rites, the king, with palms joined in reverence, self-restrained, and a joyful mind, spoke these words. (38)
Being self-controlled and pure, [he should recite] this which is about to be spoken. || 38 ||
Just as the attainment of nectar, just as rain during a drought, and just as the recovery of sight for one who is blind—such is your arrival. (39)
"According to what is appropriate for a mortal," and the word "cultivator" is to be understood as the remainder [of the phrase]. || 39 ||
The birth of a son to one who was childless through union with a wife as desired, the attainment of the object seen in a dream, and likewise this arrival of yours—[all these have occurred]. (40)
The acquisition of wealth by the poor; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 40 ||
Just as there is union with what is desired, just as there is the arrival of what is wished for, and just as there is the recovery of what was lost, so too is this arrival of yours. (41)

By means of that which was desired and longed for for a long time—such as the attainment of jewels, mantras, and prosperity—and by means of the beloved and most cherished son, brother, or other relative; [the word] "from afar" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 41 ||
Just as Harṣa rejoiced at the return of the deceased through his journey to the sky, so too, O Brahmin, do I rejoice at your arrival; welcome to you, O great sage! (42)
The phrase "joy from your arrival" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. || 42 ||
Indeed, who would not feel joy at dwelling in the world of Brahmā?
O Sage, I tell you this as the very truth: your arrival is likewise so. (43)
"And what is your supreme desire? What may I do for you?
O Brahmin, you have arrived as a worthy recipient, being most righteous. (44)
The first question concerns the subject of what is to be given; the second concerns the subject of service to be performed. || 44 ||
Formerly, you were known by the title of royal sage (rājarṣi), your splendor illumined by asceticism;
having now attained the status of a brahmin-sage (brahmarṣi), you are worthy of worship by me, O Blessed One.
He establishes his very fitness as a recipient of worship with the words "Previously" (pūrvam). The connection is: "having attained the status of a Brahmarṣi through asceticism. || 45 ||
Just as joy would arise in me from being sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
so too does the joy from seeing you cool my inner self, as it were.
It cools by means of the cessation of heat and brings happiness; the word "iva" (as if) is used for the purpose of a metaphorical identification (*abhedotprekṣā*) with the primary meaning. || 46 ||
Free from desire, fear, and anger, devoid of passion and free from affliction— O Brahmin, it is most wonderful that you have come to me.

It is well known that desire and the other [afflictions] are the causes for approaching others. Attachment (*rāga*) is an excess of craving for sense objects, arising from the coloring of the mind in the form of those objects. (47)
And I perceive myself as having entered a pure field, free from all impurity, like the lunar orb emerged [from the clouds], O best of those who know what is to be known through the Vedas. (48)
The sense is that because places frequented by celestial sages (*devarṣi*) are indeed sacred fields (*kṣetra*), your presence makes even this house so;

therefore it is free from stain— that is, devoid of sin— and for that very reason, due to the excellence of its merit, it is imagined (*utprekṣā*) to have emerged there from the attainment of the nectar-filled lunar orb.
I consider your arrival to be like that of Brahmā himself in person;
O Sage, I am purified and graced by your visit.
Purified by dharma, he was graced with both fame and prosperity. || 49 ||
O virtuous one, by the merit of your arrival, that which has been delighted today makes my birth fruitful and my life well-lived. (50)
He clarifies that very point with the words "tvad" and so forth. || 50 ||
Having seen you arrived here, having honored and bowed to you,
I bow within myself alone, like the ocean beholding the moon.

The meaning is that, because he was increased by merit and joy, he did not feel crowded within his own body, as if it were a vast vessel; the words "of the ocean at its boundary" are to be supplied [to complete the simile]. || 51 ||
"O bull among sages, whatever task you have come for, or for whatever purpose, know that it is already accomplished; you are always worthy of my honor. (52)
Know that both of these were done for the sole reason that you are always worthy of honor. || 52 ||
O Kauśika, you should not hesitate regarding your own duty;
O Blessed One, there is nothing that I cannot give to you, whatever you may request.
I shall certainly do even that which others are unable to do, and I shall certainly give even that which is impossible to give;
for if the object being given is bestowed upon you, a worthy recipient such as yourself, it becomes meaningful through the attainment of such a proper reception. This is the intended sense. || 53 ||
"You ought not to deliberate upon this matter according to dharma;
I am the doer of all for you, and you are the supreme deity."

Out of great enthusiasm, he states again what was already said in the first half [of the verse]: "Of the task," etc. He rules out that greed and other such factors are the cause by saying, "the agent acts out of duty" (dharmataḥ). || 54 ||
Having heard these exceedingly sweet words, spoken with gentleness by the knower of the self for his own spiritual welfare,
that bull among sages— whose virtues and fame were far-renowned and who was distinguished by his excellences— attained the highest joy. (55)
"By one who knows the self and is cognizant of the power of his own asceticism"—this is a qualifying phrase for the sentence "distinguished by virtues. (55)
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Arrival of Viśvāmitra," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Arrival of Viśvāmitra," in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Seventh Canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having heard those words of the lion among kings, which were of wonderful extent—
With his hair standing on end and filled with great luster, Viśvāmitra addressed him.
Then follows the praise of the king, the announcement of the obstacle to the sage’s sacrifice,
and the description of the envoy's departure for Rāma to slay the Rākṣasa.
The *adbhutavistara* is that which is endowed with an extensive exposition of marvelous and wondrous meanings. || 1 ||
O tiger among kings, this is indeed worthy of you alone upon this earth—
you who are born of a great lineage and abide in the tradition of Vasiṣṭha.
This is appropriate and fitting. In this regard, there is a qualifying phrase containing a reason: "By virtue of your lineage and by virtue of your teachers...
[O tiger among kings, carry out the decision regarding the matter that is in my heart; uphold the dharma. (3)

First, determine that which is intended in his heart—the decision regarding the task, the determination of the duty related to it; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Fearing that this might sometimes be unrighteous or impossible, he says: "Dharma. (3)
"O bull among men, I am practicing the Dharma for the sake of attaining perfection;
however, terrible Rākṣasas stand in my way as obstacles."
He says that very thing with the words beginning "I": "dharma" means sacrifice; "samātiṣṭhe" means I shall undertake. || 4 ||
Whenever I worship the hosts of gods with sacrifice,
at those very times the night-stalkers destroy my sacrifice.
To the hosts of the wise, the multitudes of gods.
When that sacrifice had been performed by me many times, those leaders of the Rākṣasas covered the earth with flesh and blood.
When it has been prescribed and performed. || 6 ||
When that assembly of sacrifices had thus become desolate, he,
having exerted himself in vain, returned from that place with his enthusiasm lost.
When the obstacles have been dispelled by the Avadhūta, [it occurs] in the "cluster of sacrifices," that is, in the collection of rites. || 7 ||
O King, my mind does not incline toward releasing anger;
for such was that deed, that no curse can take effect upon him.
To the question, "Why were they not dispelled by that very curse? he says: "And not... (verse 8).
Such was that sacrificial initiation of mine in that great rite;
by your grace, may I attain its great fruit without obstacle.

"May I, by means of such [a power] as anger, curses, and so forth, cause [them] to reach [this state]. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of the root itself; thus, "may I cause them to attain" means "may I attain. || 9 ||
"O Noble One, please protect me, who am distressed and have come seeking refuge;
for the hopelessness of those who seek aid is indeed a defeat. (10)

"Sattame" means "most excellent. However, if the reading is "sattama," it is a vocative. "Abhibhava" means contempt, [implying] the contempt of the most excellent ones. Or, it may be read as a single compound word. || 10 ||
You have a glorious son, Rāma, who possesses the prowess of a proud tiger, who is equal to Mahendra in valor, and who is the destroyer of the Rākṣasas. || 11 ||
Since the word "him" (tam) is seen later on, the word "who" (yaḥ) must be supplied here. [The following are] the qualifiers intended to establish the desired meaning:
"O tiger among kings, you ought to give to me that son, Rāma, whose valor is truth, who wears the sidelocks of youth, who is heroic, and my eldest. (12)
He whose prowess is truth and whose prowess is unfailing; he who has side-locks at the roots of his ears as a crest, perfected in the conduct of a Kṣatriya.
For, protected by me with my two-fold divine splendor,
he is indeed capable of crushing the heads of those Rākṣasas who have done him harm.
But surely, how is this boy capable [of such a task] since he is untrained in weapons? To this he replies: "capable. He is "protected," meaning guarded.
The phrase "those who do harm" refers either to the sacrifice or to the world, as the sense requires. "In the crushing of the head" means in the severing of the head. || 13 ||
And I shall bring about for him manifold and infinite welfare,
by which he will become worthy of worship even by the three worlds.

The bestowal of the science of weapons is a supreme boon; it takes many forms according to the variety of weapons, and its power is indeed infinite. Furthermore, having encountered Rāma—who is like a lion born in a forest thicket—those night-stalkers will not be able to stand before him when he is enraged.
Like deer in a forest grove. || 15 ||

"To remain"—the word "in front" (puraḥ) is to be supplied. [Regarding "vaneriṇa"]: in the *iraṇa* grass, that which arises in the forest and is called *iraṇa*; because of its flimsiness, it is incapable of protecting the deer. Alternatively, there is a word-break as "raṇe" (in battle). || 15 ||
No man other than the enraged Kesarin is capable of fighting those Kakutsthas, just as no one can fight rutting elephants except for a furious lion.
Anticipating the king's intention that "they should be restrained by my servants or by me," he says:
"And of them... [referring to] from Kākutstha, the subject Rāma. || 16 ||
For those wicked ones, intoxicated by their own prowess in battle, are like the Kālakūṭa poison;
they are the servants of Karadūṣaṇa, resembling wrathful Yamas.

To the question "Whence [does this come]?", he says: "By valor," and so forth. "Utsiktāḥ" means arrogant. It is not merely by their own strength, but also by the strength of their master; thus he says: "By Khara," and so forth. || 17 ||
O tiger among kings, they will not withstand the arrows of Rāma,
just as particles of dust cannot endure a stream of water from a cloud.

If that is so, how can they be overcome even by Rāma? To this he says: "Of Rāma... [The dust] "continuously moving" means incessantly emerging. The meaning is: just as dust particles, though capable of being overwhelmed by a shower of rain, are not capable of being overwhelmed by a downpour of tears, so it is here. || 18 ||
And you ought not, O King, to harbor affection for your son;
there is nothing in this world that great-souled men should not give away. (19)

"Let it be so; nevertheless, a son is difficult for fathers to abandon. Anticipating this objection, he says "na ca" (nor). [The word] "sneham" refers to the natural affection or attachment that thinks, "This is my son. To the question "Why is that?", he says "na tat" (not that). For instance, Śibi, Dadhīci, Alarka, and others gave even their own bodies, eyes, and so forth—this is the sense. || 19 ||
Ah, now I truly understand; know that those Rākṣasas have been slain, for wise men such as we do not engage in actions when the outcome is uncertain.

"There is not even a suspicion of misfortune here, but rather a triumph of victory," he says with the word "Hanta. "Nūnam" expresses certainty. "I recognize [this] through asceticism"—this is the ellipsis. "You too, know [this]"—this is the ellipsis, meaning "by my word.
He confirms this very point with "na hi" (for it is not so). || 20 ||
I know the high-souled Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses;
so too does the greatly effulgent Vasiṣṭha and those others who possess far-sighted vision.

"Great" (mahāntam) refers to the Self (ātmānam) which is unconditioned by the limiting adjuncts of the individual soul (jīvopādhi); that is to say, the Lord (īśvara). Alternatively, it means the Great-Souled One (mahātmānam) by virtue of His power. "And Vasiṣṭha knows" is to be supplied by changing the grammatical form [from masculine to neuter]. The same applies to what follows.
"Far-sighted" (dīrghadarśinaḥ) means those whose nature is to perceive things that are obstructed or distant, due to the perfection of yoga (yogasiddhi). || 21 ||
If righteousness, greatness, and fame reside in your mind, then you ought to grant me the son for whom I long. || 22 ||
If it is established in your mind that dharma, greatness, and fame must be protected,

then [act] so that the qualification "the most beloved son" is properly intended— that is, correctly resolved— or so that the adverbial phrase "in a manner that is perfectly intended" is realized. || 22 ||
And my sacrifice shall last for ten nights; during this time, O Rākṣasas, those enemies who act as obstacles to my sacrifice must be slain by Rāma.
The *daśarātra* is that which is to be accomplished in ten days and nights. || 23 ||
In this matter as well, O Kakutstha, let all your ministers, headed by Vasiṣṭha, grant their permission; therefore, dismiss Rāma.
In this matter, the connection is that all your ministers, even those headed by Vasiṣṭha, [are of one mind];
therefore, by their granting of permission... || 24 ||
O knower of time, O Rāghava, act in such a way that this time does not pass me by;
may prosperity be yours, and do not set your mind on grief. (25)
The connection is that time, consisting of spring and so forth, which serves as a constituent part of the sacrifice, does not pass by. || 25 ||
Even a very small task, when performed at the proper time, becomes a source of benefit;
yet even a great service, if performed at the wrong time, comes to naught.

The meaning is that assistance, which consists in favoring one with the means to achieve their desired ends, reaches a state of being even more delightful than great joy—joy that arises from the expenditure of much wealth and effort. || 26 ||
Having spoken these words, which were consistent with righteousness and purpose,
the righteous and highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, lord of sages, became silent.
He concludes the sage’s statement with the words: "Thus, in this way. (27)

Having heard the words of the eminent sage, that man of great majesty remained silent, unable to speak a fitting reply; for one does not find satisfaction except through speech endowed with sound reasoning.
And the world, its desires fulfilled, becomes wise. || 28 ||

That action in which there are words that are logically consistent (*yuktiyukta*) and established as fit for expression—that is what is meant by "thus. One might object: "Why bother considering logical consistency? It can simply be said. To this he replies: "The wise one" (*dhīmān*). For while the world is satisfied even by the fulfillment of its desires, the wise person is not satisfied even when those desires are fulfilled unless it is accompanied by a discourse consistent with reason.
The meaning is that he is pleased by reflection on what is logical and well-founded. || 28 ||
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Words of Viśvāmitra," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vālmīki’s Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Words of Viśvāmitra," in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eighth Canto.
Vālmīki said:
Having heard those words spoken by Viśvāmitra, that tiger among kings—
For a moment he remained motionless, and then spoke these words with dejection: || 1 ||
Here, out of affection for King Rāma, his unfitness for battle is described;
furthermore, having recognized the strength of Rāvaṇa and the others, his despondency is portrayed. (1)
He is motionless because he has attained a progressively higher state; he is intent upon the previously described state of Rāma, as will be further explained. || 1 ||
This lotus-eyed Rāma is less than sixteen years of age;
I do not see in him the fitness for battle with the rākṣasas.
"His age is slightly less than sixteen years"—this is a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound. The implication is that he does not even possess the fitness for battle, let alone against the Rākṣasas. (2)
"O Lord, I am the master of this full akṣauhiṇī army;
surrounded by it, I shall give battle to the flesh-eaters. (3)
If so, is this effort useless? No; he says "this" [referring to the following]. As for the definition of an *akṣauhiṇī*:

one elephant, one chariot, three horses, and five foot-soldiers constitute a *patti*. Each subsequent unit is tripled by all its constituent parts. [The larger units are: *senāmukha*, *gulma*, *gaṇa*, *vāhinī*, *pṛtanā*, *camū*, and *anīkinī*.
"Ten *akṣauhiṇīs* constitute a *daśākinikya*," thus stated Amarasiṃha himself, summarizing what is well-known from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources. || 3 ||
For these servants are indeed brave, valiant, and skilled in counsel;
here, with bow in hand, I myself shall be their protector at the head of the battle.
In this battle; a protector means a guardian. || 4 ||
Together with these, I shall give battle even to heroes as great as Mahendra, like a lion against rutting elephants.
Even greater than Mahendra are the great ones. || 5 ||
The child Rāma does not know strength and weakness in battles;
other than the inner apartments, no battlefield has ever been seen by him.
Surely, one should simply say "the battlefield was not seen by him"; thus, the qualification "another" (anyā) is redundant.

If that is the case, then it is an avyayībhāva compound meaning "within the city," specifically the inner apartments (antaḥpura). [He was] in the middle of the city for the sake of practicing and playing with weapons:
"He was neither equipped with supreme weapons nor skilled in combat."
He was an expert in the battlefields of millions of brave warriors with their new weapons.
Those weapons which are wielded after being grasped are *śastras*; those which are hurled after being thrown are *astras*.

The connection is that these belong to "tens of millions of heroes on the battlefields. One who knows that is one who knows warfare. The sense is that he possesses no expertise (*vaiśāradya*)—indeed, even knowledge regarding it is far from him. || 7 ||
One should always practice meditation exclusively in flower gardens, city parks, and in the groves and bowers of pleasure gardens.

"Thorough cultivation" (pariśīlanam). The word "of this" (asya) is to be supplied [as the object]. However, in the masculine reading, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose cultivation is limited" (parimitaṃ śīlanam asya). || 8 ||
He knows how to sport together with the princes upon his own courtyard grounds, which are strewn with offerings of flowers.
In which [courtyards], offerings consisting of strewn flowers were the very worship; in their own, that is, their private, courtyards and quadrangles. || 9 ||
"O Brahmin, today, due to the reversal of my fortune, he has become exceedingly pale and emaciated, like a lotus-colored deer turned white by frost. (10)
The word *atitarām* (exceedingly) is connected with both the word ending in the fifth case (*atitarām*) and with the words *hariṇaḥ* (tawny/pale) and *kṛśaḥ* (emaciated).

*Hariṇaḥ* means pale. In this regard, there is an illustration: "shining like a lotus" (*padmābhaḥ*), meaning having the appearance of a lotus; the suffix *ka* is applied here according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. He [is] like frost, that is, like snow (*tuṣāra*). || 10 ||
Unable to recognize himself nor to move about his home grounds, his soul overwhelmed by inner anguish, he remains merely silent. (11)
"To dwell" means to move about; it does not mean "to play," because that would result in the verb becoming intransitive. || 11 ||
O leader of sages, for his sake, I, along with my wife and servants, have surely become as devoid of essence as a cloud in autumn. (12)
"Caused by that" means having that as its cause; [it refers to] essencelessness, a lack of enthusiasm and strength, or a lack of happiness. || 12 ||
"Such is this young son of mine, now overcome by mental anguish;
how can I give him to you to fight with the night-stalkers? (13)

By describing him as "of such a form" (referring to his body), "a child" (referring to his age), and "overpowered by mental anguish" (referring to his intellect and so forth), his incapacity and his unworthiness for being sent on this mission are demonstrated. Furthermore, the implication is that it is especially improper for him even to fight, let alone with the night-stalkers. || 13 ||

O virtuous one of great intelligence, the affection for a son leads to true happiness even more than association with young women, even more than the essence of nectar, and even more than sovereignty.
Anticipating the objection, "Surely for you who desire dharma, what is the use of that son-love which is its opposite? he says, "Even" (api).
The meaning is that the fruits of dharma are indeed the aforementioned pleasures, and those do not exceed the pleasure derived from a son. || 14 ||
Those things which have miserable endings, involve great undertakings, and cause exhaustion in the three worlds—even the virtuous perform them without doubt out of affection for their sons. (15)
Even those who are virtuous and righteous find that the hardships of asceticism are far-reaching and difficult to accomplish over a long period. 15.
O tiger among sages, men may renounce their vital fluids, wealth, wives, and even happiness for the sake of pleasure; yet they do not renounce a son, for such is the inherent nature of living beings.
"pleasure is abandoned"—this is the consequence [of the teaching] through the perspective of transformation (vipariṇāma). || 16 ||
The Rākṣasas were performers of cruel deeds and experts in treacherous warfare;
Rama fought them in this manner, for such a stratagem alone was exceedingly difficult to withstand.
In this manner, Rāma remained as previously described; or, "in this manner" means by such a reasoning. || 17 ||
For, being employed by Rāma, I cannot endure to live for even a moment;
though I desire life, you ought not to lead me away to Rāma. (18)

He says in four verses beginning with "viprayukta" that if Rāma were sent away, the destruction of the Rākṣasas would not be possible; on the contrary, it would result in my own death along with my son. Furthermore, the implication is that in comparison to the duty of sacrifice (*yajñadharma*), you would incur a great unrighteousness (*adharma*). || 18 ||
"O Kauśika, nine thousand years have passed since my birth;
these four sons were produced by me with great hardship. (19)

[Objection: But was it not stated in the earlier *Rāmāyaṇa* that "O Kauśika, sixty thousand years have passed since I was born"? How then can this [statement] be said without contradicting that? [Reply: True. Therefore, the syntactical connection is not to be understood literally; rather, four sons were produced by means of the Aśvamedha and Putreṣṭi sacrifices, which are difficult to accomplish even over nine years. || 19 ||
Among them, the lotus-eyed Rāma is the preeminent one;
without him, the other three cannot sustain their lives here.
Among them, Rāma alone is the principal one, just as the vital breath (prāṇa) is among the bodies; for this very reason, he is their most beloved.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Without him... (verse 20).
That very Rāma is being led by you toward the Rākṣasas;
if that be so, know me to be as good as dead this instant, deprived of my son. (21)

The meaning is: "He by whose glance the deaths of the other three occurred—that very Rāma, who is like Death itself, is being led against the rākṣasas; therefore, you must consider me as already dead, for I am now deprived of all four. || 21 ||
Indeed, my supreme affection for my four sons lies in this very [Rāma];
therefore, you ought not to take away Rāma, who is the eldest and composed of dharma.

What need is there to speak of the death of four? Intending to show that even the mere sight of Rāma was sufficient to bring about his own death, he says, "of four. It is "consisting of dharma," meaning abundant in righteousness. || 22 ||
O Sage, if it is your desire to destroy the army of the night-stalkers,
take with you my force, fully equipped with its four divisions.
If I do not take Rāma, then how can there be success in this matter? To this he says: "niśācara... etc.
The fourfold army (*caturaṅgabalam*) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. || 23 ||
What is the prowess of those Rākṣasas? Whose sons are they, and how did they come to be? What is their size, and who are they? Describe these clearly to me. (24)
Thinking that one should not attack without full knowledge, he who desires to know the enemy's strength asks: "What is their vigor?
The remainder of the question is: "And how do they behave? "What is their measure? in terms of number and size. And "who are they" by name? (24)
O Brahmin, how should Rāma act toward those demons who fight with deceit—whether by means of my young children or by me? (25)
It must be performed, it must be countered; if the reading is "it must be struck," the meaning is clear. || 25 ||
"Tell me everything, O Blessed One, regarding how those of ill fortune must stand in the great battle, for the Rākṣasas are indeed arrogant in their prowess. (26)
They are exalted by their vigor and are indeed renowned for their power. || 26 ||
For it is heard that there is a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa of great prowess,
the brother of Vaiśravaṇa himself and the son of the sage Viśravas.
He clarifies that very point: "It is heard," etc. (27).
If that evil-minded one indeed creates an obstacle to your sacrifice, then we shall not be able to withstand him in battle, O evil-souled one. (28)
The word *kila* expresses probability; it is to be construed with "if he should say. Then, in that case... [28]
O Brahmin, from time to time, beings possessing great power and prosperity attain their rise among other creatures, and they dissolve again through the power of Time.
To explain why that is so, he says: "In time" (kāle). "Separately" (pṛthak) means according to a fixed rule, such as occurring only at certain times or in certain places.
"Vīryāṇi vibhūtayaśca" (powers and manifestations) is a karmadhāraya compound containing a dvandva within it. || 29 ||
But now, at this time, we are not capable of standing before our enemies, Rāvaṇa and the others; such is the certainty of destiny.

He asks what follows from that, and answers with the word "now" (adya). The intention is that they were not capable even then, and are all the more so now at this time. [This refers to] destiny (niyati), which is to say, fate (daiva) or God (īśvara). || 30 ||
Therefore, O knower of dharma, show favor toward my little son;
for you are indeed the supreme deity for me, who am of such meager fortune. (31)
That son, my dear child, is to be pitied; for he is incapable of fulfilling the desires of those who seek him, being but a mere infant.
Neither gods, nor dānavas, nor gandharvas, nor yakṣas, nor birds, nor serpents are able to fight Rāvaṇa in battle—how much less can mere men? (32)
To the question, "Whence indeed does such misfortune come to you?", he says: "O God. By "men" (puruṣāḥ), human beings are meant. || 32 ||
In battle, the Rākṣasa assumes the prowess of those possessed of great heroism;
therefore, we were not able to withstand him in combat with our children. (33)

The Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa seizes or, as it were, robs even the great and most worshipful ones, such as Indra and others, of their prowess—this being understood in the context of fighting in battle. Regarding him with whom we were not capable [of contending], what can be accomplished by his children? Or rather, even together with his children, such as Indrajit and the rest.
"We were not capable," this is to be connected with the preceding [verse]. || 33 ||
This is yet another time that makes the virtuous appear weak;
for even Rāghava has fallen into a state of wretchedness, worn down by old age.
He states another reason for his inability with the words "this" (ayam): he is one by whom the virtuous have been made "pelavīkṛta," that is, rendered weak.
Rāghava himself is worn out and frail due to old age; or rather, Rāghava—namely Rāma—is himself the carpenter (*vardhaka*), and he alone is the one who is worn out (*jarjara*). 34.
Or rather, O Brahmin, I shall not release that son of Madhu, who is like a salt-mine, a destroyer of sacrifice, and resembling an asura. (35)

The word "athavā" (or) indicates an alternative view. The phrase "jajñaghnaṃ tava" (the slayer of your son) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The phrase "kathayatu bhavān" (may you tell) is the ellipsis.

He is "asuraprakhya" (resembling an asura) because he was born from a demoness; yet, because he cannot be conquered by the power of Śiva’s trident and because he is the cause of Māndhātṛ’s death, the word "naiva" (not at all) is used for emphasis. || 35 ||
Furthermore, the two sons of Sunda and Upasunda are like the son of Vivasvat;
they cause obstacles to sacrifices. Tell me this, and I shall not give you my son.
Or rather, the word "athavā" (or) is supplied [from the previous verse]. Mārīca and Subāhu were the two sons of Sunda and Upasunda. || 36 ||
If you do not lead me away, O Brahmin, then I am truly slain by you;
otherwise, I see no eternal victory for myself. (37)

If you think, "Even though he has not been given [to me], I shall certainly take Rāma by the power of my asceticism," to that he says: "Now" (atha), etc. "By you" (te) means by you. "Then" (tat) refers to the aforementioned manner. The genitive case is used because the agent alone is intended to be expressed as the residual factor (*śeṣa*). The particle "eva" (certainly) is for the purpose of excluding the Rākṣasa. Otherwise, it would mean "without dying. "Śāśvatam" means certain. || 37 ||
Having spoken these gentle words, that scion of Raghu remained submerged for a moment in the surging waves of doubt regarding the sages' doctrines;
the high-souled one could not find certainty even for an instant.
He was bewildered like one tossed upon the waves of the ocean. || 38 ||

That descendant of Raghu, Daśaratha, was for a moment as if submerged in a turbulent mass of great waves consisting of doubts— such as whether the sage’s desired mission of sending Rāma and slaying the Rākṣasa should be undertaken or not, and whether it would succeed or fail— and thus he could not even ascertain a firm decision. For he was like one in a surging ocean.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "he became as if bewildered. || 38 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Speech of Daśaratha," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Speech of Daśaratha," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa.
The Ninth Canto.
Vālmīki said:
Having heard those words of his, [Rāma’s] eyes were overwhelmed with affection.
The wrathful Kauśika replied with these words to the lord of the earth.
In this [section], the anger of Viśvāmitra is described through words regarding the power of that asceticism,
as well as the gradual pacification of the king by Vasiṣṭha.
The meaning is: having heard that speech which was characterized by eyes whose vision was simultaneously agitated and overwhelmed with affection. || 1 ||
Having promised "I shall do it," you ought not to abandon your vow;
having become a lion, you now desire the state of a deer.
"Having heard" means having accepted. "He," meaning the well-known Bhāvan, the venerable one—"you"—is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
otherwise, the two second-person forms would be untenable. || 2 ||
This reversal of fortune for this lineage of the Raghavas is unworthy;
never indeed do hot rays arise from the cool-rayed moon.

This perversion of the lineage of the Raghavas, characterized by the speaking of falsehood, is improper. He supports that very point through the method of negative instance (*vyatireka*) with the word "not" (na). || 3 ||
If you are not able [to grant my request], O King, I shall go back the way I came.
O descendant of Kakutstha, you who have failed in your promise, may you be happy along with your kinsmen.
Not capable, not able. || 4 ||
Vālmīki said: Then, when the great-souled Viśvāmitra was thus overcome with anger,
the entire earth trembled and fear entered the gods.

"Enveloped" means pervaded. "In the Great-Souled One" refers to him who possesses the majesty of ascetic power (*tapas*). Because her husband was at fault, she herself became an offender; thus, fear entered the gods: "Through her asceticism, she will create a slayer of Rāvaṇa and others, and he will conquer even us"—the word "and" (*ca*) implies that he will conquer others as well. || 5 ||
Perceiving that the Great Sage, the friend of the world, was overcome by anger, the wise Vasiṣṭha, firm in his vows and possessed of fortitude, spoke these words.

"Jaganmitra" means "friend of the universe. Alternatively, "Viśvāmitra" means "friend of all," as is well known from the etymological significance of that name, according to the rule *mitre carṣau* which lengthens the vowel of the preceding word. Although Vasiṣṭha was also capable of countering that anger through his own wrath, he nevertheless did not [do so].
He became enraged; for the sense is that he possessed fortitude and other such qualities. || 6 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
You, the illustrious Daśaratha, born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, are like another Dharma incarnate, adorned with the virtues of the three worlds. (7)
He is adorned with all those qualities that are renowned among the virtuous throughout the three worlds.
