Becoming steadfast and firm in your vows, you ought not to abandon dharma;
you are renowned throughout the three worlds, endowed with righteousness and glory. (8)

The meaning is that he remained for all this time one whose vow was the observance of his promise, and who was thus distinguished; the words *bhavat* (you) and the second person are as before. He was endowed with righteousness and glory, and was renowned throughout the three worlds. || 8 ||
"Adhere to your own duty; you ought not to abandon dharma. You should carry out the word of the sage, the lord of the three worlds. (9)

"Observe the duty of fulfilling one's promises toward oneself and one's own people! Having made a solemn vow before the three worlds, 'I shall do it,' O King, you who now fail to perform that for him—
therefore, release Rāma, lest he take away your merit consisting of sacrifices and charitable works."
The syntactical connection is: "he should take that. || 10 ||
Even though you were born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku and are yourself Daśaratha, if you do not uphold his word, who else will? (11)

According to the maxim that "as is the conduct of kings, so indeed is the conduct of the subjects," you maintain the boundaries of the people; yet, if you were to act untruthfully, you would cause them to become untruthful as well. || 11 ||
Sentient beings do not abandon the boundaries established by the conventions set forth by you and others; therefore, you ought not to forsake them. (12)
By means of that which is sublime and set in motion, even ignorant beings who are like mere creatures [attain their goal]. 12.
Guarded by that lion among men as nectar is by fire,
the Rākṣasas will not be able to overcome him, whether he has mastered the divine weapons or not.
By Viśvāmitra, that lion among men, the best of men. "By fire" means it is well known that the nectar situated in Indra’s abode is protected on all sides by a fire acting as a rampart.
"Having mastered the weapons" means he has been trained in the use of missiles. The ellipsis is to be supplied: "they will not be able to overcome him. || 13 ||
He is Dharma incarnate; he is the best among the valiant;
he is preeminent in wisdom in this world and the ultimate refuge of asceticism.
In order to establish the point already stated, he elaborates upon the power of Viśvāmitra with the words "This one" (eṣa). His supreme *ayana* is his abode. || 14 ||
He knows every kind of weapon in the three worlds, among all things moving and stationary;
no other man knows these, nor shall anyone ever know them.
The ellipsis is "it is well known" regarding the moving and the unmoving; or, it connects with the subsequent clause: "no one else knows [this] among the moving and the unmoving. || 15 ||
Neither gods nor any sages, nor asuras, nor rākṣasas, nor nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas, even when assembled together, are equal to the sage. (16)
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "they are not equal in power. If it is asked, "How can this be consistent,

since it is impossible for even each of the great sages such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Agastya, or the gods such as Brahmā and others, to have less power?"— if that is so, then from the perspective of ultimate reality (tattvadṛśā), this...

There is no fault [in our position], for this statement was made with reference to the state of being Brahman as a conceited, limited state belonging to others. Furthermore, they do not possess similarity even to the state of being Brahman; because in that [state of Brahman] there is an absence of difference, that [similarity] which is constituted by difference is impossible there. And thus says the Śruti: "Neither the gods nor [the asuras were able to surpass] him, for he is not subject to non-existence (abhūti)."
"For he indeed rules over them; thus he becomes [their master]. || 16 ||
In former times, when he had attained the kingdom, Kṛśāśva gave this weapon— which was extremely difficult for enemies to conquer— to Kauśika.
The ellipsis is "produced by Dṛśāśva. The ellipsis is "given by Rudra, who was gratified by his ascetic penance.
This is well known from the earlier Rāmāyaṇa. || 17 ||
For those sons of Kṛśāśva, resembling the sons of Prajāpati—
heroes, radiant and of great prowess— followed after him.
They are the deities of the missiles (astradevas). Rudra, the son of Prajāpati, is their counterpart in the act of destruction. "Vīra" means those who are valiant;

"ojas" refers to the power capable of conquering enemies. Because Viśvāmitra had brought them under his control through the power of his asceticism (tapas), they followed him and served him like attendants. The past tense is not intended here [the action is understood as continuous]. || 18 ||
Jayā and Suprabhā were the two slender-waisted daughters of Dakṣa;
their offspring numbered one hundred and were exceedingly invincible.
He names the principal ones among them with the words beginning "Jaya" and so forth. The two Dākṣāyaṇīs are the daughters of Dakṣa. || 19 ||
In former times, Jayā, having obtained a boon, gave birth to fifty sons for the purpose of slaying the armies of the gods; they were capable and able to move at will.

He shows them by dividing [the list], saying "fifty. The phrase "having obtained boons" is to be understood as "by means of service to their husbands. In the expression "of the divine armies," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent; therefore, by virtue of their fitness, the slaying of the asuras alone is obtained. || 20 ||
Suprabhā gave birth to another fifty sons named Saṃgharṣas, who were invincible, of formidable appearance, and exceedingly powerful.
Because they are habituated to overcoming the weapons of others through their competitive spirit, they are called by that name; they are of ill appearance and fierce countenance.
Such a man of great vigor and immense splendor is Viśvāmitra, the sage of the world.
You ought not to allow your resolve regarding the journey to Rāma to become despondent.

The sage perceives the entire world through the power of yoga and, being of such a nature, beholds it directly; therefore, the sense is that since he has already seen even Rāma’s future victory as it were before him, it is not appropriate for his intellect to be distressed. || 22 ||

While this most eminent of Great Beings, the Lord of Sages, stands nearby, even though death has arrived for this virtuous man, he attains immortality; therefore, do not fall into despondency like one who is utterly deluded. (23)
Strengthening that very point, he says: "In this... *Sattva* means power.
Even for a common person (*puruṣa*), he attains immortality—by implication, that person does.
And thus, even for a common person, merely by being in its proximity, [he attains] even from what has been obtained... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
On the contrary, there is no fear of death; rather, there is the attainment of immortality. Since he is protected by that Rāma of great power, fear of insignificant rākṣasas is utterly impossible;
therefore, do not despair like a fool—this is the meaning. || 23 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Consolation by Vasiṣṭha," in the *Vairāgya-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Consolation by Vasiṣṭha," in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgya-prakaraṇa*) within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Tenth Canto.
Vālmīki said:
While Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus, King Daśaratha addressed his son.
With a heart full of joy, he summoned Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Dispatched there by the king, Yāṣṭīka went, learned of Rāma’s conduct,
and having returned, reported everything in full to the king.

"So be it. Because the fruit of the speech—namely, the joy—is directed toward another, the root *brū* takes the *parasmaipada* (active voice). The present participle (*śatṛ*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetau*). || 1 ||
Daśaratha said: "O doorkeeper, bring quickly and without hindrance the mighty-armed Rāma, whose prowess is truth, together with Lakṣmaṇa, for the sake of the auspicious rite."

"Without hindrance" means for the sake of merit, or for the sake of the sage’s sacrifice being accomplished free from obstacles; alternatively, it was said with the intention that his word might not prove false. This very point is also illuminated by the word "swiftly. || 2 ||
Thus dismissed by the king, he went to the inner apartments and,
returning in just a moment, spoke to the lord of the earth.
He was sent forth, dispatched; [he went] to Rāma’s palace situated within the inner apartments. || 3 ||
O King, Rāma, who had crushed all his enemies with his arms, remained dejected in his palace at night,
like a bee within a lotus.
Dejected, with a despondent mind. || 4 ||
"I shall come in a moment," he says, yet he meditates all alone;
with a weary mind, he does not wish to remain in the presence of anyone. (5)
A *kṣaṇa* is the latter part of a *ghaṭikā*. The word "on one side" (*ekataḥ*) is also connected with the verb "speaks.
The sense is that speaking is merely by way of words and not preceded by [the intention of] the mind; for his primary activity is indeed meditating. || 5 ||
Thus addressed by him, the king consoled all those followers of Rāma and questioned them in due order.
She comforted those followers of Rāma who had arrived with the doorkeeper to announce Rāma’s conduct, lest they fail to report it properly due to being unassured.
When asked by the king, "What is Rāma like? Of what nature is he?", the dejected servants of Rāma spoke these words to the lord of the earth: (7)
One question concerns action; the other concerns states such as emaciation and despair. || 7 ||
O Lord,
maintaining this very same outlook toward your son Rāma, whose body is now withered by exhaustion, we too are weary and dejected.

Her body, as slender as a sacrificial staff, was like a mere frame; she was exhausted and distressed. The sense is: if even those who merely behold her experience such exhaustion and emaciation, what need is there to speak of her own state? (8)
Ever since Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals,
arrived from his pilgrimage with the brahmin, he has been dejected in spirit.

*Rājīva* means a lotus. Since the word *āgataḥ* ("having come") is understood from the context— because it is established by the phrase "from which day he came and stayed"— the mention of "staying" (*sthitaḥ*) is indeed necessary as an additional qualification,
just like "dejection," because staying occurs daily.
Despite our diligent entreaties, this very person—
whose face remains unfaded [even at evening]— performs or does not perform his own daily duties.
"Daily routine" (āhnika) refers to one's own activities such as eating and so forth. The phrase "or does not perform" is used to indicate a lack of concern or disregard. || 10 ||
Dejected during bathing, worship of the gods, giving gifts, eating, and other such activities,
the Lord does not eat even when requested, for he is never satiated.
The analysis [of the compound] is either "deva-arcana and dāna" (worship of the gods and giving), or "deva-arcana and ādāna" (worship of the gods and taking). || 11 ||
In the courtyard, he does not sport in playful diversions with the amorous women of his inner apartments who have set up swings,
just as a cātaka bird does not delight in showers of rain.
The phrase "with women" is to be understood as the ellipsis. A *dolā* is a swing. *Aṅgaṇe* means in the courtyard or play-area.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that he does not sport in the same manner as a *cātaka* bird, which sports while enjoying those showers together with the rain-drops. || 12 ||
O King, the series of armlets and bracelets set with ruby buds does not delight him as much as the sky delights the earth when it descends within his reach.

The sky is sewn and inlaid with rubies shaped like buds. The heaven is near the range of sight. In the vine-circled houses, amidst the breezes carrying flowers during the glances of sporting women, he becomes exceedingly despondent. (14)

Alternatively, there is a word-division (*padabheda*) such that it means "where there are various gazes (*lokāni*) by playful young women (*vadhūbhiḥ*)" as they look on, or "where there are gazes (*lokāḥ*) belonging to playful young women (*vadhūnām*). Or, in a single compound (*ekapadya*), the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "where the flower-breezes (*kusumavāyavaḥ*) blow like arrows (*iṣavaḥ*), which are indeed the glances (*vilokāḥ*) of the sporting young women. The "coiling" (*valayanam*) of the creepers refers to their encircling.
"Valaya" refers to the houses associated with him; that is to say, in the groves. || 14 ||
Whatever substance is appropriate, delicious, delicate, and captivating to the mind—with that very thing, one suffers as if with eyes filled with tears. (15)
"Appropriate for enjoyment," meaning not contrary to worldly custom or sacred scripture; "peśalam," meaning clever; "cittahāri," meaning captivating to the mind.
(15) "Why are these city women, who cause such suffering, manifesting themselves?"—thus he censures the amorous women during their dance performances. (16)

The construction is as follows: having seen them quivering, shining with gestures (*hāva*), expressions (*bhāva*), loveliness (*lāvaṇya*), playful charms (*vilāsa*), and so forth, or dancing—why does one revile them as "givers of suffering"? The reading *prasphūranti* is straightforward. || 16 ||
Like one acting in a state of madness, he does not take delight in blameless food, bedding, vehicles, amusements, bathing, or seats.

The suffix *lyuṭ* in "śayana" (bed) and "āsana" (seat) is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), while others hold it to be used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). It refers to that by which or in which they sport. "Aninditam" means faultless; this qualifies all [the preceding terms]. || 17 ||
"What is prosperity? What is adversity? What is home? What are gestures?
Having declared that "all this is indeed unreal," he remains alone in silence. (18)
By gestures and by desires; unreal and without essence. || 18 ||
He does not engage in jests, he does not sink into enjoyments, nor does he remain occupied with worldly affairs; he maintains only silence. || 19 ||
He rises up and rejoices; he sinks down and clings; he does not persist in undertakings or tasks, nor does he apply himself to them with resolve.
Women with creeper-like tresses waving and eyes rolling in playfulness do not delight him, just as does a doe a tree in the forest. (20)

Those [women] whose locks of hair possessed dangling clusters of flowers, jewels, and the like; their playful gestures (*helā*) were movements born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). In the case of the female deer, the flower-clusters were like their locks of hair. Their eyes were flickering, moving as if with playfulness (*helā*). (20)
In solitary places, at the ends of the quarters, on riverbanks, and in forests,
he finds delight in the wilderness as if among creatures for sale.

In the forests, that is, in the woods; among creatures, that is, among common folk who are like mere animals; just as a man sold by fate finds pleasure only in solitary places and the like, so it is here. || 21 ||
By that very disposition of turning away from the giving of clothing, drink, and food,
he followed after the ascetic king who lived according to the dharma of a wandering mendicant.
By that well-known [fact], it follows and imitates the very state of the wandering mendicants (parivrāja), such as their possession of qualities like non-attachment and so forth. || 22 ||
O Lord of Men, dwelling all alone in a region devoid of people, he neither laughs with his singular intellect, nor sings, nor weeps. (23)
By the one, which is the primary. || 23 ||
Seated in the bound lotus posture with a mind empty of thought, he remains alone, resting his cheek upon the palm of his left hand.

To the question of what he does there, he says: "bound" (baddha). He whose mind is fixed upon the ultimate reality (paramārtha) as its object remains established; the sense of "meditating" (dhyāyan) is understood by implication. || 24 ||
He does not harbor pride, nor does he desire sovereignty;
he neither rises nor sets amidst the fluctuations of pleasure and pain.
In this world, rising and setting are but joy and dejection; the persistence of pleasure and pain is merely the pursuit of the desirable and the undesirable.
We do not know: where does he go? What does he do? What does he strive for? What does he contemplate? Whence does he come? And how, and why, does he run after things? || 26 ||
He strives; he desires. He pursues; he follows after. || 26 ||
Day by day he grows thin; day by day he turns pale;
day by day he falls into despondency, like a tree at the end of autumn. (27)
*Virāga* means dispassion (*vairāgya*). In the case of a tree, it refers to discoloration, that is to say, the state of being discolored. || 27 ||
O King, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa followed him in exactly the same manner;
they stood there like his very own reflections.
"Anuyātau" means followed out of affection; by implication, it is understood that they followed Rāma. "Tādṛśau eva" means exactly like him—just as Rāma was. || 28 ||
Although questioned again and again by his servants, kings, and mothers,
he said nothing at all and remained silent, devoid of desire.

Rāma’s intention was that because they said "nothing," there was nothing at all that could be used as a defense. He remained "motionless," meaning devoid of any physical gesture that might reveal his inner thoughts. || 29 ||
"Do not set your mind upon enjoyments that are pleasing only at first sight"—thus [spoke] the virtuous friend standing by his side. (30)
"Āpāta" means falling upon; it is the contact between the sense objects and the senses. By the word "mātra," the bitterness of transformation (pariṇāma) is indicated.
One who "becomes" [thus] is a "bhavya"—one possessed of discernment—but not everyone. (30)
Amidst women delightful with various luxuries and in social gatherings,
one who lacks affection perceives only destruction, as if it were standing right before him.
A social gathering is a place for pleasure. || 31 ||
"Life has been spent through activities devoid of attaining the state free from exertion"—thus he sings again and again in a faltering tone. (32)
"By men devoid of attainment, through activities directed toward external objects—it is implied—that [life] has been spent in vain.

Alternatively, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between 'by activities devoid of attainment' and the subject; in this case, it is implied that 'it was spent by me. [He spoke] with a *kākali* voice—a sweet yet indistinct speech. (32)
To his attendant who stood by him and said, "Become an emperor," the sage laughed with a distracted mind, as if at one who was prattling like a madman. (33)

"One who has performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, who is the lord of the circle [of kings], and who rules by the command of the king—he is a *samrāṭ*. Regarding the phrase "with a mind elsewhere": it means one whose mind is fixed on another object, such as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is called *samrāṭ* because it shines forth perfectly by its own nature. Because of his lack of full realization, the sage reflects upon that.
She does not listen when something is spoken, nor does she look at what is before her;
she shows contempt everywhere, even toward objects that are most excellent.
Having thoroughly examined every object according to its qualities and its results, he finds that even though he has attained what is excellent and suited to him—
even in the sky-lotus or the great forest of the sky—
no wonder arises in his mind regarding this matter. (35)

Now, one might object: "Is it not appropriate to feel wonder at an object that is worthy of wonder due to the excellence of its qualities and so forth? How then can there be contempt toward it? To this he replies with the word "api" (even). That very mind in which there might be wonder directed toward external objects is itself thus [disregarded]. The meaning is: such a mind is the locus of such wonder. How so? Because it is of the nature of space, or resides in space.
"In the great forest" means "similar to such a lotus pond"—this is the ellipsis.

The two words "doubt" (*dvi*) indicate the two-fold impossibility. Just as a forest in the sky and a lotus pond in a forest are utterly impossible, so too is wonder (*vismaya*) in the Self and the mind in the mental faculty.
The meaning is that, due to this certainty, no wonder arises in him regarding external objects. || 35 ||
Even when situated in the midst of beloved women, his mind— difficult to pierce like a massive rock— is not pierced by the arrows of Love, just as a great stone is not split by torrents of water.
They do not cause division nor do they split; [the suffix] ṇic is used in the sense of commissioning or attribution. "Dhārā" refers to streams of water. || 36 ||
"Do you desire wealth as the sole refuge in times of misfortune?"— having thus instructed him, he bestows his entire possession upon the petitioner.
"Āvāsam" means a dwelling place; "arthine" means to a petitioner. || 37 ||
"This is adversity, this is prosperity"—such is the delusion born of mental construction that has arisen in the mind; thus he sings these verses. (38)
"Consisting of conceptualization" means abundant with conceptualization; "delusion" means error. || 38 ||
"Alas! I am ruined! I am helpless!"—even while crying out thus, people do not attain detachment; rather, they simply say, "How strange this is! (39).

"Devoted to lamentation"—the ellipsis is "due to separation from what is dear. Thus, the intended meaning is that even though he perceives, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that suffering arises from passion and the like. (39)
While Rāma, the slayer of enemies and a great śāla tree in the forest of the Raghus, remains in this state, we have come to extreme distress. (40)
By the term *raghupāda*, the Raghu dynasty is indicated. *Śāla* is a well-known species of tree. The particle *eva* (only/just) serves to exclude other causes. || 40 ||
"O mighty-armed one, O lotus-petal-eyed one, we do not know what we should do for him whose mind is in such a state; for you alone are our refuge in this matter. (41)
"What shall we do for the sake of dispelling our grief?"—this is the ellipsis. || 41 ||
O Lord, he laughs at the king or the Brahmin who stands before him as his instructor, as if they were ignorant, remaining unperturbed and treating them with contempt.

"Surely, let his delusion be removed by those learned in ethics through instruction on worldly conduct? To this he replies with the verse beginning "The king... (rājānam iti). The ellipsis to be supplied is "the instructor [in] the practices of royal policy. He disregards [them], thinking: "That which has arisen, this vast thing called the world," and so forth.
Having reached the firm conclusion that "this is not a real entity, nor am I," he remained established [in that state]. || 43 ||

"It goes" (*yāti*) means that which is subject to motion; the sense is that it is perishable. "This, this"—referring to the manifold variety perceivable by external vision—is expansive and extensive. That which "dwells" (*vasati*) is a reality (*vastu*) that is eternally of one form. And as for that which is perceived by the intellect as "I," having determined that it is not such a reality but rather of an entirely different nature, one who desires to know it [proceeds].
He remained established. || 43 ||
O Lord, you have no attachment to women, nor to yourself, nor to friends, nor to the kingdom, nor to your mother;
you have no attachment to prosperity or adversity, nor to anything external.

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*), there are five locative cases; regarding the object itself, when its status as a cause is intended to be expressed, there are two instrumental cases. The preceding elaboration is merely an expansion of what was stated in general terms by the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*). || 44 ||
He is free from attachment, free from hope, free from desire, and without support;
he is neither deluded nor liberated—because of this, we are tormented exceedingly.

The distinction between *āsthā* (reliance) and *āśaya* (inclination) lies in their respective objects being dependent on self or others. Because there is no such distinction [in his case], he is free from effort (*nirīha*) and free from desire (*niriccha*). If one asks, "Even if there is no external object, how can he be suffering since the cause of suffering is absent?"—to this he replies: "He is without support" (*nirāspada*). This means that his rest is established in the immutable Self. He is not deluded, because he possesses discernment (*viveka*). Nor is he...
The liberated [state] does not arise because of the non-arising of repose. || 45 ||
"What is the use of wealth? What is the use of mothers? What is the use of a kingdom? What is the use of worldly striving?
Thinking thus within himself, he remained intent on giving up his life.

"Intent on giving up his life": the sense is that since defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like are themselves the seeds of birth, he thought that for one devoid of them, liberation would be achieved simply through the departure of the vital breaths; such was his intention. || 46 ||
He fell into extreme distress regarding his wealth, life-span, kingdom, friends, father, and mother, like a cātaka bird during a drought. || 47 ||
In the case of *avagraha*, which is the obstruction of rain. || 47 ||
Thus, may he who is devoted to compassion arise to completely uproot this calamity that has descended upon his offspring, spreading like a branching creeper. 48.
[She is] "tokeputre" (rich in offspring), meaning she is extensive and abounding through the spreading and expansion of branches such as the Cindā and Kārśya.

[The word] "āpallatām" [is derived from] "āpatti"; due to its archaic nature (ārṣatva), there is an elision of the letter *l*. Alternatively, it is "āpadyate," thus "āpat," meaning the state of having fallen into [calamity]. Or rather, the division is "āpat tām. Thus, [the compound] "toke āpat" is formed with the words separated.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: the preceding words ending in the accusative case are qualifiers of the word "tām" (her). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "May you exert yourself fully (*samudetu*)—that is, may you strive thoroughly—to uplift, meaning to uproot her. || 48 ||
O Lord, for one whose nature is such, the expansive web of saṃsāra, though endowed with all its splendors, acts as a counter-poison.
"Ābhogi" means possessing a fabricated appearance; "veṣa" refers to a fabricated display. "Prativiṣāyate" means it behaves like a counter-poison (pratikūla-viṣa). || 49 ||
Who indeed on this earth could be such a great being, capable of establishing him in this worldly affair? (50)

Who indeed could be such a great being, possessed of such great power, as to be capable of bringing one who has become thus into the natural course of worldly affairs? The meaning is: no one at all. The particle *eva* is an expletive.
Alternatively, the ellipsis is "except for you"; the sense is that only one who is like you would be capable of this. || 50 ||

Having cast aside delusion from his mind, the high-minded one indeed brings all suffering and darkness to the state of goodness and fruitfulness; just as the sun, dispelling the gloom upon the earth, attains its true nature as the maker of day.
Since darkness, characterized by distress, obstructs discernment, he who— having dispelled all such delusion from Rāma’s mind—
brings his own goodness, namely his capacity for instruction, to fruition regarding this very Rāma; he...
The connection with the preceding is: "Who indeed could be such a high-minded person? In that regard, there is an illustration:
"it leads, in the same way. (51)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Despair of Rāghava," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Despair of Rāghava," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The eleventh canto.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O highly wise ones, if it be so, then you [should honor] the descendant of Raghu."
Let them bring him here swiftly, as deer do a deer.
By the command of Viśvāmitra, Rāma was brought into the assembly hall;
therein is described the king’s consolation and his inquiry regarding the seed-syllables of the Ādhyātma and other systems.

If, in the manner thus described, you are weary, distressed, and deluded regarding this matter—O highly wise ones, skilled in investigation—[consider] the deer, the leader of the herd; by "deer" are meant those animals that follow him. This delusion of the Lord of the Raghus arises neither from calamities nor from passion.
For one possessed of discernment and dispassion, awakening itself is the great exaltation.

That state of dullness which arises from calamities or from passion is indeed delusion (*moha*). However, this [state] belongs to one possessed of discernment and so forth, and because it has awakening as its fruit, it is indeed awakening; the meaning is that it is truly a great exaltation. || 2 ||
"May Rāma come here in an instant, and may we also be here in an instant;
we shall dispel his delusion just as the wind scatters a thick cloud from a mountain. (3)

The two words *kṣaṇa* and *śabda* mean "swiftly. The connection [in the verse] is with the phrase "right here" (*ihaiva ca*). The second occurrence of the word *iha* is intended to indicate that the removal of delusion occurs at the very place of arrival. *Ghana* means a cloud. || 3 ||
When this delusion has been skillfully wiped away, that joy of the Raghus will find rest in that supreme state, just as we have.

Now, one might ask: even when delusion has been removed, what is the accomplishment of that? To this he says: "In this... [verse 4]. When that has arrived—that is, in one's own self, which is the supreme state of Viṣṇu well-known from the scripture, "That is the supreme state of Viṣṇu"—[one attains it].
He will attain truthfulness, joy, wisdom, rest, and freedom from affliction;
he will achieve plumpness and a beautiful complexion, as if having drunk nectar.

*Satyatām*: the state of being an uncontradicted reality. *Muditām*: joy; the elision of the *t* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). It means the nature of supreme bliss. *Prajñām*: the nature of undivided knowledge. Alternatively, it may mean that well-known wisdom which arises when there is the manifestation of joy (*mudi*). In the context of drinking nectar (*amṛta*): [the text continues with the description of the nectar].

The meaning is, respectively: the realization of the fruits of dharma as declared by the Vedas; the attainment of happiness in heaven according to reality; and the possession of divine knowledge. [Furthermore, there is] corpulence and a beautiful complexion in the body. (5)
And with a fully satisfied mind, the honorable one will carry out his own traditional course of conduct, unbroken and in accordance with established custom. (6)
[Objection: Since worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is well-known to be rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), its cessation should occur just as a shadow vanishes when the umbrella is removed;
yet that [cessation] is undesirable for living beings. To this, he says: "His own" (*nijām*). "His own" means appropriate to his own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
"Prakṛtām" means commenced or undertaken. Even though his desires are fully satisfied, nevertheless, for one who lives, there remains all worldly activity.

The meaning is that, since worldly activity must necessarily be undertaken because it cannot be abandoned, and since there is no reason to abandon the established practice and adopt another, and because he intends to favor those who follow his own conduct, he will continue to carry out his own uninterrupted lineage of worldly activity. || 6 ||
There will be a Great Being who knows the high and low of the world,
who has transcended pleasure and pain, and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same.
"Surely, by practicing that [meditation], one would become attached to it there; consequently, as before, one would still be subject to states of pleasure and pain.
To this he says: "He will be... *Sattva* is the strength of firmness in knowledge born from reflection and so forth.
*Para* is the causal reality (*kāraṇa-tattva*), and *avara* is the effected reality (*kārya-tattva*). He is one by whom both of these are known in the world. Alternatively:
By whom it is known that for all living beings in the worlds, the supreme— which is the nature of the highest human goal— and the inferior— which consists of worldly objects—

both the supreme unmanifest (avyākṛta) and the inferior known as Hiraṇyagarbha, are in reality none other than Brahman itself and do not exist separately; for this very reason, being free from attachment, he regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
The meaning is that he is devoid of pleasure, pain, and so forth. || 7 ||
When the Lord of Sages had spoken thus, the king, his heart filled with joy,
dispatched a succession of messengers once again to bring Rāma back.
By the use of the word "furthermore" (bhūyas), it is understood that even before Vasiṣṭha’s speech, other messengers besides the doorkeeper had already been dispatched.
After this much time had passed, Rāma rose from his seat in his own home and went into the presence of his father, like the sun rising from the mountain.

Then, immediately after the arrival of the doorkeeper, Rāma rose from his own seat; the connection with the following verse is that in this much time—limited by the conversation with the sage—he went to the place of his father. || 9 ||
Accompanied by a few servants and his two brothers, he went to that meritorious abode of his father, like the lord of the gods to heaven.
It is meritorious because it is frequented by great sages such as Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others. || 10 ||
Then Rāma saw Daśaratha from afar,
surrounded by a multitude of kings like Vāsava by a host of gods.
It was attended on both sides by Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra,
and garlanded by a multitude of ministers who were experts in the meaning of all the scriptures.

Served with endearing, beneficial, and sweet speech, and cherished; they expand and disseminate all the meanings of the scriptures in the world—thus they are "those who have expanded the meaning of all scriptures" (*sarvaśāstrārthatata*).
And those who are wise (*jña*)—[the word *teṣām* follows here, referring to them]—are the ministers; by their assembly (*vṛndena*). 12.
He was attended by beautiful women with lovely chowries in their hands,
standing in their appropriate places like the quarters of the sky personified.
With the quarters, that is, with the directions. || 13 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others, as well as Daśaratha and his kin,
beheld Rāghava from afar as he approached, resembling Guha.
Approaching nearby; Guha is Kārttikeya. || 14 ||
He was resorted to by all who seek his service, like the snowy mountain by the coolness that sustains living beings within its womb— profound yet radiant.
He describes what they saw at that time with five verses beginning with "sattva":

[The mountain] was resorted to like the Himālaya because of its coolness—coolness being the state of being both refreshing through the alleviation of heat and frosty. The four epithets beginning with "sattva" are applied to this very coolness through wordplay (śleṣa).
It is pervaded within by *sattva*—the cause of peace and solitude, the quality of purity, and the multitude of living beings;
it is filled with all things, like the full moon together with its digits, and is fit for being entered;
and it is profound, with an unfathomable interior, yet clear—such is the appropriate connection [of these adjectives]. (15)
Gentle, equanimous, and of auspicious appearance, with a mind noble through discipline, he possessed a lovely and tranquil body, a vessel for the welfare of others. (16)

Gentle and pleasant to behold; with limbs that are even, neither deficient nor redundant; lovely and captivating; tranquil and not fierce; [the means] for the sake of another's goal, namely the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha). 16.
The onset of youth had fully arisen, yet it was graced by the tranquility of the aged;
it was a joy of an undisturbed mind, wherein all desires were as if already fulfilled.

He whose youth has begun with a correct exertion; who is as beautiful as an elder through tranquility; who is undisturbed due to the departure of lack of discernment; and who is without bliss because he has not yet attained supreme bliss. || 17 ||
Having reflected upon the course of the world, which is the sphere of pure qualities, it was as if taken possession of by those very qualities out of a singular longing for the Great Being. (18)

The course of the world is the movement of saṃsāra. It is the domain and object of those with pure qualities, or of persons possessing pure virtues. It is properly resorted to by all qualities through the very greed of great being (mahāsattva). || 18 ||
He was revealing the unsurpassed, noble, and sublime state that fills the hollow of the inner heart, through a state of mental activity that was entirely undisturbed. (19)

[He was] one who, through an undisturbed mode of being and a state of stability, even amidst the perfection of all means of accomplishment, demonstrated and indicated a resting in the awakening to reality; or, "supreme" (anuttama) may be an epithet of Rāma. || 19 ||
Thus filled with a multitude of virtues, the scion of Raghu was visible from afar,
his garments and limbs radiant and pure, adorned with a smile of measured grace.
The descendant of Raghu bowed down; this is the connection with the following verse. "Ambarapallava" means a garment that is like a sprout.
He was one whose own necklace and garment-sprouts were both so pure and white that they seemed to conceal his smile, being themselves limited in measure.
He prostrated with his head, which bore the shimmering rays of a moving and beautiful crest-jewel,
possessing the splendor of a divine mountain swaying upon the trembling earth.
The crest-jewel is the ornament of the head; Devācala is Sumeru. || 21 ||
While the Lord of Sages was speaking thus, the lotus-eyed Rāma then approached to perform the salutation at his father’s feet.

Thus, while the lord of sages Viśvāmitra was speaking in the manner described in the seven verses beginning with the account of creation, Rāma then approached to perform the salutation at his father’s feet; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 22 ||
First [he honored] his father, and afterwards the sages, both of whom were highly respected;
then the brahmins, then his kinsmen, and then the groups of teachers and friends.
The two sages Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra were honored above all even by those worthy of honor; Rāma was their friend, possessing a beautiful heart. || 23 ||
And then he accepted with his gaze, his head slightly bowed,
and his speech that succession of prostrations offered by the circle of kings.
"With the head slightly bowed"—this indicates propriety toward those for whom such humility is appropriate. || 24 ||
Having received blessings from the two sages, Rāma, with a perfectly composed mind and as beautiful as a celestial being, approached the holy presence of his father.
With a perfectly equanimous mind regarding the gain or loss of desired objects. || 25 ||
Then the lord of the earth, intent on venerating his feet,
quickly embraced him upon his head and kissed him again and again.
The phrase "having smelled on the head" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "He embraced him" means he embraced him face-to-face. || 26 ||
Likewise, that slayer of enemy heroes, with deep affection, embraced Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa,
just as a royal swan embraces two lotuses.
"Just as [he kisses] Rāma, so too [he kisses her]; just as a royal swan [kisses] a lotus"—this is the simile for the act of kissing. || 27 ||
Then, as the king was saying, "O son, stay on my lap," he sat down upon a garment spread by his attendants on the ground.
On her lap—that is, on her embrace—upon her garment—that is, her cloth—she sat down. || 28 ||
The king said:
"O son, you have attained discernment and are a vessel for all that is auspicious;
do not subject yourself to distress with an intellect as worn-out as Jada's. (29)

Like one who is dull-witted or lacking discernment; "jīrṇayā" means with one that is worn out or slackened; "khedāya" means for the sake of dejection; "ātmā" refers to the individual soul (jīva). || 29 ||
The meritorious state proclaimed by aged Brahmins and gurus is attained by one such as you who practices accordingly, but not by one who pursues delusion.

By elders such as fathers and others; by gurus, that is, teachers. Because it is the means for accomplishing the duty of protecting one's progeny—[it is said]: "O son, calamities remain far away and exceedingly feeble only so long as no scope is given to delusion. (31)

The meaning is that when not present, they remain at a distance and do not approach; but when present, they become extremely fragile, remaining on all sides as something most insignificant and incapable of performing their function. The meaning is that in the expansion of delusion (*moha*), however, they become the opposite of that. || 31 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O prince of mighty arms, you are a hero; by you these enemies that are the sense-objects—so difficult to sever and so difficult to assail—have been conquered.

You alone are a hero, since you have conquered the enemies that are the sense-objects (*viṣaya*). Well-known enemies are indeed difficult to eradicate, yet they are not undertaken for their own sake; however, the enemies that are the sense-objects are produced by oneself for the sake of another kind of suffering. Why, like one ignorant of this, do you remain in this ocean of delusion which is fit only for the ignorant?
You sink away into that which is full of surging waves and characterized by dullness.

"Even though you are such as this, why do you sink, like one ignorant of that [Reality] and like one ignorant of the Self, into the ocean of delusion which is fit for the ignorant? The 'billows' are the great waves that cause agitation; 'dullness' is the stupor of ignorance, the veil.
Viśvāmitra said:
Tell me, O mind: having abandoned the flickering longing for eyes like a cluster of moving blue lotuses, for what reason do you now become deluded? 34.
Anxieties tear away the mind, just as rats gnaw through a house. || 35 ||

*Ādhi*s are mental afflictions that tear at the mind and cause despondency. "In what is their culmination? means: in which desired object, when fulfilled, do they come to an end? Alternatively, it is a question regarding their essential nature: "What are they based upon? and "What are they? It is a question regarding their cause: "By what [are they produced]? and a question regarding their classification: "How many are they?"
The word "by what cause" (*kāraṇena*) is connected with the word "by what" (*kena*). "Ākhanas" refers to those who dig into a house; that is, mice (*mūṣaka*). || 35 ||
I believe you are not the proper object for improper anxieties;
even lowly worries are useless for you in times of calamity.
"But surely, pledges, causes, and so forth are well-known in the world; why then are they being asked about? To this he says: "I think.

It is true that they are well-known, but you are not the most appropriate or fitting place (pada) for them when they are out of place. One who is in distress or poor would be such a place. And for you, they are useless in times of calamity and incapable of providing a remedy.

It does not exist; for by the power of the father alone, all calamities have been dispelled. Moreover, those mental anxieties were cast off by themselves, because he is full, being endowed with every form of good fortune—this is the intended meaning. || 36 ||
"Speak quickly whatever you desire, O sinless one, and you shall obtain it all; furthermore, by this means, mental afflictions shall no longer pierce you."
"Yathābhimatam" means without transgressing what is desired; that is to say, without concealing the intended object.

"Anagha" contains a reason within it. The connection is: "You shall obtain everything indeed that is desired," such that by the attainment of those desires, further anxieties shall not pierce you. || 37 ||
Having heard these words of his, which were filled with the grace of appropriate meaning, the wise prince, the banner of Raghu’s lineage,
abandoned his grief even as the rain-cloud thundered.
Just as a peacock is inferred from its plumage, so too is the accomplishment of the desired object inferred. || 38 ||
Having heard these words— which were spoken by the wise Viśvāmitra, whose inner intent was such that it manifested (*vilāsa*) the display of appropriate matters corresponding to his own desires—
the illustrious banner of Raghu’s lineage, perceiving the accomplishment of his desired object, cast off his grief.
The connection [is as follows]: when there is a cloud carrying water, the peacock cries out repeatedly. || 38 ||
Thus ends the eleventh sarga, titled "The Consolation of Rāghava," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition. || 11 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Consolation of Rāghava," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twelfth Sarga.
Vālmīki said:
Having been thus questioned by the lord of sages, Rāghava regained his composure.
And he spoke words that were beautiful, full of meaning, and delivered with deliberation.
In this [work], it is described that enjoyments are of the nature of suffering, that sense objects and the like are unreal, and that even prosperity is ultimately detrimental.
Having regained his composure—that is, having attained perfect tranquility—he spoke slowly and gently, as if out of respect for the gravity of the matter, and thus it was beautiful. (1)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, now that I have been questioned by you, I shall relate everything exactly as it is, even though I am ignorant; for who can transgress the words of the virtuous?
"Who would leap over [your command]?"—the sense is that I speak thus for the sake of fulfilling your command, and not out of audacity. || 2 ||
I, for my part, was born here in this, my own father’s house; I have gradually attained growth and remain here, having acquired knowledge. (3)

Having thus subdued the Sage with words of humility, he demonstrates his own emergence of inquiry through discernment and dispassion— arising from the purity of mind produced by the practice of dharma— under the guise of recounting his own life story, in four verses beginning with "As for me... (3).
Thereupon, O leader of sages, having become devoted to righteous conduct, I wandered over the earth— girdled by the oceans— for the purpose of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
He has wandered; because the root has the sense of "going," the suffix *kta* is used in the active (kartṛ) voice. || 4 ||
Then, after such a length of time, as I was removing this attachment to worldly existence, there arose in my mind this very reflection. (5)
Such is he whose characteristics will be described hereafter. || 5 ||
With my mind enveloped by discernment, I myself thereafter reflected upon this with an intellect devoid of relish for worldly enjoyments.
The "taste" for enjoyments is passion; [one should practice] with that voided.
What indeed is this so-called happiness, this continuous succession of saṃsāra, wherein the world is born for death and dies for birth? (7)
What is the name of happiness? The meaning is: none at all. "Continuity" means expansion. The sense is that it is precisely the absence of happiness that is expressed by this statement. || 7 ||
All these states of being, including the movements of the mobile and immobile worlds, are entirely unstable;
they are the masters of calamities, evil, and the very ground of worldly prosperity.

"Granted that it may be so, nevertheless, pleasure is indeed experienced in the intermediate stages of manifestation (vibhava-bhūmis). To this he replies: "The engagement in enjoyment is of two kinds—dependent on means provided by destiny and dependent on acquired means—and even the stages of manifestation, together with their characteristic activities, [are of these two kinds]."

Objects such as garlands, sandalwood, food, and drink, which exist only for the duration of their manifestation, do not grant happiness because they are unstable; the meaning is that they cause suffering at the times of non-attainment and separation.
Anticipating the objection that you might expect pleasure from them even during the time of enjoyment, he says: "They are the lords of calamities."

"Patayaḥ" means masters; that is to say, they are the most excellent. However, because they give rise to defects such as passion (*rāga*) and lead to the ultimate calamity, they are in fact of that very nature [i.e., calamitous]. While those not prohibited are thus [desirable], those that are prohibited, though seemingly "good," are actually sinful because they produce sin. Consequently, since they are like food mixed with poison, there is no happiness in enjoying them.
The meaning is that it is established that there is no happiness in saṃsāra. || 8 ||
Like iron rods, phenomena are mutually unattached;
they cling together solely through their own mental construction.
If these do not grant happiness, then how are they connected to one another as the producers of happiness? To this he says:

"This... All entities are by their very nature like iron rods or needles, unattached to one another and devoid of connection; however, through this [notion], "this is mine"— The final sentence is incomplete in the source text, so the translation reflects that incompleteness.

By means of mental constructs such as "I shall accomplish this enjoyment in this manner," they are merely joined and connected through the relationship of action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*). Likewise, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*),
this expansive world is seen to be dependent upon the mind.
The mind appears as if non-existent; by what have we been so utterly deluded? || 10 ||
It is not only the mere relationship between entities that is dependent on the mind; rather, even their birth, maintenance, and destruction are so.

If that is the case, one might argue that the mind alone should be the means to happiness; to this he says: "The mind. In discernment (*viveka*), it appears as if non-existent or empty. Thus, happiness cannot be accomplished through it either. [The opponent asks: "By what, then, could there be happiness for such a long time?"
We are deluded. || 10 ||
Alas, we of deluded intellect have been dragged away by that which is non-existent, like bewildered deer in the forest lured by the water of a mirage from afar. 11.

Therefore, by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he shows that this is indeed an illusion (*bhrānti*) with the words "asataiva" (by that which is non-existent). The meaning is: because of the absolute non-existence of both happiness and its means within *saṃsāra*. They are "drawn away" (*vikṛṣṭāḥ*) in a manner that is painful (*kaṣṭam*). It is understood that, in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), it is the hope for happiness that is like the water of a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇāmbhaḥ*).
"Deluded deer" means foolish antelopes. || 11 ||
Not sold by anyone, yet we remain as if sold; alas, we are all fools, even though we know the magic of Śambara.

"Established" means being under the control of another; that is the meaning. "Though knowing" means even though we consider ourselves wise, we are indeed deluded. "Śāmbara" means pertaining to Śambara;
the sense is that this is an illusion (māyā). || 12 ||
What indeed are these enjoyments called within these manifold phenomena, which are so utterly wretched?
For we have remained here in vain through delusion, our minds bound by attachment.

What indeed are enjoyments but mere fragments of sensory pleasure? Because they are by nature seen and then lost, they are merely a source of endless suffering. Those who hold the delusion that these are truly bound [to them] remain in such a state. || 13 ||
It is understood now that for a long time we have remained in vain in the forest;
we fools have fallen into delusion, like bewildered deer in a pit.

The word *ā* expresses remembrance and longing. It has been known for a long time. What is that? He says: "In vain indeed have you fallen into delusion. "In the forest" means in a pit or a hollow within the forest. (14)
What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments? Who am I, and what is this that has come?
Let that which is false remain false; indeed, to whom does anything belong, and what is it that has come? (15)

"Who am I? What is the nature of this world of appearances? For what purpose has it come into being? What is the use of my kingdom, and what is the use of enjoyments? Is all this entirely false, or is there something true within it? In that regard, is the vision real, or is the object of vision unreal? Whatever is false, let that alone be false; but not—"
This is a reversal. If that [consciousness] were of the nature of the knower (mityātva), what would have happened to anyone? The sense is that there would be no harm whatsoever. || 15 ||
O Brahmin, as I reflected in this way, a distaste for all worldly existences then arose within me,
just as a traveler feels toward desert wastes.

Thus, for one who reflects and investigates in the manner described by the nine verses beginning with "What indeed is this?"—*arati* meaning a lack of relish—the [mind] becomes like a desert, a waterless land. || 16 ||
Therefore, O Blessed One, tell me this: what is it that perishes? What is it that is born again? And what is it that grows? (17)

Having thus described the manner in which his own inquiry arose, he indicates the points to be investigated with the five verses beginning with "tadetad" (That this...). Because that [world] is insubstantial within the *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), first, regarding its destruction and origination, he says "imamidam" and so forth.
This visible world, established by the evidence of universal experience as being real, is as follows:

It perishes entirely and becomes as if non-existent. Is this because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence? If someone were to say that it is indeed non-existent, then it is born again and attains existence. If this [entity] undergoes modifications such as growth and so forth—which are external to both existence and non-existence—and if even that...

If the previous state perishes and arises as another state, then there would be a contradiction with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the impossibility of conventional practices such as growth and so forth. If the previous state does not perish,
then it follows that both states would exist simultaneously, which contradicts the nature of a change of state.

In that case, they would be non-existent; and if there were no difference, then the state and the possessor of the state would be synonymous. For the sake of answering these three questions—concerning the permanent entity, the state, and their relationship as synonyms—the chapters on Origination, Persistence, and Cessation are presented. Alternatively, this...
Does the body perish? Does it arise again? Does it grow? The meaning is that there is no purpose whatsoever for its birth and so forth. || 17 ||
Old age, death, calamity, birth, and prosperity increase again and again through their appearance and disappearance. (18)
It is not merely that wealth does not exist; rather, there is even a succession of misfortunes. Thus he says, "Old age," etc.
Since even prosperity is a cause of misfortune, it is counted among misfortunes. (18)
Behold, by those very same wretched enjoyments, we have indeed been reduced to a state of decay, like mountain trees battered by the winds. (19)

Now, one might object that the body does indeed have a purpose because it is the cause of enjoyment; anticipating this, he says: "by enjoyments," etc. The repetition "by those very ones, by those very ones" is intended to highlight the distaste [of such enjoyment], as it is like grinding what is already ground, since there is no novelty in them. These people are greedy for enjoyments. "Weariness" means looseness or frailty. Thus, even enjoyments are nothing but a source of harm.
The state of being. || 19 ||
Like insentient beings, men stand about making sounds in vain through the winds called "life-breaths," just like hollow bamboo flutes. || 20 ||

Thinking that even for those possessed of wisdom, if the means for the ultimate cessation of suffering are not accomplished, that wisdom is indeed in vain and they are practically insentient, he says: "They are insentient. In vain means without utility for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). "Veṇus" refers to *kīcakas*, which are bamboos that resound when stirred by the wind. (20)
"How can this suffering be stilled?"— thus am I tormented by anxiety,
like an old tree by a fierce fire dwelling within its hollow.
He provides the answer to the question, "By what cause are you deluded? with the words: "It is pacified. || 21 ||
Although my heart is as solid as a stone due to the sufferings of saṃsāra,
I do not weep with falling tears, solely out of fear of my own people.
The meaning is: one whose heart is completely filled—solid, without gaps, and densely packed—like a stone with the sufferings of saṃsāra;
[he fears] that even his own people, his kinsmen, would weep for his sake. || 22 ||
Those functions of my mind are empty, rendered tasteless by the dryness of weeping;
only discernment, abiding within my heart, perceives them in solitude.

The meaning is: my discernment alone beholds this state—wherein there is weeping that is dry and tearless, devoid of emotion and empty of affection, and consequently, artificial smiles and expressions of speech produced by joy and other such causes which are themselves lacking. || 23 ||
I am utterly bewildered as I reflect upon this state consisting of existence and non-existence;
like a fortunate man [unperturbed] by poverty, I remain far removed from the activities of worldly existence.

Reflecting upon and contemplating that state which is characterized by the abundance of the non-existence— that is, the destruction— of all beloved objects; or alternatively, reflecting upon and contemplating that state which is a modification of ignorance, the absence of that supreme bliss characterized by the cessation of all suffering, [he perceives it] as being intensely [filled] with the activities of saṃsāra.

I am bewildered; just as one who is fortunate and endowed with wealth and other blessings becomes bewildered upon remembering his former state when he encounters poverty—brought about by fate far beyond his merit or good fortune—in that same way [I am bewildered]. 24.
Fortunes, intent on deception, delude the functioning of the mind, shatter the string of virtues, and bestow a web of suffering. (25)
[The opponent objects: "Surely your desired goal will be accomplished by riches alone, for there is the popular saying: 'What indeed is difficult for the wealthy to obtain?
To this, he replies with the words "mohayantī" (deluding). "Vipralambhaḥ" means deception or fraud. || 25 ||
To me, wealth is not for the sake of joy; it is like wheels of accumulated anxiety, and houses, though filled with wives, are like those of men facing terrible calamities.

He elaborates on that very point with the verse beginning "cintā" (thought). For the wealthy, there are wheels set in motion for the sake of accumulation—that is, for piling up [wealth]—by means of the grinding of their streams of anxiety into pieces as small as sesame seeds. For those in the grip of fierce calamities, these wheels are fashioned from causes that are expanded and fragile through the constant contemplation of the various states of fault, namely, the enemy of poverty.
O Sage, my mind finds no peace, like that of a forest elephant bound in chains. || 27 ||

My mind finds no ease or stability because of the constant contemplation of the various visible and invisible defects and miserable conditions of the body and its states—conditions supported by the reason that their fragility is ever-present. (In the case of the elephant: [My mind finds no ease] because of the constant contemplation of the various visible and invisible defects and miserable conditions of the state of being an elephant, supported by the reason that its fragility is ever-present.
And by reflecting upon the miserable conditions of things such as wood that is fragile because it covers a pit devoid of width—this is the meaning. || 27 ||

From time to time, in this world where the light of consciousness has vanished into the dense mist of sharp delusion during the night, the wicked— thieves of hundreds of sense-objects, exceedingly clever, active, and intent—
have set out in every direction to seize the singular treasure of discernment.
Who among those wise men would abandon such excellent warriors when they are capable in battle? (28)

In this world, during the night characterized by ignorance, among people who possess the characteristic of delusion—that is, a lack of inquiry—there are hundreds of thieves in the form of sense objects, exceedingly clever, who at all times and in every direction roam everywhere, intent on destroying the treasure of discrimination. [The word] "in battle" (*raṇe*) means in the conflict; having abandoned the wise for the sake of slaying them... [the rest of the verse follows].
Apart from those who possess the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), what other brave warriors are capable? The meaning is that none at all.

The particle *iva* is intended to indicate the extreme rarity even of those who might resemble such [knowledgeable ones]. The underlying sense is that without the destruction of darkness (*tamas*), their slaying is impossible. || 28 ||

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The First Affliction," in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage) tradition. 12.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The First Affliction," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
This noble lady stands here, fashioned within this worldly existence.
O Sage, even that Śrī surely causes delusion and brings about misery.
That which is beloved by all the deluded, which always bestows enjoyments that lead to misfortune,
and which is fraught with manifold defects— that Fortune is censured until the end of creation.

Having thus demonstrated the worthlessness and harmfulness of sense-objects, he begins to demonstrate that the prosperity which is the root of acquiring those objects is likewise of such a nature, with the words beginning "This... and so forth. In this saṃsāra, while remaining present and not having departed, it is conceived by deluded people to be "noble" or "excellent" because it is the cause of abundant pleasure.

[This is] the remainder. In reality, however, even that [wealth] is surely for the sake of total delusion alone; because it brings about slaughter, bondage, hell, and so forth—it is "kadarthadā" (giving what is useless), meaning it either gives things that are not obtained, or things already separated, or things that cause misery, or it gives base and harmful riches rather than discernment—thus it is called *kadarthadā*. || 1 ||
Like a river in the rainy season, she carries forth vast, dull-witted [beings] who are agitated by the fire of endless waves of intense passion.

It carries away— that is, it brings about helplessness and draws in— those who are expansive, numerous, and dull-witted fools, whose endless waves are successions of desires abundant with exultations and efforts.
In the case of the river, [it refers to those] abundant with upward-moving dance (*ullāsa*), thereby increased and infinite.
Her many daughters of anxiety, nurtured by manifold indulgence, become restless and prevail over her like the waves of a river. (3)
From this Fortune (Śrī) there arise daughters characterized by anxiety, who have been nurtured and increased by their own wayward and wicked behaviors. (3)
For this unfortunate woman does not fix her step in one place; like one who is burnt, she runs hither and thither with her conduct unsteady.

Just as some unfortunate woman, having been burned by leaping upon fire out of delusion, does not fix her foot in one place— that is, she does not set her foot down— but rather runs here and there with unsteady movements, so too Fortune (Śrī) is unstable in her conduct; she does not abide in a fixed place according to the scriptures.
Producing intense burning and with her limbs utterly wasted, she, when her body is touched,
brings about only her own destruction, like a streak of soot on a lamp-flame.
The meaning is: belonging to the illustrious one (*śrīmataḥ*), [the lamp] which, having its parts touched by expenditure, embezzlement, and so forth, produces extreme burning;

"within" (*antaḥ*) means in the middle—that is, quite unexpectedly (*akāṇḍa eva*). "Destruction" (*vināśam*) refers to that of itself or of its user. In the case of the analogy of the line of a lamp (*dīpalekhāpakṣe*), "having its parts touched" (*parāmṛṣṭāṅgikā*) means its constituent members have been contacted. Regarding destruction...
The example of collyrium is given to illustrate its being rooted in darkness. || 5 ||
Indeed, like the nature of a king, a fool— without even investigating merits and defects— clings to one who has approached him, regardless of whether that person is difficult to support.
Though difficult to ascend and achieved only with great hardship, it does not belong to those who possess merit or are righteous; rather,
by the power of one's own desired merit, it supports whoever happens to be nearby— just as the nature or disposition of kings is such that they are often deluded in many ways.
It is well known that people feel affection for those who are righteous and virtuous, but they also associate with whoever happens to be nearby.
By that very same action, this [suffering] follows along with expansion,
just as the milk of the venomous serpent of the faults spreads out.

This prosperity does not attain expansion through those very actions— such as warfare, gambling, or trade— for which milk is the fruit; rather, it expands through the expansion of the venomous serpents of faults such as greed for wealth, kingdom, and gain, as well as violence and falsehood.
The meaning is that, on the contrary, [wealth] serves as a cause for their expenditure through sacrifices, gifts, and so forth. || 7 ||

People are cold and soft in their touch toward both others and their own kin only so long as they have not been made harsh by prosperity, just as frost remains cold and soft until it is driven away by a whirlwind (*vātyā*).
By the term "cold and soft touch," qualities such as compassion, courtesy, and affection are implied. *Vātyā* is a collection of winds.
They have been made harsh—[the word *kṛtaḥ* is used in the singular in both instances, though it appears as a plural in some versions]—they have been rendered unbearable.
8 Those who are wise, heroic, grateful, refined, and gentle—they have been soiled by prosperity, like jewels covered by a handful of dust. 9
He clarifies that very point with the words "the wise. This is clear. || 9 ||
"O Blessed One, prosperity does not lead to happiness; indeed, it increases only suffering.
When guarded, it brings about destruction, just as a poisonous creeper leads to death. (10)
She who is protected and guarded brings about—that is, accomplishes—destruction, which is the means of perishing; [she brings about] death, that is, dying. || 10 ||
One who is illustrious yet beyond reproach, one who is brave yet not boastful, and one who is a lord yet possesses an even gaze—these three types of men are rare to find. (11)
Now, one might object that some individuals are indeed seen who are prosperous, righteous, and renowned;
to this he replies with the word "śrīmān" (the prosperous one). This is clear. || 11 ||
For this is a treacherous and dense cave for those who experience suffering,
a great slope of the Vindhya mountains for the lordly elephants of thick delusion.
Of the serpents who experience the characteristic of suffering. || 12 ||
She is the moonlight for the night-lotus of the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause, and the moonlight for the white water-lily of suffering;
she is the gale for the lamp of right vision, and the river surging with a flood of waves.

Meritorious deeds, which are like lotuses characterized by such qualities, have [this person] as their night—that is, the cause of their closing. Likewise, [this person] is the moonlight that causes the night-lotuses of suffering to bloom. A "good vision"—meaning either a compassionate gaze or the vision of ultimate reality—is the whirlwind for the lamp of that [vision].

It is a mass of wind, like a surging river filled with a flood of waves. For her as well, the state of clouds and the like—arising from the agitation of extinguishing the lamp—is an increaser of the poison of despondency;
it is a marshland for conceptual constructions and a source of distress for the serpent of fear. (14)

Agitation, fear, and delusion—these are the nature of those clouds; the "first stage" (ādi-padavī) is the initial path, such as the preceding wind. The "furrowed field" (kedārikā)—the division of the field—is for the crops of conceptual constructions (vikalpa). It is "possessing serpents" (bhoginī), meaning it generates a fear characterized by exhaustion (kheda) and gain (āya); thus, it is "partaking of fear" (bhayabhāgavatī). [The phrase] "for exhaustion" (khedāya) [is used].
Or it may be a separate word. || 14 ||
She is the frost for the creepers of dispassion, the night of the owl of transformation,
the fang of Rahu for the moon of discernment, and the moonlight for the lotus of goodness.
The "modifications" (vikāra) are the modifications of the mind, such as desire and the like. || 15 ||
Like Indra’s bow, it is captivating with its various flickering colors;
like a darting flash of lightning, it arises and perishes, resting upon the dull matter of the body.

The *indrāyudha* is the rainbow of Śakra; likewise, even when the reading is *candrāyudha*, it refers to those who are like the half-moon—namely, fools. It is they who are generally seen to be possessed of wealth (*śrīmantaḥ*). || 16 ||
She surpassed the female mongoose of the forest by her lack of fickleness;
she excelled the mirage by her intentness on avoiding deception. || 17 ||
By whom the forest mongooses were conquered through fickleness and treated with contempt—those born of a mongoose lineage are of low birth;
here the word *na* is not the negative particle *nañ*. "Deception" (*vipralambhana*) refers to the inclination toward trickery. The intensity of the mirage in summer is well known. || 17 ||
Like a wave, she does not remain still for even a moment;
like a flickering lamp flame, her movement is within a sphere that is exceedingly difficult to comprehend.

Never remaining still for even a moment in a single form—because its nature is always subject to decay and growth—its course is difficult to discern, its range being one whose conditions are inconceivable and hard to perceive. (18)
Like a lioness, she crushes (or strikes down) the pride of the elephant-king host;
like the edge of a sword, she is cool yet possesses an exceedingly sharp disposition. (19)

Those very lords of elephants, whose people are distracted by conflict and eager for battle, themselves resort to those who are sharp—both literally sharp [weapons] and sharp-minded, cruel-hearted [men]. In the *karmadhāraya* compound, there is the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the preceding word "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*). || 19 ||
Behold, I see no happiness at all— save for suffering— in this ill-fated Fortune, who has been snatched away by misfortune and who clings to me with a malignant affliction. (20)

She is meaningful through the stolen property of others, or she desires those who have been stolen away by death; she is characterized by such conduct. In her, evil anxieties are deeply settled and hidden like thieves.
Misfortune has been driven far away from her, yet it returns again with even greater zeal.
Alas! Shameless wicked people always seem to embrace [or cling to] one.

By the reference "him" (*tam*), the word "whose" (*yasya*) is understood. Thus, the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) of that very person—by whom Alakṣmī has been driven far away as if by a co-wife—is drawn toward him with renewed affection; yet this state, which was once enjoyed by the co-wife, is difficult to achieve and momentary in its duration.
With her body twisted as she moved through the coils of the serpent, she was like the goddess Lakṣmī, who had emerged from a chasm as a flowering creeper. || 22 ||
*Kadartha* refers to a miserable purpose, such as falling or death; that which is to be accomplished or obtained by means of such recklessness is *kadarthasādhyā*.
With bodies entwined by the coils of serpents, their limbs were encircled. In a chasm, such as the pit of an old well or similar cavity. || 22 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Renunciation of Lakṣmī," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 13.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Rejection of Lakṣmī," in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*. 13.
The fourteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Life is as fragile as a drop of water hanging from the tip of the corner of a young leaf.
Like one who has gone mad, it departs suddenly, abandoning the body. || 1 ||
In this world, the life, youth, and lifespan of a fool are censured, for they are seized by disease, illness, and old age, and defiled by desire and other passions.

He says that even life, like prosperity, does not lead to happiness, beginning with the words "āyuḥ" (life) and so forth. Like a drop of water or a particle of frost hanging at the very tip of the corner—the edge—of a leaf, it is fragile and unstable. The word *unmattam* (mad/unstable), ending in the nominative case, is the first [word] referring to the simile; [the word *āyuḥ*], ending in the accusative case, is the second.

Or [the suffix *ka* denotes] a comparison with the body (*śarīra*). The suffix *kan* is used in the sense of "inopportune" (*akāṇḍa*)—meaning at an improper time—as well as in the senses of contempt and compassion. (1)
For those whose minds are worn out by attachment to the venomous serpents of sensory objects,
and whose self-discrimination is immature, life is merely a cause of exhaustion.
For those men whose minds have been completely loosened by attachment to the serpents characterized by sense-objects, no mature discernment exists within themselves. (2)
But for those who have understood that which is to be known and have come to rest in the expansive state,
for whom existence and non-existence are a source of confidence, bliss arises.
Is this the case even for those who know Brahman? No; he says "But those who... regarding the expanded state (*vitata-pade*), that is, in the unlimited reality.
That [state] in which there is equanimity—meaning the steadiness of the mind—regarding existence and non-existence, or gain and loss. || 3 ||
O Sage, we have reached a certainty established through limited forms; we find no peace in this life, which is like a mass of lightning amidst the clouds of saṃsāra. (4)
Those for whom a firm conviction has been established regarding the body and other such limited forms—that the nature of the self is exactly this much—are "contented," meaning they are happy. || 4 ||
It is as reasonable to attempt to wrap the wind or to break open space,
or to string together the limbs of a corpse, as it is to place one's hope in this life.
*Āsthā* means trust. || 5 ||
Like an autumn cloud, like a lamp without oil,
or like a restless wave, that which has passed away is perceived as such.
"Pelava" means slight. "Asneha" means devoid of oil. The word "āyuḥ" (life) is connected either by transposition or by being separated [from its position]. || 6 ||
I may exert myself to grasp a wave, the moon’s reflection, a mass of lightning, or a lotus in the sky; but I do not place my hope in life, whose stability is destroyed.
In the *hata* and *sthita* meters, there is instability. || 7 ||
With an unquiet mind, the deluded person strives for a long, empty life only for the sake of suffering, just as a female mule carries a fetus within her womb only to her own destruction.

The absolute cessation of craving is the rest of the mind. [The phrase "empty of happiness" means empty and useless. "Extended" means vast. "Seeks" means desires. A mule (*aśvatarī*) is born from a mare and a donkey; its fetus emerges only by tearing open the belly.
It is well-known. || 8 ||
O Brahmin, in this ocean of creation where the world-process flows like foam, life does not please me, being as transient as water upon a creeper-like body.

In this wandering through saṃsāra, in this revolving of worldly existence, the well-known vine of the body—the creeper of the physical frame—is like foam produced from a transformation of water in the ocean of creation, due to its extreme instability. Therefore, the meaning is that in this [world], life—that is, living—does not please me. || 9 ||
That by which the attainable is fully attained, by which one no longer grieves, and which is the abode of supreme bliss—that is called true life. (10)
That which is necessarily to be attained and worthy of being reached, consisting of the supreme human goal;
[it is] of bliss—that is, the happiness of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 10 ||
For even trees live, and deer and birds live;
but he alone truly lives whose mind does not live by means of mental fabrication.

By means of reflection, the fruit of reflection, the awakening to reality, or the destruction of latent impressions, one does not live [in the ordinary sense], but becomes voided of worldly existence.
Only those beings born in this world have led a truly virtuous life who are not born here again; all others are but aged donkeys.

The connection [of the verse] is that they alone have become those who lead a virtuous life and possess a praiseworthy existence. Even those who are aged and long-lived may have an unpraiseworthy life like that of a donkey; this is because their self-conception is fixed upon an impure body—such is the intended meaning. || 12 ||
Scripture is a burden to the undiscriminating; knowledge is a burden to the passionate;
the mind is a burden to the unpeaceful; and the body is a burden to one who has not realized the Self. 13.
