A burden is like a burden, a cause of futile exertion; and even knowledge, though it be knowledge, is likewise [a burden] when it takes the form of all such toil. Life, mind, intellect, ego, and likewise one's endeavors—all these lead only to suffering for the person of dull wit, just as a load leads to suffering for the bearer of the load. (14)
*Īhitam* means what has been striven for or undertaken. He explains the meaning of the word *bhāra* (burden) himself with the words beginning "as if for one bearing a burden," and so forth.
The mind that finds no rest and is never satisfied is the supreme abode of calamities,
a nest for the birds of disease, and the firm seat of the exhaustion of life.
Rest is the cessation of all fatigue; fulfillment is the state of having one's desires satisfied; and exertion is the means to fatigue. || 15 ||
Casting off weariness every day, gradually and incessantly,
one is destroyed by time, just as a mouse destroys an old burrow.

Since the requirement for the word *pratyaham* (daily) is satisfied by its connection with *utsṛjya khedam* (having cast aside weariness), the word *anāratam* (unceasingly) is not redundant. The meaning is that one's lifespan is destroyed. || 16 ||
The body is consumed by fierce diseases that take refuge in its cavities and inflict the burning pain of poison, just as the forest breeze is swallowed by savage serpents.
By those [beings] whose nature is to inflict burning pain like poison; "is consumed" is the ellipsis—[consumed] by life-force (āyuḥ); "by beasts of prey" means by serpents. || 17 ||
Like an old tree being gnawed by cruel woodworms, he is torn apart by base and cruel sufferings that dwell within him and flow forth incessantly.

With [the fluids] flowing and streaming forth—blood, impurities, and so on; in the case of the reading *dhuṇa*, it refers to dust—[the body] is completely cut and severed by sufferings, such as the pains of disease and the like. Even with the reading *āghṛṣyate*, the meaning is the same. *Ghuṇas* are wood-worms. || 18 ||
Surely, like a rat beheld by a cat, he is watched incessantly by death with a mind of intense greed to swallow him quickly. (19)
*Nigaraṇa* means swallowing. *Ghanagardham* means with intense longing; [it describes acting] in such a way that there is abundant desire. || 19 ||
By the void woman who is a prostitute of incapacity, yet pregnant with qualities such as fragrance, food is completely digested by old age, just as a great meal is consumed by digestion. 20.

Just as one becomes powerless and one's strength is depleted by an old courtesan, so too does life—or the person—waste away through old age. In this regard, there is an illustration: it is like food being consumed by a glutton who eats excessively. || 20 ||
Within just a few days, having been thoroughly understood,
youth is abandoned with indifference by the wicked man, just as a good person is abandoned by a wicked person.

Having recognized that youth is devoid of application toward the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), [one should treat it] with disregard; or "gatādaram" may be understood as an adverbial modifier. It is well known that a person is treated with respect by the virtuous only so long as he is not recognized as a wicked man. || 21 ||
Form is constantly coveted by Death, that supreme libertine, who is the friend of destruction and the kinsman of old age and death. (22)
The best of ornaments is the finest of men; beauty is like physical form; and it is life or the person that is desired.

(22) In this world, there is nothing so utterly devoid of quality and as fragile as this life, which is constantly abandoned by stability and the manifestation of happiness, and is destined for death. (23)

The connection is as follows: there is nothing else in this world like this life—which is constantly abandoned by that [state] renowned as liberation-in-life (jīvanmukta), which is characterized by ease, radiance, and stability, and which is superior, yet fragile, extremely trivial, and devoid of qualities. || 23 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Censure of Life," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣi tradition. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Contempt for Life," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa.
Fifteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
It has arisen in vain through delusion; it increases in vain.
I am terrified by the enemy of false ego, which consists of delusion. || 1 ||
In this context, egoism is specifically censured as the foundational pillar for the undertaking of all misfortunes,
and as the root of the creeper of possessiveness.
In this way, even egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is not a cause of happiness; on the contrary, it is the root of all defects.

Due to delusion (*moha*), that is, ignorance (*ajñāna*), as the cause, egoism has arisen in vain and increases pointlessly on all sides; the meaning is that no human goal (*puruṣārtha*) exists therein. Its material cause (*upādāna*) is also nothing but delusion.

He shows this with the words "by that which consists of falsehood. Alternatively, there is a word-break as "āmaya" (disease). The meaning is: by the enemy called egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), which has the nature of destroying [the self], like a disease. || 1 ||
Under the very influence of egoism, this world of manifold forms subjects those who are most wretched to the torment of the sheath of defects. (2)
Such is this saṃsāra, characterized by various forms consisting of the goal, the means, the fruit, and their functioning; beginning from time without beginning— starting from the infinite past—
it has experienced a succession of endless sufferings such as birth, death, and the hells, even while doing so.
Furthermore, because they repeatedly desire those fragments of pleasure as their causes even at the cost of thousands of hardships,

they do not engage in virtuous conduct within the treasuries of the senses— those who are more wretched than the wretched, who are addicted to sense objects, and whose characteristics are the defects of passion, hatred, and evil vices such as pernicious latent tendencies.
Through the power of ego comes calamity; through ego come heavy sorrows;
through the power of ego comes worldly striving—there is no enemy greater than ego; indeed, ego is my disease. (3)
He elaborates on that very result by way of illustration: "By the power of egoism," and so forth.

*Āpad* refers to physical suffering; *ādhayaḥ* are mental afflictions; *īhā* is passion or wicked conduct; *mama āmayaḥ* is my disease. Even in the reading *manomayaḥ*, it is an instance of elided parts (*luptaikadeśa*), meaning either "the disease of the mind" or "a modification of the mind."
Relying upon that supreme and ancient enemy, egoism, I neither eat nor drink water, O Sage; how much less could I enjoy worldly pleasures?
*bhuje bhuñje*; the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is Vedic; or there is a reading *bhaje*. || 4 ||
The night of saṃsāra is long, and the illusion that deludes the mind is vast;
then, through the fault of egoism, one is caught like a deer in a snare by a hunter.
In the darkness characterized by saṃsāra, there is a long and extensive snare that binds deer.
Those sufferings which are long-lasting, uneven, and great—
born from the ego-sense— they have gone forth like *khadira* thorns.
The uneven places were difficult to cross. He went from the mountain. Khadira trees are a specific species of tree. || 6 ||

I renounce the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which has the moon, the enemy of the moon (Rāhu), and the face of the lion as its aspects; which possesses the excellence of a lotus and the thunderbolt; and which is like a cloud and the autumn season. (7)

Rāhu is the son of Siṃhikā. The compound "himamaśani" is an upamita-samāsa (compound of comparison), meaning "like a hailstone. His equanimity—his vision of all beings as equal—is itself a cloud, because it rains down compassion upon all living creatures. || 7 ||
I am not Rāma, nor do I have desire for worldly objects, nor does my mind dwell upon them;
I wish to remain in peace within my own self, just like the Victorious One.

It is shown that upon the abandonment of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), pride of body, possessiveness, and so forth, subside of their own accord—this is expressed by the words "I am not" (*nāham*). "Peaceful" (*śānta*) means free from enmity; the meaning is that one perceives all beings with the same equanimity as one's own self (*ātmaupamyena*). "The Victor" (*jina*) refers to the Buddha; just as he was devoted to non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), so too [should one be]. Even toward those who are censurable, there is virtue.
The example of the Jina is given according to the principle that "it should be grasped"; or alternatively, the reading is "jita" (conquered). || 8 ||
Whatever I have eaten, offered in sacrifice, or performed under the influence of egoism—all that is indeed insubstantial; only the state of being empty of egoism is the true reality.
A non-entity is that which is void or devoid of essence. || 9 ||
O Brahmin, if there is an "I," then in times of calamity one is pained by that "I";
if it does not exist, one is happy; therefore, freedom from egoism is better.
O Sage, having abandoned the ego through a tranquil mind, I remain free from agitation; for the flood of enjoyments has its foundation in transience. (11)
Since anxieties have their root in an unpeaceful mind, the agitation caused by disease ceases through its pacification. Now, one might ask:

why would it not be so through the very attainment of enjoyments? To this he replies: "the flood of enjoyments. It is fragile, being dependent upon the body, the senses, objects, and so forth. Thus, when each of these individual components perishes, the resulting onset of anxiety is unavoidable.
The state of being. || 11 ||
O Brahmin, as long as the cloud of egoism expands,
so long does the cluster of *kuṭaja* flowers of craving blossom.
Egoism alone is like a cloud that obscures the multitude of lights arising from discernment; thus it is not perceived anywhere. It expands on all sides and stretches out the limbs.
When the cloud of egoism has subsided, craving becomes like a fresh flash of lightning.
With the movement of the flame of a dying lamp, it goes away somewhere with extreme speed.
In this context, "conduct" (vṛtti) means having a similar character. || 13 ||
In the great Vindhya mountain of egoism, the intoxicated great elephant of the mind roars with thunderous slaps, like a rain-cloud with its peals of thunder.
Its similarity to the Vindhya mountain arises from its immobility and its difficult accessibility. It "visphūrjati" means it roars.
With "āsphota"—meaning with the striking of dense clouds or, alternatively, with the striking of dense stones and the like—it possesses the enthusiasm for battle.
Here, in this great forest of the body, dwells the lion of dense egoism.
By this vast radiance which shines forth, this entire world is pervaded.

It has been expanded by those various causes of pride; it has spread throughout the world through the accumulation of seeds such as good and evil deeds. The sense is that this is according to the Vedic scripture: "For with every thought, he produces this food through his actions. || 15 ||
The succession of many births, strung upon the fine threads of craving, has been fashioned by the fierce hunter of egoism into a necklace around his neck. (16)
A "lava" is a single portion. A "succession of births" is a succession of bodies. A "khiṅga" is a libertine. || 16 ||
O Sage, this enemy that is ego has here spread out a web consisting of sons, friends, wives, and so forth, devoid of any counsel or mantra.

The remainder [of the definition] is that *tantra* consists of means such as sons, friends, and so forth, devoid of [esoteric] *tantra* and *mantra*, which serve as methods for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), causing madness (*unmāda*), and the like.
*Tantra* is thus a worldly and rational means. 17.
When this notion of "I" has been swiftly wiped away by oneself, all these mental afflictions are likewise completely wiped away. (18)
When it has been wiped away and cast out by the eradication of its root. || 18 ||
When the water of the "I" has subsided, the mist of delusion in the sky of the mind, which gradually destroys tranquility, vanishes somewhere beyond reach.

For those of dull faculties, the eradication of egoism—which is to be accomplished through awakening attained only after long practice—is a task that destroys tranquility and cuts short peace. It is a mist of delusion and a frost of great confusion residing in the sky of the mind. For me, whose mental state is free from egoism, yet who now sinks in grief due to my own folly—
O Brahmin, you ought to explain here whatever is appropriate.

I do not, with effort, resort to this abode of egoism— which is the dwelling place of all calamities, unstable, situated within [the body], abandoned by the one possessed of supreme virtue, and surrounded by extreme suffering.
O high-souled one, instruct me with what remains.

Having thus described egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), the misfortune caused by it, and the fruit of its eradication, he—stating his own attainment of the qualification for hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) resulting from the abandonment of that [egoism]—seeks instruction with the words:
"Of all calamities... [The egoism] is "internal," meaning residing in the heart; it is "freed from the highest qualities" such as tranquility (*śānti*) and so forth.
The word *ahaṃkṛti* means the form of egoism, which is a state, a mark, or a characteristic. The word *pada* means a settled position, protection, or the ultimate goal.
"Instruct me" (*anuśādhi*) means teach me along with that which remains to be accomplished. The word "the reality of the Self" (*ātmatattvam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 21 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth sarga, titled "Loathing of Egoism," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Loathing of Ego," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa. || 15 ||
The sixteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Through the service of noble persons and the performance of virtuous deeds, one attains freedom from the decay caused by defects.
The mind moves restlessly, like a film of phlegm within the wind. || 1 ||
In this work, the defects of the mind and the intellect are fully elucidated by Rāma through numerous arguments as well as abundant illustrations. (1)

He states that even for the intellect (*citta*) and the mind (*manas*), there is no quality of being a cause of happiness, but rather they are solely causes of suffering, by means of the verse beginning with "doṣaiḥ" and so forth. The two ablative cases are used in the sense of eliding the suffix *lyap*. The meaning is: having abandoned the service of the noble ones—which must necessarily be performed by virtuous seekers of liberation according to the saying, "They say that service to the great is the door to liberation."
By the defects such as desire and the like, it reaches a state of decay, that is to say, a looseness characterized by an incapacity for accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

It moves like a tuft of peacock feathers in a stream of internal wind—that is, amidst the flow of the inner air—because it is "unsteady," meaning its nature is fickle. He will later state that even the movement of the mind is dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*). || 1 ||
It runs aimlessly and restlessly here and there, wretchedly from afar to even further distances, just like a village dog. (2)

He demonstrates that very point with an illustration, beginning with the words "itaśca" (and from this). The meaning is: without investigating what is appropriate or inappropriate. "Suvyagra" means extremely agitated. "Dīna" means miserable due to not obtaining the means for its own fulfillment anywhere. "Kauleyaka" means a dog. || 2 ||
One attains nothing anywhere, even through the acquisition of great wealth;
one does not reach internal fullness, like a small casket with water.
A *karaṇḍaka* is a specific type of container for storing clothes and other items, constructed from strips of bamboo, cane, or similar materials. || 3 ||
O Sage, the mind is eternally empty, yet it is ensnared by the net of vain hopes; it finds no peace, like a deer strayed from its herd.
It is empty both of itself and of its objects. A *yūtha* is a collection of animals of the same species. (4)
Maintaining a state as flickering as a wave, it possesses a nature that is torn and shattered;
having abandoned even for a moment its long-standing persistence, it finds no stability within the heart. (5)
The disjunction of gross parts is *ālūnatā* (tearing apart); that of subtle parts, however, is *śīrṇatā* (fraying). This is due to the force of action (*karma*). (5)
The mind, agitated by its own conceptualizations, rushes in ten directions,
like the waters of the milk-ocean churned by the strike of Mount Mandara.
Agitated by reflections and the pursuit of sense objects, it has fallen into various disturbances. || 6 ||
I am unable to restrain this great ocean consisting of the mind, which is filled with waves and swirling eddies, and garlanded with the crocodiles of illusion.

O Brahmin, the deer-like mind of man runs far astray, possessing whirlpools formed by the zeal for attaining enjoyments that surge like waves; it is intent on plunging into them and yearns for the sprouts of dūrvā grass of sensual pleasure, without considering its fall into the abyss.
Falling into a chasm means falling into the abyss of hell. || 8 ||
My mind never abandons its own state of being mangled and shattered by its agitated activity, just as the ocean does not abandon its restlessness.
The state of being torn and shattered has been explained. || 9 ||
With its flickering disposition, the mind— restless with a multitude of anxieties—
does not maintain steadfastness in a single place, just as a lion does not remain in a cage.

*Cañcura* means extremely fickle. It is derived from the root *car* with the suffix *yaṅ*, followed by the suffix *ac*; due to the elision of *yaṅ* before *ac* (*yaṅo'ci ca*), the substitution of *nu* for the reduplicated syllable occurs (*caraphalośca*), and the substitution of *u* for the following vowel occurs (*utparasyātaḥ*). *Dhṛti* means fortitude.
[The mind] is already fickle by its very nature, but when it is further agitated by a multitude of anxieties, it becomes even more so.
The meaning is that even when forcibly restrained, it does not maintain its composure. || 10 ||
Mounted upon the chariot of delusion, the mind carries away the bliss of equanimity from the body—its agitation destroyed—just as a swan extracts milk from water. (11)
Since superiority and inferiority are merely imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), in the ultimate sense, the Self possesses a single uniform nature within all beings.

That very state, when experienced as such by those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), is called "equanimity" (*samatā*) and "bliss. And because that [equanimity] is eternally established simply by not mounting the chariot of delusion, it is attained even in this very body; yet, for one who has mounted the chariot of delusion—
The sense is that because it has been seized by the mind, only the notion of the self as being nothing more than a worthless body remains. || 11 ||
O Lord of Sages, the fluctuations of the mind have dissolved upon the bed of manifold conceptualization; they do not awaken, and for that reason I am distressed and agitated. (12)
The tendencies of the mind that flow toward the internal have become dissolved and are as if asleep upon the bed characterized by the conceptualization of attachment to numerous dualistic objects,
unless awakened by the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher.
They do not awaken even through thousands of investigations conducted by their own individual intellects; because of that lack of awakening, I am distressed. 12.
O Brahmin, with my self remaining within the thread of craving that has been firmly knotted and embraced, I am bound by the mind as a bird is trapped in a net.

The term *jālakena* (by means of a net) is a qualification [of the hunter], meaning "by one whose self is situated within that which has been embraced"—that is, placed inside—through mutual identification and association such as "I am this" and "this is mine. Alternatively, the meaning is: by the hunter (*vyādha*) acting as the agent, who is situated upon the line of craving for prey (*āmiṣatṛṣṇāsūtra*), and by means of the net (*jālaka*) acting as the instrument. || 13 ||
O Sage, I am consumed by my mind as dry grass is by fire—with the continuous smoke of indignation and the turbulent flames of anxiety. (14)

He whose smoke is *amarṣa*—that is, anger itself—which is pervasive and spread abroad; and who is agitated by the flame that is anxiety: through this metaphorical construction of the presence of smoke and so forth, it is the similarity to fire that is intended to be expressed, not actual fire-hood; thus there is no contradiction between the metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Under the view that [the term] qualifies the object of comparison (*upamāna*), it is not tolerated.

"It is endured" means *amarṣa* (impatience); likewise, "unbearable" refers to such smoke. "It is thought about by those who are burned" means *cintā* (anxiety); thus it should be explained as "flame. The same applies elsewhere as well. || 14 ||
O Brahmin, by my cruel mind—which has become dull-witted and follows its wife, Greed—I have been devoured as if by a dog devouring a corpse. 15.

"I have become dull and ignorant"—this is the ellipsis. "By the cruel" means by the harsh one. "Craving like a wife" is either a simile-compound (*upamita-samāsa*) or a metaphor (*rūpaka*). Elsewhere, it refers to a dog-like wife whose belly is always unfilled; by such a wife, who follows her like a hound, a corpse has been brought to a state of dullness—that is, to the state of being carried.
The connection is with the phrase "like a corpse. || 15 ||

O Brahmin, I have been carried away by the mind— which is insentient in nature and characterized by a fluctuating motion like the tossing of waves— just as a tree on a riverbank is swept away by a torrent.

In the case of the mind (*cetas*), it refers to one whose mental fluctuations (*vṛttayaḥ*) are as tremulous as waves and are struck back when encountering unattainable objects. In the other sense, it refers to that in which the waves are tremulous and possess the nature of surging; [the *ḍa* and *la* sounds are interchangeable here].
It is for the purpose of falling into an intermediate state, or for wandering in emptiness.
Like a blade of grass by a fierce wind, I have been carried far away—my mind has been led to a distance. || 17 ||

By the practice of Dharma, one ascends to heaven; in its absence, one falls unexpectedly to wander right here among births as insects, moths, and the like, devoid of even a trace of happiness. Thus says the Śruti: "They return again by this very same path," and, "But those who do not travel by either of these two paths, they become these small, crawling creatures."
In the case of comparison, this is clear. || 17 ||
Constantly intent on crossing this ocean of saṃsāra, I have been dammed like a flood of water by a bridge in the form of my evil mind. (18)

"Intent on crossing the ocean of saṃsāra and striving for departure"—in the reading where "jaladhau" (in the ocean) is used as a locative case, the meaning is: "I am intent on crossing, yet I have been held back and stationed right within this ocean of saṃsāra," just as the floodwaters of a small river are dammed by a bridge. || 18 ||
As I was going from the netherworld (pātāla) to the earth, and from the earth back to the netherworld, I have been ensnared by this evil-minded one, like a well-wood [is caught] by a rope-loop. (19)

By the words "earth" (*pṛthvī*) and "netherworld" (*pātāla*), the upper and lower regions resembling them are indicated. [It is] like a ring-shaped object fixed on three wooden spokes with a weight tied to one end by a rope for the purpose of pulling water and other loads;
[it is] merely false, appearing in a vast form, yet fragile when subjected to inquiry.
I am seized by this evil-minded one, like a child possessed by a Vetāla. || 20 ||

Just as a phantom spirit (vetāla) imagined for the purpose of frightening children expands before a child’s mind, yet upon the passing of childhood becomes non-existent through investigation, so too the mind—which is difficult to conquer by the intellect of the ignorant—becomes utterly devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvarūpa) through discernment; such is the meaning. || 20 ||
O Brahman, his mind and its grasp are more intensely hot than fire, more difficult to traverse than even a mountain, and firmer than even a diamond; thus, they are hard to restrain.

Because it cannot even be grasped through suffering, it seizes the characteristic of the mind; thus it is a "grasper" (*graha*), a *piśāca* demon that is exceedingly hot because it constantly causes torment. The method is more difficult; "transgression" (*atikramaṇa*) means bringing under control (*vaśīkāra*).
It is firmer and harder to pierce than even a diamond (*vajra*); or rather, it is more cruel than even a thunderbolt (*aśani*). || 21 ||
The mind falls upon worldly activities like a bird toward pieces of meat;
in an instant it reaches detachment, like a child leaving his toys. 22.

It falls—that is, it immediately becomes attached—to objects that are its tasks; [it seeks] cessation, that is, withdrawal, even from virtuous activities long practiced—this is the ellipsis. Just as a child, having at some time obtained a toy as a cause, [is drawn back], being of a dull nature, fickle, and characterized by the movement of wide whirlpools.
O Father, this serpent devoid of the ocean of the mind leads me far away.

All the adjectives are clearly applicable equally to both the ocean and the mind. "Ahitavyāla" refers to that in which there are six enemies, such as desire (kāma) and the rest, who are like predatory serpents. || 23 ||
O virtuous one, even more difficult than drinking up the great ocean, or uprooting Mount Sumeru,
or even consuming fire, is the restraint of the mind.
It is uneven and more difficult. || 24 ||
The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist. When it is extinguished, the world is extinguished; therefore, it should be treated with diligent effort. (25)
That which is to be treated must necessarily be removed, like a disease. || 25 ||
These hundreds of joys and sorrows surely come from the mind alone,
just as [beasts] come from forests such as Agava;
when that [mind] has become attenuated through the power of solitude.
O Sage, I believe those very things indeed dissolve away with skillful means. || 26 ||

He clarifies what has already been stated by means of an illustration: "from the mind" (*cittāt*). The word "surely" (*nūnam*) expresses conjecture. "Arrived" (*abhyāgatāni*) means grown or developed.
"From the foremost mountain" (*agavarāt*) refers to the Vindhya and other such preeminent peaks. "Attaining thinness" (*tanutām*) means reaching a state of subtlety;
that is to say, becoming like parched seeds due to the absence of latent impressions (*nirvāsanatayā*). || 26 ||
I have set my mind upon conquering that enemy against whom the great ones have bound their hopes for victory through all their virtues; yet,
due to the absence of inner attachment, I do not welcome even the Goddess of Fortune herself.
Like the moon [dispelling] a streak of clouds characterized by dullness, impurity, and playfulness. || 27 ||

When that mind has been conquered by great seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*), there is the victory—that is, the attainment—of that [state] wherein all qualities such as tranquility (*śānti*) and self-restraint (*dānti*) reside, and wherein the fragments of bliss culminate in unsurpassed bliss. The meaning is that it is bound by hope. "In this very body" means: if one has known [it] here, then the Truth exists; otherwise, it does not.
"Should he not know this here, there would be great ruin," according to the Śruti; thus, I am prepared and striving.

By means of the attainment of dispassion (vairāgya), which is characterized by the absence of worldly attachment, she enlivens, inspires, and adorns those within the inner mind who are dull, foolish, and impure. She whose "enlivening" (vilāsa) consists of dullness as the cause of delusion and impurity as the cause of sin.
Or [it refers to] that [cloud-streak]. In the case of the cloud-streak, the meaning is that it shines, being dark blue and soiled by water. || 27 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Wickedness of the Dispassionate Mind," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa composed by Valmīki, according to the tradition of the Rishis. || 16 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Wickedness of the Mind Regarding Dispassion," in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventeenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"By this endless thirst, which is like a female jackal in the inner darkness of the heart..."
O Kauśika, rows of faults, like owls, flicker in the sky of consciousness.
Here, craving alone is censured; it is the mother of the flood of all evils, the giver of death through wretchedness and misery, and that which causes the entire world to wander.

When the reality of the Self— the abode of supreme love within the heart and born of the heart— is obscured by the blinding darkness of ignorance, which is difficult to endure and difficult to eradicate, then in this sky of consciousness, that is, in the individual soul (jīva),
there appear rows of owls characterized by defects such as passion and the like. || 1 ||
My essence and tenderness have been consumed by anxiety, which brings internal burning; I am being dried up by it, just as mud is dried by the heat of the sun.
In whom the essence and softness—whether as affection and compassion, or courtesy and humility—have been utterly suppressed or stolen away;

or [in whom] the essence and softness, well-known [to others], have reached a state like that of mud; or else, by whom the essence and softness have been perfectly hidden or lost, such as I am now, reduced to withering, that is, to a state of emptiness.
This is the meaning. || 2 ||
In the great forest of my mind, which is crowded with the darkness of delusion and empty, the demoness of hope has become a frantic dancer.
In the case of emptiness, by means of investigation; in the case of the forest, by means of people. || 3 ||
With frost formed by her eloquent speech and radiant with groves of gold,
the chickpea-cluster of her thought surely comes into full bloom.

The misty spray of water-drops formed by the words of her various piteous lamentations is radiant because it produces a paleness [in her] through an excess of longing for the forest near the gold (*kāñcana*)— or, in another sense,
by the turn of phrase that chickpeas (*caṇaka*) grow only with frost-water, the frost-water drops were produced by the night.

In this [place], where a cluster of chickpea plants—characterized by anxiety and possessing a brilliant splendor due to the nearby grove of thorn-apple trees—blooms in the field; indeed, it is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): "Surely, with a mind agitated by craving, she has come here merely for the sake of wandering within."
It has arrived like a wave of uneven splendor in the ocean.

With a restless disposition, her mind agitated; elsewhere, with her waist trembling—thirst, like a wave in the ocean, has brought about an excessive internal wandering, namely, an enthusiasm for acquiring wealth that is characterized by violent surges and thick with hardship; elsewhere, it leads only to aimless roaming.
The meaning is that she has attained a dissimilar dance in the higher realms. || 5 ||
Here on the mountain of my body flows the river of craving, surging with waves of restless form and the roar of unrestrained turbulence.

The river characterized by craving—which possesses the roaring waves of active engagement such as insults and false speech that are unrestrained and surging; which, for that very reason, has a tremulous form due to its aforementioned ripples and flows, crossing from one sense-object to another—is flowing, coursing through the mountain of my body. (6)
Like an old blade of grass driven by a whirlwind, the *cātaka*-bird of my mind has been led away somewhere by turbid craving, which delights in obstructing its momentum. (7)

*Vega* means his own restlessness. *Udita* means exerted. He was led away by the force of the wind—the gusts of passion—to some unsuitable object, in order to drink the essence of the samādhi known as the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*). || 7 ||
Whichever excellence of virtue I take as my firm refuge,
that very thing thirst cuts away for me, just as a rat gnaws at a string.

Regarding the abundance of virtues such as discernment and dispassion, whatever reliance I place upon them, I wander in the wheel of thought like an old leaf in water, like an old blade of grass in the wind, or like an autumn cloud in the sky. (9)
In milk, in the water of a whirlpool. || 9 ||
We, whose intellects are powerless, are unable to reach our own proper station;
we are bewildered by the snare of thought, like birds caught in a net.
To go toward—that is, to attain—one's own abode, one's own foundation; that is to say, the ultimate form. || 10 ||
O dear one, I have been so scorched by the flame called craving that I do not hope for the cessation of this burning even through ambrosia.
I suspect; I consider it possible. || 11 ||
Having gone far, far away from here, and having met again and again, the mare, intoxicated by thirst, wanders swiftly toward the ends of the quarters. (12)
The repetition is for the purpose of including objects that are separated or remote. || 12 ||
Craving, which associates with the insentient, causes one's movement up and down;
it is perpetually agitated, knotted, and like the rope at the top of a waterwheel. (13)

She by whom the coming and going—the movement to and fro between heaven and hell—are brought about and accomplished in accordance with the objects consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);
she who is agitated and set in motion; [she who is characterized by] the identity and connection between the enjoyer and the enjoyed—these four epithets are indeed well-known. || 13 ||
Like a powerful ox driven by a rope, people are swiftly led away by this craving, which is woven within the body and is impossible for all to sever. (14)

"Bound within the body and the inner mind"—in some versions it says "bound" (*grathitayā*)—meaning bound or strung together; in the analogy of the ox's rope, it means strung through regions such as the nose. It is "dragged," meaning burdened by the weight of thousands of means for achieving results in this world and the next.
By the ever-pulling thirst for sons, friends, wives, and so forth, this snare is spread throughout the worlds by Kirātī, as if among birds. (15)

By means of that craving which is of such a nature—constantly pulling and attracting—it is as if a net is spread among the birds; likewise, this well-known net consisting of sons, friends, wives, and so forth, is woven by it among people in the worlds.
Like a dark night, this craving terrifies even the steadfast, blinds even the discerning eye, and exhausts even the joyful. 16.
Steadfast means wise and courageous; possessing insight means having the eye of discernment and being renowned;
"śarvarī" means night. || 16 ||
Crooked, soft to the touch, and signaling the imbalance of poison, craving—like a black female serpent—bites even when only slightly touched. (17)

She possesses a thousandfold guile (*kauṭilya*). Her touch is tender, intent upon a mere fragment of pleasure, and she is the acquisition of sense-objects (*viṣaya*). Yet in its ultimate consequence, she is habituated to proclaiming that instability which resembles the objects themselves—such as enmity, bondage, and slaughter. She utterly deludes, as if biting with her fangs. In the case of the female serpent (*bhoginī*), the meaning is clear. || 17 ||
Tearing the hearts of men, creating a world of illusion, bestowing misfortune, and wretched—thirst is like a black female demon. 18.

She is the nature that produces all things characterized by illusion—such as deceit and the like—which are the effects of *māyā*, as well as diseases and ailments; she is misfortune, the state of being ill-fated; she is wretched and full of dejection. (18)
O Brahmin, the lute of craving—its strings being the clusters of lassitude—shines not in bliss, for it holds its hollow body wrapped around with them. 19.

She bore a body that was like a worn-out lute— a vessel encircled by lassitude, drowsiness, and the multitude of strings, which are the collection of channels (nāḍīs). For even that lute, with its strings severed through exhaustion— the laziness of failing to provide the inner gourd— and its gourd covered with stitches, is likewise worn out and cracked.
Even a sage does not shine in that undistracted, unsurpassed bliss which is obtained through the destruction of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Thus it has been said:
"Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving. (19)
Ever exceedingly filthy, bestowing bitter madness, long-stretched, thick with affection, craving is like a creeper in a deep abyss. (20)
That which is bitter and results in suffering is intoxication; such is the nature of that gift and conduct. The rest is clear.

A "mountain-creeper" (*gahvaravallarī*) is a vine growing in a mountain cave. For it is well known among those who have seen it that, because it is never touched by the rays of the sun, it is constantly moist with thick sap and possesses abundant resin. || 20 ||
Bringing no joy, empty, fruitless, and raised in vain;
inauspicious and cruel—craving is like a withered flower-cluster. (21)

Regarding the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the meaning is clear. In other cases, it is "empty of flowers. It is "elevated" because it stands upon the upper branches of mango trees and the like; it is "cruel" because, being withered, it consists mostly of thorns. || 21 ||
Even when her mind is not won over, craving pursues everything; yet it obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman longing for love.
By which [woman] the mind is neither attracted nor brought under control; "fruit" means gain or enjoyment; "an aged woman" refers to an elderly courtesan. || 22 ||
In the great multitude of saṃsāra, crowded with various flavors, craving is like an aged dancer upon the stages of the expansive worlds. (23)
By various sentiments such as grief and delusion—in the case of the dancer, by [the dramatic rasas] such as compassion, laughter, and disgust—upon the stages, that is, in the dance halls. || 23 ||
In the long wilderness of saṃsāra, craving is a spreading poisonous creeper, blossoming with old age and bearing a succession of fruits that fall and rise. (24)
In the forest, in the dilapidated wilderness; "tata" means extensive. || 24 ||
Even when she is unable [to achieve her goal], there too she adopts a dancing gait;
devoid of joy, craving dances like an aged actress. (25)
The ellipsis is "he is not able to accomplish it. Elsewhere, the ellipsis is "if he were to go there. It is devoid of bliss because of weakness, due to a lack of enthusiasm. || 25 ||
When the mist thickens, she quivers; when light arrives, she becomes still;
and when obstacles are difficult to overcome, the fickle peahen of anxiety sets foot upon them. (26)

It manifests and dances in the mist, in the rain, and in the frost; likewise, it manifests and dances in the light of discernment (*viveka*), characterized by clarity, and in the autumn. It places its foot—meaning its resolve—and its nest upon those things that are difficult to traverse and inaccessible. (26)
Abounding with dull waves and long remaining empty within its depths, craving is like a river in the rainy season that rises in agitation for only a moment. (27)
For a long time, it is empty of fruits and water out of season; even during that season, it is empty at intervals within its course.
"Exultation" refers to the increase resulting from the abundance of fruits and water. A river of the rainy season is one that flows only during the monsoon. || 27 ||
Leaving behind one who has perished, craving moves on from man to man like a restless bird, seeking another tree as it stands. (28)
She was ruined, her purpose destroyed; she was restless with craving and distressed by hunger and thirst. || 28 ||
Though she has already stepped upon what is unassailable, though she is satisfied, she still seeks further fruit;
she does not remain long in one place—thirst is a restless female monkey. (29)
"In the unassailable, the hard-to-reach, and the difficult to cross; the determined step and the placing of the foot; the fruit, the gain, and the unripe seed. (29)
"Having done this, that comes to pass"—all of it is indeed inconsistent;
yet craving strives unceasingly, like a divine impulse. (30)
Having begun this auspicious or appropriate task, even before it is completed, this inauspicious, inappropriate, improper,
and contrary-to-order undertaking suddenly arrives and pursues him; yet he does not desist, but instead exerts himself incessantly at all times.

For the sake of auspicious and inauspicious results, just as the activity of the Creator follows the karma of living beings, so it is: "In one moment thirst—the bee within the lotus of the heart—descends to the underworld; in another moment it ascends to the vault of heaven; in another moment it wanders through the groves of the directions. (31)
In the heart-lotus is the six-footed humming bee; the rest is mostly as explained previously. 31.
Craving alone is the giver of long-lasting suffering among all the defects of saṃsāra;
it casts even one dwelling in the inner apartments into extreme peril. (32)

It bestows long-lasting suffering; it bestows enduring misery. Like a long fishing line, it drags one into the presence of the executioner and bestows the sufferings of death and so forth. He establishes this very point with the words: "Even while staying in the inner apartments," etc. (32).
Craving is a garland of clouds that bestows supreme dullness, obstructs the highest light, and is dense with the mist of delusion. 33.

*Jāḍyam* means dullness, folly, or coldness. *Paramālokaḥ* refers to the supreme light, the Self, and the sun. It deludes (*mohayati*) the distinction between the directions, such as east and west; thus, *moha* is non-discrimination. Because of that mist (*nīhāra*) consisting of such delusion, it is dense and difficult to traverse. || 33 ||
For all classes of living beings engaged in the cycle of existence, craving is like a binding rope that has woven together the garland of their minds. (34)

Like a garland formed by many animals strung together by neck-cords, this craving— transverse, long, of variegated colors, defective, extended, and foul in its condition— is empty, consisting of empty states, and bearing the likeness of Indra’s bow. (35)

She is possessed of various colors because she is colored by diverse objects; she possesses a form that causes manifold wonder. She is devoid of qualities (*viguṇā*), meaning she lacks true virtues and is devoid of the bowstring. The "man" (*puruṣa*) is dark, and he is her support (*saṃsthiti*); she is empty (*śūnyā*) because of her inherent worthlessness and is a non-entity (*avastu*). She is the "abode of emptiness" (*śūnyapadā*) because she resides within the sky of the mind.
The bow of Śakra is the Indrāyudha (Indra’s weapon). || 35 ||
She is a thunderbolt to the crops of virtues, a harvest-season for calamities,
frost to the lotuses of consciousness, and a long night for the darknesses.

She is a thunderbolt to the crops characterized by virtues; she is frost, meaning a destroyer, to the lotuses of consciousness—that is, the lotuses of awakening. But for calamities, she is the autumn that increases them, meaning she is one in whom calamities have borne fruit.
Likewise, she is the winter night to the darknesses. 36.
She is the actress in the drama of saṃsāra, the female bird in the aviary of the workplace,
the doe in the forest of the mind, and the lute for the concert of Smara.
Of the office—characterized by activity—or of the nest, that is, the upper chamber of the house; "mental" refers to the desires of the mind; "vallakī" means a lute. || 37 ||

She is the wave of the ocean of worldly affairs, the chain for the elephant of delusion, the beautiful creeper upon the banyan tree of creation, and the moonlight for the night-lily of suffering. (38)
It is called *nyagrodha* because it grows downwards; it is the banyan tree (*vaṭa*). Its beautiful creeper is a climbing vine. [This refers to] the *kairavas*, the night-lotuses (*kumuda*).
A single jewel casket for the sufferings of old age and death, she is eternally intoxicated, a playful courtesan of mental anguish and physical disease. (39)
A small box and a casket. || 39 ||
For a moment craving is like a pure light upon its objects, for a moment it is a fragment of darkness;
for a moment it is like the path of the sky, and for a moment it is dense with mist. (40)
Light is the slight illumination of discernment; the path is like the very sky. It is pervaded by things resembling mist.
For the sake of calming the exertion of the body, craving comes to rest, just as the night—black with thick darkness—is for the cessation of Rākṣasas.

Having thus described craving (*tṛṣṇā*), he states the fruit of its pacification with the words beginning "He goes" (*gacchati*). "For the sake of the body's exertion" means for the sake of the fatigue applied to the body; that is to say, for the sake of liberation. "Tamī" refers to a night of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). It is "black" because of the dense darkness of clouds (*ghanatamas*); as such, it is like that [night].
Just as [darkness] goes to its pacification or destruction for the sake of warding off demons and the absence of the movement of night-stalkers,
so too this world, mute and with its inner disposition agitated, remains deluded only so long as the cholera of the poison of craving continues to persist. (42)

The mute one is devoid of discourse on the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra). "The world" refers to people. "One whose disposition is agitated" means one whose mind is disturbed. Just as the disease of cholera caused by the administration of a particular poison is a cause of death, so too craving—pursuing [its objects]—binds and firmly maintains them; that is to say, it does not let go. || 42 ||
This entire world abandons all suffering when freed from anxiety;
indeed, the abandonment of anxiety is said to be the mantra for the cholera of craving. (43)

In that case, what is the means for abandoning that? To this he says: "The world," etc. Here, "thought" (cintā) refers to the recollection of sense-objects. [The world] is abandoned—that is, relinquished—by such [recollection]. And thus is the word of the Blessed One: "For a person who broods over sense-objects, attachment to them arises. || 43 ||
Grasping at everything—grass, stones, wood, and so forth—with the suspicion that it might be meat, craving quivers at the end, just like a female fish in a lake. (44)
"Out of suspicion of meat," that is, with the expectation that it was edible. As it is said:

"Just as the rays of the sun quickly cause even a deep lotus to rise to the surface, so too do the thirst for women and the affliction of disease quickly bring even a profound man to a state of superficiality. (45)
Affliction by disease and thirst for women; [the breath] deep and steady [indicates] shallowness, lack of fortitude, and upward expansion. 45.
Hollow within, knotted, and possessing long shoots as their thorns, craving is like a bamboo vine that is ever fond of pearl-jewels. (46)

The knots are firm attachments, and the joints are the sprouts of craving; the thorns are sufferings, and pearls are those who are dear to them. In the case of the bamboo creepers, they are the pearl-mines for them—oh, how truly wonderful it is that even craving possesses such great intelligence!
They cut even that which is difficult to sever, by means of the stainless sword of discernment.
He shows that even discernment (*viveka*) is a cause for its destruction, saying: "Aho! (Verse 47).
Neither the edge of a sword, nor the flame of a thunderbolt, nor the glowing sparks of heated iron are as sharp as this craving that dwells within the heart, wandering there. (48)

The meaning is that while things such as the edge of a sword cause harm only occasionally because they are external, craving, however, exists within the heart and therefore causes harm at all times; thus, it is even more severe than those [external dangers]. || 48 ||
Brilliant, with a dark and sharp tip, possessing long wicks of attachment, luminous yet painful to touch through its burning nature—craving is like the flame of a lamp. (49)

That which is radiant with the splendor of enjoyments in the middle, but whose tip is dark and sharp at the end—meaning it culminates in darkness and death; that which has long stages of childhood, youth, and old age made supreme by affection for mother, wife, and son; and which is manifest and perceptible.
In the case of the lamp-flame, "affection" (sneha) refers to the oil, and "condition" (daśā) refers to the wick;
the rest is clear. [49]
Even the best of men—whether he be as wise as Meru, or heroic, or steadfast—a single craving makes him as insignificant as a blade of grass in the blink of an eye. (50)
He is like Mount Meru in his dignity; he is steadfast by virtue of his vow of non-possession. He treats the wretchedness of begging as if it were a blade of grass.
Cotton is lighter than grass, and the beggar is even lighter than cotton. Why was he not blown away by the wind? [I thought:
"This man will come to beg from me. (50)

The great slope of the Vindhya mountain is thirst itself: its dense thickets are the spreading of desires, it is terrifying, composed of masses of clouds and dust, and filled with blinding darkness and fierce mist. (51)

In which [city] there are forests that are strewn wide, extensive, dense, and places of daring deeds; or rather, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—which is hope (*āśā*)—is both extensive and dense, difficult to perceive, throughout the fourteen worlds due to states such as desire, greed, and lustfulness. Thus, it is like a binding by a thick net.
It is dense with a web of dust and abundant with pollen; the rest is clear. || 51 ||
Desire alone, having found its mark within all worlds, has become difficult to perceive even while remaining embodied;
it persists in the world like a series of flickering waves.
In the midst of the waves of the milk-and-water ocean, his power is like that of nectar. || 52 ||

How is it extensive, how is it profound, and how is it one? [The author] establishes this through an illustration based on the distinctions of the substratum, the object, sound, and so forth, stating: "It is indeed one. Thirst, though situated within the body, is truly one;
having found its mark and attained its objects among all the enjoyments within the interiors of all worlds, it exists throughout the universe.

The meaning is that on the plane of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the thirst for the body alone remains, having become difficult to perceive; it has attained the state of all forms of thirst, such as hope and desire, and thus it cannot be clearly discerned.
Just as the single power of sweetness residing in the body through the nature of the gustatory faculty [is not perceived as such by everyone].

Established within the waters of the worlds—that is, within the commonality of water found in rivers, oceans, and the like, which possess flickering rows of waves—she is called *udaka* because of its flowing (*ud-kṣaraṇa*), its cleansing (*ud-un-dana*), its moistening (*ud-klēdana*), and its swelling (*ud-am-bhana*); she is called *ambu* because of its sounding (*ud-am-bhana*). Thus, through the distinction of action and sound, she resides in that fluid, unstable water as coolness (*śītā*).

Just as [the water] has reached a state of being difficult to distinguish, such that it is not perceived as being only one [with the milk], so too are life, the world, the forest, water, milk, and the sky [indistinguishable]. (Amara-kośa) || 52 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Breaking of Thirst," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. || 17 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Breaking of Thirst," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa.
The eighteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
It is dense with the strings of moist entrails, subject to transformation, and prone to putrefaction.
The body flickers within saṃsāra, and even that leads only to suffering.

In this world, the body alone is censured as the source of mental and physical ailments, manifold afflictions, and the frailty of old age and death, as well as the cause of pride, craving, and the like.

One might object: "Granted that craving is the cause of suffering, nevertheless, according to the maxim 'while living, one sees auspicious things,' and because the body is well-known as the locus for the enjoyment of pleasure, and because everyone is seen to have an intense attachment toward it, it must be a cause of happiness. Anticipating this, he demonstrates that even that [the body] is indeed a cause of suffering:

By the words beginning with "ārdra" [it is meant]: the intestines (*āntrāṇi*) are the bellows of impurities such as excrement and urine located within the belly; the tendons (*tantryaḥ*) are the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*); and falling all around (*paritaḥ pātaḥ*) refers to the injury of falling and death. || 1 ||
Though ignorant, he resembles one who knows; through the wonder of his own unfolding nature, he is neither insentient nor sentient, being both capable and incapable by way of reasoning.

Though ignorant and inert, he knows that which is inert; thus, being "tajjña" (knower of that), the Self is similar to it and of its nature. By its own nature, it is not inert—it is the wonder of the Self in which the identity with the superimposed mind is projected. It is "bhavya," meaning capable of attaining the qualification for liberation.
It is not inert, nor is it like other forms of inertia. || 2 ||
One whose mind wavers between the views of the insentient and the sentient, being undiscriminating and deluded in soul, brings about nothing but further delusion. (3)

Therefore, when the mind— wavering in doubt between the perspectives of consciousness and insentience as to whether this [body] belongs to the category of the Self or the category of the non-Self— is afflicted by indecision; and when discernment (viveka) is absent due to that lack of purification— then, O Discerner of the Non-insentient, the former [the body] is delusion, which is indeed transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), because of the notion of "Self" held toward this body.
He does not perceive the goal of human endeavor, because his evil disposition is wavering; that is to say, his impure mind is flickering. || 3 ||
With a slight [cause] one attains joy, and with a slight [cause] one falls into distress;
there is no object of grief equal to the body, which is base and devoid of virtue.
By "a little" (stokena) is meant by a small amount of food, drink, and so forth, as well as by cold, heat, and so forth. "Low" (nīcaḥ) means inferior; that is to say, impure. || 4 ||
He is constantly adorned at every moment by a flower of blossoming smiles, which possesses ever-emerging and receding [teeth] and is graced with the filaments of his teeth.
In order to express their worthiness for equanimity (*upekṣā*), he represents them as trees—representing them by means of four qualities:
the four beginning with "scriptural tradition" (*āgama*) and so forth—and at every moment, at every fragment of joy, and at every season. (Verse 5)
With arms as branches and a thick trunk, with a noble stance like a pillar of ivory,
he was occupied by the bees of her eyes, his head being the broad fruit upon its pedestal.

The shoulders are his dense and lofty trunk, and the arms are the roots of its branches. The teeth are the birds that dwell there through their attachment. His hands and feet are the beautiful sprouts, while the mass of his limbs is like a thicket where birds have made their home.
The two ears are the "ears" (*śravau*); those very [ears] are tasted by the "tooth," thus they are the "tooth-tasters" (*dantarasau*), birds known as wood-peckers (*kāṣṭhakuṭṭaka*).

He is seized by them and, as if crushed by their beak-strokes, becomes perforated. A "shrub" (*gulma*) is a particular disease as well as root-sprouts; one who possesses these is so described. It is "to be done" (*kāryaḥ*), meaning it is possible to perform; [it refers to] a complete destruction.
When the mantra is perfected, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), or the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva), hold his heart-nest. || 7 ||

This tree of the body, possessing its own shade and serving as a resting place for the multitude of travelers that are living beings—whose is it as "one's own," and whose is it as "another's"? Indeed, what room is there here for attachment or detachment?

"Shadow" (chāyā) means luster, as well as the well-known shadow; "enemy" (paraḥ) means an adversary; "attachment" (āsthā) means affection, and "non-attachment" (anāsthā) means hatred. The sense is that one should disregard these two, which are inappropriate for this tree-like body. || 8 ||
O dear one, when the boat of the body has been repeatedly taken up for the purpose of crossing over,
who could possibly maintain the notion of it being a self?
[Objection: "But surely this [self], which is well-known to all people as the 'Self,' how can it be disregarded? To this he says: "O Father!

Crossing means the crossing over of the river of life or the reaching of the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra. [This occurs] in a boat—that is, in a ship—[which is like] a forest named "body," empty and crowded with many pits.
9. In the empty forest called the body, which is filled with many pitfalls...
Who can place their trust in a tree whose branches are as numerous as body hairs? || 10 ||
"Trust" (viśvāsam) means the conviction that one is fit for staying there for a long time without apprehension. || 10 ||
O dear one, within this fragile body-drum, bound together by flesh,
sinews, and bones, I remain like a cat, having lost my way.
Tendons and veins; a *paṭaha* is a specific type of drum. "In that which is not firm," meaning in that which is insubstantial and full of holes;
"in that whose sound has passed away," meaning in that which lacks the sound of instruction regarding the means for attainment or departure. || 11 ||
Grown within the forest of saṃsāra, this monkey of the flickering mind has the appearance of a wish-fulfilling creeper, yet it is gnawed by the woodworm of long-standing suffering.

Furthermore, he characterizes the body itself as a *plakṣa* tree by means of six [verses], beginning with "In saṃsāra... and so forth. *Ghuṇas* are wood-worms; it is "perforated" (*kṣata*) by them, meaning riddled with holes. || 12 ||
This body is the dwelling place of the female serpent of craving, the abode of the crow of anger;
it is the source of the merit of smiles, yet it possesses the great fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Because the bark, sprouts, and so forth of the *plakṣa* tree are auspicious and thus a cause for the arising of merit, there is "the arising of established merit" (*sthitapuṇyodgama*).
Alternatively, the reading is "the arising of flowers" (*puṣpodgama*). || 13 ||
With a mass of beautiful clusters for his shoulders and a lovely bouquet for his hands,
all the sprouts of his limbs were made to tremble by the wind.

By the word *skandha*, the arms are indicated; *latā* means branches. Amara states: "The words *śākhā* and *latā* are synonymous. The two words *ogha* and *jāla* are to be understood as distinct parts of the body. This is because the form of a *plakṣa* tree is described solely on the basis of their common genus (*jāti*).
Here, *pavana* refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 14 ||
He is the support for all the birds of the senses, with well-formed pillars of knees, lofty, endowed with the luster of a lake, and frequented by travelers in the form of desire. || 15 ||

He whose lower body—consisting of beautiful knees and middle joints—is like a pillar; as long as that [body] is endowed with the fresh luster of youth and a cool shade, so long is it frequented by the travelers of desire (Kāma). This is the meaning. || 15 ||
Upon its head is a long row of grass-like hair;
it is a hollow belly where the vulture of egoism has built its nest.
The word division is *ādi-dīrgha*. It is well known that grass sometimes grows even upon a *plakṣa* tree. || 16 ||
With its roots—the web of latent impressions—severed, this body-plakṣa tree has become difficult to grasp; devoid of the vigor of exertion, it brings me no pleasure. (17)

Its form—that is, its essential nature—is difficult to approach and hard to sever, because its root is entwined by a mass of matted locks born from the sprouting of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*). It is "distasteful" (*virasa*) due to the various stretches (*vyāyāma*) of exertion, which constitute the length of its branches; it is also "rough," being devoid of the touch of one's beloved. (17)
O Sage, this body is the great house for the dweller who is the ego; let it roll about or attain stability—what does that matter to me? (18)
Let him roll upon the ground, having fallen down, and let him turn over. || 18 ||
This house of the body is not desired by me, for its senses are like cattle bound in rows, its inner chamber is greed for strength, and all its limbs are dyed with passion. (19)

In which [house] the mistress of the home, characterized by craving, repeatedly falters and spreads; therefore, all its limbs are dyed with passion—that is, with desire—and with coloring substances such as red ochre. || 19 ||
This house of the body is undesirable to me; it is a hollow space constricted by the friction of the wooden beams of the spinal vertebrae and bound together by the ropes of the intestines.

That which has a hollow (*koṭara*) whose space is completely narrow and constricted due to the friction of the bones of the spine, which serve as its supporting beams; [the *antrāṇi*] are the long muscular tubes for the purpose of spreading out the internal organs, excrement, urine, the essence of food, and so forth. [20]
This house of my body, with its strings of spreading sinews, its mire made of blood-water, and white with the *maṅkola* flower of old age, is not pleasing to me. (21)
That in which the sinews and veins are the strings—like the wires of a lute or binding cords—is [the body].
Since the word *nāḍī* (vein) is not a term for a limb of one's own body (*asvāṅga*), the suffix *kan* is prohibited by the rule *svāṅge*. Maṅkola is a type of powder.
The stability of the body is occupied by infinite activities performed by the servant that is the mind.
This body-house of mine, with false delusion as its great pillar, is not desired by me.

"Support" (avaṣṭambha) means the counteraction of falling. "Falsehood" (mithyā) means untruth, and "delusion" (moha) means ignorance. "Pillars" (sthūṇa) refers to supporting columns; it may be understood as a *karmadhāraya* compound [meaning "falsehood-delusion-pillars"]. || 22 ||
This house of my body is not desired by me; it is filled with the wailing of children in distress, made pleasant only by a comfortable bed, and its servant-woman is consumed by wicked cravings.
In whom that very evil desire—wicked conduct, burnt, and afflicted by the pain of burning wounds—is a slave. || 23 ||
This house of the body is not pleasing to me; it is crowded with the vessels and utensils of the array of sense-objects rich in impurity, and it is encircled by the brine of ignorance.

Therefore, this house of my body—filled with impurities, abounding in defects, and never cleansed; its foundation being the hips, its pillars the thighs, its lintel the knees, its upper beam the head, and its sturdy wooden beams the long arms—is not desired by me. (25)

The ankle of the pillar of the shank is *guggulu*, serving as the position of the supporting beam; upon it rests and is established the knee, which is the capital of that pillar of the shank. That too is established through a succession [of supports] upon its own support’s support, for if the root were loose, the consequence would be the loosening of everything. The two arms are the *doṣau*. 25.
O Brahmin, this house of my body is pleasing to me; within it, the windows of the eyes are wide open, the courtyard of the house is the playing field of wisdom, and anxiety is its daughter. (26)

The "manifest senses" are the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*). "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the intellect (*buddhi*). The word "manifest" is either a qualifier of that [wisdom] or an adverbial modifier of the action. || 26 ||
This house of my body is not pleasing to me; for its beautiful moon-chamber of the ears is covered by the roof of the hair on my head, and its turrets consist of my very long fingers.
The hair on the head is the thatch; the ears themselves are the earrings, pearls, and so forth.

This body-house, with its mass of walls formed by the collection of all limbs, its thick grass-sprouts of body hair, and its hollow interior like an empty chest, is not desired by me as a dwelling. (28)
The opening of the belly, the cavity of the stomach. || 28 ||
This abode of the navel-center, filled with the constant noise of the vital winds and the sound of digestion, this body-house is not desired by me. (29)
Like a female dog (saramā), she causes wandering, wretchedness, quarrels, and the like; her inner being resounds with hunger. "Bhāṅkāra" refers to a terrifying sound. || 29 ||
That house of my body, with its wide-open windows of the eyes, is not pleasing to me, as it is never at rest due to the force of the wind agitated by the constant coming and going [of the breath].
This house of the body is not desired by me; it is terrifying with the door of the mouth overrun by the monkey of the tongue, and its fragments of bone-like teeth are visible.
A "markaṭikā" is well known as a wooden bolt used to bar a door. || 31 ||
This house of my body, smooth with the plaster of skin, flickering due to the movement of its machinery, and constantly undermined by the rat of the mind, is not desired by me. 32.

"Sudhā" means lime-powder; "tvag-sudhā-lepa" refers to a coating of lime on the bark, by which it becomes smooth and glossy. "Yantra" refers to mills, carts, and the like; the "saṃcāra" of their joints refers to their movement, such as rotation, or the movement of those very parts themselves. "Manaḥ-sadātana-ākhu" means a mouse that is eternally present in the mind; by it, as if dug up, there is looseness [of the joints].
My body-house is not desirable, for it is sometimes illuminated by the light of a lamp-like smile, beautiful with joy for a moment, and at other times pervaded by floods of darkness.
The smiles are indeed slight laughs; they are lamps [that dispel] the floods of darkness, which are streams of the gloom of ignorance. || 33 ||

This body-house, the abode of all diseases, a city of wrinkles and grey hair, a dense thicket of all diarrhea and all mental afflictions—is not desired by me. (34) *Valī* means the loosening of the skin. *Pattana* means a city, that is to say, a place of residence. *Ādhi*s are mental afflictions.
Those very mental sufferings constitute its essence, primarily because they are what is experienced; by them, it is dense, difficult to traverse, or like a vast wilderness. || 34 ||

Unstable due to the agitation of the senses and the constellations, empty, hollow and pithless, with the thickets of the quarters shrouded in darkness—this forest of my body is not desired by me. (35)
The senses themselves are the dice; they are the gambling pieces. || 35 ||
"O Lord of Sages, I am unable to sustain this abode of a body, just as one of little strength cannot rescue an elephant sunk in the mud. (36)
What is the use of prosperity, what of sovereignty, what of the body, and what of one's endeavors?
In just a few days, Time cuts away everything. (37)
By means of endeavors, actions, or desires, it cuts or severs. || 37 ||
O Sage, tell me: what beauty can there be in this body, which consists of blood and flesh, including its exterior and interior, and whose sole nature is destruction? (38)
"Having reflected upon everything external and internal"—this is the ellipsis. || 38 ||
O dear one, tell me, what reliance can there be for the wise upon those ungrateful bodies which do not follow the life-principle at the time of death? (39)
They do not follow, they do not pursue. They destroy the assistance provided through protection, nourishment, and so forth, in return for their own benefit.
(40) "My body is as unstable as the tip of an elephant's ear in rut, and as fragile as a dangling drop of water.
Before it abandons me, I shall abandon it. (40)

Fickle and unsteady; with hanging, dangling drops of water; trembling due to proximity to the wind stirred by intoxicated elephants; fragile like a sprout on the body; worn out, thin, and crooked—such a person, bitter and sapless, is not desired by me. (41)
Wounded by hundreds of thorns of mental and physical ailments, it is worn out and frail; thin and round, it is of a base nature.
Having for a long time fed upon and drunk from that which is as delicate as a young sprout, it becomes emaciated and, without effort, hastens toward its destruction. (42)

Like a young sprout, she is delicate and soft; "tanutām" means emaciation. If the reading is "pelavam," it functions as an adverbial modifier (kriyāviśeṣaṇa). In both cases, the propriety [of the comparison] is established through the medium of the substratum. || 42 ||
Indeed, this physical body does not feel shame as it repeatedly experiences those very same pleasures and pains, consisting of both existence and non-existence. (43)

Furthermore, those very same things previously experienced are repeated again and again. Since the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) already ascends to the mind, it is grasped by the pronoun; thus, even without reduplication—or rather, by means of reduplication—the sense of repetition is obtained. "Prākṛta" means a commoner or a vulgar person. 43.
Having exercised sovereignty for a very long time and having enjoyed the glory of wealth and power, why is this body maintained, when it attains neither height nor stability? (44)

Having cultivated [virtue] and attained height, growth, or excellence, as well as stability and imperishability—[yet] at the time of old age it undergoes decay, and likewise at the time of death it meets its end;
thus the body is exactly the same for both the wealthy and the poor, being indifferent to distinctions. 44–45.
Within the belly of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the midst of the cavern of craving, this mute tortoise of a body sleeps, as if liberated. (46)

Craving itself is a small, narrow opening like a hollow lotus. He is as if asleep, utterly deluded; therefore, he is devoid of the desire and effort conducive to liberating himself from this world; for that very reason, he is mute, lacking the speech to approach his guru and inquire of him. He is submerged in the mire of foul sense-objects by the wicked senses, which are like crocodiles.
In this ocean of saṃsāra, numerous pieces of wood that are human bodies—each fit for the single purpose of being consumed by fire—are carried along; yet among them, they recognize only a rare man.
Burning alone is the single purpose, the primary objective; "among those" means among those things suitable for that [purpose]. || 47 ||
For the discerning person, there is no purpose whatsoever in this bodily form, which is encircled by long-standing wickedness and which causes the falling of the fruit of one's downfall. (48)

*Valana* is *vala*, meaning expansion or coiling. *Nipāta* is downward movement; that whose fall (*pāta*)—meaning death—is the fruit thereof, or which terminates in that, is *nipātaphala*. Alternatively, it refers to that from which a fall occurs due to evil deeds (*duścarita*) which have such a fall as their fruit. || 48 ||
Sinking into the mire of the womb, it suddenly reaches old age;
no one knows how this "frog of the body" passes away so soon. (49)
In the mud-pits of the mire-filled pools of sensory objects, how and by what miserable conditions does the frog-like mind endure? 49.
All undertakings are devoid of essence, and bodies are like fleeting winds;
as they travel along the path of dust, they are not seen here by anyone. (50)

They are pithless and sapless. The bodies themselves are as fickle as winds or tempestuous gales. By the path of passion—meaning through the activity of *rajas*, or else by the path of the sky which is reduced to mere dust or accompanied by dust—they depart elsewhere.
O Blessed One, the movement of the wind, of a lamp, and of the mind going forth is known, but never that of the body as it comes back. (51)

Here, having drawn over from the preceding verse the going and coming, as well as the destruction and arising, of the lamp and the body, the connection is that "the [going and coming] of the body is not perceived here by anyone. || 51 ||
Fie, fie again and again upon those who are attached to their bodies and attached to the stability of the world, being intoxicated by the wine of delusion! 52.

"Reliance" (āsthā) is the conceit that [the world] possesses solidity, long-lastingness, and reality; the repetition, even though already explicitly stated, is for the sake of emphasizing its intensity. 52.
"I am not the body, nor is the body mine; likewise, this [body] is not I"—those whose minds rest thus, O Sage, are the supreme persons. (53)

Having reflected that "this body is insentient like a jar and so forth, and is not the 'I'," one whose mind has found rest— in the Supreme Self (the word *paramātmani* being understood as the remainder)— is indeed a *puruṣottama*, a most excellent person, or one who is the very nature of Viṣṇu.
Abounding in honor and dishonor, and delightful through abundant gain, those things which perceive only faults destroy a man whose attachment is bound solely to the body. (54)
Those who perceive faults possess distorted views; they should be distinguished [from the wise], for such views kill and bring one under the power of death. 54.
We have been deceived by the artifice of the ego’s wondrous display—that goblin with delicate limbs who dwells within the hollow of the body. (55)

The very wonder of egoism—such as the thirst for enjoyment and so forth—is that same female demon (piśācī). Deceived by trickery and guile, they are cheated by being made to perceive the worthless as substantial, through the theft of their true essence. || 55 ||
All this wretched wisdom has been bound to the body by this [mind] through its attachment;
alas, it alone has been deceived by the wicked villain of false knowledge. (56)

Wisdom is right understanding; the wretched one is the miserable [ignorance]; false knowledge itself is the cruel ogress; she is alone, being devoid of her own companions such as discernment and the like. || 56 ||
Not even the slightest thing in this visible world is real; yet, by that deluded soul with its illusory body, the people are deceived. (57)
When not even the slightest thing within the category of the visible is real, then the body, which falls within that same category, is likewise so;
thus, the multitude of living beings is deceived by the body—which is itself already as good as burnt away and non-existent.
The meaning is: "This is truly a marvel, a wonder! || 57 ||
In just a few days, this withered sprout of a body falls away effortlessly, like a drop from the water of a mountain stream.
If there were some purpose for the body through the deception of people, then it might be appropriate; however, that too does not exist, as he says in two [verses]: || 58 ||
This body is destined for swift destruction, like a bubble upon the ocean;
it manifests fruitlessly and in vain amidst the cycle of worldly activities.

Worldly activities, which are merely the running about of saṃsāra, are like the great whirlpool of waters; they are as fruitless as they are useless, being devoid of one's own interest and likewise devoid of the interest of others—this is the meaning. || 59 ||
O twice-born one, I have no reliance for even a moment upon this body—a city born of dreams and delusion, subject to the transformation of false knowledge, and whose destruction is most evident. (50)
From where does the unreality of the group of visible objects, such as the body, arise? To this he says: "It is false" (*mithyā*).
The meaning is that it is a modification of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is itself false. It is like a dream or a city of the Gandharvas (*saṃbhramanagara*).
Alternatively, it is the substratum for dream-delusions, since dreams are seen within one's own body. Within one's own body, according to one's desire—
Because of the scriptural statement, "it revolves"; the meaning is that the city possesses an existence equivalent to the activities of its citizens.
He who has determined stability in lightning, in autumnal clouds, and in cities of the Gandharvas— let him place his trust in war.
"Believe" means let him have faith; "in the body" refers to the physical frame. || 61 ||

Having cast aside like a blade of grass this body—which is subject to a constant succession of fragile activities, which possesses a triumphant birth amidst forceful impulses, and which is full of powerful defects—I now abide in happiness. (62)
Among those things that proceed by forceful means—characterized by fragility and rapidity and engaged in asserting their own superiority—the meaning is:

[he disregards] those various things which, like lightning or autumnal clouds, are victors over a multitude of constantly perishing effects, due to the abundance of causal conditions for destruction; having set them aside with the thought that they are trivial, he casts them away. || 62 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth sarga, titled "Loathing the Body," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, according to the Ṛṣi tradition. || 18 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Loathing the Body," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The nineteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O you whose form is as flickering as a wave, though having obtained the river of the burden of duties...
In the ocean of saṃsāra, birth and childhood lead only to suffering. || 1 ||
