In this context, even childhood is censured, for it is defiled by ignorance, hunger, thirst, disease, impurity, and restlessness, and is in a state equivalent to that of subhuman creatures.

Is it not the case that not all states of the body are of the nature of suffering, since childhood is more delightful due to being desired by all people? For even the Śruti declares the abundance of bliss in childhood: "Just as a great king, or a great brahmin, or a great prince, having attained the height of bliss, might lie down. Thus, the Śruti also establishes that childhood possesses an abundance of bliss.
"Even having obtained... (*labdhvāpi*). [The word] *kāryabhāraiḥ* means by the burdens of duties, that is, by the various engagements of what must be done;

the instrumental case is used according to the rule beginning with *prakṛtyādi*. Just as in the expression "wealthy in grain" (*dhānyena dhanavān*), there is a non-differentiated connection (*abhedānvaya*) with the meaning of the base of the secondary derivative (*taddhita-prakṛtyartha*). [The phrase] *taralākāre* means that in which the forms—the fourfold bodies—are flickering and unstable. Elsewhere...

In this ocean of saṃsāra, which is by nature restless, human birth is [the goal]; however, the creature obtains childhood solely for the sake of suffering—this is the implied meaning. By the word "even" (api), the extreme rarity of human birth is illuminated.
Thus says the Śruti: "From that state, it is indeed most difficult to escape. (1)
Incapacity, calamity, craving, muteness, dullness of intellect, greed, restlessness, and wretchedness—all these prevail in childhood. (2)
He elaborates upon the meaning of the proposition [stated] with the words beginning "incapacity" (*aśakti*). *Gṛdhnutā* is the state of having desire (*sābhilāṣatā*).

*Tṛṣṇā* refers to the object of eating and so forth; *gṛdhnutā* refers to the object of play, curiosity, and so forth; the distinction is that *dainya* (wretchedness) occurs when those [objects] are not obtained. || 2 ||
In states that are fierce with anger and weeping, and shattered by wretchedness,
childhood is a bondage like a tethering post for elephants.

The letter *ca* (and) has the sense of including the infinite, unmentioned misfortunes. *Bandhana* (bondage): the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇe*). *Ālāna* is a pillar for tying an elephant. || 3 ||
Those anxieties which do not cease at death, nor in old age or disease, nor in adversity, nor even in youth—those very anxieties that [cut through] completely cut the heart asunder during childhood;
"in old age and disease" is a collective dvandva compound treated as singular; "those such as these"; they cut all around.
They seem to cut and they cause pain—those [fingers] which are such as they are. 4.
The undertaking of animal birth is despised by all; fickle and characterized by the conduct of a child, it brings suffering even beyond death.
One whose undertaking is equal to that of those born as animals, such as cattle and the like; one who has been disregarded or reviled. || 5 ||
For whom could childhood— consisting of dense ignorance regarding reflections, fragile with its various imaginings, and with the mind already cut and shattered— be a source of happiness? (6)

In which [mind] ignorance stands clearly before one like a reflection, dense and thick; in which there are, at every moment, numerous delusive cognitions produced by the reflections of various objects. Therefore, it is fragile and soft—meaning trivial—due to various volitions, being as light as those very things imagined.
In which || 6 ||
What fear could there be for anyone in times of calamity that was experienced in childhood through ignorance at every step, out of dread of water, fire, wind, and snakes? (7)
Fear is suffering either by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or in its primary sense (*mukhya*), because from one fear another fear arises.
"By lack of understanding" means by ignorance. The word *hi* has the sense of *api* (also/even). || 7 ||
Falling with great force upon playful antics, wicked amusements, evil desires, and malicious intentions, the fool brings about supreme delusion.

The distinction between play (*līlā*) and the others is according to their being general or specific, being preceded by cognition or not, and being physical or mental. "Delusion" (*moha*) refers to the error of regarding them as having intrinsic reality (*sāratā*). (8)
Childhood, with its undertakings fashioned by conceptual construction, its difficult playfulness, and its precarious foundation, serves only to discipline a person, not to bring him peace.

Even in a fruitless undertaking, out of mere curiosity and based on the words of the foolish, the intoxicated, and the like, one may conceive a great enterprise that is ill-founded and unstable. For the sake of instruction, there are the sufferings such as the flogging with whips inflicted by teachers and others;
[therein lie] those faults, those misconducts, those evil courses, and those painful anxieties.
They all remained in their childhood state, like owls in a difficult-to-access place. || 10 ||
Difficult to traverse and difficult to cross are the Kauśikas, who have ravens as their enemies. || 10 ||
O Brahmin, fie upon those dull-witted fools who, with their minds clouded, imagine that childhood is delightful! 11.
Regarding the doubt that childhood is more delightful, he says: "Childhood," etc. For the scripture states that it is characterized by passion and so forth:
"Where the mind, in the form of a swing, flickers among its fluctuations—even though it be the most auspicious thing in the three worlds, how can that lead to contentment? (12)

He establishes that very charm [of the place] with the words beginning "yatra" (where): the grammatical connection is that even that which is inauspicious or ill-omened within the three worlds [is charming there]. || 12 ||
O Sage, for all sentient beings indeed, the mind becomes ten times more restless in childhood than it is in any other state whatsoever. (13)
It is not only for humans that this lack of fitness exists, but for all living beings; thus he says, "of all.
The point is that it is well known that the extreme fickleness of the mind is itself a cause of extreme suffering. || 13 ||
The mind is restless by its very nature, and childhood is the height of restlessness;
when these two are joined together, who indeed can be a protector against the inner turbulence of the breasts? 14.
Of the two embracing and uniting; regarding the mischief of her breasts, the harm caused by them.
O Brahmin, the fickleness of one whose mind is overcome by childhood was learned from the eyes of women, from masses of lightning, from clusters of flames, and from the waves. (15)
"Surely it was learned—that is, practiced—from the mind (citta), that is, from the consciousness (cetasa) overwhelmed by childhood"; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
Indeed, childhood and the mind, in all their various states,
are seen to be constantly unstable in their condition, like two brothers.
"Of fragile duration"; the absence of the suffix *num* is a Vedic (archaic) usage; [meaning] "of a fickle nature. || 16 ||
All forms of suffering, all faults, and all anxieties depend solely upon the fool—just as men depend upon a wealthy man. (17)
They have become suffering, consisting of abundant sufferings such as misfortunes and the like. || 17 ||
If a child does not obtain something new and delightful every single day, he falls into a state of fainting due to the imbalance caused by his sensory desires.
At that time, by means of a mental transformation caused by an unbearable imbalance due to the objects [of the senses], she fell into a swoon—that is, a faint. || 18 ||
With a little he comes under control, and with a little he undergoes change;
like a dog, the fool delights only in what is impure. (19)
*Kauleyaka* means a dog; the adjectives are common [to both]. || 19 ||
With a face constantly bathed in tears, his body smeared with mud and his mind dulled,
the child resembled a patch of ground scorched by the sun and then drenched by rain.

"Bāṣpa" refers to tears and the rising of steam; "jaḍāśaya" refers to one whose intellect is ignorant and who is insentient. Furthermore, [the presence of] vapor and the like are well known even on heated ground that has been drenched by rain. || 20 ||
Devoted to fear and food, miserable, desiring both the seen and the unseen, and possessed of a fickle intellect—childhood brings the body only suffering. (21)
Fear and food constitute "fear-and-food. That which is seen is present; that which is unseen is not present. [This refers to one] whose intellect and body are fickle. 21.
Failing to obtain the things desired by his own imagination,
the weak-minded fool suffers in misery, as if his heart were being cut away.
"Existents" (bhāvān) refers to entities (padārthān). "Viniṣkṛtta" means severed (chinna). || 22 ||
O Sage, those sufferings of childhood—which involve ill-fated aims, many deceptive and harsh obstacles, and which belong to no one else—[are experienced by the child]. (23)
"Attaining their mark" means having found their footing through evil intentions, wicked deeds, or corrupt desires;
"fierce" means cruel, employing many crooked and devious methods of deception. || 23 ||
The fool is constantly tormented by his own powerful mind, which sports with its desires, just as a forest glade is scorched by the summer heat.
A youth who has entered the house of learning encounters supreme torment, as terrifying as the unevenness of poison, like a lordly elephant at its tethering post. (25)

Furthermore, there is another affliction distinct from what was mentioned before—consisting of various undesirable things such as dependence on others and humiliation—which is a false mental construction filled with manifold desires;
this childishness, with its fragile disposition, leads to exceedingly long-lasting suffering. (26)
It is that conceptualization in which the notion of reality is imagined with respect to things that are themselves false. || 26 ||
How could that foolishness by which one, being overjoyed, desires to devour the world and seize the moon from the sky, ever lead to happiness? (27)

It is well known that sometimes a child, weeping with a desire for food, is delighted by the deception "I shall give you the whole world as food," and then desires only to eat that very thing. || 27 ||
O mighty-armed one of great intelligence, what difference is there between an internal consciousness that is powerless to ward off cold and heat, and a mere child or a tree? (28)
He whose inner mind experiences the suffering of cold, heat, and so forth, [is like] a tree, a *urvīruha*. || 28 ||
Devoted to hunger, they desire to fly with their two wings;
children who possess the nature of birds are always intent on fear and food. (29)

"Uḍḍītuṃ" means to fly up. The absence of the *iṅ* augment is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). "By the wings" refers metaphorically to the arms. "Vihagadharmiṇaḥ" means those possessing the nature of birds, that is, equal to birds. || 29 ||
In childhood there is fear of the teacher, as well as of the mother and the father;
there is fear of people and of elder children; childhood is a temple of fear. (30)

O Great Sage, in this world, the childhood of even one who has taken refuge [in you], yet whose disposition is struck down by the state of all faults and who revels in a lack of discernment, does not suffice for the complete satisfaction of anyone at all. (31)

The home of one whose disposition is struck down by all the states of vice, whose inner organ is corrupted, who is characterized by a lack of discrimination, and who is habituated to unrestrained wandering—is not at all sufficient for the satisfaction or happiness of anyone; [this is] even the meaning of the particle *cit*. The word *eva* (only) is displaced in its position. (Note: The term *vilāsinaḥ* refers to the subject, the man of pleasure; *niraṅkuśavihāraśīlasya* describes his nature; *śaraṇam gṛham* is the predicate nominative; *alam* expresses sufficiency or adequacy; *naiva* is the negation.)
The meaning is that it comes into being. || 31 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth sarga, titled "Loathing Childhood," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Loathing Childhood," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa.
The Twentieth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
Then, having abandoned the miseries of childhood, a person whose inner disposition has been struck down [by realization]...
Yet youth ascends toward a fall through its very agitation.
In this context, youth is censured as being defiled by greed, hatred, pride, envy, arrogance, and avarice, and as a dwelling place for evils such as sensual desire.

"Let it be that childhood is full of suffering due to extreme ignorance, lack of capacity, and dependence; however, youth—being free from those [defects] and colored by the savor of various enjoyments—is surely a cause of happiness and thus desirable.
This is stated with the words beginning "the misfortune of childhood," etc., out of agitation—that is, through the enthusiasm for enjoyment and delusion.
Or, his disposition is struck—that is, his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is defiled—by the Kāmapiśāca and others to be described hereafter.
Because Māṇḍavya established a limit until the fourteenth year, childhood does not lead to downfall in that way; rather, the point is that youth alone leads to downfall. || 1 ||
There, experiencing the fluctuations of his own restless mind, which is full of infinite diversions, the dull-witted one goes from sorrow to further sorrow. (2)
In that regard, concerning youth: he whose infinite amorous sports (*vilāsa*) are his activities; *vṛtti* refers to transformations such as passion and hatred; "jaḍa" means a fool. || 2 ||
Helpless, he is overwhelmed by the demon of desire, which dwells within the cavity of his own mind and causes manifold agitation. (3)
Having disregarded solitude and having treated it with contempt, one is brought under control. || 3 ||
Just as collyrium [makes eyes see], it subjects the mind of the childish— whose thoughts are fickle like those of wanton women— to the lack of restraint of their own mental fluctuations.

Therefore, he offers—meaning he grants—the unrestrained and independent movement of the minds of young women, which, like those of fickle-natured [women], possess unstable states; that is, by the absence of *vṛti* (which means either "choice" or "concealment"), they are allowed to roam at will. Just as one might grant children the freedom to look for hidden treasures and the like.
The "unveiled" (avṛtīḥ) means the absence of obstructions for the flickering rays of those eyes;
that is to say, the capacity to freely behold the treasure by disregarding the intervention of the earth, stones, and other such barriers. || 4 ||
O Sage, those very faults arising from evil undertakings— those wicked things which are of that same nature as the intention itself— destroy that very person who possesses such an intention.

In that regard, during youth, there is such an inclination; the mind is brought under the sway of thoughts of sensual desire and the like, and for that very reason, those well-known [actions] consist of evil undertakings— such as the vices of women, gambling, and quarrels— from which a person of that nature and disposition [is driven], because they are the cause of rebirth in hell and other realms, and because they must be accomplished through exhaustion and affliction.
The defects such as passion and greed plunder and destroy; by that very youth, those defects are corrupted, meaning they are brought to an extreme state. || 5 ||
Those people who have not been ruined by youth— which acts as the seed for the great hells and causes one to wander incessantly— have indeed been ruined by nothing else.
Therefore, it is called the "Great Unobstructed" (Mahānavaraka). This is clear. || 6 ||
He by whom the formidable terrain of youth— consisting of various flavors and filled with a multitude of diverse experiences— is crossed, is called steadfast.

The *rasas*—such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others—the pungent tastes (*kaṭu*) and other flavors, and the objects of desire, as well as insurmountable waters; the suffix *-mayaṭ* here denotes abundance.

Through the agency of passion, greed, and the like, and by thieves, tigers, serpents, and so forth, [the world becomes] a cause of wonder—a form radiant with light, flashing in every moment, with the thundering of dense clouds tossing about.
This youth of mine, which is like the flash of lightning, does not please me.
In which [assembly] there were dense and abundant utterances full of pride, like the thundering of thick clouds; for this very reason, it was shining like lightning. || 8 ||
Sweet, delicious, and bitter, yet corrupting and a mere ornament to the faults; youth, which resembles the surging waves of wine, does not please me.

At the time of enjoyment, the waves of wine—the playful intoxications—are sweet and pleasing to the heart; yet in their ultimate consequence, they are bitter, a source of reproach, a defect that serves as an ornament for faults. (9)
Unreality appearing as reality, which soon brings about deception—
such youth, like union with a woman in a dream, does not please me.
It bestows separation and brings about deception. || 10 ||
Youth, which is enchanting for only a moment to every man and stands before all, does not please me; it is like a city of the Gandharvas.
The meaning is that among the entire collection of objects charming for a moment, it is foremost—that is, the best.
In the alternative sense, because the sight of a city of Gandharvas is a sign of death, it means at the very front—that is, at the end—of one's entire lifespan. || 11 ||
Lasting no longer than the flight of an arrow, youth provides pleasure while being radiant with suffering; it constantly bestows only burning and nourishment, and thus it does not please me.
For as long as it takes for an arrow released from the bowstring to reach its target, for that duration it is a giver of happiness.
"Youth, which is delightful only at its onset but devoid of true essence within—resembling union with a courtesan—is not pleasing to me. (13)
Delight is that which is pleasing; true being is the state of a virtuous mind. || 13 ||
Whatever undertakings there may be, they all bestow every kind of suffering; they come together in youth, just as great portents gather at the end of an eon.

The grammatical connection is that all undertakings whatsoever which cause suffering to anyone—all these [cease] at the time of dissolution (kṣaye), that is, at the time of cosmic destruction (pralaye).
Even the Blessed One—though possessing a terrifying form—is afraid of the night of ignorance of youth, which creates darkness within the heart; even he who possesses knowledge [is afraid]. 15.

The meaning is this: even the Lord Īśvara, though possessing a terrifying form, surely fears the night of ignorance joined with youth; for otherwise, how could he ever maintain the moon of discriminative knowledge? || 15 ||
This agitation of youth causes extreme delusion, which utterly forgets virtuous conduct and brings about a failure of the intellect. (16)
"Bhrama" means delusion; "saṃbhrama" means infatuation. || 16 ||
In youth, a living being is consumed in the heart by the fire of unbearable touch born from separation from a beloved, just as a tree is consumed by a forest fire. (17)
Difficult to touch, the fire of grief is impossible to grasp; by it, one is burned in the heart, that is, in the mind. || 17 ||
For even a mind that is perfectly pure, expansive, and holy becomes turbid in youth, like a river during the rainy season.

It is stainless through the cleansing of defects; it is vast through its magnanimity; it is purifying through the instilling of virtues (*guṇādhāna*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include other unmentioned qualities such as coolness and sweetness. || 18 ||
A river with its thick, surging waves may be crossed, though it be fearsome;
but not so the thirst that agitates the heart, flickering with the restlessness of youth. (19)
The mental state is unsteady and flickering due to youth; it is that [state] in which the internal senses are made restless by the thirst for enjoyment. || 19 ||
"That beloved, those two full breasts, those graceful charms, that face—through such anxieties regarding youth, a person reaches a state of decay. (20)
Weariness is flaccidity. || 20 ||
In this world, virtuous people honor a young man who suffers from the pain of a trembling fever,
but they do not honor one who is cut down like a fragment of withered grass.

In which [world], those afflicted by thirst are trembling; the word "tu" is used to indicate that it is not merely the case that they do not worship [him], but rather that they even despise him—[for the word "not" is not found anywhere]. || 21 ||
For one afflicted by intoxication, who wears the pearls of his own faults,
youth is indeed the eternal tethering post for the great elephant of pride, leading only to destruction.
Intending to show that for the high-minded, the shattering of pride is like death, he says: "Only for destruction," and so forth.

[He refers to] the great elephant of self-conceit; or rather, to one who is as rigid as a great elephant due to his conceits—an undiscriminating person whose mind is the vast root of faults that harbor venomous serpents.
Alas, youth is a forest of trees that wither and weep. || 23 ||

Through the internal burning caused by the loss of what is desired and separation from it, there is withering; the trees themselves are merely the weeping associated with that state. Faults alone are the venomous serpents. "Batā" expresses grief. 23.
Know that youth is a lotus flower: crowded with the filaments of passion, filled with the petals of false conceptualizations, and frequented by the bees of evil thoughts. (24)

It is tasted (*rasyate*), thus it is *rasa*; this refers to the nectar-essence of a drop of pleasure. Those who flow toward or spread within that object of pleasure are passion (*rāga*) and the like; these are the filaments (*kesara*). By them, it is crowded and dense. The petals are the leaves. The *cañcarīkas* are bees. The *puṣkara* is a lotus. || 24 ||
Fresh youth is the abode of the birds of mental and physical afflictions, which frequent the shores of the lake of the hearts of those belonging to both the virtuous and the wicked factions.
Evil deeds committed, merits left undone, or worldly affairs—whether performed or not—are "bad wings" because they cause one's downfall. "Abode" means a nest. (25)
The ocean, whose youthful vigor disregards its boundaries, is like a collection of inert, playful waves that have lost all count.

Precisely because they are innumerable, the waves of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) have lost their count. These "sportive" ones are by nature inclined toward play. It is "without limit" (*anavadhi*), meaning its boundary is disregarded; or alternatively, it is that for which the very suffering of old age and so forth—which is undesirable—is disregarded as its final boundary (*maryādā*). || 26 ||
The fierce wind of youth is capable of displacing the stability of all those whose creation of virtues has been firmly rooted in passion and ignorance.

In the space of consciousness (*citākāśa*), all qualities such as clarity, luminosity, discernment, and the expansion of vision are "creations" (*sarga*)—meaning they are produced or brought forth through association with the virtuous, the study of authentic scriptures, diligent effort, and so forth.

The placement of the word at the end of the compound is due to the grammatical freedom regarding the order of the qualifier and the qualified. This applies even to those things achieved through thousands of efforts.
[Of even the qualities of those to be accomplished], that is to say, of the excellent virtues; "capable" means able to remove their stability or firmness.
In the case of the wind, it refers to the collections of qualities and the threads spun by spiders. || 27 ||
The fierce dust-storms of youth lead the face to paleness and cause the hair to become disheveled; harsh as they are, these particles of youth ascend to the highest peak.

"Pāṇḍutām" means by diseases arising from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sense objects. "Ākulaiḥ" means agitated; "avakaraiḥ" refers to heaps of refuse; "utkarāt" means from a high place; and "doṣotkarṣam" refers to the upper region due to the excess of defects. || 28 ||
The exuberance of youth in men awakens the seed of vice, cuts down the row of virtues, and is the playful manifestation of the splendor of their misdeeds. (29)

The "line" (āli) refers to the multitude of faults. It is called a "pastime" (vilāsa) because it serves as the cause for the display of the splendor of misdeeds—that is, the abundance of sin. || 29 ||
This moon of fresh youth bewilders the bee-like mind that flutters over the pollen of the body-lotus. (30)

Because its wings of discernment are obstructed by the pollen of the quality of passion (rajas), it binds the restless bee of the mind—the female bee of the intellect—within the sheath of self-identification with the body; thus, it deludes one. 30.
The lovely creeper of youth, emerging from the fragments of her body, intoxicates the bee of the mind as soon as it has alighted upon her as she reaches full maturity. (31)

In a small forest thicket or bower characterized by slender bodies, the flowering cluster of the creeper intoxicates—that is, it deludes—one with its height, excellence, and upward-reaching nature. || 31 ||
The deer of the mind, rushing toward the mirage of youth that arises from the heat of the body's vital breaths, fall into the pit of the sense objects. 32.

The body itself is a desert land; therein, youth—the very state of being young—appears like a mirage arising from the heat of the sun of desire. Those who run toward it fall into the pit or chasm characterized by the objects of the senses. 32.
The moonlight for the night of my body, the mane of the lion of my mind,
and the wave of the ocean of my life— this youth of mine brings no satisfaction.

The body itself is the night; its moonlight is the radiance. It is the mane and the hair of the shoulders of the lion characterized by the mind, for by that he shines. A "laharī" is a garland of waves. || 33 ||
This youthfulness has borne fruit in the wilderness of the body for only a few days; indeed, you ought not to find comfort in this autumnal season.

This very youthfulness, because it has borne fruit for only a few days within the wilderness of the body, has become autumn—the season of harvest. The sense is that it will soon reach its decay; therefore, you should not place your trust in it. This is an address directed toward one's own kin. || 34 ||
In an instant, the bird of youth immediately departs from the body,
just as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) slips from the hand of one with little merit in a mere moment.
He elaborates upon what has already been stated with the six verses beginning with "jhaṭiti" (instantly). || 35 ||
Whenever youth ascends to its highest peak, desires surge forth with feverish intensity; at that time, they lead only to destruction.

"Parāṃ koṭim" means the highest limit or the pinnacle of excellence; "valganti" means they go toward or reach it—that is, they become old. "Sajvarāḥ" means possessed of feverish distress. Since repetition (vīpsā) was observed in the preceding [verse], the words "tadā tadā" (then and then) should be supplied here as well. || 36 ||
Right then do the demons of passion and hatred leap about;
this entire host does not set until the night of youth has passed. (37)
They spring forth and move about especially; "yāminī" means night. || 37 ||
Exercise compassion toward youth, which is full of various transformations, wretched, and perishing in an instant, as if toward a dying son. (38)
Mutations are fluctuations of the mind and the playful diversions of the ignorant. || 38 ||
That man who, out of delusion, feels joy because of youth which is momentary and fragile, is indeed considered a great fool and a "human deer. (39)
He who, out of delusion, experiences joy because of youth that perishes in an instant is a human being who, though a man, is nothing but a beast; for he is utterly foolish. (39)
He of wicked intellect who, out of pride and delusion, lusts after youth intoxicated by passion, will soon be joined with remorse. (40)
From pride and delusion, accompanied by conceit and ignorance, one desires and clings [to objects] with the notion that they possess essence. || 40 ||
They are worthy of worship, they are great-souled, and they alone are true men on this earth—those virtuous ones who have safely crossed over the perils of youth. (41)
With ease, meaning without the impairment of non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and so forth. || 41 ||
The ocean, though filled with formidable sea-monsters, can be crossed easily;
but one's own flawed youth, surging with the force of its waves, cannot.
It is a mine or quarry for the most excellent and great crocodiles and sea-monsters;
it is characterized by its habit of surging with the force of the waves of passion and the like. "Hata" means censured. The compound *kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* is a *tatpuruṣa*. 42.
Adorned with discipline, the abode of the noble, radiant with compassion, and encircled by virtues—indeed, O dear one, such a youth is rare in this world, like a forest situated in the sky. (43)

Now, since childhood and old age are rendered unfit for the accomplishment of human goals due to ignorance and incapacity respectively— and even youth is fraught with many defects— is there not, then,
ever any hope for a person regarding the attainment of human goals through the perfection of the means?

Anticipating the objection that this might be a mere hope for human goals (*puruṣārtha*), [the author] states that it is not all youth that is censured, but only "bad youth" (*duryauvana*); whereas "good youth" (*suyauvana*) culminates precisely in human goals.
Demonstrating this through its characteristics and stating its rarity, he says: "modesty," etc. "Noble ones" (*āryāḥ*) refers to venerable people.

It is the abode—that is, the place—of sages; or rather, it is like a dwelling-place for noble and virtuous people, providing them with rest. By means of qualities such as tranquility and self-restraint, [it prevails] in the world—that is, in saṃsāra. The word *hi* has the sense of *api* (even). Even here, in this human birth...

The meaning is: what else could be so difficult to attain? "Ambaragaṃ kānanam" refers to the Nandana forest. In that context, it is adorned with *vinayas*, which are the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣas*) because they lead (*nayanti*) birds (*vīn*) into their own presence.
It is the abode of noble beings (*āryajanas*), namely the gods; for this very reason, it is exalted by compassion (*karuṇā*) and grace (*dayā*), as well as by its inherent qualities (*guṇas*).

It is "enveloped" or "surrounded" by the qualities of the wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpalatā*), such as the abundance of fruits and flowers; this should be understood as being extremely difficult to find here on earth. || 43 ||
Thus ends the twentieth sarga, titled "The Censure of Youth," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Censure of Youth," in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgya-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
Within the cage-like body, which is as unstable as a mechanical puppet made of flesh, [what is this that moves?]
What indeed can be beautiful in a woman who is characterized by sinews, bones, and joints? (1)
Even women here, whose every limb is fully formed within the multitude of manifest hells, are censured for giving men birth in hell.

He begins to analyze and reveal the true nature of those female bodies in which young men harbor the delusion of beauty, starting with the verse beginning "māṃsa" (flesh) and so forth. "Snāyavaḥ" means sinews; "grathana" means a knot, by which [the body] is like a beautiful, fleshly doll made of meat.
What is it that people consider beautiful in a woman’s cage-like body, which is as unstable and fickle as a cart or other such machine? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 1 ||
Having separated the eye from its skin, blood, and tears, look at it clearly;
if it is beautiful, why do you delude yourself in vain? (2)

Expanding upon what has already been stated, he first demonstrates the lack of beauty in discernment (*viveka*) where the eyes of youths possess playful charm (*vilāsa-vibhrama*), beginning with the word "tvak" (skin). This is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). "If it is beautiful, then prepare yourself"—this is the statement of the resulting meaning. "Why in vain?"—the words "if not" are to be supplied. [Otherwise, it would be] in vain.
It is futile. || 2 ||
"Here are the hair, here the blood"—such is this body of a woman.
What does one of vast intention gain by censuring it? (3)
He possessed a vast intention and a mind expanded by solitude. || 3 ||
O dear one, those very limbs of all embodied beings which were repeatedly cherished with garments and ointments are now being torn apart by flesh-eating scavengers. (4)
"O dear one" (*aṅga*) is a term of gentle address. "They plunder" (*luṇṭhanti*) means they attack. "Carnivores" (*kravyādāḥ*) refers to flesh-eaters such as vultures, jackals, and the like. || 4 ||
In which breast the splendor of the pearl necklace was seen to be like the surge of the Ganges waters sparkling upon the slopes of Mount Meru’s peak.

A stream of liquid; the connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: "That very breast of a beautiful woman upon which the splendor of a pearl necklace—characterized by its radiant beauty—is seen. || 5 ||
In cremation grounds at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is devoured by dogs in time, like a small morsel of food. (6)
It is relished and eaten with relish; [this refers to] the food, namely, the boiled rice.
Just as the limbs of a young camel in the forest are smeared with blood, flesh, and bone, so too are the limbs of a passionate woman; for what attachment can there be toward her?
"Coated" means accumulated, as on the trunk of a camel or a donkey; "graha" means "āgraha," which is to say, an excess of craving. || 7 ||
It is imagined that women possess only superficial charm;
O Sage, I believe that even this does not exist here, for it is solely a cause of delusion.
Knowledge born of non-investigation is considered—meaning it is deemed appropriate—to last only until its initial onset or until one falls [from one's seat].

This is because it has delusion as its sole cause and mental confusion as its sole basis; for there is no such thing as [illusory] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell or the like. Such is the sense. (8)
What difference is there between wine, which causes transformation preceded by intoxication and passion, and a woman, who bestows vast delight preceded by intoxication and passion? (9)

Of one who is subject to transformation, naturally possessed of transformations such as desire, yeast, and so forth, or subject to transformations such as stumbling and quarreling, or who causes such transformations. || 9 ||
O Sage, the elephants of human beings, tethered to the hitching post of the tongue, do not attain awakening even with the firm goads of tranquility. (10)
Completely dissolved through intoxication and delusion, they were as if asleep; "awakening" refers to the vigilance born of discernment. || 10 ||
Bearing hair like soot, difficult to touch yet pleasing to the eye,
the flames of the fire of evil deeds burn a man like straw.
Women are the flames of the fires of the wicked. He establishes this very point through their characteristics—beginning with "hair": those whose nature it is to bear hair as if they were collyrium;
who are difficult to touch (*duḥsparśāḥ*), meaning impossible to touch; yet who are pleasing to the eyes (*locanapriyāḥ*), meaning beautiful to behold. For this very reason, [they captivate] a man...
They burn like straw. || 11 ||
Even when blazing at a great distance, women—though full of passion—are yet devoid of it; for they are the beautiful yet dreadful fuel for the fires of hell.

Even though the fires of hell are blazing most fiercely in Saṃyaminī, which is very far away, there is an apparent contradiction (virodhābhāsa) arising from their own nature. Alternatively, "dāruṇam" may be taken as an adjective qualifying the fuel itself; thus, even in that case, the apparent contradiction arises from its own nature. However, the resolution is that they are "sarasāḥ" (full of essence/flavor) only because they are initially tainted by latent impressions (vāsanā).
They are sapless from the perspective of ultimate reality; thus, they are beautiful on the surface but cruel in their result. || 12 ||
Her braided hair was disheveled, her eyes were like shimmering stars,
her face was like the orb of the full moon, and she smiled with a profusion of flowers.

She whose braid of hair (*kabarī*) is the very form of the night’s darkness, or who possesses such a braid; she whose eyes are the wandering stars (*tārakā*), or whose eyes have moving pupils (*tarattāraka*) like those stars; and thus, she whose face is the orb of the moon, or who possesses a face like the orb of the moon.
The analysis of the compound is: "she has a smile that is either a heap of flowers itself, or like a heap of flowers. || 13 ||
With men agitated by her playful charms, she brings about the destruction of their undertakings;
she is a woman who utterly deludes the intellect, like a long, sleepless night. (14)
In that city, men are restless with amorous sports;
therefore, their lives must necessarily perish in vain—this is the intended meaning. || 14 ||
Delightful and sweet with flowers, adorned with sprout-like hands, rich in the playful movements of bee-like eyes, and bearing clusters of blossoms in the form of breasts. || 15 ||
He says "puṣpa" and so forth to show that [the mind] not only obstructs the goals of human endeavor but is also a cause of misfortune: "the two breasts themselves, like breasts... (15).
With limbs as fair as the filaments of a flower, yet intent on slaying men,
she brings about a state of helpless madness, like a beloved woman who is actually a poisonous creeper.

Like flower filaments [producing] flower filaments, or like the state of helplessness resulting from fainting or death for fools who serve themselves and are intoxicated by passion, it bestows a state of utter helplessness. || 16 ||

By the mere exhalation of the "existent effect" (satkārya), a person is drawn out from the cave by his beloved— who is eager to crush the serpent— as if by a female elephant drawing a snake from its hole.

Here, the female bear (*bhallukī*) is to be grasped; for it is well known that she draws out snakes and other creatures dwelling in their holes by the power of her breath and devours them. Likewise, with false honors—mere empty consolations—and with longing, the beloved woman brings about the destruction of the "serpents," that is, the libertines, by depriving them of their wealth and their hearts, even through the mere act of breathing upon them as a reassurance.
A living being is uplifted; that is to say, it is brought under control. || 17 ||
Women, scattered by the hunter named Desire, are the snares for binding the limbs of those bird-like men whose minds are deluded. (18)
"Scattered" means spread out; "vāgurā" means nets. || 18 ||
O Brahmin, the intoxicated elephant of the mind remains bound by the chain of passion to the vast post of the lalanā, as if mute. (19)
For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, wandering in the mud of the mind— the mud of wealth—
a woman is the baited hook on a line made of the cords of evil tendencies.
A hook is the barb for catching fish; the dough-ball therein is the bait. || 20 ||
A beautiful-eyed woman is a tethering post for horses like a stable for elephants, and a binding spell for men as a mantra is for serpents. (21)
Mandura and mandurā refer to a stable for horses. || 21 ||
O Sage, this variegated land of enjoyment, filled with manifold flavors, has indeed attained its supreme state here by depending upon women. (22)
This world of enjoyment, characterized by the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), has attained and reached a supreme, firm, and long-lasting stability within this saṃsāra. || 22 ||
May I always be defiled by this woman, who is like a small casket for all the jewels of faults and a constant chain of suffering.
By means of a well-sealed, firm casket; "enough" means it is sufficient; the meaning is that there is no further need.
What use have I for the breast, or the eye, or the hip, or the belly—this worthless thing whose sole essence is mere flesh? (24)
By means of that which is non-substantial and void. || 24 ||
"O Brahmin, in just a few days, a woman goes to ruin—here is flesh, here is blood, and there are bones. (25)
The state of being fragile and the state of being shattered. || 25 ||
O Sage, those women who were formerly beloved by men— whether they were robust or graceful— are now sleeping with their limbs separated among the spirits of the ancestors.
By those who are coarse and lack subtle vision; they were cherished and fondled by Lalitā in the cremation grounds, the ancestral lands. || 26 ||
O Brahmin, when leaf-sprouts are placed in the mouth by a lover with intense affection, they are drunk by women even in the wilderness.

The particular designs of tilaka made with camphor, gorocana, sandalwood, and so forth are called *patrāṅkura*. It is "drunk" or "dried"; from the root *pai* meaning "to dry," the *la*-suffix is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) because it is not transitive. || 27 ||
The hair goes to become a decorative tuft on the trees of the cremation ground, and the bones, shining like stars, appear upon the circle of the earth within a few days. (28)

The hair of women is their ornament; it is that very hair which serves as the brush for painting. Because of its ash-grey color, the dust drinks the blood, and many carnivorous beasts devour it as well.
The jackals consume the skins, and the vital breaths depart into the sky. (29)

They drink and they dry up. "Dust" means particles of earth. "Carnivores" (kravyāda) refers to those that eat raw flesh (kravya), meaning meat; the remainder of the sense is that there are many such creatures. "Śivā" means a female jackal. || 29 ||
Thus, this future state of the limbs of women has been described by me to you with certainty; why do you pursue delusion? (30)
Stability is transformation. || 30 ||
How indeed could one endowed with intelligence [allow] this thing called *lalanā*, which is the configuration resulting from the conjunction of the five elements, to fall away from the essence? 31.

How could a wise person, endowed with discernment, rush toward that which is produced by the collision of [the senses], a mere configuration and arrangement, out of passion for its flavor? Some maintain that by the word "ca" (and) in the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*, the imperative (*loṭ*) is also included. || 31 ||
Anxious thought, following after its beloved, becomes dense with spreading branches and thickets, garlanded with bitter and sour fruits, and reaches the height of a great palm tree. (32)

Suffering in the next world has bitter fruit, while worldly grief, passion, and the like, though mixed with slight fragments of pleasure, have the acidity of various [sour] things. "Utālatām" means upward expansion. || 32 ||
Due to being utterly bewildered, the mind—blinded and agitated by dense craving—falls into supreme delusion, like a deer strayed from its herd. (33)

It is understood that [he is] "distressed by thoughts that have been released. For this very reason, blinded by dense—that is, thick—greed, meaning a craving for wealth, he incurs a delusion of mind characterized by such thoughts as, "In which direction shall I go? Where shall I find wealth? || 33 ||
A young man devoted to a young woman reaches the highest state of pitiability,
like an elephant longing for a female elephant who is trapped in a pit in the Vindhya mountains.
In a pit for eating. || 34 ||
He who has a woman has a desire for enjoyment; for one without a woman, where is the ground for enjoyment?
Having abandoned a woman, one abandons birth; having abandoned birth, one becomes happy. (35)
Bhavana means the earth, or origin. || 35 ||

O Brahmin, out of fear of death, disease, old age, and the like, I do not delight in worldly enjoyments that are difficult to transcend and as fleeting as the wings of a bee, providing pleasure only at the moment of contact.
I shall become tranquil and, through diligent effort, attain the supreme state.
"Pakṣati" means the root of a wing (the shoulder). The connection is: "Out of fear of death, birth, old age, and so forth, I do not delight in enjoyments.
"I am pacified" means I have desisted. The form "upaimi" (I approach) is used in the present tense because of its proximity to the present time.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of Vālmīki, within the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa*.
The twenty-first canto, titled "Loathing Women. 21.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Loathing Women," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa.
The twenty-second canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Indeed, childhood is not yet sufficient; it forcibly drinks up youth."
Youth is followed by old age; behold their mutual harshness toward one another.
In this world, old age is censured as it is crowded with the maladies of grief, delusion, separation, affliction, and despondency, and serves as a locus for anxiety and humiliation.

Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be no happiness in youth due to the intensity of defects such as desire; however, in the state of old age, when those defects have subsided, there will be much greater happiness for one who is served at home by disciplined sons, grandsons, and others.
Anticipating this objection, [the author], wishing to explain in detail the infinity of the sources of suffering therein, says:
According to the maxim, "How can there be compassion for another's family when one has no pity for the snakes that devour one's own kin?",
old age destroys the body— just as a thunderbolt from a cloud destroys a lotus, as a whirlwind destroys an autumnal water-lily, and as a river destroys a tree on its bank.

He says, beginning with "like a hailstone of snow," that how can there be any hope for happiness in that [body], when it is the very body—the abode of pleasure and the object of supreme love for the ignorant—which is being made frail? "Himāśani" means a hailstone of snow, like a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
"Ambuja" refers to a drop of water, meaning a drop of water situated on the tip of a blade of grass.
Old age, appearing in its full maturity and causing every limb to become worn out,
swiftly brings the body to deformity, just as a drop of poison does.
"Having an aged form" is a poetic conceit (*autprekṣika*). For if she herself were not such, how could she make others so? The ellipsis is "a drop of poison was consumed. (3)
Women regard a man with long limbs, whose entire body is slack and decayed, and whose frame is worn out by old age, as being equal to a young camel.

In this context, the word *sama* is a synonym for *sarva* (all). Women look upon every man whose body is decayed by old age as they would a young camel or a camel in general. He establishes this very point with the verse beginning "śithila-": [he looks upon him] as one whose all limbs are slackened and torn asunder. || 4 ||
When people have been seized by old age, which is both effortless and merciless,
wisdom flees away like a woman who has fled from a rival wife who has struck her.
"Without effort" means without exertion. "Whose nature it is to torment" means whose character it is to bring about wretchedness. "Stricken" means humiliated. || 5 ||
Servants, sons, wives, kinsmen,
and friends likewise laugh at a man trembling with old age, as if he were a madman.
The suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of censure, as in the word *unmattaka*.
Like a vulture approaching a tree that is difficult to behold, withered, miserable, and devoid of both virtue and prowess, greed indeed assails one who has grown old.
It is long, exceedingly long. *Gardha* is an excess of longing. Regarding the tree, it refers to the branch laden with fruit.
[The verse continues: "Filled with the defect of wretchedness, long, causing a burning sensation in the heart, and the sole companion of all calamities, this craving increases in old age. (8)
Abounding in the defect of wretchedness. || 8 ||
"What painful and most terrible deed must I perform for the sake of the next world?
Indeed, in old age, this fear increases—a fear that is impossible to remedy. (9)
"Kaṣṭam" is a particle indicating dejection. || 9 ||
"Who am I, this wretch? What indeed shall I do, and how indeed shall I remain? How indeed?"—thus does dejection arise in old age. (10)
"Who am I? and so forth is merely the expression of wretchedness. The words "what" and "how" refer to the anxiety regarding the goal and the means:
"How, when, and from what person shall my food be as delicious as this?
Thus, in old age, this constant longing consumes the heart. (11)
The connection is as follows: having reached old age, this other form of decay—characterized as previously described—also consumes the mind.
Here, as well as in the preceding verse, the word *iva* (as if) is intended to indicate the discrepancy between the object and its perception. || 11 ||
Longing arises with delight, yet it is impossible to enjoy;
indeed, the heart is scorched by the weakness of one's power in old age.

The wretchedness of capacities is such that when one is able to eat, there is an inability to digest, and when one is able to digest, there is an inability to eat, and so forth. (12) Like an old female crane worn out by age, the disease—perched upon the head of the tree of the body and infested with the serpents of illness—cries out as long as it causes torment to the body. (13)

The body is harmful due to the afflictions and their oppressions. It is well known that even a boil (*piḍikā*) causes pain to the tree upon which it rests. The connection is as follows: when one is infested and seized by the serpent characterized by disease, and while one is crying out and weeping, the "Kauśika" of death appears from somewhere or other. || 13 ||
O Sage, just then, from somewhere, the owl of Death— desiring the thick darkness of blindness— is seen approaching swiftly.
Thick darkness, fainting, that very same [state] is timira, and it is also darkness (andhakāra). || 14 ||
Just as darkness pursues the evening twilight that has arisen, so too does death pursue one as soon as it perceives old age upon the body. (15)
The example serves to illustrate the preceding meaning. "Prajātām" means that which has been produced or come into being. || 15 ||
O Sage, as soon as the monkey of death sees from afar the tree of the body in full bloom with the flowers of old age, it rushes toward it with great speed.
The sense is that when it falls upon [the enemy], it is for the purpose of his destruction. || 16 ||
The city appears empty; the tree appears with its branches lopped off;
the region appears parched by drought; yet the body, though worn out by old age, does not appear so. (17)
It shines; it also gleams slightly. || 17 ||
In an instant, like a vulture seizing its prey, old age swiftly devours a man, causing him to cough as he gasps for breath.

The construction is as follows: the female vulture, whose nature it was to produce that sound—namely, a cawing cry—seized the man with speed and force, as if for the purpose of swallowing him, just as one might seize raw meat. 18.
As soon as she sees him, as if filled with longing, Old Age quickly seizes the body and for a moment plucks it away, just as a young maiden plucks a white water-lily.
It withers, that is, it destroys. A maiden is a young girl. A *kairava* is a night-lily (*kumuda*). || 19 ||
Making a whistling sound, this wind, harsh with dust, withers her body— already worn out— as a gale withers the sprout of a tree.

A whirlwind here is a mass of winds from the cold season; for it causes the body to emit whistling sounds and the like, and having covered the tree-sprouts with dust, it tears them apart—just so does old age. || 20 ||
The body, struck by old age and having reached a state of decay, bears the beauty of a withered lotus strewn over by a mass of frost. (21)
The beauty of a withered lotus is its resemblance [to her]. || 21 ||
This old age, like the rising moonlight upon the peaks of the mountain of the head,
vigorously causes the night-lily of coughing due to wind to blossom.
Old age itself is the moonlight (jyotsnā), that is, the light of the full moon (kaumudī). The head itself is the mountain peak (śikharipṛṣṭha), the upper region of a mountain.
The two diseases—asthma and cough—are themselves the white water-lily creeper (kumudvatī); they cause it to blossom with great intensity and effort. || 22 ||
Having observed that it has ripened and is withered by the alkali of old age— [the word *kūṣmāṇḍa* applies to both cases]— Time, the Lord, indeed devours the gourd-like head of men. (23)

Old age itself is the alkaline powder of salt and the like; by this, it is meant that he is smeared with a greyish hue. He is the lord and master of the "gourd-head" (śiraḥ-kuṣmāṇḍa)—[the word *kūśmāṇḍa* applies to both cases]—because he has been produced and desired by him alone. || 23 ||
The daughter of Jahnu, exerted by old age, swiftly cuts away the roots of this body-tree while its life-force is still moving. (24)
The Gaṅgā, daughter of Jahnu, as if striving without ceasing, flows swiftly through life—the stream of life—while it moves on. (24) The old age-cat, being fierce, devours the mouse of youth;
greedy for the flesh of the body, she attains supreme exultation. (25)
She digs up the hole of the sense-objects within youth itself; thus, like a rat, she devours that body which is as dear as life, being greedy and desirous of consumption. || 25 ||
Is there anything in this world that causes such misfortune as this female jackal born of the body, who brings about old age and wailing? (26)
Old age itself is a female jackal in the jungle of the body; it is shouting, weeping, and clamor. (26)

This flame of old age, consisting of the smoke and darkness of suffering, accompanied by coughing, labored breathing, and whistling sounds, blazes forth; indeed, he who is touched by it is utterly consumed.
When a piece of fresh ginger wood is being burned, it is well known that even amidst the flames there is a whistling sound.
O father, through old age, the slender body of men—whose sprouts are the white parts of the body—becomes crooked, just like a flowering creeper bent down by its blossoms. (28)
*Tanvī* means small; *tanuḥ* means the body. || 28 ||
O Sage, the elephant of death surely uproots in an instant the camphor-tree of the body, which is white with the camphor of old age.
He uproots—that is, he eradicates—the camphor tree and the plantain tree. || 29 ||
O Sage, as King Death approaches, with old age as his white fly-whisk, his army of mental anguish and physical disease marches out before him.

"Come, come!"—this refers to those who are arriving or about to arrive; [the use of the present tense] is like the present when in close proximity to the present time. "Old age" (jarā) is that which has white chowries (dhavala-cāmara). Her own (svā), belonging to herself, is the army (patākinī) of mental and physical ailments (ādhi-vyādhi). || 30 ||
"O Sage, behold those who, having entered the hollow of a mountain, were not conquered by enemies in battle, have now been swiftly defeated by an old, decrepit Rākṣasī! (31)
Those who, with fortitude, have entered even the mountain clefts and rock caverns that are difficult to penetrate; || 31 ||
Within the interior of the body-dwelling, enveloped by the frost of old age, the infant senses are not able to move even slightly. (32)
*Tuṣāra* means snow; by that, they are *balite*, meaning contracted. The *akṣāṇi* are the senses themselves, which are like *śiśavaḥ*, children. || 32 ||
Stumbling repeatedly with the third part of her staff, the old woman, like a kettle-drum, produces the sound of coughing and downward wind. 33.

She is characterized by a third leg in the form of a staff for support (*daṇḍa*); she whose lower wind is like a *kāsa* and who possesses a drum (*muraja*), a particular kind of musical instrument. || 33 ||
In this Gandhakuṭī of the wandering through saṃsāra, the beauty of the fly-whisk named "Old Age" shines forth, fixed upon the head of the staff-like body. (34)

Of this well-known one: belonging to the king called Saṃsāra—that is, to the worldly existence (saṃsṛti) or conventional life—the "fragrance" (gandha) refers both to the enjoyment of sense objects and to substances such as musk, for it perfumes (gandhayati)—that is, it scents—the mind and the assembly with passion and so forth; [it is located] in the chamber (kuṭī) of that fragrance.

The meaning is that upon the staff-like body which serves as her support, the beauty of the chowrie named "Old Age" shines forth from the head, through the spreading gentle breezes of loveliness and fragrance, and so forth. 34.
O Sage, while the city of the body remains white with the rising moon of old age,
the night-lotus of death suddenly comes into full bloom.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "while the lake of the hope for life remains. || 35 ||
Within the inner apartments of the body, which are white with the plaster of old age, women remain happily, free from incapacity, affliction, and misfortune. (36)
Lime powder. || 36 ||
O Sage, where non-existence precedes and old age triumphs over living beings, what consolation can there be here for me, of dull intellect? (37)

In which beings, among those of the fourfold body, old age first conquers—that is, overcomes—and where death, which is non-existence (*abhāva*), is the precursor (*agresara*) and the flow (*sara*); for it flows, thus it is *sarī*, meaning that which must inevitably come.
If the reading is *abhāvāgresarī*, it is clear. Among those bodies, in this very body here—
What consolation or confidence can I have? Surely this is the same for Vasiṣṭha and the others as well. [He says:
"Of what use is that miserable grasp of a wretched life, since even when one has reached old age, life continues to be lived?
Father, all the cravings of people remain unconquered within the path of old age and overwhelm them. (38)
In this wretched life, a life of suffering, what is the use of a stubborn grasp—that is, a perverse insistence? It means it is useless.
[Abandon] all cravings, that is, all desires. || 38 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Loathing Old Age," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Loathing Old Age," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
By those of small intellect, through much prattle consisting of conceptual constructions and mental fabrications, [the truth is obscured].
Driven to a state of agitation by various distinctions, one wanders within the cavern of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
Delighting all living beings— whose activities they hold dear— through the floods of their own playful manifestations,
Time alone is described here by means of its excellence in qualities, defects, and power.

Thus, the detachment from the enjoyment of fruits—both in this world and the next—has been shown regarding wealth (*śrī*), which is the object of enjoyment, as well as the thirst for enjoyment, and the youth and other stages that provide the occasion for such enjoyment. Now, [the text] describes the nature of desire (*kāma*) and so forth, beginning with the conceptualization:
"This is my object of enjoyment; I am its enjoyer; and these are the means for attaining it."

By those who have uttered countless worldly discourses through infinite mental constructions and imaginings such as, "Having accomplished this, I shall enjoy that for a long time," "This has been obtained by me today," and "I shall attain this desire";
and by those who possess the notion of self in the body, which is small, and the notion of the supreme human goal in trifling fragments of pleasure.

For those deluded people, by whom— [regarding] enemies, friends, neutrals, and so forth— there arises here a false notion (*bhrama*) that this world-system (*saṃsāra*), which is called "saṃsāra" because one wanders within it, is real; how indeed can such a notion arise for the wise within the hollow of its cavity, like [the perception of reality] in a cage of nets?
Only fools desire to grasp the fruit reflected in a mirror.

The objects of the senses are like a net that binds by drawing one in from afar; the body is like a cage that binds by confining one within its limits. Since these two, when taken together, are unreal because they are established only through delusion, how could the wise—those possessed of discernment—possibly find any reliance upon them in this worldly existence? Furthermore, no illustrative example for such a state of affairs is even well-known.
The particle *eva* is used for the sake of emphasis. He confirms that very point by means of an illustration: "only the children," etc. "In a mirror" means in a looking-glass (*darpaṇa*). || 2 ||
Even here, for those whose cultivation of pleasure is fragile, Time cuts that away entirely, just as a rat gnaws through a thread. (3)

In this very world, for those whose perception of happiness and hope for pleasure are so fragile and trivial— like a rat that, while clinging to the tip of a blade of grass above a hole, protects a worm hanging in the well by its mere thread of life— there is nothing here that this all-devouring Time does not consume.
It devours that entire world-born creation, just as the submarine fire consumes the surging ocean. || 4 ||

In this world, on this plane of worldly convention, there is no such thing born or produced that Time does not swallow; thus, the negative particle *na* is connected by repetition [to both "Time" and "swallows"]. *Ghasmara* means a devourer.
The submarine fire (*vāḍava*), namely the fire of the mare (*vaḍavānala*), [consumes] the ocean that has risen and increased due to causes such as the moon and other [planets]. || 4 ||
As the Great Lord, Time is formidable in its universal universality;
it is intent upon swallowing this entire existence of the visible world. (5)
By virtue of being the universal commonality, [time] is shared by all categories of things; time itself is Maheśvara, the Rudra of dissolution. (5)
Even for the great, O Lord, Time does not wait for even a moment;
having become the soul of the universe, it swallows the infinite world.

The genitive case in the phrase "even of the great" (mahatām api) is intended to express that action alone is the subordinate element. Even beings who are great by virtue of their power, intellect, majesty, and so forth, do not wait for even a moment; they do not look on with patience. The meaning is that [Kāla] destroys them immediately. || 6 ||
Manifesting slightly through forms known as the Yugas, the Ages, and the Kalpas,
He whose nature is the unperceivable form stands pervading all things.
Having stepped upon and brought under control. || 7 ||
Those things which are delightful, those which are auspicious undertakings, and even those as massive as Mount Sumeru—
all are swallowed up by Time, just as serpents are devoured by Garuḍa.
Cruel, hard, fierce, harsh, miserly, and base—
there is nothing that this Time has not yet swallowed even until today.
The distinction is that it is as hard as stone and the like, as cruel as a tiger and the like, and as rough as a saw and the like; it swallows and devours. || 9 ||
Time, whose mind is solely intent on devouring, eats even while swallowing; yet this great consumer is never satiated, even by the infinite multitudes of worlds.

With his mind fixed and his intellect one-pointedly directed toward the object of swallowing alone, he swallows one while disregarding the other; this is clear in the reading "girīn api" (even mountains). 10.
Time takes away, destroys, creates, consumes, and slays; for it is like an actor who performs the dance of saṃsāra in various forms. 11.

The meaning is that whatever is well-known in the world, such as seizing and so forth regarding wealth and other things—all that is performed by Time alone, which exists in the form of each respective agent. || 11 ||
Established in differentiation, it incessantly breaks apart the seeds of the elements through their non-existence in the world, just as a parrot [consumes] pomegranate seeds.

The "division" refers to the state of being manifested; it is a metaphorical conceit that [the Self] divides—that is, tears apart and devours—the fourfold seeds of living beings, such as those born from eggs and so forth, which reside therein, by means of their non-existence through bondage and by bringing about their non-existence through destruction.
The illustration is clear. || 12 ||
With the tips of his tusks of good and evil lopped off the sprouts of worldly existence,
this elephant of the life-force of the vast multitude of people roams about.

The "multitude" (*janatā*) refers to a group of people accumulated through pride and other such traits; the "row of living beings" (*jīvarājī*) is the collection of those very lives, which constitutes the "forest" (*vanī*), that great wilderness.

Time (*kāla*) is the elephant within that forest. (Alternatively, if the reading is *rājīvinī*, it means an elephant for the destruction of the lotus plant. He describes it with appropriate attributes: "splendid and foul," and so forth. It manifests.
He roars. || 13 ||
Encompassing the entire expansive forest of Brahmā, it stands pervading the vast tree that bears the great gods as its fruit, rooted in Viriñci and extending through the cosmic egg.

In which [place] there are trees characterized by the fruit in the form of deities— namely, the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) themselves, whose roots are the unquintuplicated elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūtātman*) of Viriñci (Brahmā), and which are "great" (*mahāntaḥ*), being synonyms for the great word residing at their root— and in which such [trees] exist; [his] dress (*veṣaḥ*) is an artificial expansion (*kṛtrima ābhogaḥ*).

The form of the world is illusory (*māyika*); because it possesses that [form], it is "expansive" (*ābhogi*). According to the Śruti, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)," the meaning is that it is accompanied by the phenomenal world (*saprapañca*). Time stands having completely surrounded—that is, pervading from all sides—the forest of Brahman itself, which is like a wilderness (*kānana*) due to its difficulty in crossing.

The meaning is that Kālodara alone is the witness of the arising, abiding, and destruction of all things. However, if the reading "viriñcimajabrahmāṇḍaṃ mahaddivaphaladrutam" were universal, it would mean that the cause of the universe (brahmāṇḍa) released by Viriñci is the variegated Māyā; "aja" refers to those with four faces.
In every universe, there are His pastime-forms (*līlā-vigraha*) together with that very universe; the singular number is used for the genus.
That [universe] itself is "great" (*mahat*). "By day" means the gods. The absence of the *guṇa* vowel change is Vedic.
The fourfold beings characterized by that [universe], joined with the fruits of their respective karmas, are themselves the trees.

The meaning is that it stands encompassing the Brahma-forest, which is of such a nature—expansive, possessing a semblance of artificiality, endowed with slight enjoyment, or almost entirely filled with snakes on all sides. || 14 ||
Filled with bees during the night and creating clusters of blossoms by day,
the creeper of the arts of the seasons never grows weary.

The nights are filled with bees in the form of those very nights; the days are the clusters of blossoms within them. A year, a kalpa, a day of Brahmā, a kāṣṭhā (consisting of thirty kalās)—[the Lord] desists from exhaustion, meaning He ceases [from His activity]. || 15 ||
O Sage, that crest-jewel of rogues is seen neither when pierced nor even when shattered; he is not burned even when burnt, nor is he seen even when visible. 16.
The meaning is that, although it appears as various effects, or is broken, burnt, or visible, it does not undergo destruction or the like in its own essential nature. || 16 ||
In a single moment, it is capable of raising something up, and in that same instant, it utterly destroys something else, like an expansive kingdom of the mind. (17)
He remained there, drawing in people with his wealth-producing form by means of the difficult-to-sustain gestures of a woman of wanton dalliance. (18)

The wife of Time (Kāla), who is ever playful in her own wicked pastimes suited to each respective age and nourished only by the suffering of living beings, exists deluding them through the superimposition of identity with material objects such as the physical body and senses, thereby causing them to revolve in their own cycles of heaven, hell, and so forth. || 18 ||
Out of a self-centered desire for sustenance, he was intent on making everything his own— whether a blade of grass, a particle of dust, Mahendra, Mount Sumeru, a leaf, or the ocean.

"By being self-sustaining," that is, by having a nature consisting merely in filling one's own belly; "to make one's own," meaning to bring under one's own control, which is to say, to devour. || 19 ||
Cruelty is fully present here, as is greed;
all misfortune resides right here, as does unbearable fickleness.
It is sufficient and complete; at this time. || 20 ||
He playfully impels the sun and moon as if sporting in the vault of the sky, casting his two playful hands about like a child in its own courtyard. || 21 ||
He by whom a pair of balls was repeatedly cast down and struck for the sake of play. || 21 ||
With his form encircled by garlands of the bones of all beings reaching down to his feet,
he shines like Time itself at the end of an eon, having assumed its creative power.
One whose conceptual constructions have been seized and who has destroyed the distinction between living beings. || 22 ||
At the end of the eon, Mount Meru trembles in the sky like a birch-bark leaf, tossed by the winds that have issued from the limbs of this fierce being.
His conduct was wild and unrestrained; Meru, as if being shattered on all sides by the winds issuing from his limbs, was like a piece of birch bark.
Becoming Rudra, he becomes Mahendra and then the Grandfather (Brahmā);
he also becomes Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa, and yet again, nothing at all.
Possessing immeasurable splendor, he bears within himself other creations that have arisen and fallen away like waves,
as the ocean bears its waves day and night.

Assuming other creations—that is, holding them—He constantly brings forth other creations that have arisen and those that have been destroyed; "constantly arisen" means eternally active, which may also be taken as a qualification of time. "Waves" refers to the billows. (25)
He stood like one who was stripping from the trees called Mahākalpas the hosts of gods and asuras, who were like the weight of ripe fruit.
Cutting down and causing to fall. || 26 ||
This is the time for the falling of the swarms of living beings, buzzing like gnats,
which have attained the state of massive trees within the flood of the udumbara-fruit-like cosmic eggs.

Of the multitudes of the udumbara fruits that are the cosmic eggs, which resound with the "ghuṃghum" humming of the living beings themselves—the very creatures such as mosquitoes—[as they move within]. || 27 ||
Accompanied by his beloved Action, he delights his solitary body with the night-lotus of pure existence, which is made to blossom by the moonlight of consciousness.

The moonlight is the consciousness that is the substrate of all; by its mere presence, it serves as the cause of delight for the night-lotus pond— the universal characteristic of the existence of the world— which has blossomed everywhere and attained manifestation through the various auspicious and inauspicious actions of living beings.
The sense is that, through curiosity regarding monasteries and curiosity regarding worldly affairs, there is a passing of time;
since no other time exists for one who passes his time there, he merely amuses his own body. || 28 ||
He remained standing, leaning upon his own body as a firmly established seat that was boundless, shoreless, and limitless, towering high like a great mountain.

It is firmly established, having its seat fixed upon the infinite and undivided Brahman, which is likewise infinite in extent, boundless and shoreless, and devoid of any limits in the east or north. || 29 ||
In some places he contemplates his own nature as dark with the deepest gloom, in some places as pervaded by splendor, and in some places as devoid of both; thus he remains absorbed in meditation.
In some cases, such as at midnight or with the application of collyrium, it is dark like the darkness of black shadows; [this refers to] its own nature or its own effect. || 30 ||
With his own being—which has become the very essence of countless dissolved transmigrations—he has come to a state of fixed station, like the earth burdened by its heavy load. (31)

Having established his footing— meaning being firmly rooted— in that state which is substantial due to the remaining essence of his own existence, which supports all the countless transmigrating beings who have dissolved away, and which is dense with the weight of being the universal substratum,
he neither suffers nor exerts himself; he neither comes nor goes.
It neither sets nor rises, even in hundreds of great eons.
Merely through the effortless play of initiating the world, with profound ease,
he protects by means of his own self his own vast self, which is free from egoism.

"By 'thickly' (ghanā) means with ease or non-attachment. He protects and does not destroy. It is 'extended' (ātata), meaning widespread, in such a way that it is without egoism and free from conceit. || 33 ||

He remained there, having placed upon the lake of his own self the swarm of bees that was the row of day-lotuses— now darkened by the mud of the night— and which was itself a swarm of clouds within his own soul.

The night itself is the mud because it is dark; from that [mud], she was raised up. The days themselves are a cluster of *kokanada* red lotuses. Her own self is a lake whose very nature is time. // 34 //
Having taken up a worn-out broomstick for the night,
the wretched man wanders all around the mountain, gathering gold-dust from the light.

The sense is that he is miserly and greedy; for this very reason, he is incapable of acquiring a new broom, and remains dissatisfied even when he obtains a great deal of gold from a single sweeping. "The mountain" refers to the Golden Mountain (Meru); therefore, it is understood that the "gold-dust" consists of the fragments fallen from that mountain. || 35 ||
Pointing with his finger at the corners of the house of worldly existence, he searches with a lamp of the sun, out of miserliness, asking: "What is there, and where? (36)
He describes his miserliness in another way with the words "saṃcārayan" (while moving about): "in the corners," that is, in the intermediate directions.
Beholding with his unblinking solar eye, he devours the ripe fruits of the world-guardians; this [world] is like a decayed forest.
The blinking of the eyes is the counterpart of the sun; by that [blinking], it is as if the day itself.
In due course, like a merchant of the qualities, he casts the jewels of the world into the fierce hollow of death, which is like a worn-out hut strewn with refuse.
The entire world is a dilapidated hut, a house of straw; therein are scattered those who have fallen through negligence. Death itself is a casket—a small box—within which they are placed. (38)
That very string of jewels of the world which is abundantly filled with virtues, they cut away even further, as if merely for the sake of ornamenting their own bodies. (39)

By "threads" (guṇaiḥ) is meant both the threads [of a cloth] and qualities such as knowledge and discipline. "The world" (lokaḥ) refers to people; "on its own limb" (aṅge) means on its own part, such as the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
Although it cuts everything down, nevertheless, the destruction of those possessed of virtues alone attains renown;
thus, that statement is made in these two verses. || 39 ||
The fickle moon constantly and excessively forms a circle with the garland of night-lotuses that follows it like a swan during the day, using the stars as its filaments.
In which lotus garland the stars are the long filaments, or rather the constellations themselves are the filaments.
The word "capala" (fickle) is used to avoid the impropriety of placing a swan [as a central ornament]. It "encircles" means it holds it like a bracelet.
The phrase "on the forearm of the hand of the year, which has five seasons as its fingers" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 40 ||
The hunter of the world—consisting of mountains, oceans, clouds, and mountain peaks—daily drinks even the red drops of the stars upon beholding them. (41)

The waves are the oceans; the sky is the world. Time is the butcher—the slaughterer existing at the slaughterhouse (*sūnā*), which is the place of violence—of those rams characterized by the universe, whose four horns are the mountains and so forth due to their preeminence. He [Time] scatters the stars and constellations, which are like the entrails, across the courtyard of the sky.
Seeing even those red specks, she drinks and licks them day after day; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). The middle voice (ātmanepada) is Vedic (chāndasa). || 41 ||
He is the moon for the lotus of youth and the lion for the elephant of life;
there is nothing that this thief of the trivial and the sublime does not steal. (42)
The connection is that among all categories of things—whether empty, insignificant, non-empty, or great—that which this thief does not possess does not exist. || 42 ||
Through the playful sport of cosmic manifestation, by which living beings are ground down and cast away,
non-existence delights in itself by means of the appearance of existence within its own self.
By one who has thus ground, crushed, and cast living beings into the jaws of death;

by one whose play and sport take the form of the cosmic dissolution (*saṃvarta*); who, being devoid of objective entities (*bhāva*) as if in deep sleep, [acts] through his own self which, like in deep sleep, illuminates knowledge in the form of objects, [and] through his own presiding Brahman-nature.
This is the meaning. || 43 ||
