He is the creator, the enjoyer, and the destroyer; he is the rememberer who has attained the state of all things.

Thus, having rested during the dissolution, at the time of creation once again, he himself becomes the creator, enjoyer, destroyer, rememberer, and so forth—the essence of all things; this is the remainder of the sense. || 44 ||

Indeed, the power of Time manifests here among men by suddenly revealing and then concealing the body—which, though composed entirely of parts, has no internal division between them, and which bears both beautiful and ugly forms. (45)

That whose inner secret has not been grasped or determined by anyone through parts—that is, through intellectual skills—it thus sports, manifesting, concealing, and withdrawing its entire form: a form that is "fortunate" (subhaga), meaning corresponding to the enjoyment of the fruits of merit, and its opposite, "unfortunate" (durbhaga). This is Time (Kāla).
The remainder [of the commentary]: The word "hi" indicates what is well-known. The meaning is that in this world, the power of Time over human beings is indeed well-established.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Refutation of Time," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. Chapter 23.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Refutation of Time," in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgya-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Of him whose play is so formidable, and from whom all calamities have been cast far away—
In this cycle of existence, for the prince Time, whose power is immeasurable. || 1 ||
That very Time (Kāla), accompanied by his beloved Caṇḍī,
is now described as being possessed by a prince’s eagerness for the hunt.

Now he promises to assume that very form at that same time, by means of being a great prince who sports with the curiosity of hunting—this is expressed by the word "asya" (of him). He is one whose playful pastimes (*līlā*) are wild and magnificent (*uḍḍāmara*). He is one from whom all calamities have been cast far away and dispelled. He is one of unmeasured vigor, of inconceivable prowess. He is one who shines, being renowned.
The conduct of his son Kāla—[the description of his hunting]—is described; this is the understood meaning of the phrase "his conduct is described. || 1 ||
As he thus engaged in hunting with wretched, deluded herds of living creatures and wild beasts, the thicket of the world’s forest was worn away.
The connection with what follows is that the great ocean of the duration of this very kalpa has been made into a pleasure-pool.

By "the deluded" (mugdhaiḥ) is meant the ignorant. "By the herds of deer" refers to the elements (bhūtāni) themselves. This is for the amusement of the slayer even toward those who deserve to be slain.
[It is] a lotus-bed where the beautiful submarine fire blazes in one part.
The delightful pleasure-pool is like the great ocean at the end of the eon.
By implication, in a certain region of the world-forest. || 3 ||
The world is made into a morning meal by those very same oceans of curd and milk that were once filled with pungent, bitter, and sour elements, and so forth, now all having become stale.

The word *bhūta* (being) is connected to each [item] individually. The phrase "his breakfast (*kalyavartanam*)"—meaning his morning meal—is to be supplied; it refers to the world [of beings] that are of a single form every day, accompanied by oceans of curd, milk, and so forth, yet which have become stale and remained for a long time.
Such a morning meal consisting of stale food mixed with pungent and bitter curds and other ingredients is well known among the Dravidians.
Caṇḍī, who moves through the four directions, accompanied by the entire host of Mothers, is stationed within the forest of saṃsāra; she is a tigress who destroys the multitudes of malevolent spirits.
He speaks of his beloved who is worthy of him, calling her Caṇḍī: "Like a tigress, she is the slayer of the multitudes of spirits;
stationed in the forest of saṃsāra, she is appointed for its sport. Caṇḍī, the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), is his beloved—this is the sense to be supplied. || 5 ||
The earth is the palm of her hand, and the earth is her wine-cup filled with nectar;
it is garlanded by swarms of hovering bees over lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lilies.

He describes his drinking vessel: "The earth. The earth itself—the vast earth—is his drinking vessel upon the palm of his hand. For the sake of the fragrance and beauty of the liquor, it is adorned with lotuses, lilies, and other such flowers.
Within the cage of his arms lies Nṛsiṃha, roaring and tearing asunder with fierce force.
With his mane, broad and thick shoulders, he was made into a pet bird for play. || 7 ||

While he was confined within a cage held fast by his arms, the incarnation as Nṛsiṃha was turned into a bird called Vāja for the sake of sporting in the slaughter of the Dānavas and others. Of what nature was it? It was raucous, having a habit of roaring; it was vikaṭa, possessing a formidable *āsphoṭa*, which is the sound of clapping the arms; and it was vikaṭa with its *saṭās*—that is, difficult to behold due to its manes (*kesaras*).
One whose shoulders—meaning the upper parts of the arms—are full. || 7 ||
Sweet with the lute of the bottle-gourd, possessing the radiant splendor of an autumnal sky,
the Lord Mahākāla is indeed like a playful young cuckoo.

Mahākāla, who will be described in the narrative concerning the stone, is Saṃhārabhairava; for the sake of his divine play (līlā), he has assumed the form of a young cuckoo. What is he like? He wears a garland of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa-mālā) and possesses a resonance that is terrifying to others; yet, even from such a being, [he is seen] by the gaze of those whose nature is even more fierce than his own.
It is described as such because it is indeed sweet; its dark yet clear luster is like the autumnal sky. || 8 ||
The bow named Non-Contemplation (Abhāvanā), whose form is incessantly flashing and which has discharged a volley of arrows of suffering, vibrates everywhere. (9)
"Sphūrjitam" means the sound of a twang. The bow named "Saṃhāra"—belonging to him by whom the volley of arrows of suffering has been vomited forth, that is, expelled—resounds everywhere. || 9 ||

Supreme indeed is Time, the expert in excessive playfulness, wandering, moving, and shimmering about; tearing asunder the world grown old and agitated like a monkey, he strives here within this throbbing body. 10.

Even while his targets were wandering about and he himself was moving, he pierced the mark because his arrows were unfailing; for that very reason, he shone pre-eminently above all other marksmen. For that same reason, in this decaying world, he produced—that is, brought about—the "restless monkeys": people who, like monkeys, are fickle in conduct and addicted to sense-objects.

Such was that Prince Kāla, his body quivering and his form radiant, who exerted himself and engaged in the sport of hunting; yet the metaphorical representation of him as a monkey is due to a specific poetic device (*prakrama-viśeṣaṇa*). Thus ends "The Play of Time" in the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
The twenty-fourth canto, titled "Nāma."
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Play of Time," in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twenty-fifth Canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Right here, there is another supreme crest-jewel among those of wicked conduct."
In this world, that which acts and consumes is called destiny (daiva) and time (kāla). || 1 ||
Here, over the course of another boundless time, the diverse and extensive dance of necessity, consisting of actions and their fruits, is performed.

Having thus described Mahākāla as a prince, the author begins to describe the action-constituted Time—which serves as his adjunct—for the sake of his diversion, by imagining it in two forms as dancers, starting with the words "atraiva" and so forth. Among those whose amorous play (*vilāsa*) is wicked, he is the most excellent, like a crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*). Another...

It is other than what was previously mentioned. That which "plays" (divyati)—meaning it deals with living beings by bestowing the fruits of their actions—is *daiva*, which is *kṛtānta* (the Ordainer) in the state of fruition. That which "impels" (*kalayati*)—meaning it necessarily brings about the fruit—is *kriyā* (action), which is *kāla* (Time).
Thus, the meaning is that this single entity is described in two ways according to the distinction between its prior and subsequent states. || 1 ||
Apart from mere activity, no other form is perceived for that which consists of its own vibration; it has neither action nor any intended purpose.

Therein, he describes the second [type] first, according to the maxim of the needle and the frying pan—namely, "action" (kriyā). Here, "action" refers to the accomplishment of a result; "desired" (samīhita) means that which is longed for. || 2 ||
Therefore, this entire succession of living beings, exceedingly fragile,
has been brought to a state of extreme distress by his heat, like a garland of snow.

The "continuum of beings" refers to the multitude of living creatures. "By heat" means by the sun's glare. A "garland of frost" is a mass of mist. "Distress" means destruction. The underlying sense is that all misfortune is produced by one's own karma. || 3 ||
Whatever expansive mandala of the world is seen here, that is his dance-hall; herein he dances intensely.
The expansive and all-encompassing circle of the world is described as a dance hall, a theater for dancing, where the actors are passion, hatred, and the like. (4)
And third, bearing the most terrible name Kṛtānta, the god who has assumed the form of a Kāpālika dances intoxicated in the world. (5)

Since this is the primary [topic], which can be understood only through the scriptures, he begins to describe it in detail for the sake of strengthening conviction, starting with the words "the third" and so forth.
It is the "third" in relation to what was mentioned in the previous creation; "the body of a Kāpālika" means the attire of a Kāpālika. || 5 ||
O Sage, as Kṛtānta dances like one intensely impassioned, he is constantly and supremely enamored with his beloved Niyati.

*Niyati* is the fixed necessity that the fruit of performed action must inevitably come to pass; for one who is not free from passion, the meaning is that [the action] necessarily yields its fruit. (6)

The remainder is Śeṣa, white as a digit of the moon; and the flow of the Gaṅgā—these two are threefold, both as the sacred thread (upavīta) and as that which is not worn (anvita), upon the chest of worldly existence (saṃsāra).

He describes the ornaments on his limbs with the word "Śeṣa" (the Remainder). The flow of the Gaṅgā is well-known to be threefold. By the use of the particle *ca* (and), there is a reference to those two [the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā] through the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two similar terms). *Avīte* means *prācīnāvīte* (worn over the right shoulder). *Saṃsāra* is that in which one wanders; it is the triple world (*trailokya*), and that itself is his chest. || 7 ||
O Brahman, the orbs of the moon and sun are the golden bracelets on her wrists; the playful lotus in her hand is the pericarp of the cosmic egg.
The two wrists are the roots of the hands; Mount Meru is the pericarp of the universe. || 8 ||
Studded with stars as its blossoms, with the flickering Puṣkara and Āvarta clouds as its tender leaves, that single sky was the very garment upon the waters of the universal ocean.
The drops are variegated drops. Its two sprouts are the Saṃvarta clouds over Puṣkara and Āvarta.
Its garment is the very sky, washed and cleansed; for it is well known that Kāpālikas wear a single rag as a neck-cloth with a hole in the middle suspended around their necks. (9)
Before such a person as he, Destiny, ever longing for him,
dances with unremitting fervor through her various undertakings.

With its fury never subsiding and its effort unceasing, it performs actions conducive to the enjoyment of living beings; within the hollow of the world-tent, it is restless with the desire to dance, its movement unobstructed, and it is flickering with the coming and going of things.

Of her whose form is unobstructed vibration and whose power of action is unimpeded—[she is] the life-force of the living beings who witness the dance. [In this word *nṛtyat*], by the rule "anuṭ parasyātaḥ," there is the substitution of *u* for the following *a*. || 11 ||
Her limbs were adorned with beautiful ornaments, and she was like a series of celestial realms; her massive, circular braid hung down from her head as far as the netherworld.

The phrase "becomes a beautiful ornament on the limbs of the series of worlds, including the gods, consisting of the various divisions of the universe" should be supplied as a response to every [verse]. The sky, extending down to the netherworld (āpātālam), is her hanging mass of braided hair (kabarīmaṇḍala), because of its dark color. || 12 ||
And Narakālī, wearing a garland of tinkling anklets radiant with clamor,
is strung upon the thread of evil deeds and stands with her feet in the underworld.

The garland of flower-clusters (mañjarīmālā) rests upon her feet, which are characterized by the underworld (pātāla) and belong to that Narakālī who blazes with the clamor of "kala-kala" cries and the roar of weeping, and who is set ablaze by the fires of hell. By the word *mañjarī*, anklets (pādakiṅkiṇyaḥ) are indicated; otherwise, their being strung together on a thread would be untenable. || 13 ||
The forehead-slip of Yama was painted by Citragupta with musk tilakas, prepared according to the number of his deeds.

Because he serves as the cause for manifesting the fragrance of the karma of living beings, Citragupta has become musk; by means of this instrument, upon the tablet—which is a part of the face, namely the forehead (the word *phalaka* meaning "tablet" and *lalāṭa* meaning "forehead")—Yama indeed shines, for Citragupta presides over Yama. This is established precisely by the arrangement of the two primary parts, the feet and the forehead.
In the same way, the construction of the *atirātra* components should be understood from the sense of the text according to their respective application. || 14 ||
Taking on a dark face at the end of the eons,
this goddess indeed dances again in agitation, with the loud roar of crashing mountains.
Of Kāla, the Lord of Time, the mouth—indicated by such things as the playfulness of the face, the knitting of the brows, and sidelong glances—is thus [described]. 15.
Behind them were the Prālambas, the Vibhrāntakas, the Kumārabhṛtas,
and the Barhiṇas, terrifying with the loud, resonant cries from the great cavities of their three eyes.

He elaborates upon her very manner of dancing with six verses. "Behind" means from the back. "By peacocks" (barhibhiḥ) means by pheasants. For all the words ending in the instrumental case, there is a connection with the word "shines" (rājate), which is located in the fifth verse.

The sequence ending with "by the terrifying" (bhīṣaṇaiḥ) connects with the following phrase, "by the heads of Hara. [The sound] "bhāṅkāra"— (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available text.)
A particular kind of sound. || 16 ||
With the heads of Hara, whose long, dangling matted locks and moon were scattered about, and with the whisks of Gaurī’s beautiful, swaying tresses of Mandāra flowers rising aloft; || 17 ||
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound formed with a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *candra*. [The hair] is tawny (*kabara*), and by means of those [forms], [the skull-bowls are described].

With the hollows of Bhairava’s belly having the form of mountains in a wild dance (*uttāṇḍava*), and with begging-bowls that are the bodies of Indra possessing a hundred holes, which resound; || 18 ||

The immovable mountains are represented by gourd-vessels (*tumbaka*) or *alābu* bowls, because the practice of the Kāpālikas is well-known for using such items. The word "hundred" (*śata*), which has been formed by the grammatical operation of *ekaśeṣa* and is thus plural in form, functions as the first member of a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
therefore, since Indra’s body possesses a thousand eyes, it has one thousand and seven apertures, and thus nine apertures.
The distinction from well-known bodies should be understood; there is the attainment of one thousand and seven. || 18 ||
Filling the sky with the weight of her dry skeletons and skull-topped staffs, she,
the bringer of universal destruction, terrifies even herself.
The spinal bone, which constitutes a part of the body, strikes terror—that is, it acts as if to terrify others for the sake of instilling fear. || 19 ||
With the beautiful lotus-garland that is the wheel of the head of Viśvarūpa,
he shines as she dances vibrantly during the great cosmic cycles (mahākalpas).
The various forms and diverse shapes of the heads and clusters of skulls constitute a garland of lotuses; with that garland, she dances and whirls in many ways. || 20 ||
At the terrifying sounds of the drums of the intoxicated Puṣkarāvarta clouds,
it is said that even Tumburu and the other [gandharvas] flee from her at the end of the eon.

The clouds known as Puṣkarāvarta are indeed the Saṃvarta clouds; they belong to the dancing Antaka (the God of Death), who is as fierce as a drum (ḍamara) and whose hair is the sky, beautiful with the moonlight of the stars and adorned with the lunar orb as a shining crest.

Having thus described the dance of Niyati along with its accompaniments, the author, describing the ornaments of her husband as well, says "nṛtyati" and so forth. "Antaḥ" means within the previously mentioned dance hall; "candramaṇḍalena" refers to that which will later be described as his ear-ornament (kuṇḍala).

Of the radiant and shining one; of Kṛtānta (Yama), whose hair is adorned with a crest (*avacūlin*) consisting of the sky itself as a peacock-feather plume—charming and heart-stealing due to the stars and moonlight, which serve as the likeness of the moon characterized by its stars—the [earring] is attached to the ear; this is the connection with the following verse. || 22 ||
In one ear she wore a blazing bone-ring from the Himalayas, and in the other, a lovely golden earring from Mount Meru. (23)

In one right ear, there is a bone-made ring (*mudrikā*), meaning an earring (*kuṇḍala*) in the shape of a ring suitable for a *kāpālika*. On the other, the left, is a *karṇikā*, that is to say, an earring as an ornament for the ear. || 23 ||
Right here, her two dangling earrings are the sun and moon, her two cheeks are the orbs of the moon and sun, and the range of the Lokāloka mountain serves as her girdle all around her waist.
In this context, it refers to these very two ears; "śreṇī" [is used] because of the connection to the horns and arms, or due to the distinction between the Kalpa and the Brahmāṇḍa.
Moving here and there, the lightning—
like a golden bangle— shines as a silken strip upon the garment of the clouds, fluttered by the wind.

The lightning is the pericarp of the circular earring, and the bracelet is in the shape of a pericarp; the clouds themselves, due to their various colors, constitute a patched garment made of rags such as silk cloths and the like. (25)
With maces, sharp-edged spears, lances, tridents, javelins, and clubs—
sharp weapons gathered as if by the Destroyer of the world, who has himself been exhausted by the world’s own destruction— they [assailed him]. || 26 ||

The garland of his [the Lord's] arms shines, variegated by pestles and other weapons that stand as if gathered and assembled—weapons vomited forth from the exhausted worlds of previous creations, which have passed away and been brought to their end by Death (Kṛtānta). Thus ends the verse:
"In this short noose cast by the hand of Time, which severs the bonds of saṃsāra..."
His garland, strung upon the great thread of his remaining enjoyments, shines resplendent. || 27 ||
The body of the serpent-king Śeṣa is his coil; [this is an] indication of the commonality of bodies among those who bear weapons. [The implied meaning is:
"As if strung together, bound upon the hand of Time—the aforementioned prince—by fate, he fell into the cycle of transmigration," and so forth.
A garland has been fashioned and placed upon the neck of this Kṛtānta (the God of Death), with its loops fastened.
It shines. || 27 ||
The row of bracelets formed by the seven oceans, radiant with the luster of the jewels in the makara-shaped clasps shimmering with life, is the ornament of his two arms.

The emblems such as the crocodile and others found on the bracelets of other [kings] are well known to be lifeless; in order to distinguish him from them, it is said that his is "throbbing with life. || 28 ||
The great whirlpool of worldly affairs, a succession of pleasure and pain, darkened by the dust of passion and the gloom of ignorance—its line of hair shines forth. (29)
The scriptural and natural conventions are themselves the great, characteristic whorls of hair; rajas and tamas are the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti). || 29 ||
At the end of the eon, Kṛtānta, being of such a nature, having brought to an end that dance born of Tāṇḍava along with the Maheśvaras, withdrew Maheśvara from his dancing activity.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: having created such a desire for the movement of limbs—that is, a longing for the impulse to dance—which is the origin of fame for the *tāṇḍava*, He extends this playful dance (*nṛtyalīlā*). || 30 ||
Furthermore, she performs this dance-play consisting of *lāsya*, which is the very nature of creation and adorned with the overcoming of old age, grief, and suffering. (31)
Consisting of dance and abounding in dramatic gestures. || 31 ||
Again he creates worlds, forest interiors, and other realms, as well as the arrangement of the network of living beings,
and the steady and moving beauty of refined conduct.
Just as children tirelessly create patterns in the mud. || 32 ||
The beautiful arrangement—that is, the correct practice—of the *ācāras*, which are the virtuous rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*;
[a practice] which is stable in the Kṛta and Tretā ages but unstable in the Kali and Dvāpara ages; and their composition in the form of play-dolls and the like.
Thus ends the section on Dispassion (*Vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) in the *Ārṣa Śrīvāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
The twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Play of Destiny."
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Play of Fate," in the Vairāgya-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa.
The twenty-sixth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O great sage, when this [creation] of these elements, beginning with time, had thus occurred...
"What reliance can there be here for those like me upon that which is called 'saṃsāra'? Let it be said thus. (1)
Here, the miserable condition of extensive saṃsāra is elaborated upon through its defects,
by virtue of dependence on time and other factors, for the sake of producing dispassion.

Anticipating the objection, "Let time [and other factors] act; what does that matter to you?", the author proceeds to elaborate upon his perception of defects in all things, such as time and the rest, and demonstrates the resulting attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*), which is a state of non-reliance, by means of the verse beginning with "vṛtte" and so forth. "Vṛtte" refers to conduct or character. "Āsthā" refers to reliance or confidence. (1)
O Sage, we stand as if sold by these worldly phenomena such as destiny; deluded by the dust of the phenomenal world, we are like forest deer.

Those who are deluded—meaning enchanted—by these four previously mentioned factors, such as the expansion of objects like sound and so forth, which have as their primary cause *daiva*, that is, past karma. || 2 ||
This ignoble succession of time,
intent on devouring all, incessantly casts the world into the ocean of calamity.

He whose traditional practice (*samāmnāya*)—the habitual performance of conduct—is identical to that of the ignoble; he whose tradition consists of the teachings of false teachers such as the Buddhists, which result in the unceasing and incomplete enjoyment of pleasures, life, and so forth; he who is intent on devouring, devoted solely to filling his belly; the rogue named Time (*kāla*), who [deceives] the world by setting it upon the wrong path.
The word "people" (jana) is also understood to have other meanings. || 3 ||
The god burns [the world] within with his cruel activities and evil desires,
just as fire burns the world with its hot, radiant flames.
They burn within through wicked desires; by means of cruel actions and misconduct, they burn even outwardly—this is the implied sense.
The same should also be applied to the illustrative example. || 4 ||
This destiny, which is ever intent upon its fixed course, agitates my fortitude; though it is beloved for its form as the boundary of order, it is fickle by nature due to its feminine essence.

Niyati—the beloved consort of Kṛtānta (Death), who is defined by the limits of time and the restriction of the outward activity of the senses—is intent upon those fixed [beings] devoted to meditative absorption;
she shakes—that is, deprives—them of their fortitude and steadfastness. The reason for this is as follows:
"Because of being female. || 5 ||
Like a serpent seizing the wind, Death, whose conduct is cruel, incessantly devours the multitude of living beings,
leading even the ageless body to old age.
Having brought old age upon his body, which was once undecaying and youthful, he caused it to reach that state. || 6 ||
Yama, the merciless lord of kings, does not show compassion even for one who is suffering; a person who is magnanimous toward all living beings has become rare to find. (7)
He is the lord of merciless kings; that is to say, he is exceedingly merciless. || 7 ||
O Sage, all classes of beings possess but a trifling existence;
these grounds of enjoyment are harsh, consisting only of suffering, and leading to an endless end. (8)

All classes of beings, even those ending with Brahmā, as well as all species of living creatures, are in a state of detachment; their prosperity is indeed trivial—for life is exceedingly fickle, death is utterly cruel, youth is extremely unstable, and childhood is lost in its own dullness. (9)
By dullness and delusion; it has been taken away, that is, removed. || 9 ||
The world is stained by the impurity of time; kinsmen are the bonds of worldly existence;
enjoyments are the great diseases of existence; and cravings are but mirages. (10)
*Kalana* is *kalā*, which is the pursuit of sense objects. || 10 ||
The senses themselves are the enemies who have turned truth into falsehood;
the enemy that is the mind strikes the self with its own mind. (11)

The body and so forth are grasped as the Self from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Upon their discrimination, one realizes their unreality—that is, their lack of ultimate substantiality. Alternatively, "unreality" refers to the fact that the Reality characterized by "truth, knowledge," and so on, [is not found therein]. Thus, the Self—of which the mind alone is the enemy because it is the cause of bondage—becomes identified with the mind through the ego-inflation of the mind (*manobhimāna*).
He strikes himself as it were with his own mind, making himself miserable. || 11 ||
Egoism leads to blemish; intellects are fragile;
actions yield bitter fruits; and pastimes have become centered on women. (12)

Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the internal organ characterized primarily by self-conceit; it leads to defilement, that is, to a blemish, meaning a corruption of one's true nature. Cognitions (*buddhi*), whose essence is determination, are its functions; because they are directed outward, they are extremely fragile and soft, lacking stability as they do not abide in their own true nature. Actions (*kriyā*)... [are likewise].
The activities are bodily; the pastimes are mental diversions. || 12 ||
The true wonders, which were once the objects of longing, have been destroyed; women have become banners of vice, and the aesthetic sentiments have fallen into a state of flavorlessness. (13)

The wonders of truth are the marvels of the manifestation of the Self. They are the banners and flags of faults. "Rasas" refers to attachments. "Nīrasatām" means the state of being devoid of attachment, or alternatively, the state of objects being undesirable. || 13 ||
When a thing is known as non-existent, the mind is surrendered to the ego;
when beings are pierced by the realization of their non-existence, the end of existence is not attained. (14)

The object, though supramundane, is known through its nature as a collection of causes and effects; the mind is given over to it—that is to say, it is fixated upon it. Pierced by non-existence, they are seized by destruction. O holy one, because of the impermanence of all things, the intellect, with its inner depths agitated, suffers in solitude.
The disease of passion manifests, yet dispassion does not approach. || 15 ||
The statement beginning with "he does not approach" and so forth is an expression of extreme rarity in the world, and not because it contradicts his own initial undertaking. || 15 ||
The vision impaired by the quality of passion (rajas) causes darkness (tamas) to increase;
and the essence (sattva), the ultimate reality, is not attained, being exceedingly remote. 16.
It is realized; it is attained. || 16 ||
Stability has become instability; death is facing its arrival;
fortitude has fallen into despondency; and delight is fixed eternally on that which is unreal. (17)
Staying means living; [it applies] to that which is non-substantial and trivial. 17.
The intellect is clouded by dullness, the body is intent solely on falling, old age seems to blaze within the frame, and past misdeeds throb with renewed force. (18)
By "sluggishness" is meant stupidity; "having falling as its sole ultimate" means having destruction as its only conclusion. || 18 ||
Youth departs with effort, the company of the virtuous is far away; there is no refuge anywhere, and truthfulness does not arise. 19.

To the objection, "How is it that there is no destination for you, who are righteous? he replies with the words "in some [place]": the sense is that even the attainment of heaven and such is impermanent and resembles the pleasure of a dream. || 19 ||
The mind is as if utterly bewildered within; joy has gone far away.
Compassion does not arise with its usual brilliance; base conduct approaches from afar. (20)
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is contentment upon seeing the happiness of others. By the term "lowliness," its causes—such as envy (*asūyā*) and so forth—are included.
A person who is intent on falling and rising alternately goes from steadfastness to instability;
the embrace of the wicked is easily obtained, but the company of the virtuous is difficult to find. (21)
Lack of fortitude means instability. Falling and rising refer to death and birth, or ascending and descending. Embrace means attachment. || 21 ||
All things come and go; the cultivation of existence binds one to becoming.
This constant succession of beings is merely led here and there.
*Bhāvanā* means latent impression (*vāsanā*). Even when objects have disappeared, that [impression] does not disappear; thus it is the binder in existence, the cause of bondage.
The "succession of beings" refers to the multitude of living creatures. The word "by time" is to be understood as the ellipsis. (22)
For even the directions are no longer visible, and even place is subject to the designation of "other";
even the mountains crumble—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? (23)
The quarters (diśaḥ) are those in which there is no fear of time. He elaborates on that very point with the word "deśa.

"Deśa" means the instruction for the conventional usage of existence; or rather, it is called "deśa" because it points out (diśati) or provides space (avakāśam) to living beings. It refers to a contrary designation (apadeśam) other than the actual designation (vyapadeśāt).
Regarding conventional discourse: it means that [the opponent's position] itself has no room for application. || 23 ||
Even the sky is devoured by existence, and even the world is consumed; even the earth falls into distress—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? (24)
Even the external space, being existent by virtue of its existence, is pervaded by the Lord, whose nature is pure being. || 24 ||
Even the oceans dry up, even the stars perish, and even the perfected ones (siddhas) meet their end; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
They have attained perfection through yoga, mantras, elixirs, and other means distinct from [ordinary] knowledge. || 25 ||
Even the Dānavas are torn asunder, and even Dhruva’s life is impermanent;
even the immortals are slain—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even Śakra is assailed by their mouths, and even Yama is brought under control;
even Vāyu loses his nature as wind—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
It is assailed by the mouths, it is relished, it is thoroughly restrained, and it reaches a state of cessation. || 27 ||
Even the moon attains the state of the sky; even the sun goes to fragmentation;
even fire goes to extinction—what reliance can there be on a person such as I?
The state of space, which is emptiness. || 28 ||
Even Parameṣṭhin, though steadfast, is carried away; even Hari, though unborn, is led off; even Bhava falls into non-existence—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
*Niṣṭhā* means completion; *hriyate* means it is withdrawn or gathered together. || 29 ||
By whom time is reckoned and destiny is led,
and even the infinite sky is dissolved— what reliance can there be on a person such as I?
Time has been previously described as threefold; here, "space" refers to the external space beyond the enclosure wall.
By some who bestows delusion, whose form is unknown through the reality that is inaudible, unspeakable, and difficult to perceive, the worlds are being mocked.

That which is inaudible is beyond the range of the sense of hearing; that which is unspeakable is inaccessible to speech; and that whose subtle form is a reality difficult to behold is inaccessible to the eyes and other senses. "Form" (*mūrti*) refers to the gross form.
They are "mocked"—that is, displayed by *māyā* within one's own self. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), it is merely imagined.
The meaning is that he demonstrates this. || 31 ||
Having attained even a fraction of egoism, there is no one in the three worlds who is not afflicted by that which dwells within them all.
"Having attained," that is, having reached, "a portion of egoism," meaning a part of the sense of self; the word "among those who remain" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 32 ||
Like the sun upon the ridges of rocky mountains, one who has become like a horse is constantly driven about, as helpless as a forest stone. (33)

To establish that he is the subduer of all, he describes his unrestrained sovereignty with the three verses beginning with "śilā" (stone). [The chariot] has attained the state of being a chariot together with its horses; for there is the Vedic scripture: "He who dwells in the sun," and so forth. Impelled by the Lord mounted upon it, it traverses impassable terrains such as stones, mountains, and embankments.

Just as round stones of crystal and the like are driven downward with force by water flowing swiftly from a mountain peak, so too is one helpless and lacking self-mastery; [it is] like the sun and other luminaries [driven by the wind],
[and] the terrestrial globe, which is the abode for the hosts of gods and asuras dwelling within it.
He is enveloped by the wheel of the sacrificial hearths, like a ripe walnut encased in its shell. || 34 ||

The earth is the ground itself, which is the sphere (*golaka*), as is well known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*). It is encircled—that is, pervaded on all sides—by the *dhiṣṇya*, the wheel that serves as the abode of the gods, namely the celestial sphere (*jyotiścakra*).

An *akṣoṭa* is a particular kind of fruit. Even during the cycles of the ages (*yugāvarta*), when the earth undergoes transformations such as burning and submersion, [it remains] until the end of the kalpa.
The qualification "matured" (pakva) is used to indicate the firmness resulting from the non-destruction of the wheel of light. || 34 ||
The gods in heaven, the men on earth, and the serpent-beings in the netherworlds—all are brought to a state of decay in a mere instant by [him] alone. (35)
"By mere thought, by mere volition. Thus, the sense is that even the absolute dependence of the world [upon him] is a great defect. || 35 ||
And Kāma, having acquired prowess through battle with the Lord of the Universe, has displayed his valor in a disorderly manner; having assailed the world, he leaps about.

He also mentions other defects with the words beginning "kāma" (desire) and so forth. "Akrameṇa" means in an improper manner. "Ākramya" means having overcome or brought under control. If one were to fear the Controller, the Lord, then he would not be unrestrained; but he is not like that, as he says: "jagadīśāna" (the Lord of the world). || 36 ||
Spring, with its intoxicated mango trees and showers of pollen from the blossoms, perfumes the circle of all directions and drives the mind to restlessness. (37)
"Spring itself is a rutting elephant, and the shower of flowers is itself a shower of ichor"—this is a *vyastarūpaka* (distributed metaphor).
"Fickleness" is a fusion (*saṃbheda*) of the two emotional states (*bhāva*) of fear and madness. || 37 ||
Even great discernment is not capable of steadying the mind when its form has been gazed upon by the tremulous eyes of an enamored woman. (38)
I consider only the Buddha truly happy, for with a mind cooled within himself, he acts for the benefit of others while being consumed by compassion for the suffering of others. (39)
The Buddha is the person who has awakened to reality; the implication is that such awakening is exceedingly difficult to attain. || 39 ||
Who is able to count the waves in the ocean of life—waves that arise and perish, falling into the submarine fire of Time? (40)
The reason for their perishability is "time"; the word "entities" (bhāvāḥ) is to be supplied as the subject. || 40 ||
All men indeed, due to delusion, are bound by the snares of evil desires;
like deer caught in thickets of faults, they are shattered within the wilderness of birth. (41)

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: deer, wild animals, or birds situated within the *gulma* clusters characterized by the aforementioned defects, being bound by the hunter with the snare of false hope, are scattered throughout the wilderness of worldly existence (*janma-jaṅgala*).
(41) Thus, the succession of births in this world is utterly diminished.

Through these evil deeds here in this world, the lifespan of people becomes like a noose made from the creepers of a tree in the sky; we do not know what the fruit of such acts will be, even for those who possess discernment. (42)

By those evil deeds performed with the faults mentioned by them—the practice of optional rites and prohibited acts—one's lifespan is exhausted; the fruit thereof is heaven, hell, and so forth. If a tree were to exist in the sky, there might also be a creeper there; likewise, this misery of clinging to worldly support is as worthless as hanging by a noose around one's neck.

The meaning is that its existence ends with its falling away. Let alone the means for its cessation being far off, even the mere thought of it is difficult to obtain; thus he says: "Not indeed" (na hi). || 42 ||
"Today is a festival, this is the season,
and here are your kinsmen; this is a happy time with special enjoyments"—
thus, fruitlessly weaving a web of such false imaginings, [he remains].
In this world, people whose minds are as fragile as a trembling lotus-stalk are perishing. || 43 ||
He says "now" because the collection of conditions for its loss is extremely easy to encounter at every moment: "it flows away," that is, it disintegrates.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Malignant Play of Fate," in the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Valmiki. 26.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mischievous Play of Fate," in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Furthermore, O dear one, in this world-nature which is exceedingly beautiful and delightful...
Nothing whatsoever comes from that collection of objects by which the mind might attain supreme rest. || 1 ||
The defects in both those things already mentioned and those not yet mentioned, which are obstacles to the supreme good, have been proclaimed here in detail for the sake of dispassion.
Having thus detailed the various defects in each of the entities mentioned and those left unmentioned,

he concludes: "In this nature of the world— which is charming only at first sight but in reality unpleasant— there is not even the slightest collection of objects that, once obtained, brings the mind ultimate rest or the state of having all desires fulfilled."
The meaning is that no other reality besides that enters the mind, nor is it obtained. || 1 ||

When childhood has passed and the deer of the mind—restless with its imagined play—is worn out in the thickets of desire, and when the little body has reached a state of decay, the world suffers only in its utter desolation. (2)

Wives alone are caves—the mountain caverns. One is especially tormented and distressed [by them]. Having cast far away the lotus-pond of the body, which is struck by the frost of old age and devoid of human purpose, and when the bee of life has departed in an instant, the lake of worldly existence for a person has utterly dried up. (3)
Life itself is but a fleeting bee; worldly existence here consists of the undertakings of this life. Whenever it surely reaches its fruition, then and there it provides pleasure.
Yet, for men, it is a withered tree, burdened by the weight of old age and laden with many new blossoms, as Time brings them to decay.
It produces delight and pleasure—[delight] from death, as the word "mṛtyoḥ" is understood. For men, the body itself is a creeper or vine. || 4 ||

In this world, the river of craving flows on, its exceedingly powerful current engulfing the entirety of all infinite categories of objects; it is skilled at rubbing away the roots of the fine trees of faults that stand upon its banks.

Those who are skillful and capable in that regard [are those who can perform] the scraping of the roots or the cutting down of the ramparts, which is more essential, more forceful, or more powerful. || 5 ||
Bound by the straps of skin upon the ship of the body, tossed about and wandering in the ocean of existence,
the unsteady woman is being churned by the five crocodiles known as the sense-faculties as she sinks downward.

Bound by the leather straps of the monastic robe, this leather boat—well known in the Deccan—is tossed about and agitated by the waves; and because of its inherent lightness, it reels, sinks downward, and is on the verge of drowning, being further churned even by the crocodiles that are the sense organs. For therein no steadfast ones are found, only the unsteady.
It is that [state] in which living beings possess discerning wisdom and are endowed with the quality of detachment.

These deer of our minds, wandering through the forest of the creeper of craving, roam about the hundreds of branches of the trees of sensual desire; they waste away their time, yet they do not obtain the fruit.

A forest where creepers spread is a "creeper-forest" (latākānana). Because of the qualifying phrase "wandering among hundreds of branches," the "deer" (mṛga) here refers to monkeys (śākhāmṛga); they spend their lifespan there. || 7 ||
In times of hardship, they have cast far away despondency and delusion; in times of well-being, their minds are not captivated by pride.
Such great men, whose inner hearts remain unaffected by beautiful women, are exceedingly rare in this day and age.
In hardships and calamities, as well as in health and prosperity, they are delightful with a mind that is not elated and not proud.
There is also the particle *na*, which has the sense of a negative (*nañ*); its compound [is formed] with that. || 8 ||
Those who cross the ocean of battle, which has the waves of the sword’s edge as its current, are not heroes in my view;
rather, those alone are heroes here who cross this ocean of the body and senses, with the mind as its wave.
In whom the jars are the collections that are themselves the waves; those who cross over possess the state of reflecting upon the excellence of my heroism. || 9 ||

No particular activity is seen belonging to anyone that, delightful with its unafflicted ultimate fruit, brings the world—whose mental fluctuations are struck down by evil desires—to a state of rest upon reaching it. (10)

[Objection: "But surely, let action itself be the means in that case. To this he replies: "akliṣṭa" (unafflicted). The particle *eva* has the sense of "even" (*api*). No action whatsoever of anyone is seen to be delightful by virtue of its fruit—which is "unafflicted," meaning free from affliction or destruction, and which has "paryanta," meaning the end of saṃsāra, as its nature. For example, here:
The world accumulated through karma perishes; likewise, the world accumulated through merit perishes in the hereafter—such is the Vedic scripture.
The sense is that since there is an inevitable destruction of whatever fruit is produced by action, the loss of what is desired culminates in suffering.
"Having reached" (etya) means having resorted to a particular action; "rest" (viśrāntim) means well-being. || 10 ||

Those great ones who, bound by unshakable fortitude, fill the caves of the world’s directions with their fame, their homes with their majesty, and Fortune herself with the power of their virtue—such as these are not easily found in this world. (11)

Considering that in the absence of the dawning of fortune, even those things of minor fruit—such as fame, majesty, and prosperity—cause the destruction of virtues like fortitude, and [the same applies] to liberation, he says "kīrtyā" (by fame) and so forth. By "śriyā" (by prosperity), he means by wealth. "Gṛham" means the house of the supplicant.

By "sattvabalena," he means by the power of *sattva*—namely, the strength of *sāttvika* qualities such as forbearance, modesty, and magnanimity—one attains prosperity (*lakṣmīm*). For by that [power], she appears as if full.
He shines. || 11 ||
Whether situated within a mountain crag or dwelling inside a house of diamond,
all fortunes, along with the speed of supernatural powers, as well as all calamities, constantly come to him.

However, since the attainment of every desired object by everyone everywhere becomes easy when good fortune arises, [the author], intending to show the futility of human effort, says: "Even that which stands within. This refers to a wall made of stone, a rock-like wall of a mountain; the masculine gender is used here due to the *karmadhāraya* compound. Even though it is situated in the midst of that [wall].

Because it is fashioned from vajra, it is indivisible; [the phrase] "even though situated within the ālaya" implies that all people of like fortune are included. Accompanied by the "vegas"—that is, the rapid impulses—of the *siddhis* such as *aṇimā* and so forth.
The mention of "calamities" (*āpad*) is for the sake of providing an illustration. || 12 ||
Sons, wives, and wealth are fashioned by the intellect, O dear one, appearing like an elixir; yet none of them provides assistance in the end, for therein lies a most pleasant swoon of poison.

He elaborates on what was just stated—namely, "ending in non-affliction"—with the words beginning "And sons," etc. The phrase "is imagined through delusion" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "In the end" means at the time of death. Even objects of enjoyment that are exceedingly delightful result only in suffering there, like being bound by the stupefaction of poison. || 13 ||

Overcome by despair and having reached a precarious state at the end of his physical life and youth, the living being, remembering here his own worldly possessions now devoid of dharma, burns within from the onset of old age. (14)
Devoid of Dharma and empty of the accumulation of merit. || 14 ||
Having spent the initial days with activities aimed at attaining desire, wealth, and dharma, by what means can a man’s mind—fickle like a trembling peacock feather—attain rest? (15)

In the beginning, due to the intensity of the thirst for acquiring and enjoying wealth, one is occupied with worldly activities that obstruct the attainment of Dharma through the pursuit of desire and material gain alone; these activities are as fickle as the plumage of a peacock (*barhin*). The phrase "at the end of the body's life-span" is to be understood here as well. (15)

Even by those results of action that have arrived by the power of fate—though they were previously present, their form was not attained, and they resemble the lofty waves of a river—the world is mocked, for people have diverse tastes. 16.

Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be no rest for those empty of the acquisition of merit, but why should it not exist for those like you who possess such merit, since they obtain its fruits?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that the fruits of merit—such as heaven, sons, and so forth—are *taranga-vat* (like waves), meaning they are fragile; for this very reason, they are *anavāpta-rūpaiḥ*, meaning their forms are essentially unattained, being as good as not reached at all. For (*hi*) they are distinct [from the ultimate reality].
That person who has a preference for what is not-self is mocked—that is, deceived. This is the point:

that alone is called a "gain" which, once obtained, does not depart or result in misfortune; any other gain is merely a mockery. For example, like the "gain" of a short-lived son, or like that of a fish.

It is like obtaining bait on a fishhook. Thus says the Śruti: "If one should tell someone who speaks of what is dear to himself that 'it will cause you pain,' [the other would realize the truth]. Likewise, there is no confidence to be gained from attaining that [pleasure]. || 16 ||
These and those tasks, clearly distinguished and endlessly delightful,
wear away the hearts of people through the pursuit of pleasing one's wife until the very end of old age, by means of their swift passage.

He elaborates upon the very point already stated by demonstrating the expansion of the demonic nature (āsurasaṃpad) through the passage beginning with "imāni": "These" refers to those things present that must be done immediately; "those" refers to those remote things that must be done at another time or place—thus they are distinguished, constantly contemplated, and infinitely delightful.

In their ultimate consequence, they take the form of misfortune; by pleasing their wives and people through agreeable conduct, they cause even the mind to age along with the body until its decay—that is to say, they cause one to fall away from discernment. || 17 ||

Just as the withered leaves of trees, having come together at birth, quickly go to their dissolution, even so do people devoid of self-discernment; having gathered, they depart for some unknown destination within a few days. (18)
Within just a few days, from some point [in time]. || 18 ||

Having wandered here and there to a great distance and entered his home at the close of day, when the day is emptied by the virtuous deeds of people who take refuge in discernment, who then finds sleep at night? (19)
When the day has become devoid of the company of those who possess discernment and of virtuous deeds, who would resort to sleep, if not the fool? This is the implied meaning. || 19 ||
When the entire host of enemies has been routed and prosperity has arrived from every side, while one is still enjoying these pleasures, death arrives from somewhere or other. (20)

Alas! The people on this earth are being churned by these entities—whose forms are increased from some source yet are trivial, and which vanish from sight in an instant—and they do not realize whether it is a new arrival or a fall. (21)

Agitated and whirled about by objects—that is, sense-objects—which are brought together from some indeterminate cause, she does not realize, alas, that death has arrived; for in the reading "yātam," it means she does not know that which has approached (upāyātam) and that which has gone (yātam). || 21 ||
Bound by their wretched karma, those sheep among men make Kālamukha their prey with their own dear lives;
having forcibly attained corpulence, they do not exist [any longer] due to the affliction of their bodies. 22.
With their vital breaths (*asu*), which are renowned for being dear to all living beings, those very people act as sacrificers;

they are the "human-sheep" (*naram-eṣāḥ*), the sacrificial animals. The word *hata* is used here in the sense of contempt. Being bound to sacrificial posts characterized by despicable acts, they are made to have faces of a dark color by means of soot (*doṣāñjana*).

They are being consecrated. Who are they? The meaning is: those who, by virtue of their attachment to sense objects and the nourishment of the body, have merely attained corpulence and have not practiced discernment, dispassion, and so forth. For this very reason, there is the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) that they become sacrificial animals (*saṃjñapanapaśavaḥ*) by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). This is according to the Vedic scripture: "He indeed becomes non-existent if he knows Brahman as non-existent. [And] regarding sacrifice...

This is a case of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Alternatively, those very people, those sheep, and those nourishers who themselves have remained having attained corpulence, are the ones who are made [sacrificial] and offered. Therefore, these lives (*asavaḥ*) are ungrateful; because they cause affliction to the body, they are not dear lives (*priyāsavaḥ*), but rather are enemies (*śatravaḥ*). And thus, one should not be intent merely upon the nourishment of life.

The term *bhāva* means "that which is to be cultivated. Alternatively, even those devoted to the nourishment of the body are not the true lovers of life (*priyāsava*), for by practicing the means of entering the mouth of death, they instead bring about the destruction of their own vital breaths.
Rather, only those who know reality are the true lovers of life here, because from the perspective of the ultimate truth, the vital breaths are eternal.
Fools are treated like sheep by Kālamukha; that is to say, they are not respected.

He states what their particular distinction is: because they remain having attained, through the power of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), a state of fullness and non-limitation by means of the destruction of the three bodies (śarīra-traya). Therefore...
The meaning is that the excellence consists precisely in this: that the notions of "body" and "self" no longer arise, just as they do not in goats or sheep. || 22 ||
The restless multitude on this earth comes ever swiftly and likewise goes away incessantly and swiftly; from wherever it arises, it is like a garland of waves, momentary in its destruction.
Just as she comes, so too does she go swiftly; by the phrase "from somewhere," it is indicated that her point of origin and destination are what one desires to know. || 23 ||

Women, with their red lips and eyes like restless bees, steal the hearts of men through their charm, while being solely intent on taking away their lives— just as poisonous trees and trembling creepers, with their crimson leaves and flickering bees for eyes, captivate the mind while being nothing but death.

Those with red garments, those with red lips, or those with red clothes and red sprouts; those whose eyes are like bees, as it were, or who are indeed bees; and those who are like poison-vines, unsteady upon the trees of poison. 24.
Coming from here and there, bound by a common agreement in vain, the illusory conduct regarding wife and friends among men is like a temporary association during a journey. (25)

From this human world and from elsewhere, such as the heavens or the hells, [they come] in vain—that is, quite fruitlessly. "We must meet here" is a convention based on mutual intention; she has attained her true nature through that convention. It is a gathering, a meeting of the assembly, at festivals for the gods and the like. (25)
Just as when lamps have gone out after consuming their many wicks that were bound by excessive oil, so too,
in the flickering garlands of worldly existence which are unreal, the true reality is not perceived.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: in the garlands of *saṃsāras*—which are successions of births and deaths—the ultimate reality (*tattvam*), the supreme entity, is not known, just as in the case of lamps, where there is a flow of momentary flashes followed by their cessation. All the qualifiers apply to both [the *saṃsāras* and the lamps]. "States" (*daśā*) refers to childhood and so forth.
And "vartikās" refers to wicks; "sneha" means passion as well as oil; "calācalāsu" means among those that are flickering; and "atāttvikīṣu" means among those that are unreal or false. || 26 ||

This wheel of the breast, which is the very engine of the turmoil of saṃsāra, though as fragile as a bubble in the rain-clouds of the monsoon, spreads the conviction of long-lasting stability in the mind of a heedless person. (27)
Just as a potter’s wheel, though spinning, produces the perception in the mind of an inattentive person that it is long-lasting and not spinning, so too this "breast-wheel" (*kucakrikā*)—
which is the form of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-pravṛtti*)— is impermanent like a bubble on the water of a rain-swollen river.
The meaning is that it produces the perception of long-lasting duration. || 27 ||

Virtues, once radiant with splendor, have perished by the power of fate; now, remaining only in a state of decay, they have moved far beyond the reach of consolation for people, like the winter season to a lotus.

Those very qualities— such as beauty and fragrance— which exist in a person like a lotus during youth and autumn, radiant with splendor, are now, by the power of fate, destroyed by old age and the winter season when one is worn out;
they have vanished from the consolation, the mental composure, and the very scent [of life].
The meaning is that since they have gone very far away and will become difficult to find, one should not place trust in them. || 28 ||

When a tree, having approached again and again by the power of fate, has rendered assistance with the very weight of its own body, what occasion indeed is there for consolation when that tree is being cut down by axes? (29)
In this world, trees— by the power of fate and regardless of any benefit to man—

attain an abundance of birth, growth, fruit, and flowers; yet, by the very weight of their own bodies which they must support, they repeatedly perform a service for people through their shade, leaves, flowers, and fruits, even though they themselves have committed no offense.

A tree, that is, a forest tree, is cut down—that is, felled—by axes. In this regard, in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), death will surely slay even one who has done no harm, for one who is intent upon every single step [is vulnerable]. This is the intended meaning. || 29 ||
Even from the company of a person who is charming yet whose conduct is exceedingly corrupt, and who has arisen for one's own internal destruction—
just as from a poisonous tree— one now encounters only a state of stupor.
Granted that there may be a fault elsewhere, yet what fault could there be toward one's own kin who desire one's welfare? To this he replies: "Of the mind-pleasing [world]," etc.

For it is from this [world] that the activities of affection, enjoyment, and so forth, as well as the activities of burning, wandering, and so forth, arise—excessive faults—from which come both internal tranquility and life itself.
The sense is that for one who is intent on destruction, once [that state] has arisen, fainting, delusion, or dejection is encountered; this alone is the fault. || 30 ||
What are those directions in which there are no defects? What are those regions in which there is no burning pain of suffering? What are those subjects in whom there is no transience?
What are those actions in which illusion does not truly exist? 31.
Among the views of cyclic existence, what are those views? They are mundane activities; "māyā" means deception.
For even Brahmās, who live for a single kalpa, find it impossible to calculate the number of kalpas within the flood of kalpas;
therefore, in the web of time which possesses all its parts (kalā), even the notions of shortness and length are unreal.

Now, one might raise the objection that although other beings are transitory, those beings who have attained the same world as Viriñci (Brahmā) and possess a lifespan of an entire kalpa are not transitory; anticipating this, he says "kalpa..."— that is,
in the non-calculation, or the lack of full knowledge, of the number of the floods of kalpas, both past and future, which are infinite.

Due to the lack of distinction in their infinity, even the *kalpas*—from the perspective of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others—are merely moments (*kṣaṇas*); thus, even for Viriñci (Brahmā), the so-called *kalpas* are but moments of life. Therefore, within the aggregate of time which possesses constituent parts, by the same logic applied to shortness and length, even the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*) are mere atoms from the perspective of those who perceive infinite millions of cosmic eggs.
Thus, cognitions such as smallness, largeness, and so forth should also be understood as unreal. || 32 ||

Everywhere the mountains consist of stone, the earth of clay, and the trees of wood alone; likewise, people consist of flesh, their existence bound by human effort. There is nothing here that is unprecedented or devoid of transformation. (33)
Thus, he says "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) to show that even the collection of transformations appears as unreal when the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is seen.

The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in its own sense (denoting identity). The instrumental case in "beautiful by nature" (*prakṛtyā cāru*) and similar expressions denotes non-difference. Mountains (*mahīdhra*) are in reality nothing but stones; the earth (*mahī*) is nothing but clay; people (*jana*) are nothing but flesh and so forth. How then [do they appear as] mountains and the like?

The meaning is that they possess specific natures through names, forms, and conventions created by persons. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is nothing "new" (*apūrva*) other than the previously established cause. Thus, because the same logic applies everywhere, the entire world—which is devoid of modification and has abandoned all modifications—is in fact one and the same primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that it is possible through reasoning to conceive that the ultimate reality exists. Alternatively, even if the transformations such as mountains and so forth are unreal, one might ask: "How then [can the reality] exist in their material causes, such as stone and clay?
To this he says: "Not something unprecedented" (*nāpūrvam*). For those [causes] as well, [the reality exists] in their own causes, the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The meaning is "thus" (evam). || 33 ||

When perceived by consciousness, this world—interwoven with volition and bound to the waters, situated in the sky, and distinguished by the various manifestations of objective reality—is seen as such; there is nothing else whatsoever that exists apart from it.
He clarifies the statement that stones, clay, and so forth consist of nothing but the great elements (*mahābhūta*) with the words "is perceived" (*ālokyate*).

The word division is *anu-vit-hā*. "Milk" (*payaḥ*) means water; the fire connected to it is that which is linked to it either as its cause or as its fuel. Although terrestrial fire has earthy wood as its fuel, nevertheless—[the text continues]—wood... [etc.]

The sun, moon, fire, water, and so forth—these are the five great elements (*mahābhūta*). Wind is the moving; space is the sky; that which stands and does not move is the earth, called "the stationary" (*sthā*). This very pentad of great elements is "penetrated" (*anuvidhyate*), meaning they are interconnected with one another.
When they are thus "penetrated"—that is, combined—they constitute this world through the diversity of objects such as cows, jars, and the like, by means of consciousness and the intellect (*buddhi*).
It is perceived by those lacking discrimination. "Hā" is an interjection indicating grief.

However, when one examines [reality] through the vision of discrimination (*viveka-dṛś*) by means of distinct analysis, the meaning is that there is nothing else whatsoever apart from the five elements.
Thus says the Śruti: "O Agni, that which is your red form is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water."
That which is black belongs to the food. The "fire-ness" of fire has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. Thus [it is said]. 34.
And here, O virtuous one, there is a wonder that causes amazement in the hearts of wise men;
such a thing of variegated form never becomes an object for anyone, even in a dream. (35)

Now, one might object: "If objects are thus unreal, how can there be the wondrous experience of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) and enjoyment for people? For it is not possible to make a bracelet out of silver from a mother-of-pearl shell. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The wonder... Here, even though the collection of objects is illusory, for those who are wise and discerning, and who are skilled in worldly activity, there arises a sense of wonder—just as when one sees a beautiful woman in a dream.
It is of variegated form and thus not a cause for wonder, because such a marvelous experience does not occur for everyone at all times.

Although enjoyments in dreams are well-known to all, nevertheless, this is intended to indicate that there is a marvelous experience of intense pleasure and pain over a long duration, as in the case of Hariścandra’s experiences in heaven and hell.
It has been stated that this occurs "sometimes for some. || 35 ||
Even now, although the magnitude of imagination is as vast as a creeper-fruit in the sky,
for those struck by even a fragment of greed, not even a single story consisting of noble accounts arises.

Now, one might object: "If there is such delight in enjoyment, why do you become dispassionate right now? It would be more appropriate to enjoy pleasures and then, in later life, become dispassionate and engage in self-inquiry. Anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with "adya"—that both dispassion and inquiry are always difficult to attain when one is attached to enjoyment. "Adya" means in this present, earlier stage of life.

Even when he has reached this advanced age, because he lacks discernment regarding the conceptualization of attachment to enjoyments— which, though false like the fruit of a vine in the sky— has attained greatness, he is consumed by even a tiny fragment of greed for enjoyments and their means;
thus, [this work] is abundant with the account of the Supreme Self, the most exalted of all, which consists of the discourse defining His true nature.
The very thought does not arise; the continuous investigation of that [object], however, is cast far away—this is the sense. || 36 ||
Desiring to attain the state of the supreme beings, people today are led astray by their own minds;
like a beast, they fall fearlessly from the mountain peak out of a mere longing for the fruit of the blue creeper.
He states that through attachment, not only is there a loss of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), but rather a great calamity as well: "To seize [the prey]...
He confirms this point by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter) with the words beginning "like a beast":
"A beast," such as a goat and so forth, "falls"—this is to be supplied. A "vine" that is blue-black or green, meaning one situated in a precarious place.
The creeper such as *karīra* and others is taken [as the example]. || 37 ||
With their useless parts cast aside in the interim— shadows, creepers, leaves, fruits, and flowers—
the trees growing in chasms and the men of today alike possess bodies from which all excellence has been destroyed.

In the midst of inaccessible ravines, there are certain trees—so-called "pit-trees" (*śvabhradrumāḥ*)—whose very parts, such as their shade and so forth, are placed in such a way that they are useless; that is to say, because they cannot be enjoyed by living beings even in part, they are futile. Such trees are "wasted" (*kṣatāḥ*), meaning they are pointlessly destroyed, since their utility lies solely in nourishing their own bodies.
Those men who possess the wealth of knowledge, discipline, and other such riches are indeed equal [to others]. Their birth is otherwise in vain;

for people wander sometimes through regions beautiful with gentleness and sometimes through those that are harsh, like black antelopes moving through continuous forest thickets in the intervals between countries. (39)
Although there are indeed some who are righteous in certain respects, it is said that those possessed of true discernment (*vivekin*) are rare;

thus, in accordance with the nature of the people described here, the various levels of the mind (*cittabhūmayaḥ*) are taken up. Gentleness, compassion, courtesy, forbearance, and other such beauties, as well as learning, humility, and so forth, exist in those who possess them. [These qualities are absent] in the harsh.
In those parts and sections of the forest interior that are characterized by anger, greed, and cruelty [and sharpness]. || 39 ||
Day by day, the elements bring forth events that are terrifying or delightful, yet ultimately agitated and confounding at their conclusion—
undertakings whose rising hopes are destroyed by the ripening of bitter fruits.
Whose minds are not struck with wonder by them? Not even the minds of the dead. (40)

Seeing the miserable condition of people, he is pained and, on their account, censures fate, saying "of the Creator" (*dhātuḥ*). Because the corpse is insentient and like one dead, [he blames] the Creator, that is, fate. The intention is: "If it were alive, such a state of sleep would not occur. *Divasam prati* means day by day. [This is expressed] precisely by the term *karmapravacanīya*.
The dual number is used to indicate repetition (*vīpsā*). "Frightening yet charming at first sight" means they appear delightful initially but are terrifying in their result.

The word "vā" is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Whose new undertakings—disturbed by those with minds utterly agitated by passion and the like, and whose initial success is corrupted by the ripening of bitter fruits in the end—are these?
They do not cause wonder in the minds of the discerning. || 40 ||
People are attached to desires and intent on various base and unskillful activities; indeed, a virtuous person is not easily found in this world even in a dream today.
Truly, every action is devoid of happiness and is utterly distressed by its association with suffering.
I do not know how this state consisting of life itself is to be led away. 41.

Restating the matter already discussed, he concludes by showing his own agitation regarding its cause with the verse beginning "janaḥ. By "evil gains" (kukalābhiḥ) is meant crooked cleverness. A "good person" (sujanaḥ) is one possessed of discernment. "Unattached to sufferings" (duḥkhairasaṅgaḥ) means having no connection with them; that is to say, one who is free from such [gains].
The sense is that [such a person] is inevitably bound to suffering. || 41 ||

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Impermanence of States Opposed to the Highest Good," in the *Vairāgya-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 27.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Impermanence of States Contrary to the Highest Good," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa.
Chapter Twenty-Eight. 28.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, all that is unstable, resembling a meeting in a dream.
In this [work], in order to produce a sense of distaste for all objects of enjoyment,
the nature of all phenomena as being subject to perversion is described.
They say that there is no confidence in those [phenomena] even because of seeing that all entities have a nature of incessant error;
this is stated with the words "And that which... and so forth. In a dream, "union" (saṃgama) means a gathering or meeting. || 1 ||
O Sage, that which is seen today as a dug-out pit resembling a dried-up ocean shall become a mountain shrouded by clouds by morning.
A pit has been dug. The mention of "in the morning" is an indication of [any] other time. || 2 ||
That great mountain-like sky, vast as a forest array and pervading the firmament,
in just a few days reaches the level of the earth or even sinks to the state of a well.

By means of its array of forests—that is, by its collection of woods—it licked the sky; it kissed the surface of the heavens; that is to say, it was lofty. It was great in circumference. [It was built] in just a few days. || 3 ||
That very limb which today is clothed in silk garments, garlands, and ointments, tomorrow shall be cast far away into a pit, naked as the sky.
In a pit or a hole; it will fall apart, it will become shattered. [Root] *luṭ*. 4.
In that very place where today a city is seen, vibrant with its various customs,
there arises in a few days the nature of a desolate wilderness.
Furthermore, it is restless and moves again and again. || 5 ||
O King, that man who today stands as a radiant sovereign over the realms shall, within a few days, become a mere heap of ashes.
He attains; he reaches. || 6 ||
That very forest, once vast and terrifying, resembling the expanse of the sky and covering the heavens with its banners, has now become a city.
The great forest, a vast wilderness, was like the expanse of the sky due to its breadth and its deep blue hue.
That formidable forest range, which today shines embraced by creeping vines,
in just a few days will once again become a desert land.
It has become entwined and covered with creepers; the characteristic mark of a desert region is the absence of trees, water, and creepers.
Water turns into dry land, and the earth becomes a body of water;
indeed, the entire world—including its wood, water, and grass—is overturned.
The place where water and plants reside; it becomes inverted, that is, it falls into a contrary state. || 9 ||
Youth, childhood, the body, and accumulations of wealth are impermanent;
they pass incessantly from one state to another, like waves.
A different intrinsic nature [arises] from the previous intrinsic nature. || 10 ||
Life in this world is as flickering as the flame of a lamp in a gale;
the splendor of all things in the three worlds is like the flash of lightning. (11)
A small lamp is an illuminator. || 11 ||
This succession of numerous beings falls into perversion, like a heap of seeds that is being replenished incessantly again and again. (12)
Just as a heap of seeds such as grain, being constantly filled again and again in a granary or similar vessel, undergoes transformation through depletion;
or as [the earth] sown in a field, being filled with water, undergoes transformation by becoming swollen in the form of sprouts, crops, and so forth—this is the meaning. || 12 ||
With the heavy cloth of the dust of the elements tossed about by the wind of the mind,
she is adorned with the dramatic gestures of falling, rising, and turning back and forth.

This very state of the world is the *ārabhaṭī* of *saṃsāra*— characterized by the continuous succession of agent and enjoyer, and consisting of the wandering of living beings through birth and death; it is like an actress (*naṭī*) in her performance (*ārabhaṭī*), or rather, the term *ārabhaṭī* denotes the collective group of both the actress (*naṭī*) and the warrior (*bhaṭī*), for the purpose of manifesting its own extraordinary skill.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: that very actress, the dancer of exceeding splendor, while performing a dance to manifest her own supreme skill, is perceived as if she were spinning around, creating the illusion of whirling through her intense absorption (*āveśa*).
He qualifies her accordingly: "the mind itself is the wind; by it, the multitude of beings (*bhūribhūta*) is cast about and stirred up."

She whose cloth is the very mass of passion (rajas) characterized by living beings; for this reason, there is the falling of beings into hell and the like, their rising to heaven, and their transition to the intermediate world—therefore, she is adorned with those supreme (parā), most excellent gestures (abhinaya) that manifest the absence of worldly existence. 13.
This worldly existence is perceived as a state of delusion, like an actress on the stage of saṃsāra who has entered into the frenzy of a dance. (14)
It produces the delusion of a city of Gandharvas; it is charming through its grand conduct, which is as fleeting as a sidelong glance. (15)

He describes her with two verses, beginning with "Gandharva-": "The delusion [of seeing her] is an error; the art of closing the eyes of actors and dancers is well known. She is enchanting through her side-long glances, which are curved like those of a female serpent, and through her crooked dealings. (15)
O King, the construction of saṃsāra shines like one intent on a dance, repeatedly extending its repeated contraction as flickering as lightning. 16.
The light itself, as well as the act of seeing, is flickering like lightning. || 16 ||
Those were great days, those were riches, and those were our deeds;
everything has passed from the path of memory, and we too shall depart in an instant. (17)
They were endowed with the splendor of festive abundance. || 17 ||
Day by day it undergoes decay, and day by day it is born again;
even today there is no end to this burnt-out cycle of worldly existence for one whose form has been destroyed.
The words "hatā" (struck) and "dagdha" (burnt) are terms of reproach. || 18 ||
Men go to the state of animals, and even animals attain the state of humans;
