gods likewise fall from their divinity. O Lord, what indeed is stable in this world? (19)
The state of being an animal is birth as a beast and so forth. || 19 ||
Creating day and night again and again with its web of rays,
the Sun, who is Time itself, passes them by and looks toward the limit of destruction.

Time, whose nature is time—the Sun, the maker—having passed through nights and days, [reaches] the limit of destruction for the multitude of beings he himself has created; such is the ellipsis. || 20 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all species of living beings alike hasten toward destruction, just as bodies of water do before the submarine fire.
They run after and follow it, like the submarine fire (vāḍava) [pursuing] the mare-fire (vaḍavānala). || 21 ||
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—
all these are the fuel that has been completely dried up for the submarine fire of destruction.

[The term] "vāḍava" [refers] to fire by way of a part-indication (bhāgalakṣaṇā); for, since the well-known submarine fire (vāḍava) has water as its fuel, the qualification "completely dried up" would be inappropriate [if applied to it]. || 22 ||
Wealth, kinsmen, servants, friends, and all possessions—all these have become tasteless for one who is terrified by the fear of destruction. (23)
These objects of existence appear sweet to the wise man in this world only so long as the evil demon of destruction has not entered the path of his memory. (24)
They are relished; they are pleasing. || 24 ||
In one moment he attains sovereignty, and in a moment he falls into poverty;
in one moment he is free from disease, and in a moment he is beset by illness. (25)
"For a moment" means for a short time; "people" is the word understood [in the verse]. || 25 ||
Who indeed among the wise have not been deluded by this world-delusion, which strikes down the self at every moment and bestows error? (26)
The word *nihaga* signifies either censure or perishability. || 26 ||
For a moment the circle of the sky was smeared with the mire of darkness;
for a moment it was beautiful with a soft radiance like a flow of molten gold.
He elaborates upon this very indeterminacy of duration by means of three examples beginning with "darkness" (*tamaḥ*).

The example of the sphere of space (*ākāśamaṇḍala*) is for the sake of illustration. It is thoroughly smeared—that is, touched—by mud characterized as darkness; [it is] like a flow of gold, liquid, beautiful, and tender.
With a pleasant touch, such as the light of the moon and other celestial bodies. || 27 ||
For a moment its hollows were encircled by garlands of water-lilies dark as clouds;
for a moment it resounded with a tumultuous roar, and for a moment it remained as if mute.
The clouds themselves are garlands of blue lotuses; his belly is encircled by them. Uḍḍāmara means lofty or sublime. || 28 ||
At one moment it was adorned with stars, at another embellished by the sun;
at one moment it brought delight through the moon, and at another it was entirely cast out from everything.
It is excluded from, or devoid of, all the previously mentioned states, including those beyond light, whether occurring simultaneously or successively. || 29 ||

For who, even if wise, would not tremble before this [cycle of existence], which is characterized by coming and going and by the destruction of momentary stability—like one who is truly wretched? (30)
The word *iva* is either meaningless or intended to indicate the rarity of an illustrative example; the same applies to what follows. [This refers to] by means of this state of the world. || 30 ||
Calamities come for a moment, and prosperity comes for a moment;
birth is for a moment and death is for a moment—O Sage, what indeed is not momentary? 31.
"Previously there was one person here, and by the days another man has been born;
O Blessed One, nothing whatsoever exists that is eternally uniform or truly stable. (32)
The connection [of the words] is: "In this world, there is nothing whatsoever that is eternally of one form and perfectly stable. (32)
The state of a cloth is seen in a jar, and the existence of a jar is seen in a cloth;
there is nothing perceived in this world of transmigration that does not undergo reversal.
The meaning is that when a jar is destroyed in a cotton field, it is observed to become cloth through the process of transformation into cotton. || 33 ||
It expands, produces, consumes, destroys, and emits [the world] in succession;
it revolves constantly toward every person, like night and day.

The five modifications of being—known as growth, transformation, decay, destruction, and rebirth—are expressed by the words "extends" and so forth. These modifications of being cease for the person who identifies with the body as he sequentially undergoes them; they do not remain for long, and thus they too [are impermanent].

The meaning is that they undergo transformation (*viparyasyanti*). Although Yāska lists "existence" (*asti*) among the modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*), the point is that the permeation by the existence of Brahman, which has a substratum, is not itself a modification. || 34 ||
A hero slain by one who is not a hero, or even a hundred slain by a single man—when commoners attain power, the entire world is turned upside down. (35)
It is turned around; it is inverted. || 35 ||
This multitude of people constantly pursues error, like a succession of waves arising from the perception of the movement of inert matter. 36.

The "people" (janatā) are a collection of conscious beings, while the "insentient" (jaḍa) refers to the life-force, the sense organs, and so forth—[the latter being called *jaḍa*] because of the non-distinction between the letters *ḍa* and *la*. [As it is said:
"Infancy lasts but a few days, then comes the glory of youth, and after that, old age;
even in the body there is no single constant form—what reliance, then, can there be on external things? (37)
The ellipsis "it passes in a few days" is to be supplied. || 37 ||
In one moment it becomes joyful, in another it falls into despondency;
in a moment it attains gentleness—the mind behaves like an actor in every respect. (38)
Just as an actor enacts joy, sorrow, and so forth, so it is in this case. || 38 ||
Creating this thing here, that thing there, and yet another thing elsewhere, this Creator grows weary like a child engaged in play. (39)
By these three words beginning with "iti," various causes of joy, dejection, and delusion are expressed. || 39 ||
It accumulates, produces, consumes, destroys, and emits [karma] in succession;
it revolves incessantly toward each person, like night and day. (40)

Like rice and other grains, he gathers them and brings about their accumulation through collection; by means of those [beings], he produces others, and having destroyed them, he devours them. Then, having obtained a taste for it, the Creator (vidhi) creates yet other living beings so that he may continue to eat them incessantly in the same manner. And toward the created man, joy, sorrow, and the like arise, just as days and nights do.
The meaning is that they always return after having reached [them]. || 40 ||
For living beings who appear and disappear and shine within the cycle of existence, neither calamities nor prosperities attain stability. (41)
He clarifies that very point through the instability of the cause: "In manifestation... (verse 41).
Time plays, for the most part casting everyone into calamity,
having effortlessly shaken all those who are clever in the four modes of conduct.
He who, with mere ease—that is, with utter disregard—has caused all those who are clever and capable to waver and turn back, is likewise skillful and proficient in such conduct. || 42 ||

The vast multitudes of fruits from the succession of beings in the three worlds, distinguished by their various and uneven ripenings, fall day after day from the trees of expansive saṃsāra, cast down by the wind of time. (43)

Due to the various and uneven ripening of karmas and flavors, the diverse living beings of the three worlds—each distinct from the others—are like trees characterized by those very traits. Time, which is their designated end, acts as a wind that fells them;
they fall day after day. Thus, everything culminating in such a fall is indeed corrupt; there is no basis for reliance upon anything whatsoever.
The meaning is that it is logical. || 43 ||

Thus ends the twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unceasing Error Regarding All Phenomena," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unceasing Perversion of All States of Being," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa.
The twenty-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Thus, while my great mind was being consumed by the forest fire of faults, [the Lord appeared].
The hopes for enjoyments do not quiver, like mirages in lakes.
Through the perception of faults, total world-weariness in oneself is described;
for the sake of its pacification, Rama likewise seeks instruction.

Thus, by perceiving these defects within his own mind, he demonstrates a sense of world-weariness (*nirveda*) culminating in the desire to know reality (*tattva-bubhutsā*), beginning with the words "iti" and so forth. By the word "doṣa" (defect), the perception of those defects is indicated; or rather, it refers to the discrimination (*viveka*) of the defects themselves—[as it is said]:
"In that which is great and vast with discrimination, for the mirages of deer appear only in deserts, not in lakes. (1)
Day by day this condition of worldly existence becomes increasingly bitter,
fluctuating under the power of the ripening of time, just like the flavors of a neem vine.

If the reading is *eṣā*, the meaning is clear. However, if the reading is *iti*, it means that as day after day passes, due to the progressive intensity of ripening within *saṃsāra*, the bitter tastes become increasingly more bitter—just as the vines of nimba trees, through various stages of development, reach a state where their bitter flavor becomes very intense, so too do the young trees [of worldly existence]. || 2 ||
O King, wickedness increases and goodness diminishes day by day within the hearts of people, which have become as harsh as the karañja thorn.
He states the misfortune that occurs when there is an absence of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the manifestation of desire for enjoyments (*bhoga-āśā*), beginning with the word "increase" (*vṛddhim*).
*Karañja* is a thorny tree. The sense is that this occurs because every day a quarter of one's merit (*dharma-pāda*) diminishes while a quarter of demerit (*adharma-pāda*) increases. || 3 ||
Day by day, the boundary on earth is instantly shattered, like a parched bean pod bursting without even a crackling sound. (4)

"Day by day" means every single day. Now, although there is no reduplication (*dvirvacana*) in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), it must necessarily be understood through the word "always" (*nityena*);
however, the distinction is simply that in the case of a limit (*maryādā*), it is without that [reduplication]. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
O Lord of Sages, for those burdened by anxieties regarding kingdoms and heaps of enjoyments, a solitary life characterized by the absence of anxiety is superior. (5)
"Ākalitā" means accepted or embraced. "Ekānta" means one-pointedness of mind. || 5 ||
My garden is not for my pleasure, nor are my women for my happiness;
the hope for wealth brings me no joy; I am at peace along with my mind.
The attainment of wealth through the secondary sense (lakṣaṇā) is the hope for prosperity. || 6 ||
The world is impermanent and unhappy, and craving, my dear, is difficult to bear;
the mind is afflicted by restlessness—how shall I attain peace? (7)
He says that there is no cause for liberation other than peace: "And it is impermanent" (verse 7).
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;
I remain just as I am, free from all feverish distress.
"What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments, what use for wealth, or what use for my endeavors?
Under the influence of egoism, all of this has slipped away from me. (9)
By "endeavors" (īhita) is meant desires or activities directed toward objects such as kingship; this refers to the kingdom and so forth. || 9 ||
Those who strive for the sake of liberation from those firm knots of the senses that bind them upon the rope of the succession of births—they are the most excellent. (10)

The sense organs themselves are the firm knots, because attachment to sense objects is difficult to abandon. Among those living beings who are bound by these knots to the leather thong—that is, the strap characterized by the succession of births—only those who strive for liberation from them are truly superior; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 10 ||
The minds of the proud women were churned by the fish-bannered god of love,
just as a delicate lotus is crushed by the trampling of an elephant's feet.
It was indeed churned—that is, destroyed—by the god whose banner is the makara, acting as the agent, with the haughty women as the instruments. || 11 ||
O Lord of Sages, if this is not treated today with a clear intellect, then when indeed will there ever be another occasion for the treatment of the mind? (12)

"Today, while he is still in this childhood stage"—the sense is that, according to the maxim "a tree that is tender and easy to uproot becomes difficult to uproot once its trunk has grown," so it must be done now. || 12 ||
Poison is the inequality of sense objects; poison is not called mere [physical] poison.
Sense objects destroy future births, whereas [physical] poison destroys only a single body.

The characteristics of the objects of sense—disharmony and lack of straightforwardness—are "slayers of future births" because they strike down [the self] and lead it to death even in other lives. || 13 ||
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither friends nor kinsmen, neither life nor death serve to bind the mind of the wise man. (14)

[Objection: But surely even those who know reality are seen enjoying sense objects and partaking in pleasure and so forth; thus, what is the distinction between them? To this he says: "No"—meaning, for the knower, the knower of the Self. || 14 ||
Therefore, O Brahmin, best among those who know what precedes and follows, please instruct me quickly so that I may become a knower, free from sorrow, fear, and exertion. (15)
Because it uproots the very foundation of attachment to all suffering, knowledge alone is the supreme goal of human life;

therefore, he requests instruction for that purpose with the word "tat" (therefore). "Tat" means: for the reason stated above, so that I, being a knower, may become free from sorrow, fear, and exertion—that is, I shall quickly become so. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here to indicate immediate futurity.
The connection is that he should likewise teach it quickly. || 15 ||

Ensnared by the net of latent impressions (vāsanā), crowded with the thorns of suffering [and filled with perils], abounding in falls and upheavals, the forest of ignorance is of terrifying form. (16)

To show his lack of delay in giving instruction, he demonstrates his own inability to endure excessive suffering, as well as his world-weariness and longing: "Enveloped"—in these two, "falling and rising" refers to low and high places, or misfortune and prosperity, or hell and heaven. Ignorance itself is the "forest. (16)
O Sage, I am able to endure the crushing pressure of the saw’s edge—the calamity of sense objects arising from the activities of saṃsāra—that brings about destruction. (17)
The crushing and rubbing with the tips of the teeth like saws; the widespread slaughter and mutilation by means of hope and sensual objects. (17)
"This does not exist; this exists"—through such conventional discourse, the delusion born of the eye's impurity shakes this flickering mind, just as the wind disperses a mass of dust. (18)

The delusion induced by the collyrium of ignorance— consisting of worldly activity such as engagement and withdrawal, based on the notions "this is undesirable" (leading to its avoidance) and "this is desirable" (leading to its attainment)— shakes and agitates the mind, which is inherently restless, just as the wind shakes a mass of dust.
The meaning is that it causes one to waste away through joy, sorrow, anxiety, and so forth. However, in the reading "like fire [consumes] a heap of cotton," burning is indicated. || 18 ||

The collection of living beings is like a string of pearls threaded upon the fine thread of craving; with consciousness as its clear substance, it is eternally radiant, having the mind as its central gem. (19)

Craving itself is the fine thread, and therein [the world] is woven and interlaced; the multitude of living beings—the collection of souls—is the pearls within it; and that which has the crest-jewel of consciousness as its crown, made translucent by the pervasive light of the Witness-consciousness, is such a [garland]. (19)
I shall ruthlessly tear asunder this necklace of saṃsāra, adorned with the serpent of Time, just as a lion tears through a snare.

Time is death itself, which is like a serpent; its crest-jewel is the very ornament—the necklace (muktāhāra) characterized by saṃsāra. With a mind devoid of attachment and through dispassion (*vairāgya*), I shall tear it away, just as a lion tears apart a snare—this is the sense, namely, by means of the knowledge born from your instruction.
O best among the knowers of reality, by what lamp of wisdom may you swiftly dispel for me the mist of mental darkness within the forest of my heart? (21)

The "heart" (*hṛdaya*) is the location of the lotus of the heart; because it is difficult to enter, it is like a forest. The "darkness" (*timira*) of that [forest] is ignorance (*ajñāna*), which, like a cataract of the mind, covers the eye of discernment (*viveka*). By what means is this [darkness] understood? It is understood by "knowledge" (*vijñāna*)—so called because one knows (*vijānāti*) through it—which is instruction (*upadeśa*). That very [instruction] illuminates the directions, and thus it is a "lamp" (*dīpa*). It is "blissful" (*sukhakara*) because it brings about happiness. It is "foremost" (*śiras*) because it is the primary [means]. Thus, by what blissful, foremost knowledge is [the darkness] perceived? [It is perceived] by the lamp of instruction.
O Sūrya, with that [weapon], pierce and rend [him]. || 21 ||
O Great-souled One, those mental afflictions do not even exist here for you; they do not reach destruction, for they are like dark nights by the moon when it meets with minds that are most excellent.

Those who do not come to an end through association with those of the highest mind, nor through its fruit, nor through instruction—they are like this: life is as fragile as water hanging from a mass of clouds torn apart by the wind;
enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds.
Reflecting that the torrential current of the waters of fickle youth is fleeting, I have indeed swiftly and firmly sealed my heart with this very realization for the sake of lasting peace. (23)
[Objection: "But how will instruction, even if given, bear fruit in you, a child devoid of firmness in tranquility and other virtues? [Reply:

When there are many who desire authority, and among them those who inflict suffering upon the kingdom through defects such as greed and cowardice—having perceived that these [defects] lead to misfortunes such as the destruction of mental peace through faults like thirst and restlessness, one should abandon them.

The meaning is that for the sake of peace and tranquility— which are free from all defects and capable [of achieving their aim]— the firm and unshakable seal of mastery has been applied to the mind regarding its objects.
It is as fragile as water hanging from a mass of clouds tossed by the wind.

The "canopy of clouds" refers to the expanse or the spread of clouds, or alternatively, to the clouds themselves spread out like a canopy; in their midst, the flashes of lightning are as flickering as the playful diversions of the mind associated with youth.

The word *iva* (like) is used here in the sense of "as it were. They are also "unsteady" like the current or velocity of water. Generally, a conjunction (*samuccaya*) occurs between things that are equal.
Or, by the sense of the word "seen" (dṛṣṭa), the meaning of "as if" (iva) is obtained. Having quickly—meaning swiftly—perceived and reflected upon [it]. || 23 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth sarga, titled "The Exposition of Non-Attachment toward All Objects," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Non-Attachment to All Objects," in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirtieth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
Thus, within the hollow of hundreds of millions of calamities that have arisen in this manner...
Having beheld the world submerged in the process of mental deliberation, [he turned his] mind [inward]. || 1 ||
Here, clearly revealing the agitation of his own mind through various reasons,
he requests instruction for its removal and for finding rest.
Elaborating upon the agitation of his own mind through various reasons, he extensively requests the instruction on the reality that serves as the cause for rest,

beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*). Having observed that the multitude of living beings in the world is submerged in the cavity— the hollow interior— of the dark well of saṃsāra, which has been made extremely narrow by the hundreds of misfortunes described in this manner, [he addresses] the mind.
"Reflection alone is thought"; the ellipsis "I am submerged in the mire characterized by that" is to be supplied. || 1 ||
My mind seems to reel as it were, and a great agitation arises within me;
my limbs tremble like the leaves of an aged tree. (2)
Agitation means fear. Of the "jarattaru," that is, of the withered tree. || 2 ||
A mind that is agitated by the embrace of the supreme defect of being unattained, having no secure foundation,
fears in this world like a young girl who has a weak protector.
That intellect which has not attained the highest contentment characterized by fortitude—being like a mother’s lap—is situated in the state of an infant;
it fears just as one fears in a forest or similar place. || 3 ||
These fluctuations of the internal organ roll about amidst conceptual constructions, like deer enticed by worthless objects of perception, as if from the depths of pits. (4)

The functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttayaḥ*), mocked and deceived by trivial objects of sense (*tucchair ālambair viṣayaiḥ*), fall—that is, they go—into the pit of suffering, meaning they descend into the sufferings of distraction arising from conceptual constructions (*vikalpebhyaḥ*). The dative case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*. They roll about; that is to say, they fall into the abyss of misery.
Just as deer, deceived by the appearance of hollow, dangling grass and the like, fall into pits, so it is with them. || 4 ||
Lacking discrimination, fallen, and rooted in misery rather than the state of the virtuous, these wretched ones—the eye and the other senses—have fallen like blind men into a well. (5)
Regarding this, he states the reason: "due to lack of discrimination" (*aviveka*).

The meaning is that since the eyes and other [senses] have as their locus those persons in whom discrimination does not exist—being dependent upon them—and since they are rooted only in the miserable abode of *saṃsāra* through long-standing acquaintance and firmly habituated there, and not in the true state, which is the ultimate reality (*paramārthavastu*). || 5 ||
Thought, dependent on the Lord of Life, neither remains stationary nor proceeds according to its desire, like a beloved wife in the home of her husband.

The individual soul (jīva) is indeed the Lord and the master; dependent upon him and bound to him, it attains—reaches—its state of existence, its cessation, and its desired objects and locations. || 6 ||
Wearing things down and then casting them away,
my fortitude has fallen into distress like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Objects, sense-objects, and leaves and such things are abandoned because they are struck down by the frost of discernment; what remains is the mere essence.
Having cast aside all goals, the unstable state of worldly existence has become established;
having grasped and then released the self, the condition of cyclic existence has come to rest.

He elaborates upon that very intermediate state, which brings about affliction for himself, with the words "apahastite" (cast aside). The aforementioned instability and restlessness of the mind has been described. All worldly [objects] and even those pertaining to the ultimate truth have been removed from his hand;
by means of his own discrimination alone, through a state of half-awakening, having abandoned one half and grasped the other half, he remains in this condition.
By my inner fortitude, whether wavering or firm, my intellect is mocked like a poor man by the root of a felled tree.

"Inner support" refers to the reliance on the certainty of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*); those who are "destitute" of it are those lacking that [support], meaning their certainty regarding the reality of the self is subject to doubt. My mind is like [the root of] a tree cut down by a stump acting as the agent—just as in the great darkness of my own blindness, one wonders whether it is a stump or a thief.
The meaning is that, just as the intellect is mocked by doubt— whether moving or unmoving— due to its oscillation between the extremes of truth and untruth,
so too this reality is mocked by the doubt, "Is this the truth, or is that the truth? Alternatively, my [intellect] characterized as described above...

By means of the growth of latent impressions— which, though shaken from sensual enjoyments due to the firmness of dispassion born from perceiving defects, yet remains unshaken because doubt has not been removed and because fundamental ignorance has not been eradicated— one is like a tree whose roots have not been cut; for as long as the root is not destroyed, it will sprout again.
It is being "voḍambita," meaning it is as if being imitated by that which is about to sprout. || 9 ||
The mind is restless, expansive, and wanders through the various worlds;
it does not abandon its agitation, just as the immortals do not leave their own celestial chariots.

Intrinsically restless and expansive through the latent impressions of manifold enjoyments, its fickleness has been firmly habituated by wandering through other worlds; therefore, even when forcibly restrained by the support of the knowledge of reality, it does not become steady— hence, [the mind] is not unsubstantial, effortless, free from limiting conditions, or devoid of delusion.
O virtuous one, what is that state of stability wherein sorrow is not found? (11)

It is non-trivial, the ultimate truth; free from the exertion of birth and death, devoid of the limiting adjuncts such as the body; free from delusion because the cause of delusion has been eradicated; the state of stability, the place of rest. Having gone there, having attained that— || 11 ||
How did virtuous people such as Janaka and others, who were engaged in all kinds of undertakings and devoted solely to worldly activity, attain the state of excellence? (12)
Like us, they are intent upon all undertakings for visible and invisible results; that is to say, they are devoted solely to worldly and Vedic activities conducive to those ends. || 12 ||
O bestower of great honor, how is it that a person here is not smeared by the mire of worldly existence, even though it clings to his limbs in many ways? (13)
By the mire of saṃsāra, consisting of merit and demerit, as well as grief, delusion, and so forth. || 13 ||
Relying upon what view do you great-souled ones, free from defilement, live as liberated beings while yet alive and wander here in this world? (14)
Alluring those who fear the enjoyment of sense-objects only toward further fear, how can these riches, whose very form is fragile, ever lead to spiritual excellence? 15.

The enjoyments of sense-objects are like serpents disguised as objects of enjoyment; their physical form and power are both fragile and perishable, yet crooked. In the case of the serpents, "power" refers to the potency of their venom.
[May they grant] auspiciousness and well-being. 15.
How can the lake of the intellect, trampled by the elephant of delusion and marred within by stains, attain supreme clarity? 16.

"Trampled" means churned. "Stains" refers to desire and the like, as well as mud, water-weeds, and so forth. "Serene clarity" means purity. "Intellect" (*śemuṣī*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), and that itself is a lake (*sarasī*), a great pond; for the *Mahābhāṣya* states: "In the Deccan region, large lakes are called *sarasya*. (16)
How is it that a person, even while engaged in worldly activity within the flow of saṃsāra itself, does not incur bondage, just as water [does not cling] to a lotus leaf? (17)
In the multitude, in the form of a continuous flow. || 17 ||
How can a person attain the state of excellence if they perceive this entire world as being like themselves or like a blade of grass, yet remain untouched by the desire of the mind? (18)

Regarding the suffering of others as his own and his own suffering as a blade of grass— viewing it as himself through inward vision and as a blade of grass through outward vision— he, thus perceiving, [subdues] the mind’s passion, that is, the mental fluctuations of desire and the like.
When people remember by his conduct that great man who has reached the further shore of the great ocean, they do not fall into suffering. (19)
A great person who is liberated while living. There is a great ignorance here [regarding him], because of the ocean-like nature of his characteristics.
By means of conduct—that is, by observing his character—and by recollecting him, and by recollecting him in that very manner, he is to be honored as an Ācārya; this is the meaning. || 19 ||
What would be the appropriate welfare for him? What would be the appropriate fruit? And how indeed should one conduct oneself in this utterly inconsistent cycle of existence? (20)
"Fit" means worthy to be attained because of its imperishable nature. "Welfare" (śreyaḥ) refers to liberation (mokṣa). "Fruit" refers to the result of ritual action, meditation, and so forth.
O Lord, tell me some truth by which I may understand the beginning and end of this world, for the activity of the Creator is unstable. (21)
By which instruction [is this known]? Because of non-abiding; that is, of that which is not established. In the reading *asamasthiteḥ*, it means "of that which is situated unevenly.
Of the elements (*dhātu*), of activity, and of the world—there is a reality that is undifferentiated between the prior and posterior, the beginning and the end. || 21 ||
O Brahmin, act so that the cleansing of the impurities of my mind—the moon within the sky of my heart—may come to pass without obstacle. (22)
The impurity of the mind—that is, of the internal organ together with its appearances—is ignorance. || 22 ||
What here might be accepted, what rejected, or what else?
How might this flickering mind find rest, O Mountain-Dweller? (23)
The other is neither to be abandoned nor to be adopted. || 23 ||
By what purifying mantra is this cholera-like plague of miserable transmigratory existence—causing hundreds of hardships—pacified without effort? (24)
Since diseases have sin as their root, by means of purifying that [sin] through its removal, the defects of the wind are pacified:
"How can there be a coolness within, like the unceasing blossoms of the tree of bliss,
like the full moon— [she is manifest compassion]?"
I am attaining [it] intensely. || 25 ||

O virtuous ones who know the truth, please instruct me here so that, having attained internal fullness through the intense discernment of the Teacher— standing like a cluster of blossoms on the tree of bliss— I may be fulfilled and never again grieve. (26)

O Great-Souled One, conceptual constructions constantly and excessively torment your life-force here in this world— depriving it of rest in the supreme state of unsurpassed bliss— just as dogs in the forest torment a small creature. (27)
The state of bliss (*ānandapada*) is the ultimate repose in the primary [principle] and absolute stability; that which is devoid of this is empty. They "frustrate" means they afflict it. || 27 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Purpose," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Statement of Purpose," in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) within the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the glorious *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*. || 30 ||
The thirty-first canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
[I saw] that which was as transient as drops of water hanging from the trembling leaves of lofty trees.
Upon his body, which was as delicate as the digits of the moon, the lord of longevity, || 1 ||
In this saṃsāra, life is like a miserable existence amidst thick monsoon clouds;
therefore, that means by which one attains the state of happiness is what is being asked here.

As an introduction to the question that is about to be asked, he conceives life in *saṃsāra* as being like a rain cloud through these six verses beginning with "procca" (*procca-ityādi*). All the words ending in the locative case are to be connected with the phrase "what is the means? (*ka upāyaḥ*) and so forth. "Procca" means very high or tall. "Lamba" means hanging down, fragile like a drop of water.
Although this state exists even in the winter, there is nevertheless a distinction: during the rainy season, due to the falling of torrential showers, it is more swiftly fragile.

Īśāna is Śiva; his ornament is the cool-rayed moon, which is "mild" and "slight," as if remaining as a mere digit—that is to say, difficult to perceive. During the rains, the moon itself is difficult to perceive, and therein it remains as a mere digit.
The sense is "all the more so. This too is an adjective qualifying *āyus* (life-span). It refers to the body (*deha*), which is contemptible or small;
[in some places, *dehe* is not read]. || 1 ||
The gathering of friends and virtuous people is like a circle of snares for a living being— fragile as the throat-skin of a frog croaking in a field of water-lilies.
In the fields of rice-paddies—here, "corner" refers to the central part—which are as fragile and unstable as this body;

[this is the connection with what precedes]. When the lightning-flash of false hope suddenly bursts forth, fanned by the wind of latent desires within the hearts of friends, well-wishers, and trusted kinsmen.
While the cloud of the mist of delusion thunders and flashes intensely. || 3 ||

The grammatical construction is as follows: "when the dense, continuous cloud of the fierce mist of delusion is whirled about—that is, enveloped—by the east wind characterized by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Here, *mihikā* refers to frost; it is the initial stage of clouds. *Ghana* means dense or uninterrupted.
*Garjana* is general thundering, whereas *sphūrjana* is the specific crashing of lightning; thus, there is no redundancy. (3)
The fierce peacock of greed dances with wild abandon upon the trembling,
wide-open, and resounding kuṭaja tree of misfortune.
*Lola* means fickle or restless; *kalāpin* refers to a peacock; *āsphoṭa*, *kalaha*, *kalikā*, and *puṭabheda* all mean a quarrel. || 4 ||
In this cruel cat of Death, who carries off all living beings as mice, whose movement flows unceasingly, and who falls from on high from somewhere unknown; (5)
"Every creature is indeed a mouse. It is well known that cats possess an extraordinary strength due to their consumption of many small animals during the rainy season.
"Syanda" means a flow of water. From where? From the earth; or rather, from the sound "ai," meaning from somewhere unexpected, even from the sky. || 5 ||
What is the means, what is the path, what is the reflection, and what is the refuge, by which this forest of life— whose fruit is inauspicious— might not come to be?
When suffering from forest-dwelling, wind, rain, and so forth has ceased, the means are such things as an umbrella, a canopy, or a mat.

By means of medicinal juices, pills, ointments, and the like, one may quickly travel to a distant place beyond the range of sight. One should contemplate a mantra, deity, or other [protective entity] that overcomes danger, or take refuge in a mountain cave and the like.

The means of accomplishment are asked about here just as they are well-known in the world. May she not be one whose future result—that is, the consequence occurring at a later time—is likewise inauspicious. || 6 ||
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all, which the wise do not lead even this trivial thing to a state of beauty. (7)

The wise—those whose intellects are strengthened by the power of austerity and knowledge—such as you, do not bring even an object as trivial as this to a state of loveliness; that is to say, they are incapable of so doing. Such a thing does not exist on earth among humans or the like, nor in heaven among the gods, since such was the case for Triśaṅku.
The meaning is that even the curse of the preceptor, which was destined to result in a stay in heaven for the duration of a kalpa, ended in death for Śunaḥśepa because his lifespan was long. || 7 ||

For this world, though its cycle of existence is burnt away and it is agitated by incessant mental constructs, how could it attain sweetness without being devoid of sapidity and free from delusion? (8)
"Uninterrupted" means without interval; "distressed" by the experience of suffering, and therefore "flavorless. "Deliciousness" means sapidity.
"Without delusion" means by way of dispelling delusion. The meaning is: by what means or through what method does it attain deliciousness? || 8 ||
May you take delight in bathing with milk as the ripening fruit of your hopes;
thus the earth attains [splendor] through that which is white as flowers, just as she does through honey.

The fulfillment of one's desires—the ripening that is contrary to the very nature of hope, which is the source of all suffering—is itself the "bath of milk. [He] enters into saṃsāra; this is the ellipsis. With flowers, with the bright and delightful honey of spring. (9)
By what means can the nectar-shining moon of the mind arise, its stains of desire wiped away by washing? (10)

The syntactical connection is as follows: by what means of cleansing, well-known among the wise, are the stains of desire removed from the moon of the mind soiled by that [desire], such that the nectar-shedding light—the moonlight of bliss—rises?
By one who has seen the course of saṃsāra and who has destroyed both the seen and the unseen, how indeed should one conduct oneself on the paths of the forest of saṃsāra? (11)

By whom has the course of saṃsāra been seen as characterized by having calamity as its ultimate end? By which great being—like a noble soul—have both the seen and the unseen enjoyments of this world and the next been destroyed through the firmness of discernment, dispassion, and awakening? (Note: The word "viveka" does not appear in some versions.)
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "He should be brought before us for legal proceedings. In the reading *kenaiva*, the ellipsis is: "by means of what [legal procedure]. || 11 ||
How is it that the great diseases of passion and hatred, the multitudes of enjoyments, and worldly prosperities do not afflict the living being wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra? (12)
And how is it that even when falling into the fire of the best of the wise, one is not burned, just as mercury is not consumed by fire because of its mercurial nature? 13.
"Dhīvaryā" is an address of invocation. "In Agni" means in the world of transmigration, which is like fire in its capacity to burn. "Rasa" refers to the nectar of knowledge;
[the world] is "śālin" (endowed) with that. 13.
For it is said that in this world, no worldly activity can exist without action, just as for one who has fallen into the ocean, there can be no stability without water. (14)
Now, if worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is indeed suffering, then let it be abandoned; to this he replies with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).

Without the performance—that is, the accomplishment—of worldly activities, just as for a fish or similar creature born and fallen into the ocean, a state of non-water cannot possibly exist, so it is here. (14)
Free from passion and hatred, and devoid of pleasure and pain,
there is no virtuous action here, just as a flame of fire devoid of its burning power.
"Granted that there may be suffering in improper conduct, but such suffering cannot possibly arise from virtuous action. To this he replies:
"In the three worlds, the existence of a mind characterized by mental deliberation does not perish without a cause; state, therefore, that supreme means [for its cessation]. (16)

"Let alone external worldly affairs; the flickering of the mind itself is the supreme suffering. Therefore, its very treatment must be explained," he says with the word "manas. The "thinking" (*manana*) of the mind is its support upon sense-objects; while the mind exists, that support of objects persists. Only when there is the destruction of that support of objects is there the destruction of the mind's existence, and that [is what must be explained].

Without the instruction on reasoning (yukti), which is the cause for awakening to the reality that subverts all objects [of false cognition], there is no [liberation]. Therefore, explain that reasoning thoroughly and to the utmost extent until awakening arises; that is to say, "teach it. || 16 ||
"Tell me that supreme method of worldly conduct by which, through such conduct, suffering does not come to me;
or else, explain that most excellent method of worldly conduct. (17)
How, by what means, or by whom of supreme intellect was this performed in the past, whereby the mind attains this most sacred and ultimate repose? (18)

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "By what means was that dispelling of delusion previously accomplished? By whom, and in what manner was it done? Or what reality (tattva) was attained by him? Speak according to how you know it. || 18 ||
O Blessed One, as you know, please tell me for the sake of dispelling delusion that by which the virtuous have indeed attained freedom from suffering. (19)
Or else, O Brahmin, if such a logical argument does not exist, or if someone clearly does not state it to me even though it exists; (20)

He states with the seven verses beginning with "Or else" (athavā) that, in the absence of such means, one should resort to fasting unto death (prāyopaveśana) until the end of one's life, rather than engaging in worldly activities while living. || 20 ||
Yet I myself do not attain that unsurpassed rest;
therefore, having abandoned all worldly effort and attained a state free from egoism, I remain thus. (21)
Or if, having reflected for myself, I do not attain it; then... || 21 ||
I shall not eat, I shall not drink water, and I shall not put on a garment;
I shall perform no activity such as bathing, giving gifts, or eating.
I do not remain indifferent to my duties in times of prosperity or adversity;
indeed, O Sage, I desire nothing at all except for the renunciation of this body.
Free from doubt, devoid of possessiveness, and rid of envy,
I remain here in silence alone, fixed as if in a painted image.
In silence, there is an absence of all conventional activity such as speech and so forth; in the arts of writing and painting, it is "entrusted," meaning it is inscribed.
Then, having gradually abandoned the perceptions of exhalation and inhalation,
I shall cast off this useless structure known as the body.
"Arrangement" means the form consisting of the configuration of parts. || 25 ||
"I am not this, nor is it mine, nor is there another; I shall become extinguished like a lamp whose oil is spent.
Having renounced everything, I shall cast off this physical body. (26)
The remainder [of the sentence] is "this is not mine. Another [thing] also is not mine. "Without affection" means without oil. || 26 ||
Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, Rāma— delightful as the stainless moon and whose mind was blossomed by profound reflection— [proceeded].
He became silent before the great clouds, like a peacock uttering its cry of distress out of exhaustion. || 27 ||

"The moon is the maker of coolness. Having said this, he became silent before the great gurus, such as Vasiṣṭha and others; just as the peacock, having uttered its cry, becomes silent before the clouds. || 27 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Question of Rāghava," in the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Question of Rāghava," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-second canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While he was thus speaking these words that bring about the cessation of the delusion of the mind—
In that prince Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals. || 1 ||
Upon hearing Rāma’s words, a vast wonder is described among both men and gods, and a rain of flowers fell spontaneously from the sky.
This collection of Śrī Rāma’s words, which is rooted in one's own discernment and correct inquiry, is established by its own inherent reasoning;
it is intended to demonstrate that even gods and others possess the qualification for the Brahma-vidyā to be described hereafter.
To show this, [the author] describes the praise of Śrī Rāma’s speech performed by them, as well as the great festival of their meeting with him.
The connection with what follows is that they became distinguished by the astonishment, horripilation, and other [emotions] to be described hereafter. || 1 ||
All those present there became filled with wonder, their eyes wide open,
as if their hairs stood erect on their bodies to listen to the words emerging from their mouths.

The hairs on their bodies, rising up as if eager to hear Rāma’s words and having cast off the weight of their dullness, appeared as if they were tearing through their garments—this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā) suggesting that their clothes were pierced. || 2 ||
Those whose entire worldly tendencies have been cast off by the latent impression of dispassion appear for a moment like waves tossed about in the ocean of nectar.
Those whose entire latent impressions of attachment, aversion, and so forth—the causes of worldly existence—have been cast off by the impression of dispassion. || 3 ||
Those songs of the noble Rāma were heard by listeners who, as if they were figures in a painting, were swollen with the state of inner bliss.
With ears attentive through their hearing, marked by the signs of bliss, and full-bodied;
with sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra seated in the assembly,
and with ministers headed by Jayanta and Dhṛṣṭi, who were experts in counsel.
By kings resembling Daśaratha, by citizens such as the Pāraśavas, by vassal lords and princes, and by Brāhmaṇas who discourse upon the Veda; || 6 ||
[Regarding the phrase "parśvādayaḥ": since the word *paraśu* does not occur in the *parśvādi* group and that group is not an *ākṛtigaṇa*, this must be investigated.

*Parśvādayaḥ* refers to specific regions; those belonging to them are the *tadrāja*-type suffixes, such as *pāraśava* and others. By virtue of belonging to the *parśvādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. || 6 ||
Likewise, with servants and ministers, with birds staying on the five perches, with pet animals devoid of movement, and with horses that had ceased chewing; || 7 ||
And by the groups of women led by Kausalyā, who stood at their own windows with the sound of their ornaments silenced and themselves motionless.
*vātāyana* means a window. || 8 ||
It was filled with birds dwelling in garden thickets and even in the eaves of buildings,
whose flocks of wings remained undisturbed and whose cries had ceased.
Viṭaṅka refers to the parapet or cornice at the top of a palace.
[He was honored] by the Siddhas and the sky-dwellers, as well as by the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, and by the foremost of sages headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha. || 10 ||
And by others—the lords of the gods, the Vidyādharas, and the great serpents—those words of Rāma, which possessed wonderful meanings and were most noble, were heard. (11)
The lords of the gods are the guardians of the directions; the word "heard" (śrutāḥ) is to be connected with all [of them]. || 11 ||
Then, while the lotus-eyed Rāma—beautified like the moon and appearing as the moon in the sky of Raghu’s lineage—remained silent; (12)

The Raghu dynasty alone is the sky because of its purity; [he dwells] in its full moon, the perfect moon. Fearing that if it were merely a full moon, it might be perceived as having a spot, he says "beautiful as the moon. The mention of the hare (the moon's mark) is not for the sake of indicating fullness, but rather to convey the excellence of its beauty.
The sense is: "for one's own sake. || 12 ||
Accompanied by voices of acclaim uttered by the assembly of perfected beings (siddhas),
a rain of flowers fell from the sky like a canopy.
The mention of "Siddhas" is an indicative mark for all divine classes of beings who seek liberation. A "saṅgha" (assembly) is a collection for its own sake. || 13 ||
Resounding with the humming of pairs of bees resting within the buds of mandāra flowers,
it delighted men who were intoxicated by its sweet fragrance and beauty.
Pairs are couples; joyful means contented; intoxicated means having minds that are not self-controlled. || 14 ||
Like a succession of stars scattered by the wind in the sky, it was as if the radiance of the laughter of celestial women had fallen upon the surface of the earth. 15.
"Ninunnā" means cast down; "hasitacchaṭā" means the radiance of laughter. || 15 ||
It fell like a series of drops from clouds of *vṛṣyamūka* camphor, or like a succession of lumps of fresh butter being cast down. (16)

"Vṛṣyāḥ" means having the nature of raining; "mūkāḥ" means devoid of thundering; and those clouds which are "kacantaḥ," meaning radiant with lightning—their "lavāvaliḥ" is a multitude of fragments or a collection of small portions. || 16 ||
Noble like a shower from the Himavat, resembling a collection of pearl necklaces, like a garland of rays from the moon, and like a succession of waves of milk. || 17 ||
Enveloped by lotuses with their filaments, it was filled with swarms of wandering bees and stirred by sweet,
fragrant breezes singing with the sound of *sītkāra*.
It was surrounded by lotuses abounding in filaments and stamens, and it was slightly stirred by the breezes pleasant to the touch of people. || 18 ||
With its clusters of swaying ketakī flowers, its masses of blooming white water-lilies, its falling circles of kunda blossoms, and its abodes of trembling blue lotuses; 19.
Terms such as *vyūha* and others have the meaning of a collection. || 19 ||
The courtyards, the rooftops, and the squares were filled with people;
it was beheld by the men and women residing in the city who stood with their necks upraised.
The earth was the essence (rasa), by which the courtyards were filled; [it was surrounded] by the inhabitants of the city, those dwelling within the city. || 20 ||
A rain from the cloudless sky, resembling blue lotuses, fell without agitation; it was something never seen before by any person, and it inspired wonder in all. (21)
From that very sky, which was cloudless and resembled a blue lotus, a rain fell,
stirred up by the hands of the hosts of invisible Siddhas in the firmament;
for a quarter of a Muhūrta, that shower of flowers indeed fell.
A quarter of a muhūrta is half a ghaṭikā; for that duration he fell, it is said. || 22 ||
When the assembly hall was filled with light and the rain of flowers had subsided,
those gathered in the hall heard this conversation of the hosts of Siddhas.
By him the assembly and the people present there were filled; when he had become tranquil and ceased [from worldly activity]. 23.
"Having wandered throughout the heavens for an entire kalpa among the hosts of Siddhas, we have heard this unprecedented elixir for the ears. (24)
Or rather, it is the elixir for the ears, the nectar for the sense of hearing, and the very essence of the Vedas, [resounding] throughout the heavens, in every part of the celestial realm. || 24 ||
That which was indeed spoken so magnificently by this moon of the Raghu dynasty—
due to his state of passionlessness— is truly beyond the reach even of the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati).
In which there are no objects that serve as the range [of the senses], such is that [state]. || 25 ||
Oh, what great merit has been gained by us today through hearing these words issued from the mouth of Rāma, which bring such immense joy to the intellect!
"Alas! A birth devoid of hearing such words as these is in vain"—thus [he spoke] in lamentation. || 26 ||

Because the joy of the Raghus has now spoken what was fitting— that which is beautiful with the nectar of tranquility and attained through diligent effort to the state of supreme excellence— he has instantly awakened them to the necessity of renunciation.

The collection of statements spoken by the Sage— statements which constitute a refuge (*pada*), a protection, or a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)— was uttered for the purpose of producing conviction regarding the excellence already attained and acquired through [his] birth, lineage, conduct, mastery of the Dharma, and so forth;
thus it is said in the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
The thirty-second canto, titled "The Acclamation of the Sky-Travelers."
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Praise of the Sky-Traveling Sages," in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirty-third Canto.
The Siddhas said:
Regarding these purifying words spoken by the banner of the Raghus...
It is proper to hear the final decision that is about to be declared by the great sages. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], the descent of the perfected ones (siddhas) into the assembly is described,
as well as their praise of Rāma’s words while seated in their appropriate places.

Exalting the praise of Rāma’s words and so forth offered by the Siddhas, [the author] introduces their question with the words "The Siddhas said," etc. By the word *raghu*, his lineage is indicated; the meaning is: "by that which makes [the lineage] renowned like a banner. || 1 ||
Nārada, Vyāsa, Pulaha, and other preeminent sages—
all those great ṛṣis— arrived without any hindrance.
"Come quickly without hindrance"—the word "to hear" is understood as the ellipsis. The sense is that since auspicious matters are beset by many obstacles, it is not appropriate to delay. || 2 ||
Let us fly all around this holy assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha,
which is densely packed and radiant with gold, like bees hovering over a lotus pond.

"Seamless" means full; by implication, it is understood as "prosperity. For this very reason, she is "radiant with gold," meaning possessing an excellent luster. In the case of the lotus pond, she is shining with the beauty of filaments, as if with gold. (3)
Śrī Vālmīki said:
[The remaining word "by the Siddhas" is to be supplied: Having been addressed thus by them, that entire divine succession of sages dwelling in the celestial abodes descended there into that assembly.
She was dwelling in those celestial chariots whose place of residence is the sky;
she was in that part of the vast assembly hall where Rāma and the others were located. || 4 ||
Indeed, within [the heart] was Vyāsa himself, the lord of sages, dark as a rain-cloud thick with water, standing at the head [of the assembly] with his lute still sounding, unreleased.

He describes that very [scene] with eight verses. "In front" means standing in the foremost place. "The lord of sages" refers to Nārada, by whom the sounding lute has not been cast aside. "Dark like a cloud full and swollen with water" refers to Vyāsa himself;
"in between" (antarā) means in the space between those two. The use of the word *antarā* here takes the sense of the genitive case according to the rule *antarāntareṇa yukte*.
The second [verse]: "Adorned and embellished by the leaders of sages, such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, and others"—this is to be connected with what follows. || 5 ||
It was adorned by the leaders of sages such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Pulastya,
and garlanded by Cyavana, Uddālaka, Uśīra, Śaraloman, and others.
Bhṛgu and others are their names. || 6 ||
With a deerskin poorly draped due to their mutual friction,
she possessed trembling rosaries and bracelets, and carried a beautiful water-pot.
She whose deer-skins were ill-shaped and disheveled due to being rubbed and worn away by constant handling.
Like a row of stars in the sky, rosy with the spreading of their radiance;
like a row of suns, mutually illuminating the circles of each other's faces.
By the expansion of its brilliance, it is pale-red, that is, white and red. || 8 ||
Like a string of jewels, their limbs were adorned with various colors;
like a string of pearls, they enhanced each other's exceeding beauty.
It was like a rain of wish-fulfilling gems from a different sky, like a second solar disc,
or like a succession of full moons gathered together over a vast expanse of time.
"Another" means distinct from what is well-known. "Accumulated over a very long time" means gathered together in one place after a great length of time. || 10 ||
Where Vyāsa shines like a mass of stars in a cloud over the ocean,
Nārada shines here like the moon amidst a multitude of stars.
Vyāsa was on one side and Nārada on the other; this is the implied meaning. || 11 ||
Pulastya shines here like the lord of the gods among the deities,
while Aṅgiras shines like the sun among the gods.
As that perfected army fell from the sky toward the earth,
the assembly hall of Daśaratha, filled with sages, then rose up.
To the earth, the boundary-ground, the assembly-ground; as she was falling, that is, entering [the ground]. || 13 ||
Mingled together, those sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers shone resplendently,
their bodily lusters mingling with one another as they illuminated the ten directions.
By the mutual, blended splendors and radiances of their limbs. || 14 ||
With hands covered by bamboo staffs and holding play-lotuses,
their hair-tufts were overspread with sprouts of dūrvā grass, and their locks of hair were adorned with crest-jewels.
"Some hold a play-lotus"—the remainder [of the description] is to be supplied as appropriate. || 15 ||
With matted locks of tawny hue, their heads were adorned with crowns;
they wore rosaries upon their forearms and were encircled by garlands of jasmine.
Those whose heads and crowns were adorned—meaning their heads and crests were encircled with garlands—and whose forearms [were likewise decorated]. (16)
Clad in garments of bark and rags, draped with garlands of *kauśeya* silk,
they had waist-bands dangling and clusters of pearls swaying.

There is a distinction between rags and bark garments based on their specific types. Adorned with peacock feathers, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra honored all those sky-dwellers in due order with offerings of water for the hands and feet, words of welcome, and other honors. (18)
Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, along with the great hosts of sky-dwellers, honored them with respect through offerings of water for their feet, gifts worthy of guests, and words of welcome.
With all due reverence, the king worshipped the multitude of Siddhas;
and the multitude of Siddhas likewise greeted the king with inquiries concerning his welfare.
With conversation accompanied by inquiries after his welfare, and with discourse appropriate to the occasion. || 20 ||
Having received mutual hospitality through various expressions of affection and zeal,
those who move in the sky and those who dwell upon the earth sat down upon their seats.
*Praṇaya* is affection; *satkriyā* is hospitality consisting of the zeal for giving, honoring, and other such acts appropriate to that affection;
and *viṣṭareṣu* refers to seats. || 21 ||
With words, a rain of flowers, and cries of "Well done," they honored Rāma from all sides as he stood bowed before them.
With words consisting of pleasant conversations and discourses, and with expressions of "well done" and praise. || 22 ||
And there he sat down, resplendent with royal fortune, along with Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and the ministers. (23)

In that context, "among them" refers to those present there; "this Rāma" and "Viśvāmitra and the others" are to be understood as connected with the seventh half-verse, namely, "then sat down," meaning they were seated. || 23 ||
Nārada and Devaputra, Vyāsa the foremost of sages, Marīci, Durvāsas, and likewise the sage Āṅgirasa; || 24 ||
Kratu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Śaraloman, the lord of sages, Vātsyāyana, Bharadvāja, and Vālmīki, the bull among sages; || 25 ||
Uddālaka, Ṛcīka, Śaryāti, and likewise Cyavana. || 26 ||
These and many others, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, were high-souled leaders established there, having realized all that is to be known. || 27 ||
Those by whom the reality of the self, which must necessarily be known, or the object of knowledge itself, has been realized, are the most excellent leaders. 27.
Together with Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, those learned sages, Nārada and the others,
spoke these words to Rāma, whose face was bowed in humility.
The *anūcānas*—those who have duly studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs from a teacher—with their faces bowed in humility. (28)
"Oh! What most noble speech has been uttered by the prince—speech endowed with auspicious qualities and pregnant with the essence of dispassion! (29)
He elaborates upon those very statements with eighteen verses beginning with "Aho! [Verse 30]: "It is auspicious (*kalyāṇa*), as will be described;

it is established in what is to be said (*pariniṣṭhita-vaktavya*); it is endowed with wisdom (*sa-bodha*), appropriate (*ucita*), clear (*sphuṭa*), noble (*udāra*), pleasing (*priya*), worthy of the noble (*āryārha*), and moreover, it is unagitated (*avihvala*) and manifest (*sphuṭa*)."

In which [speech] the matters to be expressed have been determined and finalized as being exactly thus after deliberation; which is "with awakening," meaning accompanied by the realization of the true nature of things, and not merely established through conceptual construction; for this very reason, it is "fit for an assembly of the learned"; "clear," meaning with distinct phonemes; and "noble," meaning containing a vast and excellent intention.

Pleasant, bringing joy to the heart, worthy and appropriate for the noble, and unwavering in mind—whose wonder does this speech uttered by Rāghava not inspire? It is clearly expressed, distinct, desirable, and its clarity brings satisfaction. (31)

That in which the words are clearly manifested and purified by grammar; that which is desired and beneficial; that which is clear, being free from defects such as elision (*grasta*); and that which possesses excellence, being endowed with the lack of contentment resulting from the destruction of craving. || 31 ||
From among a hundred, the speech of even a single person becomes uniquely endowed with all manner of noble wonders, being exclusively capable of bestowing the desired object. (32)

From all speakers, in every respect, she possesses a sublime and excellent wonder— a refinement to be savored by those with aesthetic sensitivity— and is therefore exclusively proficient, being invariably capable, in the presentation and communication of the intended meaning.
The speech of Bharati—the voice—attains its full development and manifestation only in the foremost among the foremost, even when compared to hundreds of eloquent speakers;

it does not arise for everyone. This is because, according to the rule *pañcamī vibhaktau*, the suffix *tamap* is used to denote selection from among those distinguished by a hundred; thus, since this denotes a specific selection, the excellence of being "the most noble" is logically established. (32)
O Prince, without you, whose [wisdom] is rich with the fruit of discernment, toward whom will this extensive vine of intelligence reach its supreme blossoming? (33)

Wisdom is like an arrow that pierces subtle objects; it is that very wisdom which is a creeper or vine, attaining expansion through the flowers and sprouts of discernment and dispassion—or, in the reading with the letter *śa*, it attains illumination. (33)
That man is considered wise in whom the flame of the lamp of wisdom dwells in the heart, blazing like that of Rāma, producing an incomparable light. (34)
He produces an incomparable light, unique and not shared by others, which illuminates the true nature of all things; such is the incomparable person.
Others, however, are incapable of achieving the goals of human life and are for the most part like women—this is the intended meaning. || 34 ||
There are many and exceedingly numerous machines made of blood, flesh, and bone;
they draw objects toward themselves, yet there is no conscious being within them. (35)

The meaning is that people devoid of the aforementioned wisdom—because they possess the notion of a self in a body consisting of a machine of passion and so forth—draw toward themselves and enjoy those very objects such as sound and touch; thus, it follows that these people are mere Cārvākas, holding that there is no other conscious self. Or rather, if there were a conscious [self] within them, [it would necessarily...]

One must indeed strive for the goals of human life; since they do not so strive, the denial [of their agency] is intended as a censure, implying that they are indeed insentient like a clay pot or a wall. (35)
They undergo the suffering of birth, death, and old age again and again;
like beasts utterly deluded, they do not reflect upon this cycle of existence.
Those who do not reflect are like beasts. || 36 ||
Only rarely and in some place is a single person seen who possesses a pure disposition and is worthy of reflection upon his past and future, such as this Arimardana.
This is Rāma; he is the crusher of enemies, namely desire and the other passions. || 37 ||
Those who possess auspicious forms and yield the fruit of unsurpassed wonder are indeed rare in this world, like mango trees. (38)

Those [trees] in which there are fruits characterized by the direct realization of reality, possessing an unsurpassed and most excellent wonder—a particular sweetness; such are the *sahakāra* trees, namely mango trees. || 38 ||
The course of the world has been correctly perceived, and the wonder of one’s own discernment is seen this very day within this venerable-minded person. (39)

The wonder culminating in the vision of reality has been achieved through the very discrimination produced by one's own intellect, even at this present age; and that is a marvel—such is the intended meaning. || 39 ||
In a land, trees that are fortunate—easy to climb and abounding in fruit and foliage—may grow; but sandalwood trees do not. (40)
"Aubhagāḥ" means beautiful; the ellipsis "everywhere in the country" is to be supplied. || 40 ||
In every forest there are trees that are always laden with fruit and foliage; yet the clove tree, with its unprecedented wonder, is not always easily found.
Like the cool moonlight from the moon, like a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree, or like a trail of fragrance from a flower—such was the wonder beheld from Rāma. (42)
"Āmodalekhā" means a line of fragrance. || 42 ||
O best of the twice-born, in this burnt-out cycle of existence fashioned by the creation of a capricious and wicked fate, the essential core is indeed extremely difficult to find. (43)
The acquisition of the self through discernment occurs after that very same fate—namely, past karma—which possesses such unrestrained wickedness. || 43 ||
Those whose intellects, being repositories of glory, strive to attain the essence, are the fortunate ones;
they alone are counted as the foremost among the virtuous and are the best of men. (44)
Those who meditate are called *dhiyas*; being ever devoted to the contemplation of reality, those who strive in this way are blessed and are counted as foremost among the virtuous. || 44 ||
"No one equal to Rāma has been seen here in all the worlds; nor will there ever be anyone so discerning and noble-souled—this is our conviction. (45)
It does not exist here at present; it was not seen before, nor will it exist in the future.
Even though it produces wonder for the entire world, if that which is desired by the heart of Rāghava does not bear fruit, then we sages ourselves are clearly of ruined intellect.

By praising the necessity of fulfilling Rāma’s desire, he establishes the excellence of the qualification [of the seeker]; and by revealing the secret that is appropriate to be asked, he brings joy. Furthermore, even for the mind of Rāghava, who performs this [revelation], the desired wish characterized by the inquiry into reality (*tattvajijñāsā*) will not fail to bear fruit.
The phrase "by means of instruction from those possessing higher knowledge such as ourselves" is the ellipsis to be supplied. *No* is a particle synonymous with the negative particle *na*.

Therefore, they would be "those whose intellects are destroyed," meaning those of corrupt understanding; the implication is that their possession of higher knowledge (*abhijñatā*) would be entirely fruitless.
Consequently, it is established that [instruction] must necessarily be imparted. || 46 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third canto, titled "The Meeting of the Sky-dwellers and the Earth-dwellers," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Meeting of the Sky-dwellers and the Earth-dwellers," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa.
This chapter on dispassion is completed.
